<!-- custom-6: body_md -->
{Notational conventions}\label{notational}
Throughout the paper, ${\mathbb R}_+$ will denote the non-negative real numbers.
For any integer $n\ge0$, the closed unit ball in ${\mathbb R}^n$ will be
denoted by ${\mathbb B}^n$. The unit sphere in  ${\mathbb R}^{n+1}$ will be denoted ${\mathbb S}^n$.
 The open unit disk in ${\mathbb C}$ will be denoted by
${\mathbb D}$.

Throughout the paper, ${\mathbb H}^n$ will denote $n$--dimensional hyperbolic space.
We shall denote by ${v_{\rm tet}}$ the volume of a regular ideal tetrahedron
in ${\mathbb H}^3$, and by ${v_{\rm oct}}$ the volume of a regular ideal octahedron
in ${\mathbb H}^3$. Numerically, ${v_{\rm tet}} = 1.0149 \ldots$ and ${v_{\rm oct}} = 3.6638 \ldots$.
<!-- end custom-6 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{half or quarter}
Let $n\ge1$ be an integer.
We define an  \emph{open half-ball} 
  in ${\mathbb R}^{n-1}\times{\mathbb R}_+$ centered at a point $c \in  {\mathbb R}^{n-1} \times \{0\}$
to be a set which is the intersection of    ${\mathbb R}^{n-1}\times {\mathbb R}_+$
with an open
ball in ${\mathbb R}^n$. The
 \emph{axis} of the half-ball is its intersection with the line which passes
through $c$ and is perpendicular to ${\mathbb R}^{n-1} \times \{0\}$.
If $n\ge2$, we define an  \emph{open quarter-ball}
  in $ {\mathbb R}^{n-2}\times {\mathbb R}_+^2$
to be a set which is the intersection of $ {\mathbb R}^{n-2}\times {\mathbb R}_+^2$
with an open
ball in ${\mathbb R}^n$ whose center lies in ${\mathbb R}^{n-2} \times \{(0,0)\}$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- custom-7: body_md -->
{Manifold conventions}\label{manifolds}
It will always be understood that a  \emph{manifold} may have a
boundary, except where we specify otherwise.

All statements involving manifolds will be understood in the smooth
category, except when the 
topological
 or PL category is explicitly mentioned. 
(Such mentions will be frequent in Sections~\ref{Sec:OrbifoldBooks}--\ref{torus section}.)
 Thus
manifolds, submanifolds, and maps (including immersions and
embeddings) between manifolds will be understood to be smooth.

As is customary in $3$--manifold topology, we shall often use smooth versions of results that have been proved elsewhere in the category of PL manifolds. In all cases this is justified by standard smoothing theorems.
<!-- end custom-7 -->
<!-- custom-8: body_md -->
{Neat embeddedness}
\label{NeatEmbed}
As is standard in differential topology, we say that a submanifold $N$
of a manifold $M$ is  \emph{neatly embedded} in $M$ if
\begin{itemize}
\item $N$ is a closed subset of $M$,
\item $N\cap\partial M=\partial N$, and
\item $N$ and $\partial M$ meet transversely.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end custom-8 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{extend}
Suppose that 
$U$ is an open
subset of a topological $3$--manifold
$M$. Then every smooth structure on 
$U$ 
extends to a smooth
structure on $M$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We express $M$ as a countable union $\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} V_i$, where the $V_i$ are topological open $3$--balls, and prove by induction on $n$ that the smooth structure on $U$ extends to a smooth structure on $U \cup \left(\bigcup_{i=1}^n V_i \right)$. The inductive step involves showing  that the smooth structure on $V_n \cap \left(U \cup \bigcup_{i=1}^{n-1} V_i \right)$ extends to $V_n$. Since $V_n$ embeds in ${\mathbb R}^3$, it suffices to prove the proposition in the special case where $M \subset {\mathbb R}^3$, which is what we now assume.

The smooth structure on $U$ 
given by the hypothesis defines a differentiable manifold
$N$ whose underlying topological space is  $U$.
On the other hand, since $M\subset{\mathbb R}^3$, the manifold
$M$ admits a smooth structure; this smooth structure on $M$ restricts
to one on 
$U$, which defines another differentiable manifold $N'$
having $U$ as underlying space. The identity map of $U$ may then
be regarded as a homeomorphism $h\colon\thinspace N \to N'$.


Now choose a strictly positive-valued continuous  function $\varepsilon$ on
$U$ 
such that $\lim_{x\to p}\varepsilon(x)=0$ for every point $p \in M - U$. 
(For example, if we fix a distance function defining the topology
of $M$, we may define $\varepsilon(x)$, for each $x\in U$, to be the
distance from $x$ to the 
closed set $M-U$.)

Fix a distance function $d$ defining the topology of $N'$. 
By a theorem of Munkres
\cite[Theorem 6.3]{munkres},
there is a diffeomorphism $\ell\colon\thinspace N\to N'$ which is an
$\varepsilon$-approximation to $h$ in the sense that
$d(h(x),\ell(x))<\varepsilon(x)$ for every $x\in N$. Our choice of the
function $\varepsilon$ guarantees that $\ell$, regarded as a
self-homeomorphism of 
$U$, 
extends to a homeomorphism
$\overline{\ell}\colon\thinspace M\to M$ which fixes every point of $M - U$. Pulling back
the smooth structure
on $M$ via the homeomorphism $\overline\ell$
gives a new
smooth structure on $M$ extending the given smooth structure
on $U$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{tree thing}
Let $T$ be a finite tree, and let $V$ denote its vertex set. 
Suppose that each vertex $v\in V$ is assigned an integer $m_v\ge0$. For each  set $U\subset T$, set $n_U=\sum_{v\in U\cap V}m_v$. Then $T$ has a vertex $w_0$ such that, for each component $R$ of $T-\{w_0\}$, we have $n_R\le n_T/2$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Assume that for each vertex $w$ of $T$ there is a component $R$ of $T-\{w\}$ such that $n_R> n_T/2$. This component $R$ is clearly unique for any vertex $w$, and will be denoted $R_w$. For each vertex $w$, let  $h_w$ denote the cardinality of $R_w\cap V$. Choose a vertex $z\in V$ such that $h_z$ achieves the minimum value of $h_w$.

Since $T$ is a tree, and $R_z$ is a component of $T-\{z\}$, there is a unique vertex $z' \in R_z$ that is connected to $z$ by an edge.
Let $S$ denote the component of $T-\{z'\}$ containing $z$. Since $T$ is a tree, $V$ is the disjoint union of $R_z\cap V$ and $S\cap V$. Hence $n_T=n_{R_z}+n_S$. The definition of $R_z$ gives $n_{R_z}>n_T/2$, and hence $n_S<n_T/2$.

The definition of $R_{z'}$ gives $n_{R_{z'}}>n_T/2$. Since $n_S<n_T/2$, the components $S$ and $R_{z'}$ of $T-\{z'\}$ are distinct; in particular $S\cap V$ and $R_{z'}\cap V$ are disjoint. Since we have observed that $V$ is the disjoint union of $R_z\cap V$ and $S\cap V$, we have $R_{z'}\cap V\subset R_z\cap V$. Furthermore, we have $z'\in R_z$ but $z'\notin R_{z'}$, so that $R_{z'}\cap V$ is a \emph{proper} subset of $R_z\cap V$. This implies that $h_{z'}<h_{z}$,
contradicting the definition of $z$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- custom-9: body_md -->
{Geometric decompositions}
\label{geometry and norms}
Throughout the paper, we use standard notions from $3$--manifold topology, such as irreducibility, incompressibility, and Seifert manifolds. For a recent reference on this material, see e.g.~Martelli~\cite[Chapter 9]{Martelli:GeometricTopology}.

We shall make strong use of Perelman's geometrization theorem; see \cite{BBBMP} or \cite{Morgan-Tian-geom} for accounts of the proof.  One formulation of the theorem (cf.\ \cite[Theorems 1.1.4 and 1.1.6]{BBBMP}) is that if $N$ is a closed, orientable, irreducible $3$--manifold, there
is a (possibly empty) closed, orientable $2$--manifold ${\bf T}\subset
N$, canonical up to isotopy, such that
\begin{itemize}
\item each component of ${\bf T}$ is an incompressible torus, and 
\item each
component of the manifold $N'$ obtained by splitting $N$ along ${\bf T}$ is
diffeomorphic to either (a) a Seifert fibered $3$--manifold or (b) the compact
core of a finite-volume hyperbolic $3$--manifold. 
\end{itemize}
(The conditions (a) and (b) are mutually exclusive.) The components of
$N'$, which are well-defined up to diffeomorphism, will be called {\it
  pieces} of $N$, and the pieces that satisfy Alternative (b) will be
called  \emph{hyperbolic} pieces. For any hyperbolic piece $P$, we shall
write $\mathop{\rm vol} P$ for the volume of the hyperbolic manifold whose compact
core is diffeomorphic to $P$. If all pieces of $N$ are Seifert
fibered manifolds, we say that $N$ is a  \emph{graph manifold}.

We also recall \cite[Theorem 1.1.3]{BBBMP}
that every closed, oriented $3$--manifold $M$ is oriented-diffeomorphic
to a connected sum 
$N_1\#\cdots\#N_k$, 
where  $k\ge0$, the
$N_i$ are oriented prime $3$--manifolds, and the decomposition is
unique up to orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms and changing the
order of terms. Here it is understood that when $k=0$, the connected
sum gives ${\mathbb S}^3$, which is the identity for connected sum. We consider ${\mathbb S}^3$ to be \emph{trivial}. A non-trivial $3$--manifold is said to be \emph{prime}  it cannot be expressed as a
connected sum of two non-trivial summands. A prime
$3$--manifold is either irreducible or diffeomorphic to
${\mathbb S}^2\times{\mathbb S}^1$.

In particular, if we are given a closed,  \emph{orientable} $3$--manifold
$M$, the summands $N_1,\ldots,N_k$ are determined up to
diffeomorphism. The pieces of those $N_i$ which are irreducible will be called  \emph{pieces} of $M$.
<!-- end custom-9 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{because Perelman}
If a closed orientable $3$--manifold $M$ is
not hyperbolic, and $M$ contains no essential spheres or tori, then $M$
admits a Seifert fibration over ${\mathbb S}^2$ with at most three singular
fibers.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Since $M$ is not hyperbolic, and contains no essential spheres or
tori, it must be Seifert fibered 
by \S\ref{geometry and norms}.
Now, it follows from \cite[Proposition 10.4.14]{Martelli:GeometricTopology} that $M$ admits a Seifert fibration over ${\mathbb S}^2$ with at most three singular fibers.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- custom-10: body_md -->
{Gromov norm}\label{Gromov norm}
We will also make strong use of the Gromov norm. We recall 
from \cite[Definition 13.2.1]{Martelli:GeometricTopology}
that for any topological space $X$ 
and any integer $d>0$, there is a Gromov
(semi-)norm $\|\cdot\|$ on the vector space $H_d(X;{\mathbb R})$, 
that associates a number
$\|c\| \geq 0$ to every homology class
 $c\in H_d(X;{\mathbb R})$. We will consider
only the case where $X$ is a closed, orientable \emph{topological} $3$--manifold and
$c$ is the fundamental class $[X]$. We shall write $\|X\|$ for
$\|[X]\|$. 

According to \cite[Proposition 13.2.4]{Martelli:GeometricTopology}, if
$M$ and $N$ are closed 
oriented $3$--manifolds, and there is a
degree-$d$ map from $N$ to $M$, then
\begin{equation}\label{degree and Gromov}
 \| N \| \: \geq \: d \cdot  \|M\|.
\end{equation}

If $M$ is a closed, orientable hyperbolic $3$--manifold, it is a result
due to Gromov,  which appears
as \cite[Theorem 13.2.11]{Martelli:GeometricTopology}, that
\begin{equation}\label{genuine gromov}
{v_{\rm tet}}  \|M\|=\mathop{\rm vol} M,
\end{equation}
where ${v_{\rm tet}}$ is the volume of a regular ideal tetrahedron, as in \S\ref{notational}.

A folklore result, which generalizes \eqref{genuine gromov}, is that
if $M$ is a closed, orientable $3$--manifold $M$ and $P_1,\ldots,P_m$
denote its hyperbolic pieces, then 
$
{v_{\rm tet}} \|M\| =  \sum_{i=1}^m\mathop{\rm vol} P_i.
$
We shall not quote this fact as we do not have a reference for
it. However,  we will use
the following special case, which appears as
\cite[Theorem 6.5.5]{Thurston:notes}:
\begin{claim}
\label{all we need}
If $M$ is a closed, orientable $3$--manifold $M$ and $P$ is a
 hyperbolic piece of $M$, then
\[
{v_{\rm tet}}  \|M\| \geq  \mathop{\rm vol} P.
\]
\end{claim}
<!-- end custom-10 -->
<!-- claim-1: body_md -->
\label{all we need}
If $M$ is a closed, orientable $3$--manifold $M$ and $P$ is a
 hyperbolic piece of $M$, then
\[
{v_{\rm tet}}  \|M\| \geq  \mathop{\rm vol} P.
\]
<!-- end claim-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{running example}
Let $S$ be a compact surface with non-empty boundary. Then the product $M = S
\times I$ is an example of a $3$--manifold with corners.  If $G$ is a
finite group acting on $M$ by diffeomorphisms, the quotient ${{\mathcal N}} =
M/G$ is an example of what will be called a very good $3$--orbifold with $2$--corners. (Compare Definition~\ref{Def:OrbifoldChart}, and \S\S\ref{why corners?}
and \ref{Orbifold covers}.)
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- custom-11: body_md -->
{Orbifold charts}
\label{Def:OrbifoldChart}
Let $n$ and $k$ be non-negative integers.
An  \emph{$(n,k)$--orbifold chart} in a topological space $X$ is a quadruple
$( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi, G)$, 
where: 
\begin{itemize} 
\item $ U $ is an open subset of $X$;
\item ${\widetilde U}$ is an open subset of 
${\mathbb R}^{n-j}\times{\mathbb R}_+^j
$ for some $j$ with $0\le j\le \min(n,k)$;
\item
$G$ is a finite group of diffeomorphisms of ${\widetilde U} $; and
\item $\Phi \colon\thinspace  {\widetilde U}  \to  U $ is a continuous map that
factors through a homeomorphism from ${\widetilde U}  / G$ to
$ U $. 
\end{itemize}
We may refer to
$ U $, ${\widetilde U} $, $\Phi$ and $G$ respectively as the
   \emph{support} of the chart, the \emph{domain} of the chart, the  \emph{chart map} and the  \emph{group
   associated with} the chart.


If $( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi, G)$ is a chart in $X$, and ${\widetilde U}'$ is an open subset of ${\widetilde U}$ which is precisely $G$--invariant (in the sense that for every $g\in G$ we have either $g ({\widetilde U}')= {\widetilde U}'$ or $g({\widetilde U}') \cap {\widetilde U}'=\emptyset$), then the stabilizer of ${\widetilde U}'$ in $G$ defines a finite group $G'$ of diffeomorphisms of ${\widetilde U}'$, and 
$( \Phi ({\widetilde U}') , {\widetilde U}' , \Phi|{\widetilde U}', G')$ is a chart in $X$. A chart defined in this way will be called a \emph{subchart} of $( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi, G)$. 

We define a  \emph{transition map} from a chart $( U _1, {\widetilde U} _1, \Phi_1, G_1)$ to a chart
$( U _2, {\widetilde U} _2, \Phi_2, G_2)$ in $X$ to be a diffeomorphism
$\psi$ 
from the domain ${\widetilde U}_1'$ of some subchart $( U_1' , {\widetilde U}_1' , \Phi_1', G'_1)$ of 
$( U_1 , {\widetilde U}_1 , \Phi_1, G_1)$ of 
${\widetilde U}$ to the domain ${\widetilde U}_2'$ of some subchart $( U_2' , {\widetilde U}_2' , \Phi_2', G_2')$ of
$( U_2 , {\widetilde U}_2 , \Phi_2, G_2)$ such that 
\begin{itemize}
\item $\psi$ is equivariant with respect to some isomorphism $J\colon\thinspace G_1'\to G_2'$, meaning that $\psi(g x)=J(g) \big( \psi(x) \big)$ for all $x\in {\widetilde U}_1$ and $g\in G_1'$; and
\item 
$\Phi_2'\circ\psi = \Phi_1'$. 
\end{itemize}

Two
$(n,k)$--orbifold
charts $( U _1, {\widetilde U} _1, \Phi_1, G_1)$ and
$( U _2, {\widetilde U} _2, \Phi_2, G_2)$ are said to be {\it
  compatible} if, for every ${\widetilde x} _1\in  {\widetilde U}_1$ and every ${\widetilde x} _2 \in
{\widetilde U}_2$ with $\Phi_1({\widetilde x} _1) = \Phi_2 ({\widetilde x} _2)$, there is a
transition map $\psi$ between $( U _1, {\widetilde U} _1, \Phi_1, G_1)$ and
$( U _2, {\widetilde U} _2, \Phi_2, G_2)$, whose domain contains
${\widetilde x}_1 $, such that 
$\psi({\widetilde x}_1)={\widetilde x}_2$.
<!-- end custom-11 -->
<!-- custom-12: body_md -->
{Orbifolds with corners and manifolds with corners}
\label{Def:Orbifold}
\label{singular points}
A (smooth)   \emph{$(n,k)$--orbifold atlas} for $X$ is a collection of pairwise
compatible $(n,k)$--orbifold charts
in $X$ whose supports cover $X$. An  \emph{$n$--dimensional orbifold with
$k$--corners} 
${{\mathcal M}}$
is a paracompact Hausdorff
space 
$X$ equipped with a maximal 
$(n,k)$--orbifold atlas. 
The
space $X$ is called the  \emph{underlying space} of ${{\mathcal M}}$
and will often be denoted by ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$.
By a  \emph{chart for} ${{\mathcal M}}$ we mean a chart in the maximal atlas
  defining ${{\mathcal M}}$.
A  \emph{point} of 
${{\mathcal M}}$ is defined to be a point of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$.

Let ${{\mathcal M}}$  be an $n$--orbifold with $k$--corners.
A point $x$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is called a  \emph{$j$--corner point} of ${{\mathcal M}}$,
for a given  
integer $j$ with $0\le j\le \min(n,k)$
if for some,
and hence for every, chart $( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi, G)$ for
${{\mathcal M}}$ with $x\in U $,
the chart domain ${\widetilde U}$ is an  open subset of 
${\mathbb R}^{n-j}\times {\mathbb R}_+^j$, and
$\Phi^{-1}(x)
  \subset
{\mathbb R}^{n-j} \times\{0\}$ (where $0$ denotes the origin of
${\mathbb R}^j$). Thus every point of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a $j$--corner point for  a
unique choice of $j$.
A $0$--corner point of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is called an \emph{interior point}.

If $n$ and $k$ are non-negative integers, we define a (smooth) {\it
  $n$--manifold with $k$--corners} to be an   $n$--orbifold with
$k$--corners such that every point $x$ lies in the support of a chart such that the associated group $G$ is trivial.
(A more succinct characterization, using terminology to be introduced in \S\ref{Sec:LocalGroups}, is that an  $n$--manifold with corners is an   $n$--orbifold with
corners whose singular locus is empty.)
Specializing to the
case $k=1$, we recover the notion of a (smooth) $n$--manifold.
<!-- end custom-12 -->
<!-- custom-13: body_md -->
{Where corners arise}
\label{why corners?}
The importance of corners in this paper arises in large part from
their role in forming Cartesian products. If $n_1$, $k_1$, $n_2$ and
$k_2$ are non-negative integers, and ${{\mathcal M}}_i$ is an $n_i$--orbifold
with $k_i$--corners for $i=1,2$, then there is a canonically defined
$(n_1+n_2)$--orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}_1\times{{\mathcal M}}_2$ with $(k_1+k_2)$--corners
such that
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}_1\times{{\mathcal M}}_2}}={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}_1}}\times{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}_2}}$. In
particular, if the ${{\mathcal M}}_i$ are orbifolds with $1$--corners (that is, simply \emph{orbifolds} according to \S\ref{orb with boundary}) then
${{\mathcal M}}_1\times{{\mathcal M}}_2$ is an orbifold with $2$--corners.
<!-- end custom-13 -->
<!-- custom-14: body_md -->
{Standard group actions}\label{invariant neighborhood}
If $n$ and $j$ are integers with $0\le j\le n$, there is a standard
identification of ${\rm O}(n-j)\times{\rm O}(j)$ with a subgroup of the
orthogonal group ${\rm O}(n)$. We also have a standard identification of
the symmetric group ${\mathscr S}_j$ with a subgroup of ${\rm O}(j)$. With the
resulting identification of ${\rm O}(n-j)\times{\mathscr S}_j$ with a subgroup of
${\rm O}(n)$, the restriction to ${\rm O}(n-j)\times {\mathscr S}_j$ of the standard
action of ${\rm O}(n)$ on $\mathop{\rm int}{\mathbb B}^n$ leaves
$B\cap({\mathbb R}^{n-j}\times{\mathbb R}_+^j)$ invariant, for any open ball
$B\subset{\mathbb R}^n$ centered at $0$. This defines a
 \emph{standard action} of ${\rm O}(n-j)\times {\mathscr S}_j$ on
$B\cap({\mathbb R}^{n-j}\times{\mathbb R}_+^j)$.
<!-- end custom-14 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{general bochner}
If a compact  group $G$ acts by diffeomorphisms on an
$n$--manifold with corners $M$, and fixes a $j$--corner point $x\in M$
for some $j \leq  n$, then
$x$ has a $G$--invariant
neighborhood $V$ which can be identified diffeomorphically with 
$\mathop{\rm int}{\mathbb B}^n\cap({\mathbb R}^{n-j}\times{\mathbb R}_+^j)$
in 
such a way that $x=0$, 
and the action of $G$ factors through the standard action of ${\rm O}(n-j)\times {\mathscr S}_j$ on
$\mathop{\rm int}{\mathbb B}^n\cap({\mathbb R}^{n-j}\times{\mathbb R}_+^j)$ defined in \S\ref{invariant neighborhood}.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
This is a special case of \cite[Corollary 3.27]{log-corners}, where
the quantity denoted
by $k$ in that corollary is equal to $0$. The roles of the quantities denoted
by $l$ and $n$ in \cite[Corollary 3.27]{log-corners} are played here
by $n-j$ and $j$ respectively.

The case $j=0$ is the Bochner linearization theorem \cite{bochner}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{Bochner corollary}
If $G$ is a finite group of diffeomorphisms  of a connected $n$--manifold
with $k$--corners 
$M$,  
and if the action of $G$  restricts to the trivial action
on some non-empty open subset of $M$, then $G$ is trivial. {\hfill$\square$}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- custom-15: body_md -->
{Standard charts}
\label{about orbifolds}

It follows from 
Proposition \ref{general bochner}
that if $x$ is a $j$--corner point of an $n$--orbifold with corners
${{\mathcal M}}$, there is a chart $( U , D, \Phi, G)$ 
for ${{\mathcal M}}$ such that 
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(a)]
\item $D$ is the intersection of ${\mathbb R}^{n-j}\times{\mathbb R}_+^j$ with some open ball centered at the origin of ${\mathbb R}^n$;
\item
$\Phi(0)=x$; 
\item
$G$ is a subgroup of 
${\rm O}(n-j)\times{\mathscr S}_j$, whose action on $D$ is the standard one
(see \S\ref{invariant neighborhood}).
\end{enumerate}
Such a
chart will be called a  \emph{standard chart centered at $x$}.

The supports of standard charts for ${{\mathcal M}}$ form a basis for the topology of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$.
<!-- end custom-15 -->
<!-- custom-16: body_md -->
{Local groups}\label{Sec:LocalGroups}
If $x$ is a point of an orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$, 
 we  define a
 \emph{local group at $x$} to be a group which
  has the form ${\rm Stab}_G({\widetilde x})$
for some chart $( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi, G)$ with $x\in U$ and some
${\widetilde x}\in\Phi^{-1}(x)$. 
Changing the point ${\widetilde x}\in\Phi^{-1}(x)$ has the effect of conjugating
the local group within $G$, and changing the chart 
$( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi, G)$ has the effect of conjugating the local group by a
 transition map. Thus a local group at $x$ is uniquely determined up
 to isomorphism. Furthermore, the isomorphism between two local groups
 at $x$ is itself canonical modulo inner automorphisms. For this
 reason, we shall refer to {\it
  the} local group at a point $x$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$; it may be denoted by
$G_x^{{\mathcal M}}$, or by $G_x$ when it is clear which orbifold is involved. 

The group associated with a standard chart centered at a
point $x$ is
canonically identified (modulo inner automorphisms) with the local
group $G_x$. In particular, if $x$ is a $j$--corner point (where $0\le
j\le n$), then $G_x$ is canonically identified, modulo conjugacy in ${\rm O}(n-j)\times{\mathscr S}_j$, with
a subgroup of ${\rm O}(n-j)\times{\mathscr S}_j$.
Furthermore, the groups associated
to two different standard charts centered at $x$ are identified with
conjugate subgroups of ${\rm O}(n-j)\times{\mathscr S}_j$.
Thus 
we may regard $G_x$ as a
subgroup of 
${\rm O}(n-j)\times{\mathscr S}_j$
defined up to conjugacy. 
In particular,
$G_x$ is canonically identified, up to conjugacy, with a
subgroup of 
${\rm O}(n)$.

The order of $G_x^{{\mathcal M}}$ will be called the order of $x$; it may be denoted by $\mathop{\rm ord}^{{\mathcal M}}(x)$,
or by $\mathop{\rm ord}(x)$ when it is clear which orbifold is involved. 


A point $x$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is said to be  \emph{singular} if 
$G_x$ is non-trivial. The set of all singular points of
${{\mathcal M}}$ is a closed subset of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$, which is called the {\it
  singular set} of ${{\mathcal M}}$ and is denoted by $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$.
<!-- end custom-16 -->
<!-- custom-17: body_md -->
{Orbifolds with boundary}
\label{orb with boundary}
For any $n\ge1$ one may define an $n$--orbifold with boundary to be an
$n$--orbifold with $1$--corners. In this paper we shall use the term
 \emph{orbifold} to mean an orbifold with boundary; this is consistent
with the convention regarding manifolds that was laid out in \S\ref{manifolds}.

We define an \emph{$n$--orbifold with nonsingular $2$--corners} to be an  $n$--orbifold
with $2$--corners whose $2$--corner points are all nonsingular.

We emphasize that, according to these conventions, an orbifold (without further
specification) is permitted to have $1$--corner points but not
$k$--corner points for $k > 1$. Some of the substantive results of this
paper will concern $3$--orbifolds with nonsingular $2$--corners, but $k$--corners for
$k > 2$ will not arise after the foundational material of the present section.
<!-- end custom-17 -->
<!-- custom-18: body_md -->
{Naming convention}\label{Sec:naming}
Throughout the paper, we denote orbifolds with corners  by calligraphic letters, for instance ${{\mathcal M}}$ and ${{\mathcal N}}$. 
It will often be convenient to use a single letter to denote the
underlying space of an orbifold with corners.
When this arises, we typically use the
``math-italic'' counterpart of the calligraphic letter denoting the
orbifold with corners itself: e.g.\ $M={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$, $N={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$, etc.

In addition, we use a script letter  to denote a family of orbifolds
with corners
whose typical element is
denoted by the corresponding  calligraphic letter: e.g.\ ${\mathscr M} = \{
{{\mathcal M}}, {{\mathcal M}}' \ldots \}$. We also use a script letter to denote a
(possibly) disconnected orbifold whose typical component is denoted by
the corresponding calligraphic letter: e.g.\ ${\mathscr M} =  {{\mathcal M}} \sqcup
{{\mathcal M}}' \sqcup \ldots$. 
The distinction between collections and disjoint unions will be made
clear in each instance.
In the manifold setting, we use boldface letters to denote collections
of manifolds with corners and disjoint unions of manifolds with corners: e.g.\ ${\bf M} = \{ M, M' \ldots \}$.
<!-- end custom-18 -->
<!-- custom-19: body_md -->
{Orientations}
\label{orientable orbifolds}
An \emph{oriented atlas} for an orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$ is an atlas of charts for ${{\mathcal M}}$, 
together with an orientation of each chart domain, with the
property that every transition map is orientation-preserving.
This implies that for each
chart,
the associated group consists of orientation-preserving
diffeomorphisms of the chart domain.

An \emph{orientation} of an orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a maximal oriented atlas.
We say that
${{\mathcal M}}$ is  \emph{orientable} if it admits an orientation.
<!-- end custom-19 -->
<!-- custom-20: body_md -->
{Orbifold maps}
\label{maps and such}
Suppose that ${{\mathcal M}}$ and ${{\mathcal M}}'$ are orbifolds
with corners, and that $F$ is a continuous map from $M={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ to
$M'={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}'}}$. Let 
$( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi, G)$ and
$( U ', {\widetilde U} ', \Phi', G')$ be charts for ${{\mathcal M}}$ and
${{\mathcal M}}'$ respectively. 
A  \emph{smooth local lift} of $F$ is a pair $({\widetilde F}, \psi)$ where $\psi \colon\thinspace G \to G'$ is a group homomorphism, ${\widetilde F} \colon\thinspace  {\widetilde U}\to{\widetilde U}'$ is a $\psi$--equivariant smooth map,  and 
$F\circ\Phi=\Phi'\circ{\widetilde F}$. A necessary condition for the existence
of a smooth local lift\  is that $F(U)\subset U'$. We 
shall often leave the homomorphism $\psi$ implicit and simply say that ${\widetilde F}$ is a local lift of $F$.


Now suppose that two local lift s ${\widetilde F}_1$ and ${\widetilde F}_2$ of $F$ are
given. Thus for $i=1,2$, the local lift\ ${\widetilde F}_i$ is a map from
${\widetilde U}_i$ to ${\widetilde U}_i'$, where $( U_i , {\widetilde U}_i , \Phi_i, G_i)$ and
$( U_i', {\widetilde U}_i', \Phi_i', G_i')$ are charts for ${{\mathcal M}}$ and
${{\mathcal M}}'$ respectively. We shall say that ${\widetilde F}_1$ and ${\widetilde F}_2$ are
 \emph{compatible} if, for every ${\widetilde x} _1\in  {\widetilde U}_1$ and every ${\widetilde x} _2 \in
{\widetilde U}_2$ with $\Phi_1({\widetilde x} _1) = \Phi_2 ({\widetilde x} _2)$, there exist a
transition map $\psi$ from $( U _1, {\widetilde U} _1, \Phi_1, G_1)$ to
$( U _2, {\widetilde U} _2, \Phi_2, G_2)$ with domain $V \subset {\widetilde U}_1$, and a
transition map $\psi'$ between $( U _1', {\widetilde U} _1', \Phi_1', G_1')$ and
$( U _2', {\widetilde U} _2', \Phi_2', G_2')$ whose domain contains ${\widetilde F}_1(V)$, such that ${\widetilde F}_2 \circ\psi=\psi'\circ({\widetilde F}_1|V)$.

An  \emph{atlas of local lift s} for $F$ is defined to be a collection
of pairwise compatible local lift s whose domains cover ${{\mathcal M}}$.
A  \emph{smooth orbifold map} from ${{\mathcal M}}$ to ${{\mathcal M}}'$ is defined by a
continuous map $F\colon\thinspace M\to M'$ together with an atlas of local lift s of
$F$ which is maximal with respect to inclusion.

We shall call $F$ the  \emph{underlying map} of $f$. The local lift s of
$F$ that belong to the maximal atlas of local lift s defining $f$ will
be called
\emph{local lift s\ for $f$.}
<!-- end custom-20 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{UnderlyingMapNotEnough}
In general, a continuous orbifold map is not uniquely determined by its
underlying map of spaces. For example, consider the $1$--orbifold ${\mathbb R}$ and the
$2$--orbifold ${\mathbb R}^2/\langle\rho\rangle$, where $\rho$ denotes the
counterclockwise rotation of ${\mathbb R}^2$ through an angle $2\pi/n$ for an integer $n>1$. The identity
map of ${\mathbb R}$ and the quotient map ${\mathbb R}^2\to{\mathbb R}^2/\langle\rho\rangle$
are chart maps defining charts for these two orbifolds, whose supports
are all of ${\mathbb R}$ and all of ${\mathbb R}^2/\langle\rho\rangle$,
respectively. For each $j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, we may define a  map
$\ell_j\colon\thinspace{\mathbb R}\to{\mathbb R}^2$ between chart domains by setting
$\ell_j(x)=(x,0)$ for $x\ge0$, and $\ell_j(x)=\rho^j(|x|,0)$ for
$x\le0$. Then the $\ell_j$ are all local lifts of the same map of
spaces  $F\colon\thinspace{{\rm X}_{{\mathbb R}}}\to {{\rm X}_{{\mathbb R}^2/\langle\rho\rangle}}$, and
these local lifts determine $n$ distinct continuous orbifold maps having $F$ as
underlying map. This phenomenon will be important in connection with
the unique path lifting property for orbifold coverings (see
\S\ref{crucial fact} below).
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- custom-21: body_md -->
{Orbifold maps, continued}\label{maps continued}
If $f \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal M}}\to{{{\mathcal M}}'}$ and $f' \colon\thinspace  {{\mathcal M}}'\to{{{\mathcal M}}''}$ are
smooth  orbifold maps
between orbifolds with corners, we  define the  \emph{composition} of
$f$ and $f'$ to be
the unique orbifold map $f'\circ f
\colon\thinspace  {{\mathcal M}} \to{{{\mathcal M}}''}$ such that (a) the underlying map of $f'\circ f$
is $F'\circ F$, where $F$ and $F'$ denote the underlying maps of
$f$ and $f'$ respectively, and (b) whenever ${\widetilde F}$ and
${\widetilde F}'$ are  local lift s for $f$ and $f'$ respectively, such that the
image of ${\widetilde F}$ is contained in the domain of ${\widetilde F}'$, the composition
${\widetilde F}'\circ {\widetilde F}$ is a local lift\  for $f'\circ f$.
With this notion of composition, we have a
category of orbifolds with corners in which the morphisms are smooth
orbifold maps.

The isomorphisms in this category will be called  \emph{orbifold
  diffeomorphisms}.
The underlying map of an orbifold diffeomorphism is a homeomorphism,
and the local lift assigned to each point of its domain is a manifold diffeomorphism.

If ${{\mathcal M}}_i$ are orbifolds for $i=1,2$, there is a canonical orbifold
map $q_i\colon\thinspace {{\mathcal M}}_1\times{{\mathcal M}}_2\to{{\mathcal M}}_i$,
called a  \emph{projection,} whose underlying map is the product
projection from ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}_1}} \times {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}_2}}$ to
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}_i}}$. Moreover, ${{\mathcal M}}_1\times{{\mathcal M}}_2$ is a product object
in the category of smooth orbifolds.

By replacing ``smooth'' by ``continuous'' in the definitions given
above, we obtain the notions of a  \emph{continuous local lift} and a {\it
  continuous local lift\ class}, and a  \emph{continuous orbifold
map}. 
We also obtain the notion of composition of continuous orbifold maps,
and we have a category of orbifolds with corners in which the morphisms are continuous
orbifold maps.

We adopt the convention that  ``local lift s,''  
and  ``orbifold maps'' are understood to be
smooth except when ``continuous'' is specified. We shall also often
say ``map'' in place of ``orbifold map.''
<!-- end custom-21 -->
<!-- custom-22: body_md -->
{Orbifold covering maps}
\label{Orbifold covers}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ and ${{\mathcal M}}'$ be $n$--orbifolds with $k$--corners, and let
$f\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal M}}'\to{{\mathcal M}}$ be an orbifold map with underlying map $F$. We
shall say that a chart 
for ${{\mathcal M}}$, with support $U$ and connected chart domain ${\widetilde U}$, is {\it
  evenly covered} if  every component $U'$ of  $F^{-1}(U)$ is the
support of a chart 
for ${{\mathcal M}}'$ with chart domain ${\widetilde U}$, 
such that
the identity map on ${\widetilde U}$
is a local lift\ for $f$.
We shall say that $f$ is a  \emph{covering map} if every point of
${{\mathcal M}}$ has a connected open neighborhood which is the support of an
evenly covered chart.

If $\Gamma$ is a group of orbifold  diffeomorphisms of an orbifold 
with $k$--corners
${{\mathcal M}}$, and the action of $\Gamma$ on ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ is properly discontinuous,
then ${{\mathcal M}}/\Gamma$ inherits the structure of an orbifold
with $k$--corners, 
and the
quotient map from ${{\mathcal M}}$ to ${{\mathcal M}}/\Gamma$ is a
regular covering map. 
The orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}/\Gamma$ is a quotient object in the (smooth) category
defined in \S\ref{maps continued}, and its underlying space is
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}/\Gamma$.

Conversely, if $p \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}\to{{\mathcal M}}$  is a
regular covering map of  orbifolds with corners, 
then there is a group
$G$ of orbifold diffeomorphisms of ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$, acting properly
discontinuously on ${{\rm X}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}}}$, such that $p$
is the
composition of the quotient map ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}\to{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}/G$ 
with an orbifold diffeomorphism from ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}/G$ to ${{\mathcal M}}$.

These
observations apply in particular to the situation where a finite
group acts by orbifold diffeomorphisms on a given orbifold with
corners; this corresponds to the case of a finite-sheeted regular covering.

An orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$ is said to be  \emph{good} if it has some covering space
which is nonsingular, 
i.e.\ is a manifold with corners; 
otherwise ${{\mathcal M}}$ is said to be  \emph{bad}. An orbifold with corners  ${{\mathcal M}}$ is termed  \emph{very good} if it has some finite-sheeted covering space
which is nonsingular. 
It 
will follow from the relationship between covering spaces and
fundamental groups, to be presented  in \S\ref{path subsection},
 that every finite-sheeted  cover of ${{\mathcal M}}$ has a further
cover ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ such that the composition ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}} \to {{\mathcal M}}$ 
is
both finite-sheeted and regular. Consequently,  every very good orbifold with corners is the quotient of a manifold with corners by a finite group action. This is the setup described in Example~\ref{running example}.

For any
$n\ge2$, we define a
 \emph{hyperbolic $n$--orbifold} to be a quotient of ${\mathbb H}^n$ by a
properly discontinous group of hyperbolic isometries. In particular,
a hyperbolic orbifold (or manifold) is by definition connected and
complete in its natural metric, and has no boundary.

It follows from Selberg's lemma \cite{Alperin:SelbergLemma} that every
hyperbolic orbifold ${\mathbb H}^n/\Gamma$, where $\Gamma$  is a finitely
generated discrete group of isometries of ${\mathbb H}^n$,
 is very good. 

The \emph{volume} $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}}$ of a hyperbolic $n$--orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}={\mathbb H}^n/\Gamma$ may be defined as the volume of an arbitrary (measurable) fundamental domain for $\Gamma$ in ${\mathbb H}^n$, or equivalently as $(\mathop{\rm vol}{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}})/d$, where ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ is an arbitrary finite-sheeted manifold covering of ${{\mathcal M}}$ and $d$ denotes the degree of the covering map. 

Up to equivalence, a connected, non-orientable orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}$
has a unique orientable
two-sheeted orbifold cover ${{\mathcal M}}'$; we shall call ${{\mathcal M}}'$ the {\it
  orientation cover} of ${{\mathcal M}}$. While the existence of ${{\mathcal M}}'$ is
not hard to prove by adapting the standard proof for the manifold
setting, we shall need only the case where ${{\mathcal M}}$ is good, and the
proof is particularly simple in this case: if ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ denotes the
universal covering of ${{\mathcal M}}$, which is a manifold, we may define
${{\mathcal M}}'$ to be ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}/\Gamma$, where $\Gamma$ denotes the index--$2$
subgroup of the deck group of ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ consisting of
orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms.

For an arbitrary  good orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}$, which may be disconnected and
may have orientable components, we define the orientation cover to be
the two-sheeted cover which is the disjoint union of the orientation
covers of all non-orientable components of ${{\mathcal M}}$, together with two copies of
each orientable component of ${{\mathcal M}}$.
<!-- end custom-22 -->
<!-- custom-23: body_md -->
{Suborbifolds}
\label{Suborbifolds}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be an $m$--orbifold with 
corners,  and set $M={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$. 
Suppose that $n$ is an integer with $0\leq n \leq m$, and that $N$ is a subset of $M$ having the following property:
\begin{claim}\label{defines a suborbifold}
For every $x\in M$ there is a chart $( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi,
G)$ for ${{\mathcal M}}$, with $x\in U$, such that $\Phi^{-1}(N)$ is a
(possibly empty) $n$--dimensional submanifold with corners of ${\widetilde U}$.
\end{claim}
Then for every point $y\in N$, there exist a chart $( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi,
G)$ for ${{\mathcal M}}$, an integer $j$ with $0\le j\le n$, an open set $\widetilde V\subset{\mathbb R}^{n-j}\times{\mathbb R}_+^j
$, and a diffeomorphism $h$ of $\widetilde V$ onto a $G$--invariant open subset  of
$\Phi^{-1}(N)$ containing the set $\Phi^{-1}(y)$. By restricting the action of $G$ to $h(\widetilde V)$ and pulling
back via $h$, we obtain a group $\overline{G}$
of diffeomorphisms of $\widetilde V$ which is isomorphic to a quotient of
$G$. 
The map $\omega\doteq\Phi\circ h\colon\thinspace\widetilde V\to N$ then induces a
homeomorphism of $\widetilde V/\overline{G}$
onto an open neighborhood $V$ of $y$ in $N$.
The quadruple
$(V,\widetilde V,\omega,\overline{G})$ is then an $(n,j)$--orbifold chart 
in $N$; the set
of all charts of this form is an orbifold atlas on $N$, and therefore
defines an $n$--orbifold with 
corners ${{\mathcal N}}$
whose underlying space is $N$. 

For any subset $N$
of $M$ such that \ref{defines a suborbifold} holds, the orbifold
${{\mathcal N}}$
constructed in this way will be denoted ${\Omega_{N}}$. To say that ${\Omega_{N}}$ is defined means that \ref{defines a suborbifold} holds. By
definition, we always have ${{\rm X}_{{\Omega_{N}}}}=N$ if ${\Omega_{N}}$ is defined.



A  \emph{suborbifold with corners of ${{\mathcal M}}$ in the weak sense}, or more briefly a
 \emph{weak suborbifold with corners of ${{\mathcal M}}$}, is by definition an
orbifold with corners of the
form ${\Omega_{N}}$ for some set $N\subset M$ such that \ref{defines a suborbifold} holds. 

We observe that if ${{\mathcal N}}$  is a weak suborbifold with corners of  ${{\mathcal M}}$,  and $G$ is a group of diffeomorphisms of ${{\mathcal N}}$ whose underlying action on ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ leaves $N\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ invariant, then the weak suborbifold ${\Omega_{N/G}}$ of ${{\mathcal M}}/G$ is defined, and is canonically identified with the quotient ${{\mathcal N}}/G$.

In the case where ${{\mathcal M}}$ is an orbifold (with boundary), a
weak suborbifold ${{\mathcal N}}={\Omega_{N}}$ of  ${{\mathcal M}}$ is said to be  \emph{neatly
  embedded}  if a stronger version of \ref{defines a suborbifold}
holds, namely that for every $x\in M$ the chart $( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi,
G)$ may be chosen in such a way that the submanifold 
$\Phi^{-1}(N)$ is neatly embedded in ${\widetilde U}$.

For an arbitrary $m$--orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$, and an arbitrary
subset $N$ of $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ satisfying \ref{defines a suborbifold} for a given $ n \leq m$,
  choosing the support $U$ to be sufficiently small ensures that
the groups denoted $G$ and $\overline{G}$ in
the discussion above are canonically identified 
(up to inner automorphisms) 
with the local groups $G_y^{{\mathcal M}}$ and $G_y^{{\mathcal N}}$
respectively. Thus for every weak suborbifold with corners ${{\mathcal N}}$ of
an orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$, and every point
$y$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$, we have a surjective homomorphism  $\theta_y\colon\thinspace G_y^{{\mathcal M}}\to G_y^{{\mathcal N}}$ which is canonical up to composition with  inner
automorphisms of these finite groups.

  If  $\theta_y$ is an
isomorphism for every
$y\in {{\mathcal N}}$, we shall say that ${{\mathcal N}}$ is a  \emph{suborbifold of
  ${{\mathcal M}}$ in the strong sense.} We adopt the convention that
``suborbifold'' without qualification means ``suborbifold in the
strong sense.'' 

 
If ${{\mathcal N}}$ is a suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$, then in particular $G_y^{{\mathcal N}}$
and $G_y^{{\mathcal M}}$ are isomorphic, and therefore
$\mathop{\rm ord}^{{\mathcal N}}(y)=\mathop{\rm ord}^{{\mathcal M}}(y)$,  for every $y\in{{\mathcal N}}$. Hence $\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}
= {{\mathcal N}} \cap \Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$. These facts will be used very frequently in
later sections. They need not remain true if ${{\mathcal N}}$ is assumed only
to be a weak suborbifold; compare the second example in \S\ref{Exa:BMPSuborbifold}.
<!-- end custom-23 -->
<!-- claim-2: body_md -->
\label{defines a suborbifold}
For every $x\in M$ there is a chart $( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi,
G)$ for ${{\mathcal M}}$, with $x\in U$, such that $\Phi^{-1}(N)$ is a
(possibly empty) $n$--dimensional submanifold with corners of ${\widetilde U}$.
<!-- end claim-2 -->
<!-- custom-24: body_md -->
{Examples}
\label{Exa:BMPSuborbifold}\label{Exa:StrongVsWeak}
Here are two instructive examples, with the same ambient orbifold. Let ${{\mathcal M}}={\mathbb B}^2/C$, where $C$ is a cyclic group of rotations about $0\in {\mathbb B}^2$ of some odd
order $p>1$.

For the first example, let $f \colon\thinspace {\mathbb B}^2 \to {{\mathcal M}}$ be the projection, and let $g \colon\thinspace I \to {\mathbb B}^2$ be the embedding of a diameter. Then 
according to our definitions, the image of $I$ in $M = {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$
 is not the underlying set of even a weak suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$, because it does not have Property \ref{defines a suborbifold}. However, $f \circ g$ is an orbifold immersion (see \S\ref{more orbifold notions} below) and its underlying map is injective; this means that the image of $I$ is  the underlying set of a ``suborbifold'' in the sense defined by Boileau--Maillot--Porti \cite[Section 2.1.3]{BoileauMaillotPorti}. 

 For the second example, let $o\in{{\mathcal M}}$ be the image of $0$ under the quotient map. Then the  weak suborbifold
 ${{\mathcal N}}\doteq{\Omega_{\{o\}}}$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is defined but is not a
 suborbifold in the strong sense. Indeed, we have
$\mathop{\rm ord}^{{\mathcal N}}(o)=1\ne p=\mathop{\rm ord}^{{\mathcal M}}(o)$,  and $\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}
=\emptyset\ne\{o\}= {{\mathcal N}} \cap \Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$.
<!-- end custom-24 -->
<!-- custom-25: body_md -->
{Inclusion maps}\label{inclusions}
Let  ${{\mathcal N}}$ be a  suborbifold with corners of an orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$. Set $M={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ and $N={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$, and let $\kappa \colon\thinspace N\to M$ denote the inclusion map.  It follows from the discussion in \S\ref{Suborbifolds} that for every point $y\in N$ there exist charts $( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi,
G)$ and
$(V,\widetilde V,\omega,\overline{G})$ for ${{\mathcal M}}$ and ${{\mathcal N}}$ respectively such that the following condition holds:
\begin{claim}\label{for inclusion}
We have $y\in V\subset U$, and if $\widetilde{\kappa}\colon\thinspace\widetilde V\to{\widetilde U}$ denotes the inclusion map, then $(\widetilde{\kappa},\theta_y^{-1})$ is a local lift of $\kappa$,
where $\theta_y^{-1} \colon\thinspace G_y^{{\mathcal N}} \to G_y^{{\mathcal M}}$ is the inverse of the isomorphism $\theta_y$ defined in
\S\ref{Suborbifolds}.
\end{claim}


Each point $y\in N$ and each pair of charts $( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi,
G)$ and
$(V,\widetilde V,\omega,\overline{G})$ for which \ref{for inclusion} holds define a local lift of $\kappa$. The set of all local lifts defined in this way is an atlas of local lifts of $\kappa$, and therefore define an orbifold map from ${{\mathcal N}}$ to ${{\mathcal M}}$ with underlying map $\kappa$. This orbifold map will be called the \emph{inclusion map} ${{\mathcal N}} \hookrightarrow {{\mathcal M}}$. We emphasize that we have defined the inclusion map only when ${{\mathcal N}}$ is a suborbifold with corners in the strong sense: if ${{\mathcal N}}$ were only a suborbifold with corners in the weak sense, there would appear to be no naturally defined homomorphism to play the role of $\theta_y^{-1}$ in \ref{for inclusion}. 

If ${{\mathcal M}}'$ and ${{\mathcal M}}$ are orbifolds with corners, we
define an  \emph{embedding} of  ${{\mathcal M}}'$ in ${{\mathcal M}}$ to be a
smooth map from ${{\mathcal M}}'$ to ${{\mathcal M}}$ which is the composition of a
diffeomorphism of ${{\mathcal M}}'$ onto a suborbifold with corners ${{\mathcal N}}$ of
${{\mathcal M}}$ with the inclusion map from ${{\mathcal N}}$ to ${{\mathcal M}}$.

If 
$f$ is an arbitrary smooth map from ${{\mathcal M}}$ to an orbifold with corners
${{\mathcal N}}$, 
and ${{\mathcal Z}}$ is
any  suborbifold with corners of ${{\mathcal M}}$, we define $f|{{\mathcal Z}}\colon\thinspace {{\mathcal Z}}\to{{\mathcal N}}$ to be
the composition of the inclusion map ${{\mathcal Z}}\hookrightarrow{{\mathcal M}}$ with $f$.
<!-- end custom-25 -->
<!-- claim-3: body_md -->
\label{for inclusion}
We have $y\in V\subset U$, and if $\widetilde{\kappa}\colon\thinspace\widetilde V\to{\widetilde U}$ denotes the inclusion map, then $(\widetilde{\kappa},\theta_y^{-1})$ is a local lift of $\kappa$,
where $\theta_y^{-1} \colon\thinspace G_y^{{\mathcal N}} \to G_y^{{\mathcal M}}$ is the inverse of the isomorphism $\theta_y$ defined in
\S\ref{Suborbifolds}.
<!-- end claim-3 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{codim 1 is nice}
Suppose that ${{\mathcal N}}$ is a weak suborbifold with
corners  of an 
orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$. Suppose that
at least one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(i)]
\item\label{Hyp:Codim0} ${{\mathcal N}}$ has codimension $0$ in ${{\mathcal M}}$, or
\item\label{Hyp:Codim1Bdy} ${{\mathcal N}}$ has codimension $1$ in ${{\mathcal M}}$ and ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ is disjoint from
  ${{\rm X}_{\mathop{\rm int}{{\mathcal M}}}}$, or
\item\label{Hyp:Codim1Ori} ${{\mathcal N}}$ has codimension $1$ in ${{\mathcal M}}$ and ${{\mathcal M}}$ is
  orientable.
\end{enumerate}
Then ${{\mathcal N}}$ is a  suborbifold with
corners of ${{\mathcal M}}$ (in the strong sense).
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
According to the definition given in \S\ref{Suborbifolds}, we must
  show that the
  surjective homomorphism  $\theta_y\colon\thinspace G_y^{{\mathcal M}}\to G_y^{{\mathcal N}}$ has
  trivial kernel for every
$y\in {{\mathcal N}}$.   It follows from the discussion in
\S\ref{Suborbifolds} that we may fix a chart $( U , {\widetilde U} , \Phi,
G)$ for ${{\mathcal M}}$, with $y \in U$, such that $G_y^{{\mathcal M}}$ is identified
with $G$, while $G_y^{{\mathcal N}}$ is identified
with the group $\overline{G}$ of restrictions of elements of $G$ to 
a $G$--invariant open subset $\widetilde V$ of $\Phi^{-1}(N)$, 
and $\theta_y$ is the
restriction homomorphism from $G$ to $\overline{G}$. 
We may take ${\widetilde U}$ to be connected. To show that
$\theta_y$ has trivial kernel, we must show that any element $g$ of $G$
which fixes $\widetilde V $ pointwise is the identity. According to Corollary~\ref{Bochner corollary}
we need only show that $g$
fixes pointwise some non-empty open subset of ${\widetilde U}$. This is
immediate  if hypothesis \eqref{Hyp:Codim0}  holds.

If hypothesis \eqref{Hyp:Codim1Bdy} holds, then $\widetilde V $ is an $(n-1)$--manifold with
corners contained in the $n$--manifold with corners ${\widetilde U}$, and contains
no interior points of ${\widetilde U}$. Hence $\widetilde V $ contains a $1$--corner point
${\widetilde w}$ of ${\widetilde U}$. We may regard ${\widetilde w}$ as a boundary point of the $G$--invariant manifold  ${\widetilde U}'$ consisting of all $0$-- and $1$--corner points of ${\widetilde U}$. By Proposition \ref{general bochner},
applied with $\langle g\rangle$ and
${\widetilde U}'$ playing the respective roles of $G$ and $M$, some $\langle g\rangle$--invariant neighborhood 
$Y $ of ${\widetilde w}$ in ${\widetilde U}'$ can be identified diffeomorphically with 
the open half-ball $(\mathop{\rm int} {\mathbb B}^n)\cap({\mathbb R}^{n-1}\times{\mathbb R}_+)$
in 
such a way that ${\widetilde w} = 0$, 
and the action of $\langle g\rangle$ factors through the standard action of 
 ${\rm O}(n-1)$. We may suppose $ Y  $ to have been chosen small enough so
that $\partial  Y  = Y  \cap\partial{\widetilde U}'\subset\widetilde V $. Since the standard
action of ${\rm O}(n-1)$ on the boundary of the open half-ball $ Y  $ is effective, and
$g$ fixes $\widetilde V $ pointwise, it follows that $g$ also fixes $ Y  $
pointwise; thus $ Y  $ is the required open subset of ${\widetilde U}$ in this case.


If hypothesis \eqref{Hyp:Codim1Ori} holds but hypothesis \eqref{Hyp:Codim1Bdy} does not, we may
choose a point $z\in\widetilde V \cap\mathop{\rm int}{\widetilde U}$.  We choose a $\langle
g\rangle$--invariant neighborhood $T$ of $z$ in $\mathop{\rm int}{\widetilde U}$ which is
small enough to guarantee that $\widetilde V \cap T$ is closed in the
subspace topology of $T$. If $\widetilde V _0$ denotes the component of
$\widetilde V \cap T$ containing $z$, we may then write $ T=T_1\cup T_2$, where
the $T_i$ are $n$--manifolds with boundary and $T_1\cap T_2=\partial
T_1=\partial T_2=\widetilde V _0$. Now $g$ fixes $\widetilde V _0\subset\widetilde V $ pointwise,
and it preserves the orientation of $T$ since 
${{\mathcal M}}$ 
is orientable
in this case. Hence $g$ cannot interchange $T_1$ and $T_2$, and it
must therefore leave each of them invariant. We can now finish the
proof exactly as in Case \eqref{Hyp:Codim1Bdy}, with $T_1$ and  $z\in\partial T_1$ playing the
respective roles of ${\widetilde U}'$ and ${\widetilde w} \in \partial{\widetilde U}'$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- custom-26: body_md -->
{Suborbifolds, continued}
\label{suborbs continued}
If $U$ is an arbitrary open
subset of $M$, then 
${\Omega_{U}}$ is defined, and 
by Proposition \ref{codim 1 is nice} it
 is an $n$--dimensional suborbifold with corners (in the strong sense).
We shall call ${\Omega_{U}}$ an  \emph{open
  suborbifold with corners} of ${{\mathcal M}}$. 

In particular, 
if $( U ,
{\widetilde U} , \Phi, G)$, is any chart for an orbifold 
with corners
${{\mathcal M}}$, 
there is an open suborbifold 
with corners ${{\mathcal U}}\doteq{\Omega_{U}}$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$. 
The map 
$\Phi$ defines a
finite-sheeted regular orbifold covering map from ${\widetilde U}$ to the open
suborbifold 
with corners
${\Omega_{U}} $ of ${{\mathcal M}}$. Furthermore, if 
$( U , D, \Phi, G)$ is a standard chart, then $D$ is the
universal cover of ${{\mathcal U}} = {\Omega_{U}} $ and,
up to equivalence, is the unique connected manifold cover of ${{\mathcal U}}$.


For another example, the set of interior points of ${{\mathcal M}}$ defines an open suborbifold, called the \emph{interior of ${{\mathcal M}}$} and denoted $\mathop{\rm int} {{\mathcal M}}$.

An  \emph{open neighborhood} of a point $x$
of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is an open suborbifold with corners having $x$ as a point. 

A  \emph{standard neighborhood} of a point 
$x$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is
an open neighborhood of the form ${{\mathcal U}}={\Omega_{U}}$, where $U$ is the support
of a standard chart  centered at $x$.


Any component $K$  of $M$ is an open subset of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$, and
hence ${\Omega_{K}}$ is defined. We call ${\Omega_{K}}$
a  \emph{component} of ${{\mathcal M}}$. Note
that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is connected if and only if it has exactly one component.

We define a {\it
  suborbifold} or  \emph{weak suborbifold} of ${{\mathcal M}}$ to be,
respectively a suborbifold with corners or a weak suborbifold with
corners which is itself an orbifold. 
Note that we use this terminology even when ${{\mathcal M}}$ is not itself an
orbifold (that is, ${{\mathcal M}}$ has $k$--corner points for $k > 1$). 
This slight abuse of language is analogous
to speaking, for example, of a subfield of a ring. Likewise we may
refer to a ``submanifold'' (with or without corners) of the
general orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}$, meaning a suborbifold of  ${{\mathcal M}}$ which is itself a manifold.

If  $Z$ denotes the set of $1$--corner points of 
an orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}$, then ${\Omega_{Z}}$
is defined. We shall refer to ${\Omega_{Z}}$ as the
 \emph{boundary} of ${{\mathcal M}}$ and denote it $\partial{{\mathcal M}}$.
It follows from Proposition \ref{codim 1 is nice} that $\partial{{\mathcal M}}$
is a suborbifold (in the strong sense) of ${{\mathcal M}}$.


An  \emph{immersion} from ${{\mathcal M}}$ to an orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}'$
is defined to be a smooth map  $f\colon\thinspace {{\mathcal M}}\to  {{\mathcal M}}'$ with the property that
every point of ${{\mathcal M}}$ has a neighborhood ${{\mathcal U}}$ such that
$f|{{\mathcal U}}\colon\thinspace {{\mathcal U}}\to{{\mathcal M}}'$ is an embedding.
<!-- end custom-26 -->
<!-- custom-27: body_md -->
{Weak suborbifolds that are manifolds}
\label{when it's a manifold}
We will often encounter situations in which a 
subset $Y$ of $M$ has the property that ${\Omega_{Y}}$ is defined and
is a manifold with corners (and possibly a manifold).
We  will then write
$Y={\Omega_{Y}}$, and refer to $Y$ as a manifold with corners (or a manifold). This is consistent with
the universal convention in manifold theory whereby a manifold is not
distinguished notationally from its underlying set or topological
space. 

In particular, if $x$ is any point of ${{\mathcal M}}$ then 
${\Omega_{\{x\}}}$ is  defined, and is a
$0$--manifold.
<!-- end custom-27 -->
<!-- custom-28: body_md -->
{Notational shortcuts}
\label{more orbifold notions}


An orbifold 
with corners
${{\mathcal M}}$ is said to be  \emph{compact} or  \emph{connected} if
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ is, respectively, compact or connected.

A good many set-theoretic or general-topological operations on subsets
of $M$ can be interpreted as operations on suborbifolds with corners, in
situations where certain conditions hold. For example, if ${{\mathcal Y}}$ and ${{\mathcal Z}}$
are suborbifolds with corners of ${{\mathcal M}}$, if we set
$Y={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Y}}}}$, $Z={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Z}}}}$, and if ${\Omega_{Y\cap Z}}$ is defined, we will 
denote ${\Omega_{Y\cap Z}}$ by 
${{\mathcal Y}}\cap{{\mathcal Z}}$. 
We follow similar conventions regarding the intersection or union of
any  family of suborbifolds, for inclusion 
relations between
suborbifolds, and for set-theoretic differences of suborbifolds. 
(The intersection and union of any finite family of open suborbifolds is always defined.)

If ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a suborbifold with corners of  ${{\mathcal M}}$, if we set $Y={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Y}}}}$, and
if ${\Omega_{\overline Y}}$ is defined, we denote ${\Omega_{\overline Y}}$ by $\overline{{{\mathcal Y}}}$ and refer to it as the {\it
  closure} of ${{\mathcal Y}}$; we use a similar convention for frontiers of suborbifolds.

If $f$ is a smooth map of an orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal N}}$ into ${{\mathcal M}}$  defined
by a map $F\colon\thinspace {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}\to M$, if ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a suborbifold with
corners of ${{\mathcal N}}$, if we set $Y={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Y}}}}$, and if
${\Omega_{F(Y)}}$ is
defined, we will denote ${\Omega_{F(Y)}}$ by $f({{\mathcal Y}})$. 
If $f$ is an embedding of ${{\mathcal N}}$ in ${{\mathcal M}}$, then 
$f({{\mathcal Y}})$
  is defined for any suborbifold ${{\mathcal Y}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$; in particular the  \emph{image} $f({{\mathcal M}})$ of
$f$ is defined in this case. We follow a similar convention for
preimages. The preimage of an open suborbifold under an orbifold map
is always defined. 

We shall use a number of  locutions that generalize familiar locutions for
manifolds, and are self-explanatory; for example, to say that a map
$f$ from ${{\mathcal M}}$ to an orbifold with  corners ${{\mathcal N}}$ 
maps a suborbifold 
with corners ${{\mathcal Y}}$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$
diffeomorphically onto a suborbifold with corners ${{\mathcal Z}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$ means that
$f({{\mathcal Y}})={{\mathcal Z}}$ and that $f|{{\mathcal Y}}\colon\thinspace {{\mathcal Y}}\to{{\mathcal Z}}$ is a diffeomorphism.
<!-- end custom-28 -->
<!-- custom-29: body_md -->
{Straightening angles}\label{what's sta}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be an arbitrary  $n$--orbifold with nonsingular
$2$--corners. 
Set $M={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$, and let $K\subset M$ denote the set of all
$2$--corner points of ${{\mathcal M}}$. If we set $V\doteq M-\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}\supset K$, then
with the conventions of \S\ref{when it's a manifold}, $V={\Omega_{V}}$ is
an open
submanifold with corners of ${{\mathcal M}}$. On the other hand,
${{\mathcal W}}\doteq{\Omega_{M-K}}$ is an open suborbifold (with boundary) of
${{\mathcal M}}$.

Let $V'$ denote the manifold
(with boundary) obtained from $V$ 
by the standard operation of straightening the angles\ 
(see Douady and H\'erault's appendix to \cite{borel-serre}). 
Then $V'$ has the same underlying set as $V$, and the smooth manifold
structure of $V'$ --- which may in particular be regarded as a (smooth)
orbifold structure --- agrees with the orbifold structure of 
${{\mathcal W}}$ on
the open subset $(M-K)\cap V$ of $M$. Hence there is a unique 
orbifold structure on $M$ which restricts to the orbifold-with-corners
structure of ${{\mathcal W}}$ 
and to the smooth manifold structure of $V'$. The
resulting orbifold (with boundary)
will be said to be  \emph{obtained from ${{\mathcal M}}$ by straightening the angles.}
<!-- end custom-29 -->
<!-- custom-30: body_md -->
{Strata}[\rm{cf.\ Choi~\cite[Section 4.5]{Choi:Orbifolds}}]
\label{strata def}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be an 
orbifold with corners. 
For each
positive integer 
$p$, let $Z_p({{\mathcal M}})$ denote the subset of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ consisting of
all points whose order is $p$. 
We define a  \emph{stratum} of ${{\mathcal M}}$ to be a
subset of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ which is a connected component of $Z_p$ for some $p >
0$.  


It follows from this definition that the strata of ${{\mathcal M}}$ form a
partition of $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$.

 Let $( U , D, \Phi, G)$ be any standard chart
  centered at an arbitrary 
point $x\in{{\mathcal M}}$. Thus for some $j\le n$ we have
$D=(\mathop{\rm int} {\mathbb B}^n) \cap ({\mathbb R}^{n-j}\times{\mathbb R}_+^j)$ and $G\le{\rm O}(n-j)\times{\mathscr S}_j$.
For each subgroup $H$ of
  $G$, let $R_H\subsetD$ denote the set of all points whose
  stabilizer in $G$ is precisely $H$.
Thus if 
$W_L\subset {\mathbb R}^{n-j}\times{\mathbb R}_+^j$  denotes the fixed set
of a subgroup
$L$ of $G$---which is the intersection of ${\mathbb R}^{n-j}\times{\mathbb R}_+^j$ with
a linear subspace of ${\mathbb R}^n$---we have 
\begin{equation}\label{what RH looks like}
R_H=D\cap \Big( W_H-\bigcup_{H< L\le G}W_L \Big).
\end{equation}

If $y$ is any point of $D$, and we set $H={\rm Stab}_G(y)$ and $p=|H|$, 
then $y$ has a neighborhood $V\subset D$
such that ${\rm Stab}_G(z) \leq H$ for every $z\in V$. Hence for any $z\in
V$, we have $| {\rm Stab}_G(z) | =p$ if and only if ${\rm Stab}_G(z)=H$. This means
that 
\begin{equation}\label{why was six}
V\cap\Phi^{-1}(Z_p)=V\cap R_H.
\end{equation}
 It follows 
 from \ref{why was six} 
that:

\begin{claim}\label{was six}
A subset of $D$ is a component of $R_H$ for some $H\le G$
if and only if it is a component of $\Phi^{-1}(\sigma)$ for some
  stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$.
Hence a subset of $U$ is a component of $\Phi(R_H)$ for some $H\le G$
if and only if it is a component of $U\cap\sigma$ for some
  stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$.
\end{claim}

It follows from \ref{was six} and the definition of the sets $R_H$
that for any stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$, all points of
$\Phi^{-1}(\sigma)$ have the same stabilizer in $G$. As this holds for
 every standard chart $( U , D, \Phi, G)$  for ${{\mathcal M}}$, we deduce:
\begin{claim}\label{was three}
For any stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$, the local groups of all points of
$\sigma$, regarded as subgroups of ${\rm O}(n)$, all coincide up to
conjugacy. Thus $\sigma$ has a  \emph{local group} which is a subgroup
of ${\rm O}(n)$, well-defined up to conjugacy. It will be denoted by $G_\sigma$.
\end{claim}

Again considering an arbitrary  stratum  $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$ and an arbitrary standard chart
$( U , D, \Phi, G)$, 
observe that \eqref{what RH looks like} implies that for each
subgroup $H$ of $G$, the set $R_H$ is a manifold with corners, and
that for any $k\le n$, the set of $k$--corner points of $R_H$ is the
intersection of $R_H$ with the set of $k$--corner points of $D$. 
Note that $H$ is the largest subgroup of $G$ that acts trivially on $R_H$.
Hence, if we set $E={\rm Stab}_G(R_H)$, 
then
$H$ is a normal subgroup of $E$, and the action of $E$ induces an
action of $E/H$ on $R_H$. This action is free (since ${\rm Stab}_G(y)=H$ for every 
$y\in R_H$), and thus the quotient is a manifold. 
This proves:

\begin{claim}\label{was too}
For each stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$, 
the weak
suborbifold ${\Omega_{\sigma}}$ of  ${{\mathcal M}}$
is defined, and
is a (smooth)
manifold
with corners. Thus according to the convention of 
\S\ref{when it's a manifold} 
we
may write $\sigma={\Omega_{\sigma}}$ and regard $\sigma$ as a
manifold
with corners. 
Furthermore, for each $k \leq n$, the set of $k$--corner points of $\sigma$ is the
intersection of $\sigma$ with the set of $k$--corner points of ${{\mathcal M}}$. 

In particular,  each stratum of
  ${{\mathcal M}}$ has a well-defined  \emph{dimension}. A stratum whose
  dimension is a given integer $d$ 
may be called a
  \emph{$d$--stratum}. 
\end{claim}

The proof of \ref{was too} shows that for 
any  stratum  $\sigma$, and any standard chart
$( U , D, \Phi, G)$ centered at a point of $\sigma$, we have
$\dim\sigma=\dim R_G$. In particular: 
\begin{claim}\label{was four}
A stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$ has dimension $n$ if and only if
  $G_\sigma=\{1\}$. 
Hence
 $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ is the union of all
  strata of ${{\mathcal M}}$ having dimension strictly less than $n$.
These will be called \emph{singular strata}.
\end{claim}


Finally, we observe, as a consequence of \eqref{what RH looks like}, that 
for 
{\color{green}any  stratum  $\sigma$, and} any standard chart
$( U , D, \Phi, G)$, the collection of all components of the sets 
$R_H$ with $H \le G$ is
finite; and that for each set $J$ in this collection, $\overline{J}-J$
  is a union of sets in the collection having lower dimension than
  $J$. Hence:
\begin{claim}\label{missing piece}
The set of all strata of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is locally finite, and for each
stratum $\sigma$, the set $\overline{\sigma}-\sigma$
  is a union of strata having lower dimension than
  $\sigma$.
\end{claim}
<!-- end custom-30 -->

<!-- custom-31: body_md -->
{Orbifold fundamental groups}
\label{path subsection}
The treatment of orbifold fundamental groups in this subsection is
inspired by the material in Boileau, Maillot, and Porti~\cite[Section
2.2]{BoileauMaillotPorti}. However, we have had to reorganize the
material here, and coordinate it with the material in \S\S\ref{maps and such} and \ref{maps continued}, in order to guarantee
functoriality of the orbifold fundamental group, which is used strongly
in the later sections of this paper.


The unit interval $I$ is a $1$--manifold, and in particular a
$1$--orbifold. We define an  \emph{orbifold path} in an orbifold with
corners ${{\mathcal M}}$ to be a continuous orbifold map (see \S\ref{maps and such}) from
$I$ to ${{\mathcal M}}$. The underlying map of an orbifold path $\alpha$ is a
path $A$ in the topological space ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$; the initial and
terminal points of $A$ will be called the initial and
terminal points of $\alpha$. The  \emph{image} of the orbifold path
$\alpha$ is defined to be $A(I)$.

We emphasize that in general an orbifold path is not uniquely
determined by its underlying map. Indeed, Example~\ref{UnderlyingMapNotEnough}
 can easily be adapted to illustrate this.



Suppose that $\alpha$ and  $\beta$ are orbifold paths in ${{\mathcal M}}$, that
the terminal point of $\alpha$ is a nonsingular point $c\in{{\mathcal M}}$,
and that $c$ is the initial point of $\beta$. Let $u$ and $v$ denote
the unique orbifold self-maps of $I$ whose underlying maps are given
by $t\mapsto t/2$ and $t\mapsto (t+1)/2$ respectively. Then there is a
unique orbifold path $\alpha\cdot\beta$ in ${{\mathcal M}}$,
called the  \emph{concatenation} of $\alpha$ and $\beta$,
 such that
$(\alpha\cdot\beta)\circ u=\alpha$ and $(\alpha\cdot\beta)\circ
v=\beta$ (where composition of orbifold maps is defined as in
\S\ref{maps continued}). 
The uniqueness assertion depends on the assumption that $c$ is
nonsingular.

An  \emph{orbifold homotopy} between orbifold paths $\alpha_0$ and
$\alpha_1$ in ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a continuous orbifold map $h\colon\thinspace I\times
I\to{{\mathcal M}}$ such that $h\circ q_i=\alpha_i$ for $i=0,1$, and $h\circ
r_i$ is a constant orbifold path for $i=0,1$, where $q_i,r_i\colon\thinspace I\to
I\times I$ are the orbifold maps whose underlying maps are given
respectively by $q_i(t)=(t,i)$ and $r_i(t)=(i,t)$.

If $h$ is an orbifold homotopy between orbifold paths $\alpha$ and
$\alpha'$, and $h'$ is an orbifold
 homotopy between $\alpha'$ and another orbifold path $\alpha''$, then
 there exists an orbifold homotopy $H$ between $\alpha$ and
 $\alpha''$ such that the equalities of orbifold maps $H\circ ({\rm id}\times u)=h$ and $H\circ ({\rm id}\times
 v)=h'$ hold, where $u$ and $v$ are the maps defined above. (The
 homotopy $H$ is not in general unique, although its underlying map is
 determined by those of $h$ and $h'$. The construction of the maximal
 atlas of local lifts defining $H$ requires a little care.) This shows
 that homotopy of orbifold paths is an equivalence relation.

Suppose an orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$ is equipped with a nonsingular basepoint
$\star$. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are orbifold loops based at $\star$,
i.e.\ orbifold paths having $\star$ as both initial and terminal point,
the orbifold homotopy class of $\alpha\cdot\beta$ depends only on those of
$\alpha$ and $\beta$. Thus the set 
$\pi_1({{\mathcal M}}, \star)$ of all orbifold homotopy classes of orbifold loops based at
$\star$ inherits a binary operation. With respect to this operation, $
\pi_1({{\mathcal M}},\star)$ is a group. 

Now suppose that $f$ is a continuous orbifold map from an orbifold
with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$ to an orbifold
with corners  ${{\mathcal M}}'$.
Then for any orbifold path $\alpha$ in
${{\mathcal M}}$, 
the composition of orbifold maps
$f\circ\alpha$ is  an orbifold path in
${{\mathcal M}}'$.  Furthermore, if $h$ is an orbifold homotopy between orbifold paths
$\alpha$ and $\alpha'$ in ${{\mathcal M}}$, then $f\circ h$ is a homotopy
between $f\circ\alpha$ and $f\circ\alpha'$. Using these observations
and the definition of the group operation in the orbifold fundamental
group, one deduces that if ${{\mathcal M}}$ and ${{\mathcal M}}'$ are equipped with nonsingular basepoints
$\star$ and $\star'$, and if $f$
carries $\star$ to $\star'$, then $f$ induces a homomorphism
$f_* \colon\thinspace\pi_1({{\mathcal M}},\star)\to \pi_1({{\mathcal M}}',\star')$. 
This makes
$\pi_1$ a functor from the category of orbifolds with corners,
equipped with nonsingular basepoints (and with continuous basepoint-preserving orbifold
maps as morphisms), to the category of groups.

If an orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$ is connected, then for any two points $x,y\in{{\mathcal M}}$ there
is a path with initial point $x$ and terminal point $y$. If $\alpha$
is any such orbifold path, there is a well-defined isomorphism from
$\pi_1({{\mathcal M}},x)$ to $\pi_1({{\mathcal M}},y)$ given by
$[\gamma] \mapsto [\overline{\alpha}\cdot\gamma\cdot\alpha]$. From this one
deduces that if $f\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal M}}\to{{\mathcal M}}'$ is an 
orbifold map between connected orbifolds with corners, replacing one
consistent pair of nonsingular basepoints for ${{\mathcal M}}$ and ${{\mathcal M}}'$ by another has
the effect of precomposing and postcomposing $f_*$ by group
isomorphisms. In particular, it makes sense to say that 
$f_*\colon\thinspace\pi_1({{\mathcal M}})\to \pi_1({{\mathcal M}}')$ is injective, or
surjective, without specifying basepoints.

These observations apply when ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a connected suborbifold with corners of a connected orbifold
with corners
${{\mathcal M}}'$ and $f$ is the inclusion map. We shall say that
${{\mathcal M}}$
is \emph{$\pi_1$--injective} in ${{\mathcal M}}'$ if the inclusion homomorphism 
$f_* \colon\thinspace\pi_1({{\mathcal M}})\to \pi_1({{\mathcal M}}')$ is injective. 
An arbitrary suborbifold ${{\mathcal Y}}$ of an arbitrary orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}$ will
be termed \emph{$\pi_1$--injective} in ${{\mathcal M}}$ if each component of
${{\mathcal Y}}$ is $\pi_1$--injective in the component of ${{\mathcal M}}$ containing it.


An orbifold path $\alpha$ in an orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal M}}$ will be
termed  \emph{generic} if $\alpha^{-1}(\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}})$ is a finite subset
  of $(0,1)\subset[0,1]$. The following fact is crucial in relating
  orbifold fundamental groups to orbifold covering spaces:

\begin{claim}\label{crucial fact}
Suppose that $f\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal M}}'\to{{\mathcal M}}$ is an orbifold covering, and that
$\alpha$ is a generic orbifold path in ${{\mathcal M}}$. Let $\star$ denote the
initial point of $\alpha$, and let $\star'$ be a 
point of $f^{-1}(\star) \subset {{\mathcal M}}'$.
Then there is a unique orbifold
path $\alpha'$ in ${{\mathcal M}}'$ which is a lift of $\alpha$ (in the sense
that $f\circ\alpha'=\alpha$) and has initial point $\star'$.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{crucial fact}, one writes $\alpha$ as a concatenation of orbifold
paths $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m$ where each $\alpha_k$ has
nonsingular  initial and terminal points $i_k$ and $t_k$; we have
$i_{k+1}=t_k$ whenever $1\le k<m$,  and the  image of each $\alpha_k$
is contained in  the support of an
evenly covered chart $( U_k ,
{\widetilde U}_k , \Phi_k, G_k)$. If $F$ denotes the underlying map of $f$,
and $U_1'$ denotes the component of $F^{-1}(U_1)$ containing $\star'$, it follows from the definitions that
$\alpha_1$ admits a lift to ${{\mathcal M}}'$ whose image is contained in
$U_1'$, and that $G_1$ acts transitively on all such lifts. Since
$\star$ is nonsingular, there is a unique lift $\alpha_1'$ of $\alpha_1$ to
${{\mathcal M}}'$ having initial point $\star'$. The same argument shows that
if $1\le k<m$, and if $\alpha_k'$ is a lift of $\alpha_k$, there is a
unique lift of $\alpha_{k+1}$ whose initial point is the terminal point
of $\alpha_k'$. Now \ref{crucial fact} follows by induction.


The usefulness of \ref{crucial fact} arises from the following fact,
which 
in turn follows from Assertions \ref{was six} and \ref{what RH looks like} in the discussion of strata:


\begin{claim}\label{homotop to generic}
Any path in an orbifold with corners, whose initial and terminal
points are nonsingular, is homotopic to a generic path.
\end{claim}

The following fact is easier to verify than \ref{crucial fact},
because there is no uniqueness assertion, and the step involving the
group action is therefore not needed:

\begin{claim}\label{lifting homotopies}
Suppose that $f\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal M}}'\to{{\mathcal M}}$ is an orbifold covering, and that $h$
is an orbifold homotopy between orbifold paths $\alpha_0$ and
$\alpha_1$ in ${{\mathcal M}}$. If $\alpha_0'$ is a lift of $\alpha_0$ to
${{\mathcal M}}'$, then $h$ admits a lift which is a homotopy from $\alpha_0'$
to some lift of $\alpha_1$.
\end{claim}



Using \ref{crucial fact}, \ref{homotop to generic}, and \ref{lifting homotopies}, it is now quite straightforward to establish the
direct generalization of the familiar facts relating
manifold covers and fundamental groups to the context of orbifold covers of connected orbifolds with
corners, equipped with nonsingular basepoints. These include the lifting criterion (for a
basepoint-preserving map between orbifolds with corners equipped with nonsingular
basepoints) and the correspondence between connected covers of an orbifold with
corners and subgroups of its fundamental group. In particular, ${{\mathcal M}}$ has a universal cover ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ 
that is simply connected, and there is an isomorphism
between the orbifold fundamental group $\pi_1({{\mathcal M}})$ and the deck group of  ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}} $. Compare \cite[Theorems 2.1 and 2.2]{BoileauMaillotPorti}.
<!-- end custom-31 -->

<!-- custom-32: body_md -->
{Size and weight of a subset}
\label{size 'n' stuff}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be an orbifold
with corners, 
and let $Z$ be a subset of
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$. We define the  \emph{size} of $Z$, denoted
 $\mathop{\rm size}(Z)$, to be $\mathop{{\rm card}}(Z\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}})$; note that $\mathop{\rm size}(Z)$ may
 be an infinite or a finite cardinal. In the case where 
$\mathop{\rm size}(Z)$ is
 finite,  we define the  \emph{weight} of $Z$, denoted $\mathop{{\rm weight}}(Z)$,
 to be 
$\sum_{x\in Z\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}}\mathop{\rm ord}(x)$.
<!-- end custom-32 -->
<!-- custom-33: body_md -->
{Orbifolds of dimension $1$}
\label{folded}
Any compact, connected $1$--orbifold is either a manifold
diffeomorphic to ${\mathbb S}^1$ or $I$, or is diffeomorphic to the quotient of
${\mathbb S}^1$ or $I$ by a reflection $\tau$. The orbifold ${\mathbb S}^1/\tau$ has one
$1$--stratum and two $0$--strata, whereas $I/\tau$ has one
$1$--stratum and one $0$--stratum. We shall refer to an orbifold
diffeomorphic to $I/\tau$ as a \emph{folded arc.}
<!-- end custom-33 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{Prop:LocalStructure2Orbifold}
For any stratum  $\sigma$  of  a $2$--orbifold  ${{\mathcal S}}$,
exactly one of the following alternatives holds.
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:$(1)$]
\item  
$\sigma\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal S}}=\emptyset$ (so that $\dim\sigma=2$ and
  $G_\sigma=\{1\}$ by 
Assertion \ref{was four}).
In this case, for any
  standard neighborhood ${{\mathcal U}}$
 of a point $x$ of $\sigma$, the set
  $U\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ is disjoint from $\Sigma_{{\mathcal S}}$. If
  $x\in\mathop{\rm int}{{\mathcal S}}$ then $U$ is an open $2$--disk. If
  $x\in\partial{{\mathcal S}}$ then $U$ is homeomorphic to an open half-ball in
${\mathbb R}\times{\mathbb R}_+$.
\item   $\sigma$ has dimension $0$ and is contained in $\mathop{\rm int}{{\mathcal S}}$, and $G_\sigma$ is a cyclic group of rotations
  of some order 
$p > 1$. 
Furthermore, $\sigma$ is a full component of
  $\Sigma_{{\mathcal S}}$, and if ${{\mathcal U}}$ is a standard neighborhood of the unique point $x$
  of $\sigma$ then ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ is 
homeomorphic to
an open disk.
In this case, $x$ is called a \emph{cone point} of
  order 
$p$. 
\item $\sigma$ has dimension $1$, and $G_\sigma $ is an order-two cyclic group
  generated  by a reflection. 
For every point $x$ of $\sigma$ and every standard neighborhood ${{\mathcal U}}$ 
  of $x$ in ${{\mathcal S}}$, the intersection of $U\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ with
  $\Sigma_{{\mathcal S}}$ is contained in $\sigma$. If $x\in\mathop{\rm int}{{\mathcal S}}$, there
  is a homeomorphism of $U$ onto an open half-ball in ${\mathbb R}\times{\mathbb R}_+$, mapping 
  $U\cap\sigma$ to the boundary of the half-ball.
If $x\in\partial{{\mathcal S}}$, there
  is a homeomorphism of $U$ onto 
an open quarter-ball 
  in ${\mathbb R}_+ \times {\mathbb R}_+$, mapping
  $x$,  $U\cap\sigma$ and $U\cap{{\rm X}_{\partial{{\mathcal S}}}}$ into
  $(0,0)$,
  ${\mathbb R}_+ \times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times{\mathbb R}_+$ respectively.
In this case, $\sigma$ is called a \emph{mirror
    stratum}, and its points are called \emph{mirror points}.
\item $\sigma$ has dimension $0$ and is contained in $\mathop{\rm int}{{\mathcal S}}$,
  and $G_\sigma$ is a dihedral group of order 
$2p$ for some $p > 1$,
  generated by reflections about two lines that meet at an angle of
  $\pi/p$. 
Furthermore, if ${{\mathcal U}}$ is a standard neighborhood of the
  unique point $x$ of $\sigma$, then $U\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ is 
homeomorphic to
an open quarter-ball 
in ${\mathbb R}_+ \times {\mathbb R}_+$, 
 with $x$ mapping to $(0,0)$, and 
 the two
  components of $\partial U-\{x\}$ mapping to intervals in 
   ${\mathbb R}_+ \times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times{\mathbb R}_+$ and contained in mirror strata.
    In this case,  $x$ is called a \emph{bi-mirror point} of order
$2p$.
\end{enumerate}


We shall denote by ${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal S}}}^{\rm mir}}\subset\Sigma_{{\mathcal S}}$  the union of all
mirror and bi-mirror strata of ${{\mathcal S}}$. It follows from the assertions
above that ${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal S}}}^{\rm mir}}$ may be described as the closure of
the union of  all mirror strata of ${{\mathcal S}}$, or as the
set of all points whose local group contains an orientation-reversing
element.  It also follows from the assertions above that ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal S}}}}$ is a topological
$2$--manifold, and that $\partial {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal S}}}}={{\rm X}_{\partial{{\mathcal S}}}}\cup
{\Sigma_{{{\mathcal S}}}^{\rm mir}}$. In particular, if ${{\mathcal S}}$ is orientable then  $\partial
{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal S}}}}={{\rm X}_{\partial{{\mathcal S}}}}$.
{\hfill$\square$}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- custom-34: body_md -->
{Reflective\ coverings}
\label{reflective}
Let ${{\mathcal S}}$ be a $2$--orbifold, set $S={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal S}}}}$, and let ${\widetilde S}$
denote the topological $2$--manifold obtained by doubling $S$ along the
$1$--manifold $\mu\doteq{\Sigma_{{{\mathcal S}}}^{\rm mir}}\subset\partial S$. Thus ${\widetilde S}$ is a union of
two topological submanifolds $S_0$ and $S_1$, where each $S_i$ is equipped
with a canonical homeomorphism $h_i$ onto $S$. The $h_i$ agree on
$R\doteq S_0\cap S_1$, and map $R$ homeomorphically onto $\mu$. Let
$F\colon\thinspace{\widetilde S}\to S$ denote the map such that $F|S_i=h_i$ for
$i=0,1$. Then there 
exist a unique $2$--orbifold ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}$ and a unique two-sheeted orbifold covering
map $f\colon\thinspace{\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}\to{{\mathcal S}}$ such that
${{\rm X}_{{\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}}}={\widetilde S}$ and  $F$ is the underlying map of $f$. 
We shall call ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}$ the {\it
  reflective\ covering} of ${{\mathcal S}}$. 

We have $R\doteq S_0\cap S_1=F^{-1}({\Sigma_{{{\mathcal S}}}^{\rm mir}})$, 
and the underlying map of 
the non-trivial deck transformation of ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}$
interchanges $S_0$ and $S_1$.

We have
