${\Sigma_{{\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}}^{\rm mir}}=\emptyset$, and the singular points of ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}$ are as follows. For any order--$p$ cone point $x \in {{\mathcal S}}$, the preimage $f^{-1}(x)$ consists of two order--$p$ cone points, namely $h_0^{-1}(x)$ and $h_1^{-1}(x)$. For any  order--$2p$ bi-mirror point  $x \in {{\mathcal S}}$, the preimage $f^{-1}(x)$ is a single order--$p$ cone point, namely ${\widetilde x} = h_0^{-1}(x) = h_1^{-1}(x) \in R$. 
If
$( U , D, \Phi, G)$ is a standard chart  for
${\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}$ centered at ${\widetilde x}$, then $\Phi^{-1}(R)$ is a union of $p$
diameters of the open disk $D$. Thus $R$ is  \emph{not} in general the
underlying set of a suborbifold of ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}$. Likewise, $S_0$ and $S_1$
are not in general the
underlying sets of  suborbifolds of ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}$. 

For any small enough neighborhood $U$ of ${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal S}}}^{\rm mir}}$ in $S$, if we
set ${{\mathcal U}}={\Omega_{U}}$ and ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}=f^{-1}({{\mathcal U}})$, the covering
$f|{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\colon\thinspace{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\to{{\mathcal U}}$ is equivalent to the (orbifold)
orientation cover of ${{\mathcal U}}$. However, the reflective\ covering of
${{\mathcal S}}$ is not in general equivalent to its orientation covering. For
example, if ${{\mathcal S}}$ is a non-orientable closed $2$--manifold, regarded as a closed
$2$--orbifold with empty singular set, the orbifold orientation cover
of ${{\mathcal S}}$ coincides with its usual manifold orientation cover, but its
reflective\ cover is a disjoint union of two trivial covers.
<!-- end custom-34 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{Prop:LocalStructure3Orbifold}
If ${{\mathcal M}}$ is  an orientable $3$--orbifold with nonsingular
$2$--corners, then
for any stratum  $\sigma$  of   ${{\mathcal M}}$,
exactly one of the following alternatives holds.

\begin{enumerate}[\:\:$(1)$]
\item \label{ThreeOrbNonsing}
$\sigma\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}=\emptyset$ (so that $\dim\sigma=3$ and
  $G_\sigma=\{1\}$ by 
Assertion \ref{was four}).
In this case, for any
  standard neighborhood ${{\mathcal U}} $ of a point $x$ of $\sigma$, the set
  $U\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal U}}}} $ is disjoint from $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$. If
  $x\in\mathop{\rm int}{{\mathcal M}}$ then $U$ is an open $3$--ball. If
  $x\in\partial{{\mathcal M}}$ then $U$ is homeomorphic to  
an open half-ball in
  ${\mathbb R}^2 \times {\mathbb R}_+$, 
with $x\in\partial U$.
 \item \label{ThreeOrbCone}
  $\sigma$ has dimension $1$, and $G_\sigma$ is a cyclic group of rotations
  of some order $p > 1$. 
Furthermore, 
if ${{\mathcal U}} $ is a standard neighborhood of a point $x$ of $\sigma$, then 
there is a homeomorphism $j$ from $U\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal U}}}} $ to 
an open ball in ${\mathbb R}^3$ (if $x\in\mathop{\rm int}{{\mathcal M}}$) or to
an open half-ball in ${\mathbb R}^2 \times {\mathbb R}_+$ (if $x\in\partial{{\mathcal M}}$).
In the respective cases, $j(U\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}} )$ is an  axis of the
ball or the  axis of the half-ball.


\item \label{ThreeOrbNode}
$\sigma$ has dimension $0$ and is contained in $\mathop{\rm int}{{\mathcal M}}$, 
 and $G_\sigma$ is a spherical triangle group, given by a presentation
$$\langle \xi,\eta:\xi^{p_1}=\eta^{p_2}=(\xi\eta)^{p_3}=1\rangle$$
for some integers 
$p_1,p_2,p_3$
satisfying $1<p_1\le p_2\le p_3$ and $1/p_1+1/p_2+1/p_3>1$. 
Furthermore, 
if ${{\mathcal U}}$ is a standard neighborhood of the
unique point $x$ of $\sigma$, then 
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal U}}}}\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ has the form
  $\{x\}\cup\tau_1\cup\tau_2\cup\tau_3$, where for $i=1,2, 3$ the set $\tau_i$ is a component of
  the intersection of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ with a $1$--dimensional stratum of order 
$p_i$; and there is a homeomorphism
 of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ onto an open ball $E\subset{\mathbb R}^3$ which
carries $x$ to the center $c$ of $E$, and carries each $\tau_i$ onto
$\rho_i-\{c\}$ for some radius $\rho_i$ of $E$. 

\end{enumerate}

In particular it follows that $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ is an orientable topological
$3$--manifold and
that $\partial {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}={{\rm X}_{\partial{{\mathcal M}}}}$.
Furthermore,
every stratum of
${{\mathcal M}}$ has dimension $0$, $1$ or $3$, and $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ is homeomorphic to a $1$--complex.
{\hfill$\square$}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- custom-35: body_md -->
{Cone strata and nodes}
\label{what's a node}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be an  orientable $3$--orbifold with nonsingular $2$--corners,
and let $\sigma$ be a singular  stratum of
    ${{\mathcal M}}$.
If Alternative \eqref{ThreeOrbCone} 
of the conclusion  of
    Proposition \ref{Prop:LocalStructure3Orbifold} holds, 
we shall call $\sigma$ a  \emph{cone stratum
  of order 
$p$}, where $p$ is the integer given by \eqref{ThreeOrbCone}. When Alternative \eqref{ThreeOrbNode}
holds, we call the unique point of $\sigma$ a  \emph{node of type
  $(p_1,p_2,p_3)$}, where   $(p_1,p_2,p_3)$ 
is the triple given by \eqref{ThreeOrbNode}. 

We define a   \emph{dihedral
  node} of ${{\mathcal M}}$ to be a node of type 
$(2,2,p)$ for some $p \geq 2$.

Now, suppose that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is compact, and that  $\tau$ is a $1$--stratum of $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, equipped with an orientation. If there is a continuous map 
$\alpha\colon\thinspace [0,1]\to{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ 
which restricts to
an orientation-preserving 
diffeomorphism of $(0,1)$ onto
the $1$--manifold $\tau\cap{{\rm X}_{\mathop{\rm int}{{\mathcal M}}}} $, 
such that $\alpha(1)$ is a
node, then $\alpha(1)$ is called a \emph{terminal node} of $\tau$. 
Note that an oriented $1$--stratum can have at most one terminal node.
Note also that $\alpha(0)$ may be the same node, a different node, or a $1$--corner point of ${{\mathcal M}}$.

For each node
$x$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$, there are exactly three oriented $1$--strata of
${{\mathcal M}}$ having $x$ as their terminal nodes. The orders of these
oriented $1$--strata are 
$p_1$, $p_2$ and $p_3$, where $(p_1,p_2,p_3)$
is the type of $x$. It may happen that two of these oriented strata
are defined by distinct orientations of the same underlying stratum.
<!-- end custom-35 -->
<!-- custom-36: body_md -->
{Orbifold Euler characteristic}\label{Euler}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a compact $n$--orbifold with 
$n\le2$, or a compact, orientable $3$--orbifold with nonsingular
$2$--corners. According to Assertion \ref{missing piece}, since ${{\mathcal M}}$ is
compact it has only finitely many strata; and for each stratum
$\sigma$, the set $\overline{\sigma}-\sigma$ is a union of strata. 
It then follows that $M$ admits a PL
structure with the property that the closure of each stratum 
of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a PL subset. (See \S\ref{folded} when
$n=1$; Proposition \ref{Prop:LocalStructure2Orbifold} and the
triangulation theorem for $2$--manifolds~\cite[Theorem 4.1]{Thomassen:Jordan-curve} when $n=2$; and
Proposition \ref{Prop:LocalStructure3Orbifold} and
the triangulation theorem for $3$--manifolds~\cite[Theorem 8.1]{moise-tame}
when $n=3$.)
Hence for each stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$, the sets
$\overline{\sigma}$ and
$\overline{\sigma}-\sigma$ are compact PL spaces and therefore have
well-defined Euler characteristics. We define the  \emph{Euler
  characteristic of ${{\mathcal M}}$} 
  to be
\begin{equation}\label{that's what chi is}
\chi({{\mathcal M}})=\sum_\sigma\frac{ \chi(\overline \sigma) - \chi(
\overline{\sigma}-\sigma)}{ \mathop{\rm ord}(\sigma)},
\end{equation}
where $\sigma$ ranges over the strata of ${{\mathcal M}}$.

In the special case where ${{\mathcal S}}$ is a compact, orientable $2$--orbifold, 
the only singular points are (isolated) cone points, and \eqref{that's what chi is} immediately implies 
 the well-known formula
\begin{equation}\label{hurwitz}
\chi({{\mathcal S}})=\chi({{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal S}}}} )-
\sum_{x\in\Sigma_{{\mathcal S}}}\bigg(1-\frac1{\mathop{\rm ord}(x)}\bigg).
\end{equation}

Under the general hypotheses of this subsection, 
it follows from the observations made above that $M \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ admits a triangulation in
which $\overline{\sigma}$ and $\overline{\sigma}-\sigma$ are subcomplexes for each
stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$. 
Now, definition \eqref{that's what chi is} implies
 that for such a triangulation we have 
\begin{equation}\label{in terms of simplices}
\chi({{\mathcal M}})=\sum_\tau (-1)^{\dim\tau}\frac{1}{\mathop{\rm ord}(\tau)},
\end{equation}
where $\tau$ ranges over the open simplices of $M$, and
$\mathop{\rm ord}(\tau)$ denotes the order of the stratum containing $\tau$. In
particular 
 the right hand side of \eqref{in terms of simplices} is independent of the choice of a triangulation of
$M$ with the stated properties. Compare \cite[Definition on p.~39]{BoileauMaillotPorti} and \cite[Section 2.4]{CHK:OrbifoldBook}.






From the formula \eqref{in terms of simplices} it follows readily that 
if ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ is an $n$--sheeted
covering  of
 ${{\mathcal M}}$, where $n<\infty$, then
$\chi({\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}})=n\chi({{\mathcal M}})$. The same formula implies that if ${{\mathcal Y}}$ and ${{\mathcal Z}}$ are
compact suborbifolds with corners  of ${{\mathcal M}}$
 such that
${{\mathcal Y}}\cap {{\mathcal Z}}$ and ${{\mathcal Y}}\cup {{\mathcal Z}}$ 
are defined (see \S\ref{more orbifold notions}), 
then $\chi({{\mathcal Y}}\cup{{\mathcal Z}})=\chi({{\mathcal Y}})+\chi({{\mathcal Z}})-\chi({{\mathcal Y}}\cap{{\mathcal Z}})$.
<!-- end custom-36 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
It can  be shown
that if the dimension and orientability assumptions are removed from the discussion in
\S\ref{Euler}, then for each stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$, 
the sets
$\overline{\sigma}$ and
$\overline{\sigma}-\sigma$ are compact locally triangulable PL spaces.
Shmuel Weinberger has pointed out to us that, as a consequence of the results of \cite{hanner} and \cite{west}, 
such spaces are homotopy-equivalent to compact CW complexes, and therefore
have
well-defined Euler characteristics. Furthermore, if $\chi({{\mathcal M}})$ is defined
by \eqref{that's what chi is}, then the assertions in \S\ref{Euler}
involving finite coverings, unions and intersections still hold. As
we will not need these results, we omit the proofs.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{very good near cone stratum}
Let $\sigma$ be a cone stratum in an orientable $3$--orbifold
${{\mathcal M}}$. Then $\sigma$ has an open neighborhood ${{\mathcal W}}$ in ${{\mathcal M}}$ 
that
is very good. In fact,
${{\mathcal W}}$ has a degree-$\mathop{\rm ord}(\sigma)$ regular covering ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal W}}}}$ which is
a $3$--manifold, and the covering projection $\phi\colon\thinspace{\widetilde{{{\mathcal W}}}}\to{{\mathcal W}}$ maps
$\phi^{-1}(\sigma)$ diffeomorphically onto $\sigma$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
It follows from Proposition \ref{Prop:LocalStructure3Orbifold} that
$\sigma$ is a locally flat 
one-dimensional 
topological
submanifold of the topological manifold
$M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$. Therefore, according to 
\cite[Theorem 8.1]{moise-tame},
there is a PL structure on $M$ in which $\sigma$ is a PL
submanifold. Hence, by orientability, there is an open neighborhood $W$ 
of $\sigma$ in $M$, with $W\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}=\sigma$, such that the topological pair $(W,\sigma)$ is
homeomorphic to $(\sigma\times \mathop{\rm int} {\mathbb B}^2, \sigma\times\{0\})$. In
particular, 
if we fix a transverse orientation of $\sigma$, then
each closed curve $\gamma$ in $W-\sigma$ has a well-defined winding
number
about $\sigma$, which we will denote by 
$d(\gamma)\in{\mathbb Z}$. 


If $U$ is the support of a standard chart centered at a point
of $\sigma$, and $U\subset W$, then by the definition of a cone
stratum, $U\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}=U\cap\sigma$ 
is an unknotted open arc in the open ball $U$; hence 
for any closed curve $\gamma$ in $U-(U\cap\sigma)$, the winding number
of $\gamma$ about $U\cap\sigma$ is defined and is equal to
$d(\gamma)$. If $p$ denotes the order of the cone stratum $\sigma$,
and if $\overline{d}(\gamma)$ denotes the image of $d(\gamma)$ in ${\mathbb Z}/p{\mathbb Z}$
for an arbitrary  closed curve $\gamma$ in $W-\sigma$, we deduce:
\begin{claim}\label{I need this}
If $U\subset W$ is the support of a standard chart centered at a point
of $\sigma$, and $\gamma$ is a closed curve in $U-(U\cap\sigma)$, 
then $\gamma$ represents the identity in $\pi_1({\Omega_{U}})$ if and only if $\overline{d}(\gamma)=0$. 
\end{claim}
Now suppose that $\gamma$ is a closed curve in $W-\sigma$ which
represents the identity in the fundamental group of ${{\mathcal W}}\doteq{\Omega_{W}}$. Then the continuous
orbifold map $\gamma\colon\thinspace {\mathbb S}^1\to{{\mathcal W}}$ extends to a  continuous
orbifold map $\delta\colon\thinspace {\mathbb B}^2 \to{{\mathcal W}}$. We may choose $\delta$ so
that $\delta^{-1}(\sigma)$ is a finite set $\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$. If
$U_1,\ldots,U_m$ are pairwise disjoint supports of standard charts for
${{\mathcal M}}$ centered at $x_1,\ldots,x_m$, we may choose subdisks
$D_1,\ldots,D_m$ of ${\mathbb B}^2$ centered at the $x_i$ such that
$\delta(D_i)\subset U_i$; the restrictions of $\delta$ to 
$\partial D_1,\ldots,\partial D_m$ then define closed curves
$\gamma_i$ in the $U_i$, and each $\gamma_i$ represents the identity
in $\pi_1({\Omega_{U}}_i)$. In view of \ref{I need this} it now follows
that $\overline{d}(\gamma_i)=0$ for $i=1,\ldots,m$, and hence that
$\overline{d}(\gamma)=\sum_{i=1}^m\overline{d}(\gamma_i)=0$. This shows that 
for every closed curve $\gamma$ in $W-\sigma$ which
represents the identity in $\pi_1({{\mathcal W}})$, we have $\overline{d}(\gamma)=0$. From
this it follows that there is a well-defined homomorphism
$h\colon\thinspace\pi_1({{\mathcal W}})\to {\mathbb Z}/p{\mathbb Z}$ given by $h([\gamma])=\overline{d}(\gamma)$.
Let $\phi\colon\thinspace{\widetilde{{{\mathcal W}}}}\to{{\mathcal W}}$ denote the $p$--fold covering of ${{\mathcal W}}$ defined by the
subgroup $\ker h$ of $\pi_1({{\mathcal W}})$
(see \S\ref{path subsection}). 


If $U\subset W$ is the
support of a standard chart centered at a point of $\sigma$, 
another application  of \ref{I need this}  shows that 
the
composition of the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1({\Omega_{U}})\to\pi_1({{\mathcal W}})$ with $h \colon\thinspace \pi_1({{\mathcal W}})\to {\mathbb Z}/p{\mathbb Z}$ is an isomorphism. Hence
 the induced covering $\phi^{-1}({\Omega_{U}})$ of ${\Omega_{U}}$ is diffeomorphic to the
 universal cover of ${\Omega_{U}}$, which is a ball. As this holds for all
 choices of $U$, the $p$--fold cover ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal W}}}}$ of ${{\mathcal W}}$ is a manifold.
It follows from the construction that $\phi$ maps
$\phi^{-1}(\sigma)$ diffeomorphically onto $\sigma$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- claim-12: body_md -->
\label{I need this}
If $U\subset W$ is the support of a standard chart centered at a point
of $\sigma$, and $\gamma$ is a closed curve in $U-(U\cap\sigma)$, 
then $\gamma$ represents the identity in $\pi_1({\Omega_{U}})$ if and only if $\overline{d}(\gamma)=0$.
<!-- end claim-12 -->
<!-- custom-37: body_md -->
{${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant smooth structures}
\label{wuzzaccordant}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be 
an orientable $3$--orbifold, so that $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ is an
orientable topological $3$--manifold by Proposition \ref{Prop:LocalStructure3Orbifold}.
A smooth   $3$--manifold structure 
on $M$
 will be termed \emph{${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant} if it 
satisfies the following conditions: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item\label{Itm:Accord1} Each stratum of ${{\mathcal M}}$, with the smooth structure given by
Assertion 
\ref{was too},
is a submanifold of $M$.
\item\label{Itm:Accord2} If $\sigma$ is any cone stratum
of ${{\mathcal M}}$, and if $p=\mathop{\rm ord}(\sigma)$,  then there exist an open subset $U$
of  $M$ with $U\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}=\sigma$, 
such that the
self-map $(z,t)\mapsto(z^p,t)$ of ${\mathbb D}\times \sigma $ is the
composition of the 
underlying map of  
some orbifold covering map ${\mathbb D}\times \sigma \to {\Omega_{U}}$ with some manifold diffeomorphism $\zeta\colon\thinspace  U\to {\mathbb D}\times \sigma $. 

\end{enumerate}


We observe that if a smooth  structure on $M$ is ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant, then
in particular Condition \eqref{Itm:Accord1} above must hold for every  
codimension--$0$
stratum of ${{\mathcal M}}$. Hence the smooth manifold structure that
$M-\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ inherits from $M$ coincides with the smooth manifold
structure that ${\Omega_{M-\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}}}$ possesses as an open suborbifold
of ${{\mathcal M}}$.
<!-- end custom-37 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{smooth underlying}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be 
an orientable $3$--orbifold.
Then there exists an ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant smooth structure on the
topological $3$--manifold $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
We let ${{\mathcal M}}'\subset{{\mathcal M}}$ denote the complement of the set of
nodes in $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ 
(see \S\ref{what's a node}).
The orientability of ${{\mathcal M}}$ implies that the singular strata of
${{\mathcal M}}'$ are all one-dimensional.
For each singular stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}'$, Lemma
\ref{very good near cone stratum} gives
an open suborbifold ${{\mathcal W}}_\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}'$, 
{\color{green}with ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal W}}_\sigma}}=\sigma$,} and
a finite-sheeted regular cover
$\phi_\sigma\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal W}}}}_\sigma\to {{\mathcal W}}_\sigma$ with cyclic  deck
group $G_\sigma$ of order $p_\sigma\doteq\mathop{\rm ord}(\sigma)$, such that ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal W}}}}_\sigma$ is a
$3$--manifold, and  $\phi_\sigma$ maps $S_\sigma\doteq\phi_\sigma^{-1}(\sigma)$
diffeomorphically onto $\sigma$.
We may take
the ${{\mathcal W}}_\sigma$ to be pairwise disjoint as
$\sigma$ ranges over the cone strata of ${{\mathcal M}}'$. 
For each $\sigma$,
the (possibly non-compact) $1$--manifold $S_\sigma$ is then $G_\sigma$--invariant.
Fix a $G_\sigma$--invariant tubular neighborhood $V_\sigma$ of $S_\sigma$ in
${\widetilde{{{\mathcal W}}}}_\sigma$. 
Since $G_\sigma$ is cyclic of order $p_\sigma$ and
${{\mathcal W}}_\sigma\subset{{\mathcal M}}$ is orientable,
$V_\sigma$ may
be diffeomorphically identified with ${\mathbb D}\times S_\sigma$ in such a way that some generator of
$G_\sigma$ acts on $V_\sigma$ by $(z,s)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/p_\sigma}z,s)$. We may then
identify $\phi_\sigma(V_\sigma)$ homeomorphically with ${\mathbb D}\times S_\sigma$ in such a way
that $\phi_\sigma|V_\sigma$ is the map $(z,s)\mapsto(z^{p_\sigma},s)$. 
The standard smooth
structure on ${\mathbb D}$ and the smooth structure  on $S_\sigma$ inherited
from ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal W}}}}_\sigma$ define a smooth structure on the product
${\mathbb D}\times S_\sigma$, and therefore on  $\phi_\sigma(V_\sigma)$. 


On the other hand, the open suborbifold  ${{\mathcal M}}'-\Sigma_{{{\mathcal M}}'}=M'-\Sigma_{{{\mathcal M}}'}$ of ${{\mathcal M}}'$ is a
smooth manifold. 
For each singular stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal M}}'$, the smooth structure
of   ${{\mathcal M}}'-\Sigma_{{{\mathcal M}}'}$ agrees on $\phi_\sigma(V_\sigma)-\sigma$ with
the smooth structure that we have constructed on $\phi_\sigma(V_\sigma)$. 
Hence
there is a smooth structure on $M'$ that restricts to the smooth
structures that we have described on the sets $\phi_\sigma(V_\sigma)$ and on
$M'-\Sigma_{{{\mathcal M}}'}$. By Proposition \ref{extend},
this smooth
structure on $M'$ extends to one on $M$. It follows from the
construction that this smooth structure on $M$
is ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{not unique}
The ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant  smooth structure given by Proposition
\ref{smooth underlying} is not in general unique, and it is not clear
to us whether there is a canonical ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant  smooth
structure for a given  orientable $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}$. At
several points in this paper it will be necessary to make a choice of 
 ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant  smooth
structure; our final results are independent of these choices.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- custom-38: body_md -->
{Suborbifolds and transversality}
\label{Suborbifolds-of-3orbifolds}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be an orientable $3$--orbifold.
If $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ is  equipped with an
${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant 
smooth $3$--manifold structure, 
we shall  often refer to it 
as the  \emph{underlying manifold}
of ${{\mathcal M}}$.
In particular, it makes sense to  speak of smooth submanifolds
of $M$, and of transversality between such submanifolds. A
smooth submanifold of  $M$ will be said to be  \emph{transverse
  to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$} if it is transverse to all the strata of
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ (which are themselves smooth submanifolds of
$M$ by the definition of ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordance).



If $M$ is equipped with an ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant smooth structure,
and if $F$ is a neatly embedded submanifold
of $M$ of 
dimension at most $2$
which is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, then ${\Omega_{F}}$
is defined and is a neatly embedded suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$ (in the
strong sense). To verify this, we must check that Condition
\ref{defines a suborbifold} holds with $F$ playing the role of $N$,
and that the homomorphism $\theta_y$ defined in \S\ref{Suborbifolds} is
an isomorphism for every $y\in F$.   Condition \eqref{Itm:Accord1} of \S\ref{wuzzaccordant} 
implies that \ref{defines a suborbifold} holds when the given
point
$x\in M$ is nonsingular, and that $\theta_y$ is
an isomorphism when the point $y\in F$ is a nonsingular point of ${{\mathcal M}}$.
Condition \eqref{Itm:Accord2} of \S\ref{wuzzaccordant} 
implies that \ref{defines a suborbifold} holds when 
$x\in M$ lies in a cone stratum of ${{\mathcal M}}$, and that $\theta_y$  is
an isomorphism when $y\in F$ lies in a cone stratum. In view of
transversality, the case when
$y\in F$ is a node of ${{\mathcal M}}$ does not arise. Thus ${{\mathcal F}} \doteq {\Omega_{F}}$ is defined.

According to \S\ref{Suborbifolds}
we then have $\Sigma_{{{\mathcal F}}}=
F\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$. 
In particular, we have $\mathop{\rm size} F=\mathop{{\rm card}} \Sigma_{{{\mathcal F}}}$ 
(where $\mathop{\rm size} F$ is defined as in 
\S\ref{size 'n' stuff}, 
and is finite if $F$ is compact).
It also follows from \S\ref{Suborbifolds} that
$\mathop{\rm ord}^{{\mathcal F}}(x)=\mathop{\rm ord}^{{\mathcal M}}(x)$ for each $x\in F$; hence if $F$ is
compact
then $\mathop{{\rm weight}}(F)$ 
is the sum of the orders of the singular points of
${\Omega_{F}}$.


We will sometimes encounter the special case in which a  submanifold $F$ of
  $M$ is  \emph{disjoint} from $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$. 
In this case,
${\Omega_{F}}$ is a manifold having the same underlying set and the same
smooth manifold structure as the given submanifold  $F$ of
$ {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$. Thus the convention laid out in 
\S\ref{when it's a manifold},
according to which we write $F={\Omega_{F}}$, leads to no ambiguity.


The observation 
  made above about obtaining suborbifolds from submanifolds
  transverse to the singular set
has a partial converse: if ${{\mathcal M}}$  is an orientable $3$--orbifold, then every orientable, neatly\  embedded
 $2$--suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$
has the form ${\Omega_{F}}$ for some orientable, neatly\  embedded
two-dimensional submanifold $F$ of $ {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$. (This becomes false
if one removes the hypothesis of orientability. For example, if $\rho$
is a $\pi$--rotation of ${\mathbb S}^3$ and $C$ denotes the fixed circle
of $\rho$, then for any $2$--sphere $Y\supset C$ the suborbifold
${{\mathcal N}}\doteq Y/\langle\rho\rangle$ of ${{\mathcal M}}\doteq
{\mathbb S}^3/\langle\rho\rangle$ is defined, but  ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ contains $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ rather than being transverse to  $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$.)
<!-- end custom-38 -->
<!-- custom-39: body_md -->
{Splitting an orbifold}
\label{new splitting}

There is a notion of splitting an orbifold along a suitable
type of suborbifold, which generalizes the familiar notion of
splitting a manifold along a neatly\  embedded codimension-$1$ submanifold.

Suppose that ${{\mathcal S}}$ is a neatly\  embedded, $(n-1)$--dimensional
suborbifold of an  $n$--orbifold (with boundary) ${{\mathcal M}}$. 
We shall
say that an $n$--orbifold with $2$--corners ${{\mathcal M}}'$ is  \emph{obtained by splitting ${{\mathcal M}}$
  along ${{\mathcal S}}$,} and that an orbifold immersion
$\iota\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal M}}'\to{{\mathcal M}}$ is  \emph{associated with the splitting,} if 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\iota|\iota^{-1}({{\mathcal M}}-{{\mathcal S}})\colon\thinspace \iota^{-1}({{\mathcal M}}-{{\mathcal S}})
\to ({{\mathcal M}}-{{\mathcal S}})$ is an orbifold
  diffeomorphism, and
\item for every $x\in{{\mathcal S}}$ there is a connected open neighborhood
  ${{\mathcal V}}$ of $x$ in ${{\mathcal M}}$ such that $\iota^{-1}({{\mathcal V}})$ has exactly
  two components, and $\iota$ maps each of these components
  diffeomorphically onto the closure, relative to ${{\mathcal V}}$, of a component
  of ${{\mathcal V}}\cap({{\mathcal M}}-{{\mathcal S}})$.
\end{enumerate}


If ${{\mathcal M}}'_1$ and ${{\mathcal M}}'_2$ are two orbifolds with $2$--corners  obtained by splitting
${{\mathcal M}}$ along ${{\mathcal S}}$, and if $\iota_1$ and $\iota_2$ are the
associated immersions, one can deduce directly from the definition of
splitting that there is a unique diffeomorphism $\alpha\colon\thinspace
{{\mathcal M}}'_1\to{{\mathcal M}}'_2$ such that $\iota_2\circ\alpha=\iota_1$. In view
of this uniqueness property of an orbifold with $2$--corners obtained
by splitting, we shall refer to  \emph{the} orbifold obtained by splitting
${{\mathcal M}}$ along ${{\mathcal S}}$ if such an orbifold exists, and denote it by
${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal S}}$. To say that ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal S}}$ is defined means
that such a split orbifold exists. We shall refer to the associated
immersion as the  \emph{canonical immersion} $\iota\colon\thinspace
{{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal S}}\to {{\mathcal M}}$.

Whenever  ${{\mathcal M}}' \doteq{{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal S}}$ is defined, we have
$\Sigma_{{{\mathcal M}}'}=\iota^{-1}(\Sigma_{{{\mathcal M}}})$. Furthermore, 
$\iota^{-1}({{\mathcal S}})$ 
is
defined and is disjoint from
$\mathop{\rm int}{{\mathcal M}}'$; by Proposition \ref{codim 1 is nice},
$\iota^{-1}({{\mathcal S}})$ 
is a suborbifold of $\partial{{\mathcal M}}'$ (in the strong
sense). The set of $2$--corner points of ${{\mathcal M}}'\doteq{{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal S}}$ is
${{\rm X}_{\partial(\iota^{-1}({{\mathcal S}}))}}$. 
The canonical immersion
$\iota\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal M}}'\to{{\mathcal M}}$ restricts to a
two-sheeted orbifold covering map from 
$\iota^{-1}({{\mathcal S}})$
to 
${{\mathcal S}}$. 
The non-trivial deck transformation of this orbifold covering will be called the \emph{canonical involution} of $\iota^{-1}({{\mathcal S}})$.


We recall that if $M$ is a manifold and $S\subset M$ is a neatly\ 
embedded codimension-$1$ submanifold, then
$M{\backslash \backslash} S$ is always defined.
For example, if $M$ is connected and $S$
separates $M$, we may take $M{\backslash \backslash} S$ to be the disjoint union of the
closures of the components of $M-S$, and take the canonical immersion to agree with the
inclusion on the closure of each component. In  general we may take
$M{\backslash \backslash} S$ to be the closure in $M$ of $M-R$, where $R$ is a tubular
neighborhood of $S$ in $M$; the definition of $\iota$ then requires a
little care.

While it can be shown  that, in the orbifold  context, ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}
{{\mathcal S}}$ exists under fairly broad conditions, we shall need only the case in which 
  ${{\mathcal M}}$ is an orientable $3$--orbifold and ${{\mathcal S}}$ is a neatly\ 
  embedded, orientable two-dimensional suborbifold
of ${{\mathcal M}}$; and in this case, there is a construction of ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}
{{\mathcal S}}$ which is particularly well-adapted to the applications in this
paper. Choose an ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant smooth structure on 
$M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$, which exists by Proposition \ref{smooth underlying}. By an observation made in \S\ref{Suborbifolds-of-3orbifolds}, we have ${{\mathcal S}}={\Omega_{S}}$ for some neatly\ 
  embedded, orientable two-dimensional submanifold $S$
of the orientable $3$--manifold $M$. By the discussion above, $M'\doteq
M{\backslash \backslash}
S$ is defined. If $J\colon\thinspace M'\to M$ denotes the canonical
immersion, it is straightforward to check that 
there exist a unique
$3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}'$ and a unique orbifold immersion
$\iota\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal M}}'\to{{\mathcal M}}$ such that ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}'=M'$ and  $J$ is the
underlying map of $\iota$. 
Furthermore, Conditions
(1) and (2) above hold with these choices of ${{\mathcal M}}'$ and
$\iota$. Thus ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal S}}={{\mathcal M}}'$ is defined in this situation, and it
follows from the uniqueness pointed out above that ${{\mathcal M}}'$ is
independent of the choice of an ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant smooth structure.
<!-- end custom-39 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{split injective}
Let ${{\mathcal S}}$ be a neatly\ 
  embedded, orientable, $\pi_1$--injective two-dimensional suborbifold
of a connected, orientable $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}$. 
Let ${{\mathcal M}}'$ denote a component of ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal S}}$, and let 
$\iota \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal M}}' \to{{\mathcal M}}$ denote the canonical
immersion. Then the induced homomorphism
$\iota_*\colon\thinspace\pi_1({{\mathcal M}}') \to \pi_1({{\mathcal M}})$ 
is injective.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
When ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a manifold, this is standard, 
and one of the standard proofs involves constructing the universal
covering of the given manifold as a tree of spaces
(cf.\ Scott and Wall \cite{scott-wall}). We shall adapt this proof to the orbifold
setting, using
the orbifold versions of standard results in
covering space theory (see \S\ref{path subsection}).

We shall denote by $\tau$ the canonical involution of $\iota^{-1}({{\mathcal S}})$ (see \S\ref{new splitting}). 



 Any orbifold covering
space of ${{\mathcal M}}$ induces an orbifold covering of  ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal S}}$. To
prove the lemma, it suffices to 
construct an orbifold covering space ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$ such that every
component of the induced orbifold
covering space of ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal S}}$ is simply connected. (It is
not necessary to show that ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$  itself is simply connected,
although this could be done.)

For $n\ge0$ we shall recursively define orbifolds ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_n$, orbifold
immersions $p_n\colon\thinspace{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_n\to{{\mathcal M}}$, and orbifold embeddings
$j_n\colon\thinspace{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_n\to{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_{n+1}$ such that $p_{n+1}\circ j_n=p_n$. For
each $n$, each component of the suborbifold $p_n^{-1}({{\mathcal S}})$ of
    ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_n$ will be either properly embedded in ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_n$ or
    contained in $\partial{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_n$. 
Furthermore, if  the  components of $p_n^{-1}({{\mathcal S}})$ that are
    contained in $\partial{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_n$ are faithfully indexed as $({\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}_\alpha)_{\alpha\in J_n}$,
where $J_n$ is some index set,
then for each  $\alpha\in J_n$ 
 here will be a simply connected 
suborbifold ${{\mathcal E}}_\alpha$ of ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_n$, containing ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}_\alpha$,
 such that
    $p_n|{{\mathcal E}}_\alpha\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal E}}_\alpha\to{{\mathcal M}}$ is the composition with
    $\iota$ of
    some covering map $p_\alpha$ from ${{\mathcal E}}_\alpha$ to a component of ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal S}}$.

We take ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_0$ to be a simply connected orbifold
covering of some component ${{\mathcal M}}_0$ of ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal S}}$, and define
$p_0$ to be the composition of the covering map with $\iota$. 

Now suppose that
${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_n$ and $p_n$ have been constructed. For each $\alpha\in J_n$, set ${{\mathcal S}}_\alpha=p_\alpha({\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}_\alpha)$ and ${{\mathcal T}}_\alpha=\tau({{\mathcal S}}_\alpha)$.
The simple connectivity of ${{\mathcal E}}_\alpha$ and the 
$\pi_1$-injectivity of ${{\mathcal S}}_\alpha$ imply that ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}_\alpha$ is simply
connected. Likewise, if ${{\mathcal M}}'_\alpha$ denotes the component of
${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal S}}$ containing $\tau({{\mathcal S}}_\alpha)$, and if we fix a simply
connected covering $q_\alpha\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal F}}_\alpha\to{{\mathcal M}}'_\alpha$ and a
component $\widetilde{{\mathcal T}}_\alpha$ of $q_\alpha^{-1}(\tau({{\mathcal S}}_\alpha))$, then
$\widetilde{{\mathcal T}}_\alpha$ is also simply connected; hence for each 
$\alpha\in J_n$ we may fix a lift
$\widetilde\tau_\alpha\colon\thinspace{\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}_\alpha\to\widetilde{{\mathcal T}}_\alpha$ of $\tau|{{\mathcal S}}_\alpha\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal S}}_\alpha\to{{\mathcal T}}_\alpha$ which
is an orbifold diffeomorphism.

Consider the
disjoint union
of $\widetilde M_n\doteq{{\rm X}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}}}_n$ with all spaces of the form
${{\mathcal F}}_\alpha$, where $\alpha$ ranges over $J_n$. Define $\widetilde M_{n+1}$ to be the quotient space of this disjoint
union obtained by identifying ${{\rm X}_{{\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}}}_\alpha$ with ${{\rm X}_{\widetilde{{\mathcal T}}_\alpha}}$, via the
underlying homeomorphism of
$\widetilde\tau_\alpha$, for each  $\alpha\in J_n$. There is a
well-defined map $P_{n+1}\colon\thinspace \widetilde M_{n+1}\to {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ which restricts
to $P_n$ on $\widetilde M_n$ and to $q_\alpha$ on  ${{\mathcal F}}_\alpha$, for each $\alpha\in J_n$. There exist a
unique orbifold ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_{n+1}$ and a unique orbifold immersion
$p_{n+1}\colon\thinspace{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_{n+1}\to{{\mathcal M}}$ such that
${{\rm X}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_{n+1}}}=\widetilde M_{n+1}$ and $P_{n+1}$ is the underlying map
of $p_{n+1}$. The natural map from $\widetilde M_n$ to $\widetilde M_{n+1}$ is the
underlying map of an orbifold embedding $j_n$. With these definitions,
${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_{n+1}$, $p_{n+1}$ and $j_n$ have the properties required to complete the
recursion step. (If  the  components of $p_{n+1}^{-1}({{\mathcal S}})$ that are
    contained in $\partial{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_{n+1}$ are faithfully indexed as $({\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}_\beta)_{\beta\in J_{n+1}}$,
then for each  $\beta\in J_{n+1}$ there is a unique $\alpha\in J_n$ such that ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal S}}}}_\beta\subset {{\mathcal F}}_\alpha$. We may then take ${{\mathcal E}}_\beta={{\mathcal F}}_\alpha$ and $p_{\beta}=q_\alpha$.)
This completes the recursive construction.


The  directed system defined by the ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}_n$ and the
$j_n$ has a well-defined direct limit ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ in the category of orbifolds.
The maps $p_n$ then define a covering map ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}} \to {{\mathcal M}}$ which has the
required properties.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- custom-40: body_md -->
{Special types of orbifolds}
\label{spherical etc}
An orbifold (of any dimension) will be termed  \emph{discal} or {\it
  spherical} if it is covered by a ball
or a sphere respectively. A
$2$--orbifold will be termed  \emph{toric} or  \emph{annular} if it is
covered by a torus or annulus respectively. A  \emph{solid toric
  orbifold} is a $3$--orbifold which is covered by a solid torus. 

  These definitions apply to
both orientable and non-orientable orbifolds. 

If ${{\mathcal N}}$ is an orientable discal
$2$--orbifold then  ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ is a disk, and 
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}$ either is empty or consists of a single cone point.
If ${{\mathcal N}}$ is an orientable annular
$2$--orbifold then either ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ is an annulus and
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}=\emptyset$, or ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ is a disk and
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}$ consists of two cone points of order $2$. 

If ${{\mathcal N}}$ is an orientable discal
$3$--orbifold, 
then the Orbifold Theorem  
 \cite{BoileauMaillotPorti,
  CHK:OrbifoldBook} implies that
 $N\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ is a topological $3$--ball.
 If ${{\mathcal N}}$ is 
a  solid toric
$3$--orbifold, then the Orbifold Theorem similarly implies that
$N\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ is  a (topological)  solid torus or  $3$--ball.
Furthermore, if $N$ is a solid torus then $\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}$ is either  the
empty set or a single cone stratum which is a
core curve of $N$. If $N$ is a ball, then
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}$ is contained in a (tame) properly embedded disk $D \subset N$,  and consists of either two disjoint cone strata or three cone strata forming the letter $H$.

A  \emph{turnover} is an orientable $2$--orbifold ${{\mathcal S}}$ such that
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal S}}}}$ is a $2$--sphere and $\Sigma_{{\mathcal S}}$ has cardinality $3$. If
the orders of the singular points of ${{\mathcal S}}$ are $p$, $q$ and $r$, we
may refer to ${{\mathcal S}}$ as a  \emph{$(p,q,r)$-turnover.} If ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a
$3$--orbifold, we shall often use the phrase ``turnover in ${{\mathcal M}}$'' to mean a suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$ which is a turnover.
<!-- end custom-40 -->
<!-- custom-41: body_md -->
{Clean\ pairs}
\label{Clean pairs}
We define a \emph{clean\ pair} to be an ordered pair $({{\mathcal Y}},{{\mathcal Z}})$ such
that 
\begin{enumerate}
\item\label{Clean1} ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a compact, orientable $3$--orbifold with $2$--corners, 
\item\label{Clean2} ${{\mathcal Z}}$ is a
$2$--dimensional suborbifold (with boundary) of ${{\mathcal Y}}$, 
\item\label{Clean3} ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Z}}}}$ is disjoint from
 ${{\rm X}_{\mathop{\rm int}{{\mathcal Y}}}}$, and 
 \item\label{Clean4} ${{\rm X}_{\partial{{\mathcal Z}}}}$ is the set of all $2$--corner points of ${{\mathcal Y}}$.
\end{enumerate}
If $(Y,Z)$ is a clean\ pair such that $Y$ is a manifold with corners
(and hence $Z$ is a manifold), we shall call $(Y,Z)$ a  \emph{clean
  manifold pair}.

If $({\mathscr Y},{\mathscr Z})$ is a clean\ (orbifold) pair, then
$({{\mathcal Y}},{\mathscr Z}\cap{{\mathcal Y}})$ is a clean\ pair for any
component ${{\mathcal Y}}$ of ${\mathscr Y}$. A clean\ pair of this form  is called a 
  \emph{component} of $({\mathscr Y},{\mathscr Z})$. We say that $({\mathscr Y},{\mathscr Z})$ is
  \emph{connected} if it has exactly one component, or equivalently if
 ${\mathscr Y}$ is connected.

If $({{\mathcal Y}},{{\mathcal Z}})$ is a clean\ pair then
${{\mathcal Y}}$ has nonsingular $2$--corners. To see this, note that by
\S\ref{Suborbifolds} we have $
{{\mathcal Z}} \cap \Sigma_{{\mathcal Y}}
=\Sigma_{{\mathcal Z}}
$.  If $K$ denotes the set of $2$--corner points of ${{\mathcal Y}}$, we
have $K={{\rm X}_{\partial{{\mathcal Z}}}}$ by the definition of a clean pair. Hence
$K\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal Y}}={{\rm X}_{\partial{{\mathcal Z}}}}\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal Z}}$. The latter
intersection is empty since ${{\mathcal Z}}$ is an orientable $2$--orbifold, and
the assertion follows.


If ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a compact, orientable $3$--orbifold with $2$--corners and
${{\mathcal Z}}$ is a 
two-dimensional
weak suborbifold of ${{\mathcal Y}}$,
and if Conditions \eqref{Clean1}, \eqref{Clean3} and \eqref{Clean4} of the definition above hold, then
$({{\mathcal Y}},{{\mathcal Z}})$ is a clean pair. 
Indeed, Proposition \ref{codim 1 is nice} implies that ${{\mathcal Z}}$ is a suborbifold of ${{\mathcal Y}}$ in the strong sense, hence Condition \eqref{Clean2} holds also.
<!-- end custom-41 -->
<!-- custom-42: body_md -->
{Essentiality and Irreducibility}\label{Pi1Injective}
For the following set of definitions, suppose ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a compact orientable $3$--orbifold.


Let ${{\mathcal S}}_0$ and ${{\mathcal S}}_1$ be 
compact
$2$--suborbifolds 
of a $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}$, 
such that
$\partial{{\mathcal S}}_i\subset\partial{{\mathcal M}}$ for $i=0,1$.
We shall say that ${{\mathcal S}}_0$ and
${{\mathcal S}}_1$ are  \emph{parallel} if 
there is an embedding 
 $f \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal S}}_0 \times [0,1] \to {{\mathcal M}}$, such
that $f$ maps ${{\mathcal S}}_0 \times \{i\}$
diffeomorphically onto  ${{\mathcal S}}_i$ for
$i=0,1$, and $f( \partial{{\mathcal S}}_0 
\times [0,1] ) \subset \partial {{\mathcal M}}$. The image 
(see \S\ref{Suborbifolds})
of such an embedding
is called a  \emph{parallelism} between ${{\mathcal S}}_0$ and ${{\mathcal S}}_1$. A 
neatly\ \ embedded 
$2$--suborbifold
  of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is said to be  \emph{boundary-parallel}
if it is parallel to some $2$--suborbifold contained in $\partial {{\mathcal M}}$.


A connected $2$--suborbifold ${{\mathcal S}}$ of 
${{\mathcal M}}$ is called \emph{essential} if ${{\mathcal S}}$ is neatly embedded,
orientable
and $\pi_1$--injective, is not the boundary of a discal
$3$--suborbifold, and is not boundary-parallel.
A possibly disconnected $2$--suborbifold ${{\mathcal R}}$ is called \emph{essential} if every component of ${{\mathcal R}}$ is essential.

As a special case, we have the notion of an  \emph{essential turnover} in
a $3$--orbifold.

We say that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is \emph{irreducible} if ${{\mathcal M}}$ is connected and every closed  $2$--suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$ with strictly positive Euler characteristic is the boundary of 
a discal $3$--suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$. 
Since every bad $2$--orbifold has positive Euler characteristic by \cite[Corollary 2.28]{CHK:OrbifoldBook}, we observe that an irreducible $3$--orbifold cannot contain any bad, essential $2$--suborbifolds.
We also observe that every hyperbolic $3$--orbifold is irreducible.

We say that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is \emph{boundary-irreducible} if $\partial {{\mathcal M}}$ is $\pi_1$--injective.
<!-- end custom-42 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{when injective}
{\rm (cf.\ \cite[Corollary
3.20]{BoileauMaillotPorti}).}
Let ${{\mathcal W}}$ be an orientable two-dimensional closed suborbifold of the interior of
a very good, orientable $3$--orbifold
${{\mathcal M}}$. Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}
\item ${{\mathcal W}}$ is $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal M}}$.
\item for every two-dimensional 
orientable
discal suborbifold ${{\mathcal D}}$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$
  such that ${{\mathcal C}}\doteq\partial{{\mathcal D}}={{\mathcal D}}\cap{{\mathcal W}}$,
there is  a discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal W}}$ whose boundary is ${{\mathcal C}}$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
First suppose that ${{\mathcal W}}$ is  $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal M}}$. Let
${{\mathcal D}}$ be any two-dimensional 
discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$
  such that ${{\mathcal C}}\doteq\partial{{\mathcal D}}={{\mathcal D}}\cap{{\mathcal W}}$. Then ${{\mathcal C}}$ is
  a simple closed curve disjoint from the singular set of ${{\mathcal M}}$, and
  represents (up to conjugacy and inversion) an element of finite
  order in $\pi_1({{\mathcal M}})$. Since ${{\mathcal W}}$ is  $\pi_1$--injective, ${{\mathcal C}}$ 
  represents  an element of finite
  order in $\pi_1({{\mathcal W}})$, and 
is therefore the  boundary of 
a  discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal W}}$.


Now  suppose that ${{\mathcal W}}$ is not $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal M}}$.
Set ${{\mathcal M}}'={{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal W}}$, 
denote the canonical immersion
from ${{\mathcal M}}'$ to ${{\mathcal M}}$ by $\iota$,  and set
${{\mathcal W}}'=\iota^{-1}({{\mathcal W}})$
(which, as observed in \S\ref{new splitting}, is a
well-defined  suborbifold of $\partial{{\mathcal M}}'$).
Then it follows from 
Lemma \ref{split injective}
that ${{\mathcal W}}'$ is not $\pi_1$--injective in
  ${{\mathcal M}}'$. 
Fix an orbifold loop $\alpha$ in  ${{\mathcal W}}'$  which is orbifold-homotopically trivial 
in ${{\mathcal M}}'$ but not in ${{\mathcal W}}'$. 

Since ${{\mathcal M}}$ is  very good, we may fix a finite-sheeted regular cover
$p\colon\thinspace N\to{{\mathcal M}}'$ such that $N$ is a manifold. Let $G$ denote the covering
group. Since $\alpha$  is
orbifold-homotopically trivial 
in ${{\mathcal M}}'$, it follows from \ref{lifting homotopies} and \ref{homotop to generic}
that $\alpha$ admits a lift ${\widetilde\alpha}$ which is a loop in
$N$. Since $\alpha([0,1])\subset{{\mathcal W}}'$, we have ${\widetilde\alpha}([0,1])\subset
V\doteq p^{-1}({{\mathcal W}}')\subset\partial N$. Since $\alpha$  is
orbifold-homotopically trivial 
in ${{\mathcal M}}'$ but not in ${{\mathcal W}}'$, the 
orbifold loop 
${\widetilde\alpha}$  is
orbifold-homotopically trivial 
in $N$ but not in $V$. 
Hence by
Meeks and Yau's
equivariant loop theorem  \cite[Theorem 3]{MY-sphere},
$N$ contains a non-empty, $G$--invariant, neatly\  
embedded
submanifold ${\bf E}$, each
component of which is an essential disk. Let ${\bf D}$ denote the
frontier in $N$ of a 
$G$--invariant 
regular neighborhood of
${\bf E}$. Then ${\bf D}$ is itself $G$--invariant and its components are
essential disks; and in addition, no component of ${\bf D}$ is
invariant under an element of $G$ which reverses its orientation. It
now follows that
$p({\bf D})$ is a well-defined 
orientable, neatly\  embedded $2$--suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}'$  having
boundary in ${{\mathcal W}}'$, and that
each component of $p({\bf D})$  is
discal.  Since
the components of ${\bf D}$ are essential, no boundary component of
$p({\bf D})$ is the boundary of a discal suborbifold of
${{\mathcal W}}'$. Hence the image under $\iota$ of an
arbitrary component of $p({\bf D})$
is an orientable discal
weak 
suborbifold  ${{\mathcal D}}$ of ${{\mathcal M}}$
  such that ${{\mathcal C}}\doteq\partial{{\mathcal D}}={{\mathcal D}}\cap{{\mathcal W}}$,
and
there is  no discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal W}}$ whose boundary is ${{\mathcal C}}$.
Since  ${{\mathcal D}}$ has codimension $1$ in  ${{\mathcal M}}$,  and  ${{\mathcal M}}$ is
orientable, it follows from Proposition \ref{codim 1 is nice} that
${{\mathcal D}}$ is in fact a suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$ (in the  strong sense).
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{if three}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable, very good
$3$--orbifold. Let $S\subset{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ be a
$2$--sphere which is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ 
and has
size\
at most $3$  (see \S\ref{size 'n' stuff}).
 Then ${{\mathcal S}}\doteq{\Omega_{S}} $ is
$\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal M}}$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
According to Proposition \ref{when injective},
$\pi_1$--injectivity 
of ${{\mathcal S}}\doteq{\Omega_{S}} $ in ${{\mathcal M}}$
is equivalent to the assertion
that if $C$ is any simple closed curve in
$S-(S\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}})$ 
such that $C = {\Omega_{C}} $
 bounds 
an orientable
discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$,
then $C$ bounds a discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal S}} $. But since $S$ is
a sphere of size\ at most $3$, 
for \emph{every}
simple closed curve $C$ in $S-(S\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}})$ there is a disk
bounded by $C$ that contains at most one point of $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, and hence
$C $ 
bounds a discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal S}} $.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{cause gromov}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable hyperbolic $3$--orbifold. Observe
that by Proposition~\ref{Prop:LocalStructure3Orbifold}, $M \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ is a closed topological $3$--manifold,
so that the Gromov norm $\| M \|$ is defined by \S\ref{Gromov norm}.
Then $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} \geq {v_{\rm tet}} \| M \|$ (where $ {v_{\rm tet}}$  is defined as in \S\ref{notational}).
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Since ${{\mathcal M}}$ is hyperbolic, it is very good. Let ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ be a
finite-sheeted covering space of ${{\mathcal M}}$ which is a hyperbolic
manifold, and let $d$ denote the degree of the covering map
$p\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}\to{{\mathcal M}}$. 
Then  the underlying map of
$p$ is a degree-$d$ map from
${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ to $M$. 
It now follows from \eqref{degree and Gromov}, \eqref{genuine gromov}, 
and the multiplicativity  of volume under covers that
\[ 
d \cdot {v_{\rm tet}} \|M\|
\: \leq \:  {v_{\rm tet}} \| {\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}} \| 
\: = \:  \mathop{\rm vol} {\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}
 \: = \: d \cdot \mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}},
\]
which implies the result.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{Cor:SimpleVolBound}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable hyperbolic $3$--orbifold with $\mathop{\rm vol}
{{\mathcal M}} < {V_{\rm Weeks}}$. Then 
$M \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ is homeomorphic to
 a connected sum of graph manifolds.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let us fix a smooth structure on
$M$. Assume that the smooth, orientable $3$--manifold $M$ is not a
graph manifold, so that by \S\ref{geometry and norms} it has at least
one 
hyperbolic piece, say $P$. Then
by combining the result due to Gabai, Meyerhoff, and
Milley mentioned above with Assertion \ref{all we need},
Proposition~\ref{cause gromov}, and the hypothesis of the present
corollary, we find
\[
{V_{\rm Weeks}} \leq \mathop{\rm vol} P 
 \leq {v_{\rm tet}} \|M\| \leq \mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} < {V_{\rm Weeks}},
\]
a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{Def:OrbifoldFiberBundle}
Suppose that ${{\mathcal P}}$ is  an orbifold with $2$--corners, and ${{\mathcal F}}$ and ${{\mathcal H}}$ are orbifolds (with
boundary).
A smooth orbifold
map
$q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$
 is said to be an
\emph{orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration} if
for every  $x \in {{\mathcal H}}$, there exist
\begin{itemize}
\item  
an open neighborhood ${{\mathcal U}}$ of $x$,
\item a manifold ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$,
\item  a finite group ${\mathfrak G}$, equipped with  actions on ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ and  ${{\mathcal F}}$, such that the diagonal action of ${\mathfrak G} $ on
the product orbifold with $2$--corners ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times {{\mathcal F}} $ (see
\S\ref{why corners?}) is effective,
\item a 
smooth map
 $\phi\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\to{{\mathcal U}}$ 
which induces an orbifold diffeomorphism
  between ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}/{\mathfrak G} $ and ${{\mathcal U}}$, and
\item a 
smooth map
$\xi$ from 
${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times {{\mathcal F}}$ to the open suborbifold 
with $2$--corners
 $q^{-1}({{\mathcal U}})$ of $  {{\mathcal P}}$
which induces an orbifold diffeomorphism
  between $({\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times {{\mathcal F}} )/{\mathfrak G} $  and $q^{-1}({{\mathcal U}})$,
\end{itemize}
such that 
the following diagram, where $\widetilde q\colon\thinspace 
{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times {{\mathcal F}} \to{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ denotes projection to the first factor, 
commutes:
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}} \times {{\mathcal F}} \arrow[r, "\xi"] \arrow[d, "\widetilde q"] & q^{-1}({{\mathcal U}}) \arrow[d, "q"] \\
{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}} \arrow[r, " \phi"] & {{\mathcal U}}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}


A quintuple $({{\mathcal U}},{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}},{\mathfrak G},\phi,\xi)$ such that the bulleted
conditions above hold will be called a  \emph{local trivialization of}
the orbifold fibration $q$  \emph{near} the point $x$.
This notation leaves the actions implicit.

  We observe that
  if $q$ is an orbifold fibration, 
the 
underlying
map of  
$q$ 
is surjective.
We also observe
that if
$({{\mathcal U}},{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}},{\mathfrak G},\phi,\xi)$ is a  local trivialization of
$q$, then
$\xi\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times {{\mathcal F}} \to q^{-1}({{\mathcal U}})$
is a regular covering whose deck group is ${\mathfrak G}$; and $\phi\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\to{{\mathcal U}}$ is a regular covering whose deck group is
some (possibly proper) quotient of
${\mathfrak G}$.


An orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration $q\colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}}\to{{\mathcal H}}$ may also be referred
to as an orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration of ${{\mathcal P}}$ with base ${{\mathcal H}}$. An
orbifold 
with $2$--corners ${{\mathcal P}}$
equipped with an orbifold fibration over some base will be
called an \emph{orbifold bundle.}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- custom-43: body_md -->
{Standard local trivializations}
\label{Rem:StandardNbdFibration}


Suppose that $q\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal P}}\to{{\mathcal H}}$ is an orbifold
${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration, and that
$({{\mathcal U}},{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}},{\mathfrak G},\phi,\xi)$  is a local trivialization of $q$
near a point $x\in{{\mathcal P}}$.
Then for any connected open neighborhood ${{\mathcal U}}'\subset{{\mathcal U}}$ of $x$,
there is another local trivialization $({{\mathcal U}}',{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}',{\mathfrak G}',\phi',\xi')$
near $x$ given by taking
${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}'$ to be a component of $\phi^{-1}({{\mathcal U}}')$,  setting
${\mathfrak G}'={\rm Stab}_{\mathfrak G}({{\mathcal U}}')$,  
$\phi'=\phi|{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}'$, and $\xi'=\xi|({\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}'\times {{\mathcal F}})$, and
restricting  the action of ${\mathfrak G}$ on ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ to obtain an action of ${\mathfrak G}'$ on ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}'$.  (Since
the diagonal action of ${\mathfrak G}'$ on ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times {{\mathcal F}} $ is effective, it
follows from Corollary~\ref{Bochner corollary} that its diagonal action  on
${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}' \times {{\mathcal F}} $ is also effective.)
 
It follows that there is a local trivialization $({{\mathcal U}},{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}},{\mathfrak G},\phi,\xi)$ of $q$ such
that ${{\mathcal U}}$ is a standard
neighborhood of $x$ (as defined in \S\ref{Suborbifolds}), and ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$
is connected.

According to an observation made in \S\ref{Orbifold covers}, the standard neighborhood ${{\mathcal U}}$ of $x$  has only one connected manifold cover up to
equivalence. Hence 
 there is a standard chart 
 $(U, D, \Phi,G)$ centered at $x$, where $U = {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal U}}}}$,
the group $G$ is the quotient of ${\mathfrak G}$ that acts effectively on
${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$, and
the  open ball or half-ball $D = {\Omega_{D}}$ may be
 smoothly and ${\mathfrak G}$--equivariantly identified with ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ in such
 a way that $\Phi$ is the 
underlying map of 
$\phi$. Under this identification the given local
trivialization becomes 
$({{\mathcal U}},D,{\mathfrak G},\phi,\xi)$. A local trivialization of the latter
form, associated with a suitable standard chart $(U, D, \Phi,G)$
centered at $x$,  will be termed  \emph{standard}.


If it happens that
 the action of ${\mathfrak G}$ on
$D = {\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ is effective, then ${\mathfrak G}$ is also identified with $G_x$.
<!-- end custom-43 -->
<!-- custom-44: body_md -->
{Fibers and vertical weak suborbifolds}
\label{vertical weak}
If $f\colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}}\to{{\mathcal H}}$ is an  orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration, 
with underlying
map $F\colon\thinspace {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}\to{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal H}}}}$, then 
for any weak
suborbifold ${{\mathcal Z}}$ of ${{\mathcal H}}$, 
it follows from the definitions that
$Y\doteq F^{-1}({{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Z}}}})$
is  the underlying set of a weak suborbifold-with-corners
of ${{\mathcal P}}$. Following the convention introduced in
  \S\ref{more orbifold notions},
we denote the weak suborbifold-with-corners
${\Omega_{Y}}$ of ${{\mathcal P}}$ by $f^{-1}({{\mathcal Z}})$.

A weak suborbifold 
${{\mathcal N}}$ of  ${{\mathcal P}}$ is called \emph{vertical} if ${{\mathcal N}} =
f^{-1}({{\mathcal Z}})$ for a
weak
 suborbifold ${{\mathcal Z}}$ of ${{\mathcal H}}$.

In particular, 
for every $x\in{{\mathcal H}}$, we have a
well-defined 
vertical
weak suborbifold $f^{-1}(x)$ of ${{\mathcal P}}$. This
weak 
suborbifold 
is orbifold-diffeomorphic
to a quotient of ${{\mathcal F}}$ by a finite group action, and is called
the  \emph{fiber} over $x$.
<!-- end custom-44 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{Rem:NoGenericFiber}
Our definition of an orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration is equivalent to the
one given in Cooper, Hodgson, and Kerckhoff \cite[Section 2.7]{CHK:OrbifoldBook}. Our definition is weaker than
the one given in Boileau, Maillot, and Porti \cite[Section 2.4]{BoileauMaillotPorti}, where it is
assumed that
near every point $x\in{{\mathcal H}}$ there is a local trivialization
$({{\mathcal U}},{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}},{\mathfrak G},\phi,\xi)$ such that
the action of  ${\mathfrak G} $ on ${{\mathcal U}}$ is
effective. In \cite{CHK:OrbifoldBook} the orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$ is
referred to as a ``generic fiber,'' but we have avoided this term
because, in general, the map $q\colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}}\to{{\mathcal H}}$ need not have any fiber
which is 
orbifold-diffeomorphic to ${{\mathcal F}}$. 
(For example, if $\widetilde{{\mathcal F}} \to {{\mathcal F}}$ is a finite characteristic cover, then any
${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration of a given orbifold ${{\mathcal P}}$ is also
an $\widetilde{{\mathcal F}}$--fibration. In this situation, a product ${{\mathcal H}} \times
{{\mathcal F}}$ will not have any fiber diffeomorphic to $\widetilde{{\mathcal F}}$.
This also shows that an orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration
$q\colon\thinspace{{\mathcal P}}\to{{\mathcal H}}$, where ${{\mathcal F}}$, ${{\mathcal P}}$ and ${{\mathcal H}}$ are manifolds, is not necessarily
an ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration in the usual sense.)
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{Ex:SeifertManifold}
Let $M$ be an orientable Seifert fibered $3$--manifold. 
Identifying every Seifert fiber to a point produces a quotient $q \colon\thinspace M \to {{\mathcal H}}$, where ${{\mathcal H}}$ is a $2$--orbifold. Then $q \colon\thinspace M \to {{\mathcal H}}$ satisfies Definition~\ref{Def:OrbifoldFiberBundle} with ${{\mathcal F}} = {\mathbb S}^1$. The regular Seifert fibers are exactly the preimages of nonsingular points in ${{\mathcal H}}$, while the singular Seifert fibers are the preimages of cone points in ${{\mathcal H}}$.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{fibrations surject pi one}
Let $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$ be an orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration. Then
for every generic orbifold path $\alpha$ in ${{\mathcal H}}$, and for every point $z$ in the fiber over the
initial point of $\alpha$, there is a lift of $\alpha$ to ${{\mathcal P}}$
having initial point $z$. Furthermore, if
${{\mathcal P}}$ and ${{\mathcal F}}$ are connected, then the homomorphism $q_* \colon\thinspace \pi_1({{\mathcal P}}) \to
\pi_1({{\mathcal H}})$ (see \S\ref{path subsection}) is surjective.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
We begin by proving the first assertion under the additional
assumption that the image of $\alpha$ is contained in ${{\mathcal U}}$ for some
local trivialization $({{\mathcal U}},{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}},{\mathfrak G},\phi,\xi)$ of $q$. In this
case, we may select a point $(x,y)\in {\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times{{\mathcal F}}$ such that
$\xi(x,y)=z$. It follows from the assertion \ref{crucial fact} that $\alpha$
admits a lift ${\widetilde\alpha}$ to the orbifold covering
$\phi\colon\thinspace{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\to{{\mathcal U}}$ having initial point $x$. Now let
$s\colon\thinspace{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times{{\mathcal F}}\to{{\mathcal F}}$ denote the projection to the second
factor. Since ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}} \times {{\mathcal F}}$ is a product object in the smooth category of
orbifolds (see \S\ref{maps continued}), there is an orbifold path
$\beta$ in ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times{{\mathcal F}}$ such that $\widetilde q\circ\beta={\widetilde\alpha}$ and
$s\circ\beta$ is the constant path at $y$. Then $\xi\circ\beta$ is a lift of $\alpha$ to ${{\mathcal P}}$
having initial point $z$.

To prove the assertion in the general case, we write the given generic
orbifold path $\alpha$ as a composition $\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_n$,
where each $\alpha_i$ is a generic path whose image is contained in ${{\mathcal U}}_i$ for some
local trivialization $({{\mathcal U}}_i,{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}_i,{\mathfrak G}_i,\phi_i,\xi_i)$ of
$q$. Using the special case  that has been
proved, we may recursively choose lifts ${\widetilde\alpha}_1,\ldots,{\widetilde\alpha}_n$
of $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n$ such that ${\widetilde\alpha}_1$ has initial point
$z$, and for any $i$ with $1<i\le n$, the initial point of ${\widetilde\alpha}_i$
is the terminal point of ${\widetilde\alpha}_{i-1}$. Then the composition
${\widetilde\alpha}_1\cdots{\widetilde\alpha}_n$ is defined and is a lift of $\alpha$ to ${{\mathcal P}}$
having initial point $z$.

To prove the second assertion, it suffices to show that if ${{\mathcal F}}$ is
connected, and $z$ is a
point of ${{\mathcal P}}$ such that $w\doteq q(z)$ is nonsingular, then $q_* \colon\thinspace \pi_1({{\mathcal P}},z) \to
\pi_1({{\mathcal H}},w)$ is surjective (see \S\ref{path subsection}). 
By Assertion \ref{homotop to generic}, any element $g$ of
$\pi_1({{\mathcal H}},w)$ is represented by a generic loop
$\alpha$ based at $w$. By the first assertion of the present lemma,
the path $\alpha$ admits a lift ${\widetilde\alpha}$ to ${{\mathcal P}}$ whose initial point is
$z$. Since $\alpha$ is a loop, the terminal point $z'$ of ${\widetilde\alpha}$
lies in the same fiber ${{\mathcal F}}_0$ as $z$. Since ${{\mathcal F}}$ is connected, ${{\mathcal F}}_0$ is
connected, and hence by an observation made in \S\ref{path subsection}
there is an orbifold path $\gamma$ in ${{\mathcal F}}_0$ with initial point $z'$
and terminal point $z$. If we set
$h=[{\widetilde\alpha}\cdot\gamma]\in\pi_1({{\mathcal P}},z)$, then $q_*(h)=g$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{Lem:InducedCover}
Let $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$ be an orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration, where
${{\mathcal P}}$ and ${{\mathcal F}}$ are connected. Then, for every connected cover
$\theta  \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$, there 
exist an 
orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration $\widetilde q \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to {\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}$ and a cover $\upsilon  \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to {{\mathcal P}}$ such that $\theta $ and $\upsilon $ have the same degree and the following diagram commutes:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
{\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \arrow[r, "\upsilon "] \arrow[d, "\widetilde q"] & {{\mathcal P}} \arrow[d, "q"] \\
{\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}} \arrow[r, "\theta "] & {{\mathcal H}}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Such an orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration $\widetilde q \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to
{\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}$ will be said to be \emph{induced} by the orbifold
${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $\upsilon  \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to {{\mathcal P}}$ be the cover of
${{\mathcal P}}$ corresponding to the subgroup $q_*^{-1}(\theta _*(\pi_1
{\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}))$. Now, the lifting criterion (see \S\ref{path subsection}) ensures that $q \circ \upsilon  \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$ lifts to a smooth map $\widetilde q \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to {\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}$.


Since  ${{\mathcal F}}$ is connected, 
it follows from Lemma~\ref{fibrations surject pi one} that
$q_* \colon\thinspace \pi_1 {{\mathcal P}} \to \pi_1 {{\mathcal H}}$ is surjective. Thus 
\[
\big[ \pi_1 {{\mathcal H}} : \theta _*(\pi_1 {\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}) \big] = \big[ \pi_1 {{\mathcal P}} : q_*^{-1}(\theta _*(\pi_1 {\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}})) \big],
\]
hence $\theta $ and $\upsilon $ have the same degree. 

It remains to check that $\widetilde q \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to
{\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}$ is an orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration. This can be shown
by verifying that for every ${\widetilde x} \in {\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}$, a
standard local trivialization of $q$ near $x = \theta ({\widetilde x})
\in {{\mathcal H}}$ 
gives rise to
a standard local trivialization of $\widetilde q$ near ${\widetilde x}$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- custom-45: body_md -->
{Fiber-preserving actions}
\label{what's fiber preserving}
Suppose that $r\colon\thinspace M\to Z$ 
is a smooth
fibration, where $M$ and $Z$ are manifolds (with boundary). A
self-diffeomorphism $g$ of $M$ is said to \emph{preserve the
  fibration $r$} if
$g\cdot F$ is a fiber of $r$ for each fiber $F$ of $r$.
<!-- end custom-45 -->
<!-- custom-46: body_md -->
{Boundary collars and group actions}\label{collars and actions}
A  \emph{parametrized boundary collar} for a manifold 
$M$ is defined to be an embedding $c\colon\thinspace (\partial
M) \times [0,1) \to M$ such that $c(x,0)=x$ for each $x\in\partial
M$. One can construct a parametrized boundary collar for any manifold 
$M$ by fixing a vector field
$Y$ on $M$ which is
inward-pointing at every point of $\partial M$,
integrating $Y$, and restricting the resulting flow to a
small neighborhood of $\partial M$. 

If we are given an action by diffeomorphisms of a finite
group $G$ on $M$, then by averaging 
a vector field
$Y_0$  which is
inward-pointing at every point of $\partial M$, we obtain a
$G$--invariant vector field $Y$ with the same property; the construction
referred to above, with this choice of $Y$, then gives
a parametrized boundary collar $c$ for $M$
which is {\it
$G$--equivariant} in the sense that
$g\cdot c(x,t)=c(g\cdot x,t)$ for each $(x,t)\in (\partial
M) \times [0,1) $. 

Now suppose that we are given a smooth fibration $r \colon\thinspace M\to Z$ of the
compact manifold $M$ over a closed manifold $Z$, whose fiber is a
compact manifold with boundary, and that the action of $G$ on $M$
preserves the fibration (\S\ref{what's fiber preserving}).
Then the 
inward-pointing vector field $Y_0$ used in that construction given
above may
be taken (by a partition-of-unity argument) to be 
everywhere tangent to the fibers of $r$.
With this choice of $Y_0$, the
$G$--equivariant parametrized boundary collar $c_0$ given by the
construction will be
compatible with the fibration $r$ in the sense that $c_0(x\times[0,1))$ is
contained in a fiber of $r$ for each $x\in\partial M$.
<!-- end custom-46 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{FiberPreservingAction}
Suppose that $r\colon\thinspace M\to Z$ 
is a smooth
fibration with fiber $F$, where $M$ is a compact manifold with
  $2$--corners and $F, Z$ are 
compact
manifolds (with boundary).
Let $G$ be a finite group of  diffeomorphisms of $M$, and
suppose that each $g\in G$ sends fibers to fibers, 
so that there is an induced action of $G$ on  $Z$. 
Let $q\colon\thinspace M/G  \to Z/G$ denote the
unique orbifold map such that the diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
M \arrow[r, ""] \arrow[d, "r"] & 
M/G \arrow[d, "q"] 
 \\
Z \arrow[r, ""]
& Z/G
\end{tikzcd}
\]
commutes, where the horizontal arrows indicate quotients by the $G$--action.
Then $q$ 
is an
orbifold $F$--fibration.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
We first consider the case in which $Z$ and $F$ are both closed, so that $M$ is closed.

We fix a $G$--invariant Riemannian metric on $M$.

We  set ${{\mathcal N}}=M/G$ and ${{\mathcal H}}=Z/G$, and we denote by $p$ the quotient map from
$Z$ to ${{\mathcal H}}$. We set $m=\dim M$
and $n=\dim Z$, so that $F$ is a manifold of dimension $k\doteq m-n$. 

Let a point $x\in{{\mathcal H}}$ be given. Let us choose a point ${\widetilde x}\in
p^{-1}(x)\subset Z$. Set $F_0=r^{-1}({\widetilde x})\subset M$, so that $F_0$ is
orbifold-diffeomorphic to $F$. 

Let $J\le G$ denote the
stabilizer of ${\widetilde x}$ 
under the action of $G$ on $Z$, which is also the stabilizer of $F_0$ under the action of $G$ on 
$M$.
For a small enough
positive number $\varepsilon$, 
the proof of the standard tubular neighborhood theorem for smooth
submanifolds shows that
the $\varepsilon$--neighborhood $V=V_\varepsilon$
of $F_0$ in $M$ (with respect to the chosen Riemannian metric) is the
domain of a well-defined nearest-point map $t\colon\thinspace V\to F_0$, and $t$ is a
(manifold) fibration of $V$ with base $F_0$, whose fiber is an open ball of
dimension $m-k=n$. The $G$--invariance of the
metric on $M$ implies that $V$ is $J$--invariant, and that $t$ is a
$J$--equivariant 
map. Since the action of $G$ on $Z$ is induced by its
action on $M$, the map $r|V\colon\thinspace V\to Z$ is also $J$--equivariant. Hence, if
the product $Z\times F_0$ is endowed with the product $J$--action, we may
define a $J$--equivariant map $\eta\colon\thinspace V\to Z\times F_0$ by
$\eta(z)= (r(z),t(z))$. 

Note that $\eta$ is a smooth map between $m$--manifolds. We claim:

\begin{claim}\label{invertible}
For every point 
$z\in F_0$, 
the linear map $d\eta_z\colon\thinspace T_zV\to
T_{\eta(z)}(Z\times F_0)$ is invertible.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{invertible}, we let $D$ denote the $n$--ball
$t^{-1}(z)\subset V$. 
We write $T_z V=A\oplus B$, where $A$ and
$B$ are canonically isomorphic to $T_z D$ and $T_{t(z)} F_0$  respectively.
We also write $T_{\eta(z)} (Z\times F_0) = A' \oplus B$, where $A'$ and
$B$ are canonically isomorphic to $T_{r(z)} Z$ and $T_{t(z)} F_0$
respectively. 
Since $t|F_0$ is the identity map and $r|F_0$ is constant, 
$d\eta_z$ maps $B$ isomorphically onto $B$. 


Since $r$ is a fibration, $dr_z\colon\thinspace T_zV\to T_{r(z)}Z$ is surjective. But
$dr_z|B$ is the zero map, and hence $dr_z|A \colon\thinspace  A \to A' = T_{r(z)}Z$ is surjective. Since
$A$ and $A'$ are both $n$--dimensional, this means that $dr_z|A$
maps $A$ isomorphically onto  $A'$. But $t|D$ is
constant, and hence $dt_z|T_zD=0$; it follows that $d\eta_z$ maps $A$ isomorphically onto $A'$. 
Thus \ref{invertible} is established.

It follows from \ref{invertible} and the compactness of $F_0$ that some
open neighborhood of $F_0$ in $V$ is mapped diffeomorphically by $\eta$
onto an open neighborhood of $\{{\widetilde x}\} \times F_0$ in $Z\times F_0$. Again
using the compactness of $F_0$, we see that the latter neighborhood
contains one of the form ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times F_0$ where ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ is an open neighborhood
of ${\widetilde x}$ in $Z$; and since $J$ fixes ${\widetilde x}$, we may assume after
replacing ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ by a possibly smaller neighborhood of ${\widetilde x}$ that ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ is
$J$--invariant, and is disjoint from its image under every element of $G-J$. Some open neighborhood $W$ of $F_0$ is mapped
diffeomorphically onto the $J$--invariant open set ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times F_0$, and the
$J$--equivariance of $\eta$ then implies that $W$ is $J$--invariant and
that $\eta|W\colon\thinspace W\to {\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times F_0$ is $J$--equivariant. 

Let $\psi\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times F_0\to{{\mathcal N}}$ denote the composition of the
diffeomorphism $(\eta|W)^{-1}\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times F_0\to W\subset M$ with the
quotient map $M\to M/G={{\mathcal N}}$. Then the conditions of
Definition \ref{Def:OrbifoldFiberBundle} hold with ${{\mathcal N}}$, $F$,
$p({\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}})$, $J$ and $p|{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ playing the respective roles of
${{\mathcal P}}$, ${{\mathcal F}}$, ${{\mathcal U}}$, ${\mathfrak G} $ and $\phi$.
This shows that $q$ is an orbifold $F$--fibration,
and completes the proof in the case where $Z$ and $F$ are both closed.

This argument does not quite work in  the case in which $Z$ is closed but
$\partial F\ne\emptyset$, because for an arbitrary $G$--invariant
metric on $M$, the proof of the tubular neighborhood theorem does not show
that the map $t$ appearing in the argument is a fibration for an
arbitrary point $x\in{{\mathcal H}}$; to guarantee this we must exercise a little more care in
choosing the $G$--invariant metric. 
For this purpose we use 
the construction of \S\ref{collars and actions} to produce a
$G$--equivariant parametrized boundary collar in $M$ which is
compatible with the fibration $r$, in the sense defined in that subsection.

Now define a metric $\rho_0$ on 
$c_0((\partial
M)\times[0,1))$ 
by pushing forward, via $c_0$, the product of some
$G$--invariant metric on $\partial M$ with the standard metric on
$[0,1)$. There is a metric $\overline{\rho}_0$ on $M$ which agrees with
$\rho_0$ on some neighborhood of $\partial M$, and averaging
$\overline{\rho}_0$ via the action of $G$ gives a $G$--invariant metric $\rho$ on $M$ which
again agrees with
$\rho_0$ on some neighborhood of $\partial M$. This implies that
the restriction of the metric $\rho$ to some neighborhood of $\partial M$ can itself be obtained by pushing forward 
a product metric via some 
parametrized boundary collar $c\colon\thinspace (\partial
M)\times[0,1)\to M$ which is  compatible with the fibration $r$. This
is enough to guarantee that the map
$t$ appearing in the argument given above is a fibration for an
arbitrary point $x\in{{\mathcal H}}$. This  completes the proof in the case in which $Z$ is closed but
$\partial F$ may be non-empty.


To prove the proposition in the general case, we consider certain doubled
manifolds $DM$ and $DZ$. Here $DM$ is obtained by doubling $M$ along
the manifold (with boundary) 
$E\doteq r^{-1}(\partial Z)$.
The manifold $DM$ is the union of two manifolds with $2$--corners
$M_1$ and $M_2$,
each of which is identified diffeomorphically with $M$ 
and therefore
has a submanifold $E_i$ identified with $E$; and we have
$M_1\cap M_2=
E_1=E_2$.
The manifold $DZ$ is the double of $Z$ along its full boundary; it is
the union of two submanifolds
$Z_1$ and $Z_2$,
each of which is identified diffeomorphically with $Z$, and $Z_1\cap Z_2=\partial
Z_1=\partial Z_2$. There is a doubled map $Dr\colon\thinspace DM\to DZ$ which, for
each $i$,
restricts to a map from  $M_i$ to $Z_i$ that is identified with $r$;
and there is a doubled action of $G$ on $DM$ which, for
each $i$,
restricts to an action on  $M_i$ that is identified with the
action of $G$ on $M$. The hypotheses of the proposition continue to
hold when $M$, $Z$ and $r$ are replaced by  $DM$, $DZ$ and $Dr$, and
$G$ acts on $DM$ by the doubled action. By the case of the proposition
already proved, the map $Dq\colon\thinspace 
(DM)/G  \to (DZ)/G$ induced by $Dr$ is an orbifold fibration. Now
since $Z_1/G$ is a suborbifold of $(DZ)/G$, and
$M_1/G=(Dq)^{-1}(Z_1)$, the restricted map $q_1=Dq|(M_1/G)\colon\thinspace M_1/G\to
Z_1/G$ is also an orbifold fibration. The conclusion follows.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- claim-13: body_md -->
\label{invertible}
For every point 
$z\in F_0$, 
the linear map $d\eta_z\colon\thinspace T_zV\to
T_{\eta(z)}(Z\times F_0)$ is invertible.
<!-- end claim-13 -->
<!-- custom-47: body_md -->
{Orbifold $I$--fibrations}\label{Def orbifold I-bundle}
By specializing the notion of an orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--fibration (resp.\ orbifold ${{\mathcal F}}$--bundle) defined in \S\ref{Def:OrbifoldFiberBundle} to the case where ${{\mathcal F}}$
is the $1$--manifold $I=[0,1]$, we obtain the notion of an
\emph{orbifold $I$--fibration} 
(resp.\ \emph{orbifold $I$--bundle}). 


If $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}}\to{{\mathcal H}}$ is an $I$--fibration,
the \emph{vertical boundary of ${{\mathcal P}}$}, denoted $\partial_\mathrm{v} {{\mathcal P}}$, is
defined to be
$q^{-1}(\partial {{\mathcal H}})$,
which according to  \S\ref{vertical weak} is  \emph{a
priori} a weak
suborbifold of ${{\mathcal P}}$. But since $\partial{{\mathcal H}}$ has codimension $1$
in ${{\mathcal H}}$, the codimension of $\partial_\mathrm{v}{{\mathcal P}}$ in ${{\mathcal P}}$ is also
equal to $1$; hence, by Proposition \ref{codim 1 is nice},
$\partial_\mathrm{v}{{\mathcal P}}$ is a suborbifold of ${{\mathcal P}}$ (in the strong sense).
 The \emph{horizontal boundary of ${{\mathcal P}}$},
denoted $\partial_\mathrm{h} {{\mathcal P}}$, is the $\partial I$--bundle over ${{\mathcal H}}$
obtained by restricting $q$. 
It follows that every non-interior point of ${{\mathcal P}}$ belongs to either $\partial_\mathrm{v} {{\mathcal P}}$ or $\partial_\mathrm{h} {{\mathcal P}}$, and the intersection $\partial_\mathrm{v} {{\mathcal P}} \cap \partial_\mathrm{h} {{\mathcal P}}$ is exactly the set of $2$--corner points of ${{\mathcal P}}$.
If ${{\mathcal P}}$ is orientable, then  $\partial_\mathrm{h}
{{\mathcal P}}$ is the orientation cover of ${{\mathcal H}}$
(see \S\ref{Orbifold covers}).
In particular, if we assume  ${{\mathcal P}}$ is orientable, then $\partial_\mathrm{h} {{\mathcal P}}$ is disconnected if and only if ${{\mathcal H}}$ is orientable.
<!-- end custom-47 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{Ex:FiberedDisk}
Let $A = {\mathbb S}^1 \times I$.
Then the projection $q \colon\thinspace A \to {\mathbb S}^1$ is an $I$--fibration.
Now, suppose $\lambda \colon\thinspace A \to A$ is an involution acting by reflection on both ${\mathbb S}^1$ and $I$.
The quotient ${{\mathcal P}} = A / \langle \lambda \rangle$ is a $2$--orbifold
with underlying space ${\mathbb B}^2$ and two cone points of order
$2$. Furthermore, ${{\mathcal P}}$ admits an $I$--fibration over 
${{\mathcal J}} \doteq {\mathbb S}^1 / \langle \lambda \rangle$. Compare \cite[Example
2.34]{CHK:OrbifoldBook}.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- custom-48: body_md -->
{Fibrations and cleanliness}
\label{clean fibration}
If a compact, orientable $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal P}}$ is equipped with an
$I$--fibration, then $({{\mathcal P}},\partial_\mathrm{v}{{\mathcal P}})$ is a clean\ pair. Indeed,
we observed in \S\ref{Def orbifold I-bundle} that $\partial_\mathrm{v}{{\mathcal P}}$ is
a suborbifold of ${{\mathcal P}}$ (in the strong sense), establishing Condition \eqref{Clean2}. Conditions \eqref{Clean3} and \eqref{Clean4}
of the definition in \S\ref{Clean pairs}  follow from the
definition of a fibration.
<!-- end custom-48 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{fibered annular}
Let ${{\mathcal A}}$ be a compact connected $2$--orbifold which is an $I$--bundle 
over a closed $1$--orbifold ${{\mathcal J}}$. Then ${{\mathcal A}}$ is annular.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Since the fibers of ${{\mathcal A}}$ are quotients of $I$, and have non-empty
boundary by \S\ref{folded},
we have
$\partial {{\mathcal A}} \neq \emptyset$.
Thus it follows from \cite[Theorem 2.22]{CHK:OrbifoldBook} that ${{\mathcal A}}$ is very good.

Consequently, ${{\mathcal A}}$ 
is covered by a compact orientable $2$--manifold $\widetilde{{\mathcal A}}$ that is itself an $I$--bundle over a closed base. 
Thus $\chi(\widetilde{{\mathcal A}}) = 0$, 
hence $\widetilde{{\mathcal A}}$ is an annulus, and the result follows.
