<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{Cor:VertBoundaryStructure}
Let ${{\mathcal P}}$ be a compact $3$--dimensional orbifold $I$--bundle.
Then every component  of $\partial_\mathrm{v} {{\mathcal P}}$  is an annular $2$--orbifold.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The $I$--fibration $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$ induces an $I$--fibration of each
component of $\partial_\mathrm{v} {{\mathcal P}}$ over a component of $\partial {{\mathcal H}}$. 
Observe that each component of $\partial {{\mathcal H}}$ is closed. The conclusion now follows from
Proposition  \ref{fibered annular}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{Lem:SameGroup}
Let  $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$ be an orbifold $I$--fibration, 
where ${{\mathcal P}}$ is an orientable $3$--orbifold.
Let a point $x \in {{\mathcal H}}$ be given and let
$({{\mathcal U}},{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}},{\mathfrak G},\phi,\xi)$ be a standard local trivialization of
$q$  near $x$.
Then an element $g$ of ${\mathfrak G}$ reverses the orientation of $I$ if and only if $g$ reverses the orientation of ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$. 
Furthermore, ${\mathfrak G}$ acts effectively on ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$, and can therefore be identified
with the local group  $G_x^{{\mathcal H}}$ by  \S\ref{Rem:StandardNbdFibration}.
In particular, ${\mathfrak G}$ is either cyclic or dihedral by Proposition
\ref{Prop:LocalStructure2Orbifold}.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Since ${{\mathcal P}}$ is orientable, the diagonal action of ${\mathfrak G}$ 
must preserve the orientation of the product ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}} \times I$. This
implies the first conclusion of the lemma.

Now suppose that some non-trivial element
$g$ of ${\mathfrak G}$ acts trivially on ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$. Since the action of
${\mathfrak G}$ on ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}\times I$ is effective, $g$ must act non-trivially
on $I$. But any non-trivial periodic diffeomorphism of $I$ is conjugate
to a reflection; hence  $g$ reverses the orientation of $I$; as it acts
trivially on  ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$, this contradicts the first assertion.
This shows that
${\mathfrak G}$ acts effectively on ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$. As indicated in the statement, the
remaining assertions follow from 
\S\ref{Rem:StandardNbdFibration} and Proposition
\ref{Prop:LocalStructure2Orbifold}.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- convention-1: body_md -->
\label{no more Gamma}
According to Lemma \ref{Lem:SameGroup}, if  $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$ is an orbifold $I$--fibration, 
where ${{\mathcal P}}$ is an orientable $3$--orbifold, and if
$({{\mathcal U}},{\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}},{\mathfrak G},\phi,\xi)$ be a standard local trivialization of
$q$  near a point $x \in {{\mathcal H}}$, then ${\mathfrak G}$ and ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal U}}}}$ are canonically
identified with the local group $G_x$ and a disk or half-disk $D$. In such a
situation we shall therefore generally denote the  local
trivialization in question by $({{\mathcal U}},D,G_x,\phi,\xi)$.
<!-- end convention-1 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{Lem:FoldedIntervals}
Let  $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$ be an orbifold 
$I$--fibration, where ${{\mathcal P}}$ is an orientable $3$--orbifold.
Let a point $x\in{{\mathcal H}}$ be given.
If $x \in  {\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}$, 
the fiber $q^{-1}(x)$    is a folded arc.
If $x \notin  {\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}$, the
 fiber $q^{-1}(x)$  is diffeomorphic to $I$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
By \S\ref{Rem:StandardNbdFibration} and \S\ref{no more Gamma},
we may fix a standard local trivialization 
$({{\mathcal U}}, D, G_x,\phi,\xi)$ near $x$.
The fiber $q^{-1}(x)$ is diffeomorphic to $\big( \{x\}\times I \big)/G_x$, and
is therefore a folded arc if and only if the action of the local group $G_x$ on
$I$ is not orientation-preserving. 
By  Lemma \ref{Lem:SameGroup}, this is in turn equivalent to saying
that the action of $G_x$ on
$D$ is not orientation-preserving, i.e.\ that 
$x \in {\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- custom-49: body_md -->
{$I$--bundles have nonsingular corners}\label{why nonsingular}
Recall that if a compact,
orientable $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal P}}$ admits an $I$--fibration, then $({{\mathcal P}},
\partial_\mathrm{v} {{\mathcal P}})$ is a clean\ pair
by
\S\ref{clean fibration}, 
and hence that ${{\mathcal P}}$ has nonsingular $2$--corners by
\S\ref{Clean pairs}.

Recall also from 
\S\ref{what's a node}
that in a compact, orientable $3$--orbifold with 
nonsingular
corners, every singular stratum is either a
node or a cone stratum. 
For the  $I$--bundle case, we have the following stronger statement.
<!-- end custom-49 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{Prop:IBundleSingLocus}
Let  $q$
be an $I$--fibration of a compact, orientable $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal P}}$ over
a $2$--orbifold ${{\mathcal H}}$.
Then for every singular stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal P}}$, exactly one of the
following alternatives holds:
 \begin{enumerate}[\:\:(i)]
 \item\label{Itm:Vert} 
$\sigma$ is a cone stratum of some order $n$, and its closure in ${{\mathcal P}}$ is a
fiber over
a cone point of order $n$ or a bi-mirror point of order $2n$. Such a stratum $\sigma$ will be
called \emph{vertical}. 
\item\label{Itm:Horiz} 
$\sigma$ is a cone stratum of order $2$,  its image under $q$ is a
mirror stratum $\tau$ of  
${{\mathcal H}}$, and $q|\sigma$ is a diffeomorphism between $\sigma$ and
$\tau$ (which are smooth manifolds by 
Assertion \ref{was too}).
Such a stratum $\sigma$ will be
called  \emph{horizontal}. 
\item\label{dihedral alternative}
$\sigma=\{u\}$
for some dihedral node $u$,
which is a terminal node of two oriented horizontal $1$--strata (of
order $2$), 
and of one oriented vertical $1$--stratum which
projects to a bi-mirror point of ${{\mathcal H}}$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
We denote by $Q\colon\thinspace{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}\to{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal H}}}}$ the 
underlying map of 
$q$.
    
For each point $x \in {{\mathcal H}}$, 
we fix a standard local trivialization 
$({{\mathcal U}}_x, D_x, G_x,\phi_x,\xi_x)$ near $x$, following the conventions of \S\ref{Rem:StandardNbdFibration}
and \S\ref{no more Gamma}.
By
\S\ref{Rem:StandardNbdFibration}, there is a standard chart $(U_x,D_x,\Phi_x,G_x)$ centered at $x$, where
 $U_x={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal U}}}}_x$.
For each $x \in {{\mathcal H}}$, we set ${{\mathcal W}}_x = q^{-1}({{\mathcal U}}_x)$, an open suborbifold of ${{\mathcal P}}$.



According to Proposition \ref{Prop:LocalStructure2Orbifold}, every
point of ${{\mathcal H}}$ is a nonsingular point, a cone point, a mirror point
or a bi-mirror point. Hence for a singular stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal P}}$,
at least one of the following alternatives must hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item\label{Itm:SomeNonsing} For some $z\in\sigma$, the point $Q(z)$ is nonsingular.
\item\label{Itm:SomeCone} For some $z\in\sigma$, the point $Q(z)$ is a cone point.
\item\label{Itm:EveryMirror} For \emph{every} $z\in\sigma$, the point $Q(z)$ is a mirror point.
\item\label{Itm:SomeBiMirror} For some $z\in\sigma$, the point $Q(z)$ is a bi-mirror
  point.
\end{enumerate}



If \eqref{Itm:SomeNonsing} holds, and if we choose a point $z\in\sigma$ such that $x\doteq
Q(z)$ is nonsingular, then $G^{{\mathcal H}}_x=\{1\}$. Hence ${{\mathcal W}}_x$, 
which by Definition~\ref{Def:OrbifoldFiberBundle} is orbifold-diffeomorphic to 
 $(D_x\times {{\mathcal F}} )/G_x$, is a manifold, and $z\in
  {{\mathcal W}}_x$ is a nonsingular point; this is a contradiction,
  since $\sigma$ is a singular stratum. Thus Case \eqref{Itm:SomeNonsing} cannot occur.

If \eqref{Itm:SomeCone} holds, and if we choose a point $z\in\sigma$ such that $x\doteq
Q(z)$ is 
a cone point of order 
$n > 1$, then 
$G_x \cong {\mathbb Z} / n{\mathbb Z}$ acts on $D_x$
by
rotations. 
Since every $g \in G_x$ preserves the orientation
  of $D_x$, Lemma~\ref{Lem:SameGroup} implies that $G_x $ acts
  trivially on the $I$ factor of $D_x \times I$. Hence  $G_x $ acts
  on the cylinder $D_x \times I$ 
by rotations about the axis $\{0\}\times I$. Thus the singular set
of  ${{\mathcal W}}_x$ is the closed arc  $Q^{-1}(x)$. It follows that
$Q^{-1}(x)$ is  a vertical cone stratum of order $n$ of ${{\mathcal P}}$, in the sense defined in
the statement of the Proposition. Since this vertical stratum contains $z$,
it must coincide with $\sigma$. 
Thus Alternative \eqref{Itm:Vert} of the conclusion of the proposition holds in this case.

If \eqref{Itm:EveryMirror} holds, then since $\sigma$ is connected, $Q(\sigma)$ must be
contained in a single mirror stratum $\tau$ of ${{\mathcal H}}$.
Define $S = \overline{\sigma}\cap Q^{-1}(\tau)$, and observe that $\sigma \subset S$, hence $S \neq \emptyset$.

Consider an arbitrary point $w$ of
$S$. Since $v\doteq Q(w)\in\tau$,
the point $v$ is a mirror point. Hence
the generator $g$ of $G _v\cong {\mathbb Z}/2{\mathbb Z}$ acts on $D_v$ by a
  reflection; by  Lemma~\ref{Lem:SameGroup}, $g$ acts on $I$ by a reflection as well. The
  $3$--dimensional action of $g$ is
a composition of reflections through two perpendicular planes,
  which is a $\pi$--rotation about a horizontal open line segment in $D_v \times I$.
Thus the singular locus of ${{\mathcal W}}_v$ is an open arc $A$ which
contains $w$ and is contained
in an order-$2$ cone stratum $\sigma'$ of ${{\mathcal P}}$; and $Q$ maps $A$
diffeomorphically onto an arc in the mirror stratum  of ${{\mathcal H}}$
containing $v$, namely $\tau$. Furthermore, since $A$ is the full singular locus of ${{\mathcal W}}_v$, and $Q|A$ is one-to-one, the only singular point in the fiber $Q^{-1}(v)$ is $w$ itself.

In particular, $A$ is a
neighborhood of $w$ relative to  $\Sigma_{{\mathcal P}}$; since $w\in
S\subset\overline{\sigma}$, the arc $A$ must meet $\sigma$. Hence
$\sigma'=\sigma$, which shows that $\sigma$  is a cone stratum of order
$2$, and that $w\in\sigma$.
Since $w$ was an arbitrary point of $S$, we have shown that
$S\subset\sigma$. 
We have already observed the reverse inclusion $\sigma\subset S$. Since each point $w \in S = \sigma$ is the only singular point of its fiber, it follows that $Q | \sigma$ is one-to-one and  is therefore a diffeomorphism to its image.

It follows that $Q(\sigma)$ is an open subset of $\tau$. But since $\sigma=S=\overline{\sigma}\cap
Q^{-1}(\tau)$, it follows that $Q(\sigma)=\tau\cap Q(\overline{\sigma}) = Q(\overline{\sigma})$, hence $Q(\sigma)$ is also closed in $\tau$. We conclude that $Q | \sigma$ is a diffeomorphism onto the stratum $\tau$, verifying that $\sigma$ is a horizontal stratum in the sense defined in the statement
of the Proposition; 
that is, Alternative \eqref{Itm:Horiz} of the conclusion holds.


Finally, suppose that \eqref{Itm:SomeBiMirror} holds.
Let us choose a point $z\in\sigma$ such that $x\doteq Q(z)$ is a
bi-mirror point. Then $G_x$ is a dihedral group of 
some finite order $2n$. 
There is a cyclic index--$2$ subgroup $C$ of $G_x$ that acts
on $D_x$ by rotations; since the action of $C$ preserves the
orientation of $D_x$, it must act trivially on $I$ by Lemma
\ref{Lem:SameGroup}. Thus $C$ acts on $D_x \times I$ by rotations about a vertical axis. On the other hand, every element of $G_x - C$
reverses the orientation of $D_x$, and by Lemma
\ref{Lem:SameGroup} it must also reverse the orientation of
$I$. Hence such an element acts on $D_x \times I$ as a product of
two reflections, which is  a $3$--dimensional $\pi$--rotation about a
horizontal axis. From this one deduces that  $G_x$ acts on $D_x \times I$ as the orientation-preserving symmetries of a prism over a regular $n$--gon.
The singular set 
of the orbifold ${{\mathcal W}}_x$ is the union of a
closed arc $\alpha=Q^{-1}(x)$ with two half-open arcs $\beta_1$ and
$\beta_2$, such that
$\alpha\cap\beta_1=\alpha\cap\beta_2=\beta_1\cap\beta_2=\{ u \}$ for
some point $u $. If we set $\alpha'=\alpha-\{u \}$, and $\beta_i'=\beta_i-\{u \}$ for $i=1,2$, then the singular strata of  ${{\mathcal W}}_x$ are
$\{u \}$, $\alpha'$, $\beta_1'$ and $\beta_2'$. The map
$Q$ 
maps each $\beta_i'$ diffeomorphically onto an open arc in a mirror
stratum of ${{\mathcal H}}$.



Since $\alpha'$ and $\{u \}$ do not meet the frontier of ${{\mathcal W}}_x$ in ${{\mathcal P}}$, they are singular strata of ${{\mathcal P}}$. 
Each $\beta_i$ is
contained in a singular stratum $\gamma_i$ of ${{\mathcal P}}$. 
Since $z\in Q^{-1}(x)=\alpha=\alpha'\cup\{u \}$, 
the stratum $\sigma$
is equal to either $\{u \}$ or $\alpha'$, which is a vertical stratum over a
bi-mirror point in the language of the proposition.

Let us summarize what we have shown so far in this case:

\begin{claim}\label{what if four}
If \eqref{Itm:SomeBiMirror} holds for a given singular stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal P}}$, then
$\sigma$ is contained in a single fiber $Q^{-1}(x)$ for a bi-mirror point $x \in {{\mathcal H}}$.
Furthermore, either
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(a)] 
\item $\sigma$ is a vertical stratum over $x$, or
\item 
$\sigma = \{u \}$, and $u $ has a neighborhood in
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal P}}$ which is the union of a
closed arc $\alpha=Q^{-1}(x)$ with two half-open arcs $\beta_1$ and
$\beta_2$, such that
$\alpha\cap\beta_1=\alpha\cap\beta_2=\beta_1\cap\beta_2=\{u \}$. Furthermore,
if we set $\alpha'=\alpha-\{u \}$, and $\beta_i'=\beta_i-\{u \}$ for $i=1,2$, then 
$\alpha'$ is a vertical stratum of ${{\mathcal P}}$, while each $\beta_i'$ is
contained in a
stratum and is mapped diffeomorphically by $Q$ onto an open arc in a mirror
stratum of ${{\mathcal H}}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{claim}

To complete the proof of the proposition, we
note that 
 Alternative (a) of \ref{what if four} implies Alternative \eqref{Itm:Vert} of the
conclusion 
of the proposition.
Now suppose that (b) holds, and
for $i=1,2$, let $\gamma_i$ denote the stratum of ${{\mathcal P}}$ that
contains $\beta_i$. (Note that $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ are not
necessarily distinct.)
For each $\gamma_i$, one of the alternatives \eqref{Itm:SomeNonsing}--\eqref{Itm:SomeBiMirror} must hold.
We have seen that \eqref{Itm:SomeNonsing} cannot occur, and that \eqref{Itm:SomeCone} implies
that the given stratum $\gamma_i$ is 
contained in a fiber, which is
impossible since $q$ maps $\beta_i'$ diffeomorphically to its image. If
\eqref{Itm:SomeBiMirror} holds 
for $\gamma_i$, then  \ref{what if four} likewise implies that $\gamma_i$ is contained in a fiber, which we have seen is impossible.
Hence each stratum $\gamma_i$ must satisfy \eqref{Itm:EveryMirror}, and is therefore 
a horizontal stratum, in the sense defined in the statement of the
proposition. In particular the $\gamma_i$ are cone strata of order $2$; and it
follows that $u $ is a dihedral node,
which is a terminal node of two oriented horizontal $1$--strata of
${{\mathcal P}}$, and of one oriented vertical $1$--stratum which
projects to 
a bi-mirror point of ${{\mathcal H}}$. 
This is Alternative \eqref{dihedral alternative} of the conclusion of the proposition.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- claim-14: body_md -->
\label{what if four}
If \eqref{Itm:SomeBiMirror} holds for a given singular stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal P}}$, then
$\sigma$ is contained in a single fiber $Q^{-1}(x)$ for a bi-mirror point $x \in {{\mathcal H}}$.
Furthermore, either
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(a)] 
\item $\sigma$ is a vertical stratum over $x$, or
\item 
$\sigma = \{u \}$, and $u $ has a neighborhood in
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal P}}$ which is the union of a
closed arc $\alpha=Q^{-1}(x)$ with two half-open arcs $\beta_1$ and
$\beta_2$, such that
$\alpha\cap\beta_1=\alpha\cap\beta_2=\beta_1\cap\beta_2=\{u \}$. Furthermore,
if we set $\alpha'=\alpha-\{u \}$, and $\beta_i'=\beta_i-\{u \}$ for $i=1,2$, then 
$\alpha'$ is a vertical stratum of ${{\mathcal P}}$, while each $\beta_i'$ is
contained in a
stratum and is mapped diffeomorphically by $Q$ onto an open arc in a mirror
stratum of ${{\mathcal H}}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end claim-14 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{Seifert}
The structural information provided by Proposition \ref{Prop:IBundleSingLocus} is closely related to the well-known structure of orbifold Seifert fibered spaces \cite[Section 2.8]{CHK:OrbifoldBook}. For the sake of this discussion, an \emph{orbifold Seifert fibered space} is an orientable $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}$ equipped with an ${\mathbb S}^1$--fibration over a $2$--orbifold ${{\mathcal H}}$. (This generalizes Example~\ref{Ex:SeifertManifold}, where ${{\mathcal M}}$ was required to be a manifold.) In an orbifold Seifert fibered space ${{\mathcal M}}$, it is once again true that every $1$--stratum of $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ is either vertical or horizontal, with every vertical $1$--stratum projecting to a cone point and every horizontal $1$--stratum projecting homeomorphically to a mirror stratum of $\Sigma_{{\mathcal H}}$.
Furthermore, just as in Proposition \ref{Prop:IBundleSingLocus}, every $0$--stratum is a dihedral node projecting to a bi-mirror point.
Compare \cite[Pages 41--42]{CHK:OrbifoldBook}.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- custom-50: body_md -->
{Classical $I$--bundle s}
  \label{classical}
We define a  \emph{classical $I$--bundle} to be a topological $3$--manifold (with
boundary) $P$ equipped with a
locally trivial fibration $Q\colon\thinspace P\to H$ in which the base  $H$ is a topological
$2$--manifold (with
boundary), and the fiber is the unit interval $I$. 
In this situation,
$Q\colon\thinspace P\to H$ may be referred to as a
\emph{classical $I$--fibration}. 
A subset of $P$
is called  \emph{vertical} if it is saturated in the fibration $Q$. We define the {\it
  vertical boundary} of $P$ to be the submanifold $\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl}
P\doteq Q^{-1}(\partial H)$
of $\partial P$, and its  \emph{horizontal boundary, } denoted $\partial_\mathrm{h}^{\rm cl}
P$, to be its
associated $\partial I$--bundle. 

We note that smooth and PL structures play no role in this definition.
<!-- end custom-50 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{Lem:IBundleTotalSpaceOriBase}
Let $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$ be an orbifold $I$--bundle,
where ${{\mathcal P}}$ is compact, connected, orientable, and $3$--dimensional. Suppose in addition that
${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}=\emptyset$.
Then the 
underlying
 map $Q \colon\thinspace {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal H}}}}$ of $q$ 
is a classical $I$--fibration.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Let $P \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}$ and $H \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal H}}}}$.  Since 
${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}=\emptyset$,
Proposition~\ref{Prop:LocalStructure2Orbifold} says that the singular
locus $\Sigma_{{\mathcal H}}$ consists entirely of cone points; hence
Proposition~\ref{Prop:IBundleSingLocus} implies that $\Sigma_{{\mathcal P}}$ consists
entirely of vertical strata. Thus each stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal P}}$ is
the fiber over some cone point of ${{\mathcal H}}$, which will be denoted
$x_\sigma$.
In particular we have $Q^{-1}(\Sigma_{{\mathcal H}})=\Sigma_{{\mathcal P}}$.

By \S\ref{Rem:StandardNbdFibration}, for each cone point $x\in{{\mathcal H}}$,
we may fix a standard local trivialization near $x$, which by
\S\ref{no more Gamma} we may denote
$({{\mathcal U}}_x, D_x, G_x,\phi_x,\xi_x)$. We may choose the local
trivializations in such a way that  ${{\mathcal U}}_x\cap{{\mathcal U}}_{x'}=\emptyset$ 
whenever $x$ and $x'$ are distinct cone points.

Since ${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}} =
\emptyset$, Lemma~\ref{Lem:FoldedIntervals} says that for every
$x\in{{\mathcal H}}$, the fiber $\sigma_x\doteq q^{-1}(x)$ is
diffeomorphic to $I$;
  that is, the action of $G_x$ on $I$ is trivial.
Hence $(D_x\times I )/G_x $  may be canonically identified with
$(D_x /G_x)\times I $. On the other hand, according to
the definition of a local trivialization, $\phi_x$ induces an orbifold
diffeomorphism between $D_x /G_x$ and ${{\mathcal U}}_x$. Under these
identifications,  $\xi_x$ becomes a smooth map from $D_x\times I$
to $q^{-1}({{\mathcal U}}_x)$, which induces an orbifold diffeomorphism $\eta_x$
  between ${{\mathcal U}}_x\times I $  and $q^{-1}({{\mathcal U}}_x)$. The
  commutativity of the diagram in \S\ref{Def:OrbifoldFiberBundle} then
  says that $q\circ\eta_x\colon\thinspace {{\mathcal U}}_x\times I\to{{\mathcal U}}_x$ is the projection
  to the first factor. Thus $Q \colon\thinspace P \to H$  is a locally trivial fibration of topological spaces.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{Lem:SameEuler}
Let $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$ be an orbifold $I$--fibration,
where ${{\mathcal P}}$ is compact, connected, orientable, and $3$--dimensional. 
Then $\chi({{\mathcal P}}) = \chi({{\mathcal H}})$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Set $P = {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}$ and $H = {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal H}}}}$. 
Let $Q \colon\thinspace {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal H}}}}$ denote the 
underlying map of 
$q$. 

We first consider the case in which ${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}=\emptyset$. 
In this case,  $\Sigma_{{\mathcal H}}$ consists of finitely many cone points. It
follows from Proposition~\ref{Prop:IBundleSingLocus} that
for every  cone point $x$  of ${{\mathcal H}}$, the set $Q^{-1}(x)$ is a cone
stratum of ${{\mathcal P}}$, and furthermore that $Q^{-1}(\Sigma_{{\mathcal H}})$ is the
full singular set of ${{\mathcal P}}$. Since ${{\mathcal P}}$ is connected, ${{\mathcal H}}$ is
also connected; this implies that $H-\Sigma_{{\mathcal H}}$ is the unique smooth
stratum of ${{\mathcal H}}$, while $P-\Sigma_{{\mathcal P}}=Q^{-1}(H-\Sigma_{{\mathcal H}})$ is the unique smooth
stratum of ${{\mathcal P}}$.

In particular, the assignment $\sigma\mapsto Q^{-1}(\sigma)$ is a
bijection between the strata of ${{\mathcal H}}$ and those of
${{\mathcal P}}$. By \eqref{that's what chi is}, we have
$$
\chi({{\mathcal H}})=\sum_\sigma\frac{ \chi(\overline \sigma) - \chi(
\overline{\sigma}-\sigma)}{ \mathop{\rm ord}(\sigma)} \qquad {\rm and} \qquad
\chi({{\mathcal P}})=\sum_\sigma\frac{ \chi\big(\overline{Q^{-1}( \sigma)}\big) - \chi\big(
\overline{Q^{-1}(\sigma)}-Q^{-1}(\sigma)\big)}{ \mathop{\rm ord}(Q^{-1}(\sigma))},
$$
where $\sigma$ ranges over the strata of ${{\mathcal H}}$. Hence, to establish
the conclusion in this case, it suffices to show that for every
stratum $\sigma$ of ${{\mathcal H}}$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{what we need}
\chi\big(\overline{Q^{-1}(\sigma)}\big)=\chi(\overline{\sigma}), \quad \chi\big(
\overline{Q^{-1}(\sigma)}-Q^{-1}(\sigma)\big)=\chi(
\overline{\sigma}-\sigma),
\quad{\rm and}\quad
\mathop{\rm ord}(Q^{-1}(\sigma))=\mathop{\rm ord}(\sigma).
\end{equation}

If $\sigma$ is a singular stratum of ${{\mathcal H}}$, then $\sigma$ consists
of  a cone
point of some order $p$. By Proposition~\ref{Prop:IBundleSingLocus},
the cone stratum $Q^{-1}(\sigma)$ also
has order $p$, and $Q^{-1}(\sigma)$
is a closed topological arc since ${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}=\emptyset$.  The sets
$\overline{\sigma}-\sigma$ and
$\overline{Q^{-1}(\sigma)}-Q^{-1}(\sigma)$
are empty. This establishes 
\eqref{what we need} when $\sigma$ is a singular stratum.

If $\sigma$ is the nonsingular stratum of ${{\mathcal H}}$, then $Q^{-1}(\sigma)$
is the nonsingular stratum of ${{\mathcal P}}$; we have
$\overline{\sigma}=H$ and $\overline{Q^{-1}(\sigma)}=P$. The equality
of $\chi\big(\overline{Q^{-1}(\sigma)}\big)$ and $\chi(\overline{\sigma})$ therefore
follows from Lemma~\ref{Lem:IBundleTotalSpaceOriBase}. 
To establish the equality
$\chi\big(
\overline{Q^{-1}(\sigma)}-Q^{-1}(\sigma)\big)=\chi(
\overline{\sigma}-\sigma)$ in this situation, we note that 
$\overline{\sigma}-\sigma=\Sigma_{{\mathcal H}}$ and that
$\overline{Q^{-1}(\sigma)}-Q^{-1}(\sigma)=\Sigma_{{\mathcal P}}$. Since the
components of $\Sigma_{{\mathcal P}}$, which are closed arcs, are in bijective
correspondence with the points that make up $\Sigma_{{\mathcal H}}$, the desired
equality follows. Finally, the orders of $\sigma$ and $Q^{-1}(\sigma)$
are both equal to $1$. Thus \eqref{what we need} is proved for all
strata, and the proof of the lemma in the case
${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}=\emptyset$ is complete.


Now suppose that ${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}} \neq \emptyset$. Let ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}\to{{\mathcal H}}$ denote the 
  reflective\ covering of ${{\mathcal H}}$ (see \S\ref{reflective}). Lemma~\ref{Lem:InducedCover} provides an induced $I$--fibration
$\widetilde q \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to {\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}$ and a two-fold covering ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to {{\mathcal P}}$. Since ${\Sigma_{{\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}}^{\rm mir}} = \emptyset$, the case of the lemma that we have already proved, combined with the multiplicativity of Euler characteristic under covers, implies
\[
2 \chi({{\mathcal P}}) = \chi({\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}}) = \chi({\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}) = 2 \chi({{\mathcal H}}).
\]
Thus $\chi({{\mathcal P}}) = \chi({{\mathcal H}})$, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{hands-on part}
Suppose that $P_0$ is a classical $I$--bundle, and that $A$ is a two-dimensional, compact 
vertical submanifold of $\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P_0$ (so that each component of
$A$ is a topological annulus or disk). 
Suppose that $ T \colon\thinspace A \to A$ is
an involution which leaves invariant each fiber of 
$P_0$ contained in $A$,
and reverses the orientation of each such
fiber. 
Let $f \colon\thinspace P_0 \to E$ be the quotient map that identifies every orbit of $T$ to a point.
Then $E $ is a topological $3$--manifold, and
may be given the structure of
a classical $I$--bundle\ in such a way that $f$ 
carries $\overline{(\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P_0)-A}$ onto a vertical
submanifold of $\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} E$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Let  $Q \colon\thinspace P_0\to H_0$ denote the 
locally trivial fibration that defines the classical $I$--bundle\ structure of
$P_0$. 
The hypothesis implies that there is a compact $1$--manifold
$\alpha\subset\partial H_0$ such that $A=Q^{-1}(\alpha)$. The
hypothesis also implies that $A$ may be identified homeomorphically
with $\alpha\times I$ 
in such a way that $Q|A$ is the projection to the
first factor, and $ T (x,t)=(x,1-t)$ for every $(x,t)\in A$.


From this description of $T$, it follows that $E$ is a topological
$3$--manifold, and that there is a homeomorphism
$\eta\colon\thinspace P_0\to E$ which agrees with the quotient map $f \colon\thinspace P_0\to E$
outside an arbitrarily small neighborhood of $A$ in $P_0$. 
See Figure~\ref{Fig:Folding}.
In
particular, if $N$ is a regular neighborhood of $A$ relative to
$\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P_0$, which is a vertical submanifold of $P_0$,  we may take $\eta$ to be the identity on
$\overline{(\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P_0)-N}$. 
It now follows that
$Q'\doteq Q\circ\eta^{-1}\colon\thinspace E\to H_0$ is a classical $I$--fibration. 
In terms of the $I$--bundle structure of $E$ defined by $Q'$, the map 
$f$ carries $\overline{(\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P_0)-N}$ onto a vertical
submanifold of $\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} E$. Hence, by precomposing $Q'$ with a
self-homeomorphism of $E$ that maps $A$ onto $N$, we obtain a
classical $I$--fibration with the required properties.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{Prop:IBundleTotalSpace}
Let $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$ be an orbifold $I$--bundle,
where ${{\mathcal P}}$ is compact, connected, orientable, and $3$--dimensional.
Then $P \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}$,
regarded as a topological $3$--manifold,
may be given the structure of
a classical $I$--bundle\ in such a way that ${{\rm X}_{\partial_\mathrm{v} {{\mathcal P}}}}$ is a vertical
submanifold of $\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P$.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
If  ${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}=\emptyset$, 
then the result follows from Lemma~\ref{Lem:IBundleTotalSpaceOriBase}. 

Now, assume 
that ${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}\ne\emptyset$.
Let $\theta \colon\thinspace{\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}\to{{\mathcal H}}$ denote the 
  reflective\ covering of ${{\mathcal H}}$ (see \S\ref{reflective}).
Set $H={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal H}}}}$ and $\widetilde H={{\rm X}_{{\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}}}$, and let $\Theta \colon\thinspace\widetilde H\to H$
denote the underlying
map of $\theta $.
According to \S\ref{reflective}, we may write $\widetilde H$ as a union of
two topological $2$--submanifolds $H_0$ and $H_1$, such that
$\Theta $ maps $H_i$  homeomorphically  onto $H$ for $i=0,1$.

Lemma~\ref{Lem:InducedCover} provides an induced $I$--fibration
$\widetilde q \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to {\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}$ and a covering map $\upsilon  \colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \to {{\mathcal P}}$.
According to that lemma,
we have $\deg \upsilon =\deg \theta =2$; hence  ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}}$ has a
unique non-trivial deck transformation $\delta$, which is an
involution.
Lemma~\ref{Lem:InducedCover} also implies that there is a commutative diagram
\begin{equation}\label{involution-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}
 {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \arrow[r, "\delta"] \arrow[d, "\widetilde q"] & {\widetilde{{{\mathcal P}}}} \arrow[d, "\widetilde q"] \\
{\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}} \arrow[r, "\lambda"] & {\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
where $\lambda$ denotes the non-trivial deck transformation
of ${\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}$.

Let $Q \colon\thinspace P \to H$, $\widetilde Q \colon\thinspace \widetilde P \to \widetilde H$,  $\Upsilon  \colon\thinspace \widetilde P \to P$, $\Lambda\colon\thinspace\widetilde H\to\widetilde H$ and
$\Delta\colon\thinspace\widetilde P\to\widetilde P$ denote the 
underlying maps of 
$q$, $\widetilde q$,  $\upsilon $, $\lambda$ and $\delta$
respectively. 

For $i=0,1$, set $P_i=\widetilde Q^{-1}(H_i)$. Since
$\widetilde H=H_0\cup H_1$, we have $\widetilde P=P_0\cup P_1$. 
According to \S\ref{reflective}
we have $R\doteq H_0\cap H_1=\Theta ^{-1}({\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}})$, 
and the involution
$\Lambda$ of $\widetilde H$  interchanges $H_0$ and $H_1$.
It follows
that $A\doteq P_0\cap P_1=\widetilde Q^{-1}(R)$, 
and, in view of the commutativity of \eqref{involution-diagram},  that the involution $\Delta$
of $\widetilde P$  interchanges $P_0$ and $P_1$. In particular $\Delta$ leaves $A$ 
invariant, and therefore restricts to a self-homeomorphism
of $A$ which  \emph{a priori} is periodic with period at most $2$. From \S\ref{reflective}
we also have that $\Lambda$ fixes $R$ 
pointwise, which with the commutativity of \eqref{involution-diagram},
implies that  $\Delta$
leaves the set  $E_{\widetilde x}\doteq \widetilde Q^{-1}({\widetilde x})\subset A$ invariant for each point ${\widetilde x}\in R$.

If ${\widetilde x}$ is any point of $R$, then $x\doteq
\theta ({\widetilde x})\in {\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}$, so that Lemma \ref{Lem:FoldedIntervals}
gives that the orbifold fiber $q^{-1}(x)$ is a folded arc. On the
other hand, since ${\Sigma_{{\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}}^{\rm mir}}=\emptyset$,  Lemma \ref{Lem:FoldedIntervals}
gives that the orbifold fiber $\widetilde q^{-1}({\widetilde x})$ is diffeomorphic to
$I$. Hence $ \Delta |E_{\widetilde x}$ is an 
orientation-reversing  involution of $E_{\widetilde x}$ for each ${\widetilde x}\in R$. In
particular $ \Delta | A $ is an involution.


According to \S\ref{reflective}, we have
${\Sigma_{{\widetilde{{{\mathcal H}}}}}^{\rm mir}}=\emptyset$. 
Lemma~\ref{Lem:IBundleTotalSpaceOriBase} then implies that $\widetilde Q \colon\thinspace \widetilde P \to \widetilde H$ is a locally trivial fibration of topological spaces. Hence if we set
$P_0=\widetilde Q^{-1}(H_0)$, then
$\widetilde Q$ restricts to a locally trivial fibration  $Q_0\colon\thinspace P_0\to H_0$, and $P_0$ thus acquires the structure of a
classical $I$--bundle. From the perspective of this structure, $A$ is a vertical
subset of $P_0$, and the sets of the form $E_{\widetilde x}$ for ${\widetilde x}\in R$ are
the fibers of $P_0$ contained in $A$. Thus $\Delta | A $ is an involution
of the vertical set $A$ which restricts to an orientation-reversing
involution of each fiber contained in $A$. Furthermore, Proposition
\ref{Prop:LocalStructure2Orbifold} implies that ${\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}$ is a
one-dimensional topological submanifold of the boundary of the
topological $2$--manifold $H$;
since $\Theta $ maps $H_0$  homeomorphically  onto $H$, it follows that 
$R$ is a
one-dimensional topological submanifold of $\partial H_0$, and
hence that $A$ is a two-dimensional topological submanifold of 
$\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P_0$. Thus $P_0$, $A$ and $ T \doteq \Delta | A$ satisfy the
hypotheses of Lemma  \ref{hands-on  part}.


We have $\Upsilon \circ \Delta=\Upsilon $. Since $\Upsilon  \colon\thinspace \widetilde P \to P$ is
surjective, and 
since $\Delta$  interchanges $P_0$ and $P_1$
and leaves $A$ invariant, 
the map $\Upsilon _0\doteq
\Upsilon |P_0\colon\thinspace P_0\to P$ 
induces a continuous bijection from
the quotient space $E$ defined in Lemma \ref{hands-on part} to
$P$. Since $E$ is compact and $P$ is Hausdorff, this induced
map is a homeomorphism. It therefore follows from Lemma \ref{hands-on part} that $P$ 
may be given the structure of
a classical $I$--bundle\ in such a way that 
 $\Upsilon _0(\overline{(\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P_0)-A})$ is a vertical
submanifold of $\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P$.


Now Proposition \ref{Prop:LocalStructure2Orbifold} implies that
${{\rm X}_{\partial{{\mathcal H}}}}=\overline{(\partial H)-{\Sigma_{{{\mathcal H}}}^{\rm mir}}}$.
Hence 
\[
\overline{(\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P_0)-A}
= (Q\circ \Upsilon _0)^{-1}({{\rm X}_{\partial{{\mathcal H}}}})=\Upsilon _0^{-1}({{\rm X}_{\partial_\mathrm{v}{{\mathcal P}}}}),
\]
which with the surjectivity of $\Upsilon _0$ shows that
 $\Upsilon _0(\overline{(\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P_0)-A})={{\rm X}_{\partial_\mathrm{v}
  {{\mathcal P}}}}$. It now follows that ${{\rm X}_{\partial_\mathrm{v}{{\mathcal P}}}}$ is a vertical
submanifold of $\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- custom-51: body_md -->
{Conventions about smoothness and transversality}\label{AccordantConvention}
In the remainder of the paper, 
whenever we consider an orientable $3$--orbifold  ${{\mathcal M}}$, it will be  understood that
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ is equipped with
an ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant smooth  structure, which exists in view of
Proposition \ref{smooth underlying}.

In \S\ref{Suborbifolds-of-3orbifolds}, we described
the correspondence between orientable, neatly\  embedded
 $2$--suborbifolds of ${{\mathcal M}}$ and neatly\  embedded
two-dimensional submanifolds  of $M\doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$. This correspondence will be used very
freely, as will the connection --- also explained in \S\ref{Suborbifolds-of-3orbifolds} ---
between the singular structure of such suborbifolds of ${{\mathcal M}}$ and the 
size and weight (see \S\ref{size 'n' stuff}) of the corresponding two-dimensional submanifolds  of
$ {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$. 
We will also freely use the fact (see \S\ref{new splitting}) that an orientable $3$--orbifold can be split along a neatly
embedded $2$--suborbifold. This includes the special
case that for a clean\ submanifold $K$ of $M$ with frontier transverse
to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, we have a well-defined suborbifold ${\Omega_{K}}$.
<!-- end custom-51 -->
<!-- custom-52: body_md -->
{Clean\ suborbifolds}\label{clean}

We shall say that a suborbifold with corners 
${{\mathcal Y}}$ of a compact, orientable
$3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$
is  \emph{clean}  if
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}}{{\mathcal Y}}$ 
    is defined and is a neatly\ 
    embedded suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$, and
  \item\label{clean pair part} $({{\mathcal Y}}, \mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}}{{\mathcal Y}})$ is a clean\ pair 
 (see \S\ref{Clean pairs}).
  \end{enumerate}
  Note that \eqref{clean pair part} includes the information that
  $\dim{{\mathcal Y}}=3$ and that $\dim\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}}{{\mathcal Y}}=2$. 


If ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a \emph{weak} suborbifold of a compact, orientable
$3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$ such that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}}{{\mathcal Y}}$ 
    is defined and is a neatly\ 
    embedded \emph{weak} suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$, and if Condition \eqref{clean pair part} above holds, then it follows from an observation made in 
\S\ref{Clean pairs} that ${{\mathcal Y}}$ and $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}}{{\mathcal Y}}$  are suborbifolds of ${{\mathcal N}}$ (in the strong sense), and hence that ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a clean suborbifold. This will make it simpler to recognize clean suborbifolds.


Specializing to the case in which ${{\mathcal N}}$ is a manifold, we obtain the notion of a
clean\ submanifold with corners. 

Note that if
${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a clean suborbifold with corners of a compact, orientable $3$--orbifold
 ${{\mathcal N}}$ (so that  $N\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ has a fixed ${{\mathcal N}}$--accordant smooth structure by 
the convention of
\S\ref{AccordantConvention}),
then the induced smooth manifold structure on
 $Y\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Y}}}}$ is ${{\mathcal Y}}$--accordant, and $Y$ 
 is a clean submanifold with corners of $N$. To go
in the other direction, by analogy with   \S\ref{Suborbifolds-of-3orbifolds}, if $Y$ is a clean submanifold with corners of $N$, and $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N} Y$ is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}$, then ${\Omega_{Y}}$ is defined. Furthermore, by Proposition~\ref{codim 1 is nice},
${\Omega_{Y}}$ is a suborbifold in the strong sense.
It then follows readily that ${\Omega_{Y}}$ is a clean suborbifold.


It follows from \S\ref{Clean pairs}
that if ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a clean\  suborbifold with corners of a compact, orientable
$3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$ then ${{\mathcal Y}}$ has nonsingular corners.

If ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a clean suborbifold with corners of\  ${{\mathcal N}}$, 
then with the conventions established in
\S\ref{Suborbifolds}, the suborbifolds (with boundary)
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal Y}}$,
${{\mathcal Y}}\cap\partial{{\mathcal N}}$
and
${{{\mathcal N}}-{{\mathcal Y}}}$
of ${{\mathcal N}}$, and the suborbifold with corners
$\overline{{{\mathcal N}}-{{\mathcal Y}}}$, are defined.
Note  that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal Y}}$ is
a neatly\  embedded $2$--suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$ and that 
$\overline{{{\mathcal N}}-{{\mathcal Y}}}$ is a clean suborbifold with corners of\  ${{\mathcal N}}$.
Note also that  $\partial({{\mathcal Y}}\cap\partial{{\mathcal N}})=
\partial(\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal Y}})$. 

If ${\mathscr Y}$ is a family of clean\  suborbifolds
with
$2$--corners in ${{\mathcal N}}$, and if for all ${{\mathcal Y}},{{\mathcal Y}}'\in{\mathscr Y}$, the
suborbifold ${{\mathcal Y}}\cap{{\mathcal Y}}'$ is defined and is a union of common
frontier components of ${{\mathcal Y}}$ and ${{\mathcal Y}}'$, then
$\bigcup_{{{\mathcal Y}}\in{\mathscr Y}} {{\mathcal Y}}$ is defined and is a clean suborbifold with corners of\ 
${{\mathcal N}}$. 


We have the following immediate consequence of Lemma \ref{split injective}: 

\begin{claim}\label{because split injective}
If ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a clean suborbifold with corners of\  an orientable $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$, and $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal Y}}$ is
$\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal N}}$, then ${{\mathcal Y}}$ and $\overline{{{\mathcal N}}-{{\mathcal Y}}}$ are
$\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal N}}$.
\end{claim}
<!-- end custom-52 -->
<!-- claim-15: body_md -->
\label{because split injective}
If ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a clean suborbifold with corners of\  an orientable $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$, and $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal Y}}$ is
$\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal N}}$, then ${{\mathcal Y}}$ and $\overline{{{\mathcal N}}-{{\mathcal Y}}}$ are
$\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal N}}$.
<!-- end claim-15 -->
<!-- custom-53: body_md -->
{Bindinglike and pagelike suborbifolds}
\label{PagelikeBindinglike}

Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be a compact, orientable $3$--orbifold. 


A suborbifold
with corners
${{\mathcal B}}$ 
of ${{\mathcal N}}$ is said to be  \emph{bindinglike} if
\begin{itemize}
\item ${{\mathcal B}}$ is
  a clean suborbifold with corners of\  ${{\mathcal N}}$,
\item the orbifold obtained by straightening the angles\ of
  ${{\mathcal B}}$ 
(which is defined since the clean suborbifold ${{\mathcal B}}$ has nonsingular corners  by \S\ref{clean}; see \S\ref{what's sta})
is a solid toric orbifold, and 
\item $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal B}}$ 
is a non-empty
disjoint union of annular $2$--orbifolds which are $\pi_1$--injective in
${{\mathcal B}}$.
\end{itemize}

This definition 
implies that 
${{\mathcal B}}$ is connected and that 
${{\mathcal B}}\cap\partial{{\mathcal N}}$ 
is also a non-empty
disjoint union of annular $2$--orbifolds  which are $\pi_1$--injective in
${{\mathcal B}}$.

According to the discussion of solid toric orbifolds
in \S\ref{spherical etc}, if ${{\mathcal B}}$ is a bindinglike suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$ then
$B \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal B}}}}$ either is  a topological ball,
i.e.\ is homeomorphic 
 to ${\mathbb B}^3$, or is  a topological solid torus,
i.e.\ is homeomorphic to ${\mathbb B}^2\times{\mathbb S}^1$.
Furthermore, if  $B$ is
a topological solid torus, then the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr} B$ are annuli with non-zero
winding number in $B$.


A  suborbifold
with corners
${{\mathcal P}}$  
of ${{\mathcal N}}$ is said to be  \emph{pagelike} if 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal P}}$ is defined and neatly embedded in ${{\mathcal N}}$, and
${{\mathcal P}}$ 
admits an  $I$--fibration over a 
  connected $2$--orbifold 
with non-positive (orbifold) Euler characteristic,
such that
  $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal P}}$ is the vertical boundary of the $I$--bundle ${{\mathcal P}}$.
It then follows from \S\ref{clean fibration} that $({{\mathcal P}},\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}} {{\mathcal P}})$ is a clean pair. By an observation made in \S\ref{clean}, this in turn implies that ${{\mathcal P}}$ and $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}}{{\mathcal P}}$  are suborbifolds of ${{\mathcal N}}$ in the strong sense, and hence that ${{\mathcal P}}$ is a clean suborbifold. 

Note that this definition
implies that ${{\mathcal P}}$ is connected,
and has non-positive Euler
characteristic (by Lemma~\ref{Lem:SameEuler}), 
that ${{\mathcal P}}\cap\partial{{\mathcal N}}$ is the horizontal
boundary of the $I$--bundle ${{\mathcal P}}$, and that   $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal P}}$ is $\pi_1$--injective in
${{\mathcal P}}$. Note as well that  $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal P}}$ may be empty.
<!-- end custom-53 -->
<!-- custom-54: body_md -->
{Orbifold books of $I$--bundles}
\label{wuzza book}
We define an \emph{orbifold book of $I$--bundles} to be a compact,
connected, orientable $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$ equipped with two
clean\ suborbifolds with corners
${\mathscr B}$ and ${\mathscr P}$ such that 
\begin{itemize}
\item every component of ${\mathscr B}$ is purely
bindinglike, and  every
  component of ${\mathscr P}$ is purely
pagelike; and
\item ${\mathscr B}\cup{\mathscr P}={{\mathcal N}} $
and ${\mathscr B}\cap{\mathscr P}=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{\mathscr B}=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{\mathscr P}$.
\end{itemize}

The components of ${\mathscr B}$ and ${\mathscr P}$ are respectively
 called the \emph{bindings}  and the \emph{pages} of ${{\mathcal N}}$. 

Note that according to this definition, each component of
${\mathscr B}\cap{\mathscr P}$ is an   
orientable, annular,  neatly\  embedded suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$,
and ${\mathscr P}$ admits
an $I$--fibration in which ${\mathscr P}\cap\partial{{\mathcal N}}$ is the
horizontal boundary and ${\mathscr B}\cap{\mathscr P}$ is the vertical boundary.

Note also that every binding has a
virtually cyclic fundamental group, and that no page has a
virtually cyclic fundamental group.

It follows from an observation made in \S\ref{clean} that any union of
pages and bindings of a book of $I$--bundles ${{\mathcal N}}$ is a clean
suborbifold with corners of ${{\mathcal N}}$. Furthermore, it follows from
Assertion \ref{because split injective} and the discussion in 
\S\ref{PagelikeBindinglike} that 
every page or binding of a book of $I$--bundles ${{\mathcal N}}$ --- and more
generally  every union of pages and bindings of ${{\mathcal N}}$ --- is
$\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal N}}$, 
and so is the frontier of every page or binding. These observations
will be used extensively in the following sections.

When the structure of an orbifold book of $I$--bundles on ${{\mathcal N}}$ has
been fixed, we denote the suborbifolds ${\mathscr B}$ and ${\mathscr P}$
by  ${\mathscr B}_{{\mathcal N}}$ and ${\mathscr P}_{{\mathcal N}}$ respectively. Furthermore,
if ${{\mathcal S}}$ is any union of components of $\partial {{\mathcal N}}$,
we set
${\mathscr A}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}={\mathscr B}_{{\mathcal N}}\cap{{\mathcal S}}$ and
${\mathscr H}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}={\mathscr P}_{{\mathcal N}}\cap{{\mathcal S}}$;
  these are well-defined $2$--suborbifolds of ${{\mathcal S}}$. Note  that every component of ${\mathscr A}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}$ has
 Euler characteristic $0$,  that every component of ${\mathscr H}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}$ has
strictly negative Euler characteristic, and that ${\mathscr A}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}\cup {\mathscr H}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}={{\mathcal S}}$.
We also set 
${\bf C}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}={\mathscr A}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}\cap
{\mathscr H}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal S}}}{\mathscr A}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal S}}}{\mathscr H}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}$,
a well-defined $1$--manifold. It can be deduced from Lemma~\ref{split injective} that ${\bf C}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal S}}}$ is $\pi_1$--injective in the orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$.

We mention as a mnemonic device that ${\mathscr A}$ stands for ``annular,'' ${\mathscr H}$ stands for ``horizontal boundary,'' and~${\bf C}$ stands for ``curves.''
<!-- end custom-54 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{nodes of a book}
If ${{\mathcal N}}$ is a book of $I$--bundles then every node of the
$3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$ is dihedral.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Set ${\mathscr B}={\mathscr B}_{{\mathcal N}}$ and ${\mathscr P}={\mathscr P}_{{\mathcal N}}$. Let
${\mathscr F}$ denote the common frontier of ${\mathscr B}$ and ${\mathscr P}$. By
\S\ref{wuzza book}, ${\mathscr F}$ is an orientable, neatly\  embedded
suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$; hence by \S\ref{Suborbifolds-of-3orbifolds},
${{\rm X}_{{\mathscr F}}}$ is a neatly embedded two-dimensional submanifold of
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$, transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}$.
This implies that every node of ${{\mathcal N}}$ is either a
node of ${\mathscr B}$ or a node of ${\mathscr P}$. It follows from
the description of solid toric orbifolds given in
 \S\ref{spherical etc} that the components of ${\mathscr B}$ only have dihedral nodes.
On the other hand, the components of
${\mathscr P}$ are pagelike, which by definition implies that they admit
$I$--fibrations over $2$--orbifolds; according to Proposition
\ref{Prop:IBundleSingLocus}, it follows that every node of ${\mathscr P}$
is dihedral.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{saddy}
Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be an orbifold book of $I$--bundles, and let ${{\mathcal J}}$ be a
connected
  two-dimensional
suborbifold of   $\partial {{\mathcal N}}$ with
$\partial {{\mathcal J}}\subset{\bf C}_{{{\mathcal N}},\partial{{\mathcal N}}}$. Suppose that
$\chi({{\mathcal J}})=0$. Then ${{\mathcal J}}$ is a component of ${\mathscr A}_{{{\mathcal N}},\partial{{\mathcal N}}}$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Let us set ${\mathscr A}={\mathscr A}_{{{\mathcal N}},\partial{{\mathcal N}}}$,
${\mathscr H}={\mathscr H}_{{{\mathcal N}},\partial{{\mathcal N}}}$, and ${\bf C} = {\bf C}_{{{\mathcal N}},\partial{{\mathcal N}}}$.
Since $\partial {{\mathcal J}}\subset{\bf C}$, 
the orbifold ${{\mathcal J}}$ is a
union of components of ${\mathscr A}$ and of ${\mathscr H}$. Since the
components of  ${\bf C} = {\mathscr A}\cap
 {\mathscr H}$ are simple closed curves, $\chi({{\mathcal J}})$ is the sum of
 the Euler characteristics of components of  ${\mathscr A}$ and of
 ${\mathscr H}$ contained in ${{\mathcal J}}$. We observed in \S\ref{wuzza book} that every component of ${\mathscr A}$ has
 Euler characteristic $0$, while every component of ${\mathscr H}$ has
strictly negative Euler characteristic. Hence ${{\mathcal J}}$ is a
union of components of ${\mathscr A}$, and since it is connected, the
conclusion follows.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{just four simpler}
Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be
an orbifold book of $I$--bundles. Let ${{\mathcal B}}$ be a binding of
${{\mathcal N}}$, and suppose that  the frontier of $B\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal B}}}}$ in
$N\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ has a component $F$
which is an annulus, and that each component of $\partial F$ bounds a disk
in $\partial N$ 
whose weight\ (see 
\S\ref{size 'n' stuff}) 
is $4$. Then $B$ is a topological $3$--ball and $F$ is the full frontier of $B$ in $N$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{what weight 4 means}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma \ref{just four simpler}, it follows from
the definition of an orbifold book of $I$--bundles that a component $C$
of
$\partial F$ is $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal N}}$. 

In general, 
if $D\subset{{\mathcal N}}$ is a disk, transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}$ and bounded by a
curve $C$ which is $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal N}}$, 
the condition that $D$ has weight\ $4$ is
equivalent to saying that $D$ has exactly two singular points, each of which has
  order $2$. 
This is because, if  $D$ had exactly one singular point
  and its order were $4$, then  ${\Omega_{D}}$ would be a discal orbifold,
  a contradiction to the $\pi_1$--injectivity of $C$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ denote the components of $\partial F$. By
hypothesis, each $C_i$ bounds a weight--$4$ disk
$D_i\subset\partial N$. 
It follows from Remark \ref{what weight 4 means}
 that ${{\mathcal D}}_i\doteq{\Omega_{D_i}}$ has Euler
characteristic $0$.
Furthermore, since $F$ is a frontier component of 
$B = {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal B}}}}$,
we have  $C_i\subset{\bf C}_{{{\mathcal N}},\partial{{\mathcal N}}}$.
Hence by Lemma \ref{saddy}, 
each ${{\mathcal D}}_i$ is a component of ${\mathscr A}\doteq{\mathscr A}_{{{\mathcal N}},\partial{{\mathcal N}}}$; that is, $D_i$ is
a component of ${\bf A} \doteq {{\rm X}_{{\mathscr A}}}$
for $i=1,2$. Since the
boundaries $C_1$ and $C_2$ of $D_1$ and $D_2$ are distinct,
the components $D_1$ and $D_2$ of ${\bf A}$ are distinct
and therefore disjoint. Hence $W\doteq D_1\cup F\cup D_2$ is a
topological
$2$--sphere. 
We may regard ${\bf B}\doteq{{\rm X}_{{\mathscr B}_{{\mathcal N}}}}$ as a topological
manifold, each of whose components is a topological ball or solid
torus, and $B$ is one of these components.
Since $F\subset \partial B\subset\partial{\bf B}$ and
$D_i\subset {\bf A} \subset\partial{\bf B}$, we have $W\subset\partial{\bf B}$; and
since $F\subset B$, the component of ${\bf B}$ containing $W$ must be
$B$. Since $W$ is a topological sphere,  $B$ must be a topological ball, and $W$ must be the entire
boundary of $B$. In particular we have $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NB=F$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- custom-55: body_md -->
{Harmless components}
\label{Def:Harmless}
Let  ${{\mathcal P}}$ be a page of an orbifold book of $I$--bundles ${{\mathcal N}}$. 
Set $N={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ and $P={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}$.
Note that any component  $V$ of 
$\overline{N -P}$ is a union of underlying sets of
pages and bindings. As observed in \S\ref{wuzza book}, this implies that
${\Omega_{V}}$ is defined and is a clean\ suborbifold with corners of ${{\mathcal N}}$, so that
$V$ is a clean\ submanifold with corners  of $N$.

We
shall say that $V$ is \emph{harmless} if 
$V$ is  a topological ball and $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N}V$ 
is connected. 

Note that since ${{\mathcal P}}$ is a page of the orbifold book of $I$--bundles
${{\mathcal N}}$, each component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}}{{\mathcal P}}$ is an annular orbifold, and
hence each component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N}P$ is 
an annulus or a disk. 
It follows
that the
frontier of each harmless\ component of 
$\overline{N-P}$
is  an  annulus or a disk. 



Hence if $V$ is a harmless
   component of $\overline{N-P}$, then $V$ is diffeomorphic to either 
${\mathbb B}^2\times I$ or ${\mathbb B}^3 \cap ({\mathbb R}^2 \times {\mathbb R}_+)$. Under the diffeomorphism, $\mathop{\rm Fr}_N V$ corresponds to $\partial {\mathbb B}^2 \times I$ or ${\mathbb B}^2 \times \{0\}$, respectively.
<!-- end custom-55 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{Prop:ExpandedPage}
Let ${{\mathcal P}}$ be a page of an orbifold book of $I$--bundles ${{\mathcal N}}$. 
Set $N={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ and $P={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}$.
Let ${\bf V}$ be the union of some number of 
harmless components  of  
$\overline{N-P}$.
  Let ${\widehat P} $ denote the clean submanifold  with corners
    $P\cup {\bf V}$ 
 of $N$.
Then the following hold:

\begin{enumerate}[\:\:$(1)$]
 \item \label{ExpandedPageFrontier} 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N{\widehat P} = \mathop{\rm Fr}_N P - \mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\bf V}$.
\item\label{ExpandedPageIsBundle} ${\widehat P} $,
regarded as a topological $3$--manifold,
may be given the structure of
a classical $I$--bundle\ in such a way that 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N{\widehat P}$ is a vertical subset of $\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} {\widehat P}$.
\item\label{ExpandedPageEuler} The Euler characteristic of ${\widehat{{\mathcal P}}} \doteq {\Omega_{{\widehat P}}}$ is strictly negative,
and each component of
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{\widehat{{\mathcal P}}}={\Omega_{\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N} {\widehat P} }}$
 is an annular $2$--orbifold.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Set ${{\mathcal F}} =\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}} {{\mathcal P}}$ and $F={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal F}}}}=\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP$.
According to the definition of a
harmless component, each component of ${\bf V}$ is a  component  of  
$\overline{N-P}$ having connected frontier. This proves conclusion \eqref{ExpandedPageFrontier}.

Since ${{\mathcal N}}$ is an orbifold  book of $I$--bundles, the page ${{\mathcal P}}$
of ${{\mathcal N}}$ is equipped with an
orbifold
 $I$--bundle structure in which ${{\mathcal F}} $
is the vertical boundary. It therefore follows from  Proposition
\ref{Prop:IBundleTotalSpace} that the
topological
$3$--manifold 
$P$ may be given the structure of a classical $I$--bundle\ 
in such a way that 
$F $
is a
vertical subset of 
$\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P$.



Consider an arbitrary component $V$ of ${\bf V}$. Since $V$ is harmless,
it is homeomorphic to ${\mathbb B}^3$, and its frontier is a single annulus or
a single disk. Since $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N }V$ is a component of $F $, it is a
vertical submanifold of
$\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P$; thus the classical\ fibration of $ P$
restricts to a 
locally trivial fibration of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N }V$ over a $1$--manifold, with
fiber $I$. Since $N={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ is orientable, this fibration of
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_NV$ is trivial.



Now observe that any trivial topological
 fibration, with fiber $I$, of a topological annulus or disk contained in $\partial {\mathbb B}^3$ extends to
a trivial fibration of $ {\mathbb B}^3$. Hence the fibration 
of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N }V$
obtained by restriction extends to a trivial $I$--fibration of $V$. Since this
holds for every $V$, the $I$--fibration of $ P$ extends to a classical\
$I$--fibration of ${\widehat P} $. 
By Conclusion~\eqref{ExpandedPageFrontier},
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N }{\widehat P} $ is a union of components of $F $; hence 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N }{\widehat P} $ is a vertical submanifold of $ P $, and is therefore
a vertical submanifold of ${\widehat P}  $. 
Since $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N }{\widehat P} $ is
vertical in ${\widehat P}$ and is contained in the boundary of the
topological $3$--manifold ${\widehat P}$, it is in fact contained in 
$\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} {\widehat P}$.
This establishes Conclusion~\eqref{ExpandedPageIsBundle}.


Next
note that ${\widehat{{\mathcal P}}}\doteq {\Omega_{{\widehat P}}} $ is a union  of pages
and bindings; hence we may write ${\widehat{{\mathcal P}}}={\mathscr B}'\cup{\mathscr P}'$,
where ${\mathscr B}'$ is a union of bindings of ${{\mathcal N}}$ and ${\mathscr P}'$ is a
union of pages. Since ${{\mathcal P}}\subset{\mathscr P}'$, we have
${\mathscr P}'\ne\emptyset$; and by the definition of an orbifold book of
$I$--bundles, each component of ${\mathscr P}'$ has strictly negative
orbifold Euler characteristic. Hence $\chi({\mathscr P}')<0$. Each
component of ${\mathscr B}'$ 
becomes a solid toric orbifold upon straightening the angles, 
and hence
$\chi({\mathscr B}')=0$. Each component of ${\mathscr B}'\cap{\mathscr P}'$ is a
component of the vertical boundary of the $I$--bundle ${\mathscr P}'$ and
is therefore annular; thus $\chi({\mathscr B}'\cap{\mathscr P}')=0$. It now
follows from the discussion in \S\ref{Euler} that
$\chi({\widehat{{\mathcal P}}})=\chi({\mathscr P}')+\chi({\mathscr B}')-\chi({\mathscr P}'\cap{\mathscr B}')<0$. 

Finally, by Conclusion~\eqref{ExpandedPageFrontier},
each component of
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}} {\widehat{{\mathcal P}}} $
is also a component of
  $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal P}}=\partial_\mathrm{v}{{\mathcal P}}$,
and is therefore annular
 by
Corollary \ref{Cor:VertBoundaryStructure}. This establishes Conclusion~\eqref{ExpandedPageEuler}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- custom-56: body_md -->
{Smoothing subsurfaces}
\label{what's smoothing}

We will frequently encounter situations in which ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a closed,
orientable $3$--orbifold, and we have a topological surface
$F$ in $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ and a closed $1$--manifold $L\subset F\cap (M-\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}})$
such that 
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(1)]
\item $L$ and
$F-L$ are smooth submanifolds of $M$, and $F-L$ is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$; and 
\item
 there exist a tubular
neighborhood $J$ of $L$ in $M-\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, and
a diffeomorphism of $J$ onto ${\mathbb B}^2\times L$ carrying $F\cap
J$ onto $V\times L$, where $V$ is a union of two line radii in
${\mathbb B}^2$. 
\end{enumerate}
Such a surface $F$ is called \emph{smoothable}.
If $F$ is closed and smoothable, there is a topological ambient isotopy of
$M$ which is supported on $J$ and carries $F$ onto a smooth
closed surface $F'$ which is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$. We shall say that such a surface $F'$ is \emph{obtained  by smoothing $F$.} We observe that in this situation, 
$\mathop{\rm size}(F')=\mathop{\rm size}(F)$.
<!-- end custom-56 -->
<!-- custom-57: body_md -->
{Minimal essential spheres}
\label{minimal}
Specializing the definition of an essential suborbifold given in
\S\ref{Pi1Injective}, we shall say that a (smooth) $2$--sphere 
$S$ in a closed orientable $3$--manifold $M$ is \emph{essential} if $S$ does not bound a $3$--ball in $M$.

Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable $3$--orbifold,
and set $M={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$.
 We define an \emph{${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential sphere} in $M$ to
 be a $2$--sphere $S\subset M$ such that 
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(1)]
\item $S$ is essential in $M$, 
\item $S$ is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, and 
\item
for every
$2$--sphere $S'\subset M$ which is essential in $M$ and
transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, we have $\mathop{\rm size}(S')\ge\mathop{\rm size}(S)$. 
(See \S\ref{size 'n' stuff}. The sizes of $S$ and $S'$ are finite by transversality.)
\end{enumerate}
We define a \emph{strongly ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential sphere} in $M$ to be an ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential sphere $S$ in $M$ such that for every ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential sphere $S'$ in $M$, we have $\mathop{{\rm weight}}(S')\ge\mathop{{\rm weight}}(S)$.


Note that if ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a closed, orientable $3$--orbifold and $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ contains an essential $2$--sphere, then $M$ contains 
a strongly ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential sphere.
<!-- end custom-57 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{it's incompressible}
Let 
${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable, hyperbolic $3$--orbifold, and let
$S$ be an ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential $2$--sphere in $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$. 
Then ${{\mathcal S}} \doteq {\Omega_{S}} $ is essential in ${{\mathcal M}}$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
We first observe that ${{\mathcal S}}$ is not the boundary of a three-dimensional discal
suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$.  Indeed, if ${{\mathcal H}}$ were a discal suborbifold
with $\partial {{\mathcal H}}={{\mathcal S}}$, then by \S\ref{spherical etc}, $
H\doteq
{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal H}}}}\subset
{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ would be a $3$--ball with 
$\partial H=S$, 
and this is impossible since $S$ is essential
in $M$.


It remains
to show that 
${{\mathcal S}}$ is $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal M}}$. 
Since ${{\mathcal M}}$ is hyperbolic, it is very good. 
According to
Proposition \ref{when injective},
proving the $\pi_1$--injectivity of ${{\mathcal S}}$ amounts to showing that
if ${{\mathcal D}}$ is a two-dimensional
orientable
  discal suborbifold of
${{\mathcal M}}$ with ${{\mathcal D}} \cap {{\mathcal S}} = \partial {{\mathcal D}}$, then $\partial {{\mathcal D}}$ bounds a discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal S}}$. 
Since ${{\mathcal D}}$ is an orientable discal suborbifold, $ D \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal D}}}}$ is a 
disk transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$
  (see \S\ref{Suborbifolds-of-3orbifolds}),
 with $\mathop{\rm size}(D)\le 1$ and $\mathop{\rm size}(\partial D) = 0$.



Now the curve $C\doteq\partial D$ bounds two disks $ D_1,  D_2 \subset
S$. 
For $i = 1, 2$, 
set $n_i =\mathop{\rm size} ( D_i)$,
so that $\mathop{\rm size}(S) = n_1 + n_2$. 
According to \S\ref{what's smoothing}, the sphere $S_i$
obtained by smoothing
$D \cup  D_i$ has the same size as $D \cup  D_i$; hence
$\mathop{\rm size} S_i = n_i + \mathop{\rm size}( D) \le n_i + 1$. 
Since $S$ is essential, at least one of the $S_i$ is essential, so we
may assume after relabeling that $S_1$ is essential. The minimality
of $S$ then gives $\mathop{\rm size}(S) \le \mathop{\rm size}(S_1)$, i.e.\ $n_1 + n_2 \le
\mathop{\rm size}(S_1) \le n_1 + 1$. So $n_2 \le 1$, and it follows that ${\Omega_{
  D_2}}$
  (which is defined by virtue of transversality)
is a discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal S}}$ bounded by $\partial {{\mathcal D}}$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{Thm:HomeoTypeSpherePieces} 
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable, hyperbolic $3$--orbifold.
Let $S$ be
a 
strongly
${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential $2$--sphere in $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}} $. Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be a component of ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {\Omega_{S}} $. 
Assume that ${{\mathcal N}}$ admits the structure of an orbifold book of $I$--bundles. Then $ N \doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}} $ is homeomorphic 
 either to ${\mathbb S}^2 \times I$ or 
to a manifold obtained  from a non-trivial lens space by removing the
interiors of one or two closed $3$--balls.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{Cor:HomeoTypeReducible}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable, hyperbolic $3$--orbifold.
Suppose that 
$M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}} $ 
contains  a  
strongly
${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential $2$--sphere $S$ such that each component of
${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {\Omega_{S}} $ 
admits the structure of
a book of $I$--bundles. Then 
$M$ 
is homeomorphic to either a connected sum of two non-trivial lens spaces, or the connected sum of ${\mathbb S}^2\times {\mathbb S}^1$ with a possibly trivial lens space.
{\hfill$\square$}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{was-height def}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable $3$--orbifold, and let $S$ be a
$2$--sphere in 
$M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$
which is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$. Let $N = M {\backslash \backslash} S$, and let $\iota \colon\thinspace N \to M$ be the canonical immersion.
If $C$ is any simple closed curve in 
$\partial N$, disjoint from $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, 
then 
$C$ bounds two disks  $D_1, D_2 \subset \partial N$. 
  Recall from \S\ref{new splitting} that
$N$ is the underlying space of a
$3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal N}} =  {{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {\Omega_{S}}$, 
so that $\mathop{\rm size}(D_i)$ is well-defined.
We define the \emph{spanning size} of $C$ to be
\[
{\rm spanning size}(C) = \min \{ \mathop{\rm size}(D_1), \: \mathop{\rm size}(D_2) \}.
\]
Note that  $\mathop{\rm size}(D_i) = \mathop{\rm size}(\iota(D_i))$, and therefore ${\rm spanning size}(C)\le\mathop{\rm size}(S)/2$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{Lem:SameSpanningSize}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable $3$--orbifold. Set $M={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$.
Suppose that $S$ is an ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential $2$--sphere in $M$. 
Let $N$ be a component of $M {\backslash \backslash} S$, with canonical immersion $\iota\colon\thinspace  N \to M$.
Suppose that $J$ is a neatly\  embedded annulus in $N$ with $\mathop{\rm size}(\iota(J))=0$. 
Then the two components of $\partial J$ have 
the same spanning size.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Let $n = \mathop{\rm size}(S)$. Let $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ denote the components of $\partial J$.
Set $s = 
{\rm spanning size}(\gamma)$ and $s' = {\rm spanning size}(\gamma')$.
By symmetry, it is enough to show that $s'\geq s$.

Let $\Psi$ denote the component of $\partial N = \iota^{-1}(S)$ containing
$\gamma$.
Then $\gamma$ bounds two disks in $ \Psi$; they may be labeled
$\Delta_1$ and $\Delta_2$ in such a way that
$\mathop{\rm size}(\Delta_1)=s$ and
$\mathop{\rm size}(\Delta_2)=n-s$. 
Furthermore, $\gamma'$ bounds a disk $E\subset \partial N$ with $\mathop{\rm size}(E)=s'$.


Note that $J\cup E$ is a
smoothable topological disk whose boundary is $\gamma$, and that
$\mathop{\rm size}(J\cup E)=s'$. By a small non-ambient isotopy in $N$ we may
replace $J\cup E$ by a 
smooth,
 neatly\  embedded disk $\Delta_3$ in $N$ with
$\partial \Delta_3=\gamma$ and $\mathop{\rm size}(\Delta_3)=s'$. 
(This is a  minor variant on the smoothing operation described in
\S\ref{what's smoothing}.)

The disks $\Delta_i$ for $i=1,2,3$ all have boundary $\gamma$, and any two of
them intersect precisely in $\gamma$. Furthermore,
 the map
$\iota|(\Delta_1 \cup  \Delta_2 \cup \Delta_3)$ is
one-to-one. 
So if we set $D_i=\iota(\Delta_i)$, and $C=\iota(\gamma)$, then the
disks $D_i$ all have boundary $C$,
and any two of them intersect precisely in $C$. We have
$D_1\cup D_2 = \iota(\Psi) = S$.
By  \S\ref{what's smoothing}, for $i=1,2$, the sphere $S_i$  obtained by smoothing $D_i \cup
D_3$ has the same size as $D_i \cup
D_3$.
Since $S$ is essential in $M$, at least one of the spheres $S_1$ and $S_2$ is essential.
Since $S$ is minimal and has size\ $n$, at least one of the inequalities $\mathop{\rm size}(S_1)\ge n$, $\mathop{\rm size}(S_2)\ge n$ holds.

But we have $$\mathop{\rm size}(S_1)=\mathop{\rm size}(D_1)+\mathop{\rm size}(D_3)=\mathop{\rm size}(\Delta_1)+\mathop{\rm size}(\Delta_3)=s+s',$$ and similarly
$\mathop{\rm size}(S_2)=(n-s)+s'$. Furthermore, the definition of size\ gives $s\le n/2$, so that $s\le n-s$. Thus in any event we have $s'+(n-s)\ge n$, so we conclude that $s'\ge s$ as required.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- custom-58: body_md -->
{Spanning size of  an annulus or binding}
\label{what's the point}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable $3$--orbifold. Set $M={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$.
Suppose that $S$ is an ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential $2$--sphere in
$M$. Let $N$ be a component of $M {\backslash \backslash} S$, 
  so that according to the discussion in \S\ref{new splitting}, 
$N$ is canonically identified with ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ for some component
${{\mathcal N}}$ of ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{\Omega_{S}}$.  
If $J$ is a neatly\  embedded annulus in $N$ with $\mathop{\rm size}(\iota(J))=0$, 
then by Lemma \ref{Lem:SameSpanningSize}, the two components of $\partial J$ have 
the same spanning size. This common spanning size\ will be referred to as the
\emph{spanning size\ of $J$}.



Now suppose that ${{\mathcal N}} $  is
equipped with the structure of
an orbifold book of $I$--bundles, and
let ${{\mathcal B}} $ be a 
binding of ${{\mathcal N}}$ such that $B \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal B}}}}$ is a topological solid torus.
Then every component of 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N}B $ or $(\partial N)\cap B $ 
is a size--$0$ annulus. If $A$
is any component of 
$(\partial N)\cap B $, 
then the two components $C_1$ and $C_2$ of $\partial A$ also have the same
spanning size\ because they are isotopic in $\partial
N-(\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}\cap\partial N)$; hence if $J_i$ denotes the component
of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N}B $ containing $C_i$, we have ${\rm spanning size}(J_1)={\rm spanning size}(J_2)$.
Since $\partial B $ 
is connected, it follows that all components of 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N}B $ 
have the same spanning size. Their common spanning size\ will be
called the \emph{spanning size\ of ${{\mathcal B}}$}.
Note that we have defined the spanning size\ of a binding
  ${{\mathcal B}}$ only in
the case where ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal B}}}}$ is  a
topological solid torus
rather than a topological ball (see \S\ref{PagelikeBindinglike}).
<!-- end custom-58 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{therefore}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable, hyperbolic $3$--orbifold.  Suppose that $W$ is a (smooth) $2$--sphere in $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$, transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, such that ${\Omega_{W}} $ is a toric $2$--orbifold. Suppose that the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1({\Omega_{W}})\to\pi_1({{\mathcal M}})$ has infinite image. Then  there is a ball 
$J\subset M$ 
such that $\partial J=W$, and ${\Omega_{J}} $ (which is defined by \S\ref{clean}) is a solid toric $3$--orbifold.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Since ${{\mathcal M}}$ is closed and hyperbolic, it has a finite-sheeted regular cover ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ which is a closed hyperbolic $3$--manifold. Let $p\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}\to {{\mathcal M}}$ denote the covering projection, and $G$ the covering group. Fix a component $T$ of $p^{-1}({\Omega_{W}} )$. Since ${\Omega_{W}} $ is toric, its finite-sheeted manifold covering $T$ is a torus. Since the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1({\Omega_{W}} )\to\pi_1({{\mathcal M}})$ has infinite image, and the covering $p\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}\to {{\mathcal M}}$ is finite-sheeted,
the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1({\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}})$ has infinite image.

Since ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ is closed and hyperbolic, ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ is irreducible and $T$ is compressible in ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$. We recall that a compressible torus in a hyperbolic manifold either is contained in a ball or bounds a solid torus. If $T$ were contained in a ball in ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ then
the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1({\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}})$  would be trivial, a contradiction. Hence $T=\partial V$ for some solid torus $V\subset{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$. 

If $g$ is an arbitrary element of $G$, we have either $g\cdot T=T$ or $(g\cdot T)\cap T=\emptyset$. Hence one of the following four alternatives holds: 
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(i)]
\item\label{Vdisjoint} $(g\cdot V)\cap V=\emptyset$;
\item\label{Vcontains}  $g\cdot V\subset V$; 
\item\label{Vcontained} $g\cdot V\supset V$; or 
\item\label{Vlens} $(g\cdot V)\cup V={\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$. 
\end{enumerate}
If \eqref{Vlens} holds then ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ has a cyclic fundamental group, which is impossible since ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ is a closed hyperbolic $3$--manifold. If \eqref{Vcontains} holds, and if the inclusion given by \eqref{Vcontains} is strict, then $g^n\cdot V$ is a proper subset of $V$ for every integer $n>0$; this is impossible, since $g$ has finite order. Hence \eqref{Vcontains} implies that $T$ is invariant under $g$; and by the same argument, with $g^{-1}$ in place of $g$, \eqref{Vcontained} also implies that $T$ is invariant under $g$. 

We conclude that for each $g\in G$ we have either $(g\cdot V)\cap
V=\emptyset$ or $g\cdot V= V$. Hence $p$ maps 
$V$ 
onto a suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$ which is (orbifold-) diffeomorphic to the
quotient of $V$ by 
${\rm Stab}_G(V)$.
In particular ${{\mathcal J}}\doteq p(V)$ is a solid toric orbifold. We have
$\partial{{\mathcal J}}=p(\partial V)=p(T)={\Omega_{W}} $. Now set $J={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal J}}}}$. By orientability we have $\partial J={{\rm X}_{\partial
  {{\mathcal J}}}}=W$. Since ${{\mathcal J}}$ is a solid toric orbifold and $W$ is a
sphere, it follows
  by \S\ref{spherical etc}
that $J$ is a ball.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{what about}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable, hyperbolic $3$--orbifold.
Suppose that $S$ is a strongly ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential $2$--sphere
in $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$. Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be a component of  ${{\mathcal M}}
{\backslash \backslash} {\Omega_{S}} $.
Suppose that $F$ is a neatly\  embedded disk in
$ N \doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$, transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}$,  such that
${\Omega_{F}} $ 
(which is defined by \S\ref{Suborbifolds-of-3orbifolds})
is an annular orbifold and is $\pi_1$--injective in
${{\mathcal N}}$. Then there is a
  topological
ball $K\subset  N $ such that
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N }K=F$, and ${\Omega_{K}} $ is a bindinglike suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
According to \S\ref{new splitting},
$N$ is
canonically identified with
 a component of 
$M{\backslash \backslash} S$.
Let $\iota \colon\thinspace  N \to M$ denote the 
restriction to $N$ of the canonical immersion of 
$M{\backslash \backslash} S $ in $M$. 
Since $F$ is a disk and ${{\mathcal F}} \doteq {\Omega_{F}} $ is an orientable annular
suborbifold, $F\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}} =\Sigma_{{\mathcal F}} $ consists of two points, both of order
$2$. Now the curve $C\doteq\partial F$ is contained in some component
${\widetilde S}$ of $\partial N $, and bounds two disks $D_1,
D_2 \subset {\widetilde S}$. Set $n_i =\mathop{\rm size} (D_i)$ for $i = 1, 2$
and $n = \mathop{\rm size}(S) = n_1 + n_2$. 
According to  \S\ref{what's smoothing}, for $i = 1, 2$, the sphere $S_i$
obtained by smoothing
$\iota (F \cup D_i)\subset M$ has the same size as $\iota (F \cup
D_i)$; hence
$\mathop{\rm size} S_i = n_i + \mathop{\rm size}(F) = n_i + 2$. 
Since $S$ is essential
  in $M$,
at least one of the $S_i$ is essential,
so we may assume after relabeling that $S_1$ is essential. 
The
minimality of $S$ then gives $\mathop{\rm size}(S) \le \mathop{\rm size}(S_1)$, i.e.\ $n_1 +
n_2 \le \mathop{\rm size}(S_1) = n_1 + 2$. So $n_2 \le 2$. If $n_2$ were at most
$1$, the curve $\partial F=\partial D_2$ would represent the conjugacy
class of an element of finite order in the orbifold fundamental group
$\pi_1({{\mathcal N}})$, contradicting the $\pi_1$--injectivity of the annular
orbifold ${\Omega_{F}} $.
Hence $n_2=2$. It now follows that $\mathop{\rm size}(S_1)=n$, so that $S_1$ is ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal. The strong ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimality of $S$ then implies that $\mathop{{\rm weight}}(S)\le\mathop{{\rm weight}}(S_1)$. 

Since $n_2=2$, the $2$--orbifold ${\Omega_{D_2}}$ has two singular
points, whose orders are integers strictly greater than $1$; we denote 
these integers 
by $p$ and $q$. We then have 
\[
\mathop{{\rm weight}}(S)=\mathop{{\rm weight}}(D_1)+\mathop{{\rm weight}}(D_2)=\mathop{{\rm weight}}(D_1)+p+q. 
\]
On the other hand, since the two singular points of ${\Omega_{F}} $ are of order $2$, we have
\[
\mathop{{\rm weight}}(S_1)=\mathop{{\rm weight}}(D_1)+\mathop{{\rm weight}}(F)=\mathop{{\rm weight}}(D_1)+4. 
\]
The inequality
$\mathop{{\rm weight}}(S)\le\mathop{{\rm weight}}(S_1)$ then becomes $\mathop{{\rm weight}}(D_1)+p+q\le
\mathop{{\rm weight}}(D_1)+4$, so that $p+q\le4$ and hence $p=q=2$. 
Since $S_2$ is obtained by smoothing $\iota(F\cup D_2)$, it follows that
${\Omega_{S_2}}$ 
has four singular points, all of order $2$. Since $S_2$ is a sphere, it follows that ${\Omega_{S_2}}$ is a toric orbifold.
Furthermore, since ${\Omega_{F}} \subset{\Omega_{ S_2}}$ is annular and $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal N}}$,  the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1({\Omega_{S_2}})\to\pi_1({{\mathcal M}})$ has infinite image. We may therefore apply
Lemma \ref{therefore}, with $S_2$ playing the role of $W$, to deduce
that there is a topological ball $J\subset M$ such that $\partial J=S_2$, and
${\Omega_{J}} $ is a solid toric $3$--orbifold.
Hence $\iota(F \cup D_2)$ bounds a topological $3$--ball $K^* \subset
M$, and $K^*$ is isotopic to $J$ by a topological ambient isotopy
of $M$  which is constant on $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$. In particular, straightening the angles\ of  the
orbifold with corners ${{\mathcal K}}^*\doteq{\Omega_{K^*}}$ yields a solid toric orbifold.

Since  $S$ is essential in $M$, we cannot have $S\subset K^*$. Hence 
there is a topological $3$--ball $K \subset N$ whose frontier is $F$,
such that $\iota$ maps $K$ diffeomorphically onto $K^* \subset M$. Now ${\Omega_{K}}$ is a well-defined clean\ suborbifold with corners
 of ${{\mathcal N}}$, and is orbifold-diffeomorphic to
${{\mathcal K}}^*$; thus straightening the angles\ of  
${\Omega_{K}}$ yields a solid toric orbifold. It
then
follows from the definition in \S\ref{PagelikeBindinglike} that ${\Omega_{K}}$ is bindinglike.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- custom-59: body_md -->
{Standing hypotheses and conventions}
\label{standing}
For the remainder
of the section, the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{Thm:HomeoTypeSpherePieces} will be assumed to
hold. Thus it will be understood that we are given a closed,
orientable, hyperbolic $3$--orbifold  ${{\mathcal M}}$ and a 
strongly
${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal essential $2$--sphere $S$ in $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}
$; we shall write ${{\mathcal S}}={\Omega_{S}}$, which is a well-defined suborbifold
of ${{\mathcal M}}$ by 
\S\ref{Suborbifolds-of-3orbifolds}.
It will further be understood that we are given 
 a component  ${{\mathcal N}}$ of ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {\Omega_{S}} $, so that by
\S\ref{new splitting},
${{\mathcal N}}={\Omega_{N}}$ for some component $N$ of $M{\backslash \backslash} S$. It will be assumed that ${{\mathcal N}}$
is equipped with the structure of an orbifold book of $I$--bundles. We
shall write $n=\mathop{\rm size}(S)$.
<!-- end custom-59 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{not more than one, now}
Let ${{\mathscr B}^\ast}$ denote
the union of all bindings of ${{\mathcal N}}$ whose underlying spaces are
topological solid tori, and whose  spanning size\
is $n/2$
