(see \S\ref{what's the point}).
Then each component of $\partial N $ contains at most one component of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathscr B}^\ast}}}\cap\partial N $.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Suppose there is a component ${\widetilde S}$ of $\partial  N $ which contains
two distinct components of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathscr B}^\ast}}}\cap\partial N $, say
$A_1$ and $A_2$. Let $D_1$ denote the component of
$\overline{{\widetilde S}-A_1}$ that contains $A_2$. Then $D_1$ contains a unique
component $D_2$ of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-A_2}$. Both $D_1$ and $D_2$ are
disks. Since each $A_i$ is a component of the intersection of
$\partial  N $ with a  topological solid torus which is the
underlying manifold of a binding ${{\mathcal B}}_i$,
and ${{\mathcal B}}_i$ has spanning size\ $n/2$, 
the boundary curves of $A_i$ have spanning size\ $n/2$
and hence 
$\mathop{\rm size}(D_i)=n/2$.
Now if $J$ denotes the annulus $\overline{D_1-D_2}$, we
have $\mathop{\rm size}(D_1)=\mathop{\rm size}(D_2)+\mathop{\rm size}(J)$, and hence
$\mathop{\rm size}(J)=0$. 
It follows that ${{\mathcal J}}\doteq{\Omega_{J}}$ has Euler characteristic
$0$. Since $\partial J=\partial A_1\cup\partial
A_2\subset{\bf C}_{{{\mathcal N}},\partial{{\mathcal N}}}$, 
it follows from Lemma \ref{saddy} that ${{\mathcal J}}$ is
a component of ${\mathscr A}\doteq{\mathscr A}_{{{\mathcal N}},\partial{{\mathcal N}}}$. 
Since $J$ shares a boundary curve
with the component $A_1 \ne J$ of ${\bf A}\doteq{{\rm X}_{{\mathscr A}}}$, 
this is
a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{more four}
Let ${{\mathcal B}}$ be a binding of
${{\mathcal N}}$ such that $B\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal B}}}}$ is a topological ball, and let $F$ be a
component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NB$ which is an annulus. Then 
each component of $\partial F$ bounds a disk of weight\ $4$ in $\partial
  N$. 
(As discussed in Remark \ref{what weight 4 means}, such a disk must have
exactly two cone points, each of which has order $2$.)
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
According to Definition \ref{PagelikeBindinglike}, 
straightening the angles\ of ${{\mathcal B}}$ yields a
solid toric orbifold, and ${{\mathcal F}}\doteq{\Omega_{F}}$ is $\pi_1$--injective in
${{\mathcal N}}$. Since $B={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal B}}}}$ is a topological ball, we have $\mathop{\rm size}(\partial
B)=4$, and each singular stratum of ${{\mathcal B}}$
  is a cone stratum of order $2$ (see \S\ref{spherical etc}).
Since
$F\subset\partial B$ is a size--$0$ annulus, and ${{\mathcal F}}$ is
in particular $\pi_1$--injective in
${{\mathcal B}}$, 
any
boundary component $C$ of $F$ bounds a disk $D\subset\partial B$ such
that 
$\mathop{{\rm weight}}(D)=4$. 
Furthermore,
  ${{\mathcal D}}\doteq{\Omega_{D}}$
is $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal B}}$; since the
$\pi_1$--injectivity of ${{\mathcal F}}$ in ${{\mathcal N}}$ implies that ${{\mathcal B}}$ is
$\pi_1$--injective in  ${{\mathcal N}}$, the orbifold ${{\mathcal D}}$ is also
$\pi_1$--injective in  ${{\mathcal N}}$. We can modify $D$ by a small non-ambient isotopy in $B$ to obtain
a neatly\  embedded disk $D_1$ in $B$, disjoint from $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NB$ and
transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal B}}$,  such that  
$\mathop{{\rm weight}}(D_1)=4$, and
  ${{\mathcal D}}_1\doteq{\Omega_{D_1}}$
is $\pi_1$--injective in  ${{\mathcal N}}$. Note  that $D_1$ is
neatly\  embedded in $N$. We may therefore apply Lemma \ref{what about}, with $D_1$ playing the role of $F$,
to obtain  a topological ball $K\subset  N $
such that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N }K=D_1$ and ${\Omega_{K}}$ is bindinglike, so that straightening the angles of
${\Omega_{K}} $ yields a solid toric $3$--orbifold.
  We therefore have $\mathop{{\rm weight}}(\partial K)=8$.
Now $E\doteq\overline{(\partial
  K)-D_1}$
is a disk in $\partial N$ whose boundary is isotopic in
$(\partial N)-(\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}}\cap\partial N)$ to $C$, and
$\mathop{{\rm weight}}(E)=\mathop{{\rm weight}}(
  \partial K)-\mathop{{\rm weight}}(D_1)=4$.
Hence $C$ bounds a weight--$4$ disk in $\partial N$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- custom-60: body_md -->
{Big pages}\label{Subsec:BigPage}
Recall that our goal is to prove Theorem~\ref{Thm:HomeoTypeSpherePieces},
which describes the topological structure of $N$ 
under the standing assumptions given in \S\ref{standing}.
This topology will be anchored by (the underlying space of) a \emph{big page}, which we define now.

A page ${{\mathcal P}}$  of
${{\mathcal N}}$ is called \emph{big} if there exist a 
boundary component ${\widetilde S}$ of $N\doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ 
and a component $H$ of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}\cap{\widetilde S}$, such that every component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ has size\ at most $n/2$.
<!-- end custom-60 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{Rem:BigIsRare}
It is straightforward to show that big pages are quite rare.
Indeed, suppose ${{\mathcal P}}$ is a big page and $H$ is the component of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}} \cap {\widetilde S}$ stipulated in the definition. Let $D_1, \ldots, D_k$ be the components of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$, and let $C_i = H \cap D_i$. Observe that if $k \geq 2$ and $1 \leq i \neq j \leq k$, then $C_i$ and $C_j$ co-bound an annulus in ${\widetilde S}$, which can be shown to have non-zero size by Lemma~\ref{saddy}. Thus at most one $D_i$ can have size equal to $n/2$.
If $\mathop{\rm size}(D_i) < n/2$, then $D_i$ cannot intersect the underlying space of any  big page. If $\mathop{\rm size}(D_i) = n/2$, then another application of Lemma~\ref{saddy} implies that $D_i$ has at most one component of intersection with the underlying space of any big page. Thus ${\widetilde S}$ intersects at most two underlying spaces of big pages. A more careful version of this argument implies that ${{\mathcal N}}$ can contain at most two big pages; see the final paragraph of  \S\ref{ChaiProof}.

Despite the difficulty of satisfying Definition~\ref{Subsec:BigPage}, the next lemma shows that big pages always exist.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{big ol' lemma}
The book of $I$--bundles
${{\mathcal N}}$ has at least one big\ page.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Choose a component ${\widetilde S}$ of $\partial  N $, 
and set ${\widetilde {{\mathcal S}}}={\Omega_{{\widetilde S}}}$. 
Using the notation of \S\ref{wuzza book}, set 
${\mathscr A}={\mathscr A}_{{{\mathcal N}},{\widetilde {{\mathcal S}}}}$, ${\mathscr H}={\mathscr H}_{{{\mathcal N}},{\widetilde {{\mathcal S}}}}$,
and ${\bf C} = {\bf C}_{{{\mathcal N}},{\widetilde {{\mathcal S}}}}$. 
Then ${\bf H} \doteq{{\rm X}_{{\mathscr H}}}$ and ${\bf A} \doteq{{\rm X}_{{\mathscr A}}}$ are $2$--manifolds with boundary whose union is ${\widetilde S}$,
and ${\bf C}={\bf H}\cap{\bf A} $
is a closed $1$--manifold. 
A pair of components $A \subset {\bf A}$ and $H \subset {\bf H}$ are called \emph{adjacent} if $A \cap H \neq \emptyset$. Note that $A \cap H \subset {\bf C}$, and since every component of ${\bf C}$ separates ${\widetilde S}$,  adjacency is equivalent to saying that $A \cap H$ is a component of ${\bf C}$.
Let $T$ be the adjacency graph of components of ${\bf A}$ and ${\bf H}$. That is, every vertex of $T$ corresponds to a component of ${\bf A}$ or a
component of ${\bf H}$, and two vertices are connected by an edge if and only if the corresponding components are adjacent. Since every simple closed curve on ${\widetilde S}$ is separating, $T$ is necessarily a tree.

For each vertex $v$ of $T$,
let us denote by $K_v$ the component of ${\bf A}$ or of ${\bf H}$
corresponding to $v$, and let us set $m_v=\mathop{\rm size}(K_v)$. 
Given this definition of $m_v$, we may define 
$n_U=\sum_{v\in U\cap V }m_v$ for each  set $U\subset T$, as in the statement of Proposition~\ref{tree thing}. Note that $n_T=\mathop{\rm size}({\widetilde S})=n$. Proposition~\ref{tree thing} now gives a vertex $w_0\in V $ such that, for each component $R$ of $T-\{w_0\}$, we have $n_R\le n_T/2=n/2$. Then $L\doteq K_{w_0}$ is a component of either ${\bf H}$ or ${\bf A}$. 

If $Z$ is any component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-L}$, there is a component $R$ of $T-\{w_0\}$ such that $Z=\bigcup_{v\in R\cap V }K_v$. Hence $\mathop{\rm size}(Z)=\sum_{v\in R\cap V }\mathop{\rm size}(K_v)=n_R\le n/2$. Thus:

\begin{claim}\label{i knew it}
Every component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-L}$ has size\ at most $n/2$.
\end{claim}


We now claim:

\begin{claim}\label{i still know it}
There is a component $H$ of ${\bf H}$ such that every component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ has size\ at most $n/2$.
\end{claim}


To prove \ref{i still know it}, first note that in the case where $L$ is a component of ${\bf H}$, the assertion follows immediately from \ref{i knew it} upon setting $H=L$.



We now turn to the case in which $L$ is a component of ${\bf A}$. Then ${\Omega_{L}}$ is an annular orbifold. Hence either (a) $L$ is an annulus and $\mathop{\rm size}(L)=0$, or (b) $L$ is a disk, $\mathop{\rm size}(L)=2$, and each of the two singular points of ${\Omega_{L}}$ is of order $2$. If (a) holds, 
let $H$ be a component of ${\bf H}$ adjacent to $L$.
Since (a) holds, it now follows that $H$ is isotopic to $L\cup H$ in ${\widetilde S}\cap( N -\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}})$. Hence any component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ is isotopic in ${\widetilde S}\cap( N -\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}})$ to a component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-(L\cup H)}$, which is in turn contained in a component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-L}$ and therefore has size\ at most $n/2$ by \ref{i knew it}. Since an isotopy in ${\widetilde S}\cap( N -\Sigma_{{\mathcal N}})$ obviously preserves size, this shows that every component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ has size\ at most $n/2$. This establishes \ref{i still know it} in the subcase where (a) holds.


There remains the subcase in which (b) holds. In this subcase,
$\overline{{\widetilde S}-L}$ is a disk and has size
 $n-2$.  
Hence
\ref{i knew it} gives $n-2\le n/2$, so  that $n\le4$. 

If $n\le3$ then $\mathop{\rm size}(\overline{{\widetilde S}-L})\le1$. This means that
${\Omega_{\overline{{\widetilde S}-L}}}$ is a discal orbifold, so that $\partial L$
defines an element of finite order in $\pi_1({{\mathcal N}})$; this is a
contradiction, since $\partial L$ is a component of 
${\bf C}={\Omega_{{\bf C}}}$,
which is
 $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal N}}$ by
\S\ref{wuzza book}. 
Hence $n=4$.

Now let $H$ denote the component of ${\bf H}$ 
adjacent to $L$. 
The component $L$ of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ has size\ $2$. If $Y$ is any component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ distinct from $L$, we have 
\[
4 = n = \mathop{\rm size}({\widetilde S})\ge\mathop{\rm size}(Y)+\mathop{\rm size}(L)=\mathop{\rm size}(Y)+2,
\]
so that $\mathop{\rm size}(Y)\le2$. Thus every component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ has size at most $2=n/2$. This completes the proof of \ref{i still know it}.

Now if $H$ is the component of ${\bf H}$ given by \ref{i still know it}, there is a page ${{\mathcal P}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$ such that $L$ is a component of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}\cap{\widetilde S}$. It then follows from \ref{i knew it}, and the definition of a big\ page, that ${{\mathcal P}}$ is a big\ page of ${{\mathcal N}}$. This gives the conclusion of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- claim-16: body_md -->
\label{i knew it}
Every component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-L}$ has size\ at most $n/2$.
<!-- end claim-16 -->
<!-- claim-17: body_md -->
\label{i still know it}
There is a component $H$ of ${\bf H}$ such that every component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ has size\ at most $n/2$.
<!-- end claim-17 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{middle-sized lemma}
Let ${{\mathcal P}}$ be a page of ${{\mathcal N}}$,
and set
$ P={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}$. 
Assume that  some component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{  N } P$ is an annulus of spanning size\ $n/2$. Then ${{\mathcal P}}$ is big.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Fix a  component $F$ of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N } P$ which is an annulus of spanning size\ $n/2$,  fix a component $C$ of $\partial F$, and let ${\widetilde S}$ denote the component of $\partial  N $ containing $C$. Then $C$ is 
contained in the boundary
of some component $H$ of $ P\cap{\widetilde S}$. According to the definitions, we have ${\rm spanning size}(C)={\rm spanning size}(F)=n/2$. Hence each of the two disks contained in ${\widetilde S}$ and bounded by $C$ has size\ equal to $n/2$. These disks may be labeled $D$ and $D'$, where $D$ is a component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ and $D'\supset H$. Each component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ either is equal to $D$ or is contained in $D'$; hence each component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ has size\ at most $n/2$. It now follows from the definition that ${{\mathcal P}}$ is big.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{EveryCompBigSize} 
Let a big\ page ${{\mathcal P}}$  of ${{\mathcal N}}$
be given. Let ${\widetilde S}$ be any 
boundary component of $ N \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$, and let $H$ be any
component of the intersection of
$ P\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}$ with ${\widetilde S}$. 
Then every component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}-H}$ has size\ at most $n/2$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
The orbifold $I$--bundle structure of ${{\mathcal P}}$ implies that
$ P\cap{\widetilde S}$ has at most two components. If it has only one
component, the assertion is immediate from the definition  of a big\ page. Now suppose it has two components, $H_0$ and $H_1$. Let ${\widetilde S}_i$ denote the component of $\partial  N $ containing $H_i$. (The ${\widetilde S}_i$ are not necessarily distinct.) Since ${{\mathcal P}}$ is big, we may suppose the $H_i$ to be labeled in such a way that every component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}_0-H_0}$ has size\ at most $n/2$. It remains to show  that every component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}_1-H_1}$ has size\ at most $n/2$.

Let $q \colon\thinspace {{\mathcal P}} \to {{\mathcal H}}$ be the fibration map of the $I$--bundle ${{\mathcal P}}$.
Since the horizontal boundary $\partial_\mathrm{h} {{\mathcal P}}$ has two components ${\Omega_{H_0}}$ and
${\Omega_{H_1}}$, it follows from   \S\ref{Def orbifold I-bundle} that the base ${{\mathcal H}}$ is orientable, and that each of ${\Omega_{H_0}}$ and
${\Omega_{H_1}}$ is
orbifold-diffeomorphic to ${{\mathcal H}}$. In particular, 
$w\doteq\mathop{\rm size}(H_0)=\mathop{\rm size}(H_1)$. Each component of $\partial_\mathrm{v} {{\mathcal P}} $ must meet both components of $\partial_\mathrm{h} {{\mathcal P}}$.
In particular no component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N } P = {{\rm X}_{\partial_\mathrm{v} {{\mathcal P}}}}$ has connected boundary;
since  the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N } P$ are underlying surfaces of annular orbifolds, they must be size--$0$ annuli. Hence $H_0$ and $H_1$ have the same number of boundary curves, which we denote by $m\ge0$, and we may write $\partial H_i=\bigcup_{1\le j\le m}C_i^j$, where $C_0^j$ and $C_1^j$ are joined by a size--$0$ annulus in $ N $ for $1\le j\le m$. According to 
Lemma \ref{Lem:SameSpanningSize}, we have
${\rm spanning size}(C_0^j)={\rm spanning size}(C_1^j)$ for every $j$.

For all $i$ and $j$,
let $D_i^j$ denote the component of
$\overline{{\widetilde S}_i - H_i}$ containing $C_i^j$. For $1\le j\le m$ we have
$\mathop{\rm size}(D_0^j)\le n/2$, and we must show that $\mathop{\rm size}(D_1^j)\le
n/2$. This is vacuously true if $m=0$, so we may assume $m>0$. Since
the disks $D_1^j\subset{\widetilde S}_1$ are pairwise disjoint, we have
$\sum_{1\le j\le m}\mathop{\rm size}(D_1^j)\le \mathop{\rm size}{\widetilde S}_1=n$; hence there is at
most one index $j$ for which $\mathop{\rm size}(D_1^j)>n/2$. Thus, after
re-indexing if necessary, we may assume that $\mathop{\rm size}(D_1^j)\le n/2$ for
$1\le j<m$.  We now
  need only prove that $\mathop{\rm size}(D_1^m)\le n/2$.

For $i=0$ and $1\le j\le m$, and also for $i=1$ and $1\le j<m$, since $\mathop{\rm size}(D_i^j)\le n/2$, the definition of spanning size\ gives $\mathop{\rm size}(D_i^j)={\rm spanning size}(C_i^j)$. Note also that for $i=0,1$ we have $w+\sum_{1\le j\le m}\mathop{\rm size}(D_i^j)=\mathop{\rm size}({\widetilde S}_i)=n$. Hence
\begin{align*}
w+\sum_{1\le j\le m}{\rm spanning size}(C_0^j)&=w+\sum_{1\le j\le m}\mathop{\rm size}(D_0^j) \\
&= w+\sum_{1\le j\le m}\mathop{\rm size}(D_1^j)\\
&=w+ \Big(\sum_{1\le j<m}{\rm spanning size}(C_1^j) \Big) +\mathop{\rm size}(D_1^m)\\
&=w+ \Big( \sum_{1\le j< m}{\rm spanning size}(C_0^j) \Big)  +\mathop{\rm size}(D_1^m),
\end{align*}
which gives $\mathop{\rm size}(D_1^m)={\rm spanning size}(C_0^m)$. The definition of spanning size\ now implies that $\mathop{\rm size}(D_1^m)\le n/2$, as required.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{both verses}
Let ${{\mathcal P}}$ be a big\
page of ${{\mathcal N}}$, and set $ P={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}$. Let $F$ be a component of
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{  N } P$ such that either 
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(a)]
\item $F$ is an annulus  with
${\rm spanning size}(F)<n/2$, or 
\item 
the binding of ${{\mathcal N}}$ containing  ${\Omega_{F}}$ has a 
topological ball as its  underlying space.
\end{enumerate}
Let $V$ denote the component of $\overline{ N - P}$ containing
$F$. Then $V$ is harmless, and is disjoint from 
the underlying manifold of
every big\ page of ${{\mathcal N}}$ other than ${{\mathcal P}}$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
First we observe that if there is a
big\ page ${{\mathcal Q}}\ne {{\mathcal P}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$ such that  ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Q}}}}$ has non-empty intersection with 
$V$, then since ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Q}}}}$ is connected and disjoint from $P$ we must have
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Q}}}}\subset V$. It therefore suffices to prove that (I) $V$ is
harmless, and (II) there is no big page ${{\mathcal Q}}\ne {{\mathcal P}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$
such that ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Q}}}}\subset V$.

Consider the case in which (a) holds. We set $h={\rm spanning size}(F)$, so that 
$h<n/2$. Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ denote the components of $\partial F$. For $i=1,2$ let $H_i$ denote the component of $ P\cap\partial  N $ containing $C_i$, and let ${\widetilde S}_i$ denote the component of $\partial N $ containing $H_i$. (The $H_i$ are not necessarily distinct, and in particular the ${\widetilde S}_i$ are not necessarily distinct.) 
For $i=1,2$ let $D_i$ denote the component of $\overline{{\widetilde S}_i-H_i}$ containing $C_i$. Then $D_i$ is a disk, and it follows from Lemma \ref{EveryCompBigSize} that $\mathop{\rm size}(D_i)\le n/2$. The definitions of the spanning size\ of a simple closed curve, and  of the spanning size\ of an annulus, then imply that  $\mathop{\rm size}(D_i)$ is equal to $h$ (and is in particular strictly less than $n/2$).

We claim:
\begin{claim}\label{snores} 
For $i=1,2$, the interior of $D_i$ is disjoint from 
the underlying manifold of every big\ page of $ {{\mathcal N}}$, 
including ${{\mathcal P}}$.
\end{claim}


If \ref{snores} is false, then $\mathop{\rm int} D_i$ contains a component 
$H$ of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Q}}}}\cap{\widetilde S}_i$ for some big\ page ${{\mathcal Q}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$. But then the disk $\overline{{\widetilde S}_i-D_i}$ is contained in some component $E$ of $\overline{{\widetilde S}_i-H}$. According to Lemma \ref{EveryCompBigSize} we have $\mathop{\rm size}(E)\le n/2$. But $\mathop{\rm size}(E)\ge\mathop{\rm size}(\overline{{\widetilde S}_i-D_i})=n-h>n/2$, a contradiction. This proves \ref{snores}.

According to \ref{snores}, $\mathop{\rm int} D_i$ is in particular disjoint from $P$ for $i=1,2$. Hence:
\begin{claim}\label{shores} 
For $i=1,2$, the disk $D_i$ is a component of $\overline{(\partial N )-( P\cap \partial N )}$. 
\end{claim}


The disks $D_1$ and $D_2$, which by \ref{shores} are components of
$\overline{(\partial N )-( P\cap \partial  N )}$, 
are distinct because their boundaries $C_1$ and $C_2$ are
distinct. Hence $D_1\cap D_2=\emptyset$. Since the annulus $F$ is
neatly\  embedded in $ N $, we have $D_i\cap F=C_i$ for $i=1,2$, and
$ D_1\cup F\cup D_2$ is a smoothable 
$2$--sphere. 
By a minor variant of the smoothing operation described in \S\ref{what's smoothing},  $ D_1\cup F\cup D_2$ is non-ambiently isotopic to  a smooth $2$--sphere $R$ contained in the interior of $N$ and transverse to the singular set of
${{\mathcal N}}$, with the same
 size as $ D_1\cup F\cup D_2$.

Since $\mathop{\rm size}(D_1)=\mathop{\rm size}(D_2)=h$ and $\mathop{\rm size}(F)=0$, we
have $\mathop{\rm size}(R)=2h$.  The
canonical immersion from $ N $ to $M$ maps $R$
diffeomorphically 
to a smooth 
sphere $R'$ in $M$ which is
transverse to the singular set of ${{\mathcal M}}$ and has 
size  $2h$. Since $2h<n$ and $S$ is 
${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal, the sphere $R'$ cannot be essential in
$M$; hence $R'$ bounds a smooth  ball $W\subset M$. 
Now $\partial W=R'$ is disjoint from $S$, and since $S$ is
essential it cannot be contained in $\mathop{\rm int} W$. Hence $W$ is
disjoint from $S$. It now follows that 
$ D_1\cup F\cup D_2$ 
bounds a topological ball $K\subset
 N $. Thus we 
have $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N }K=F$. 
Since $F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N } P$, either (i) $K$ is a component of $\overline{ N - P}$ or (ii) $K\supset P$. But (ii) would imply  $ P\cap\partial N \subset K\cap\partial N =D_1\cup D_2$, which contradicts \ref{shores}. Hence (i) holds, i.e.\ 
$K=V$. In particular 
$V$ is a topological
ball and its frontier is the single annulus $F$. Thus 
$V$ is harmless, and Assertion (I) is established in this case.

To prove Assertion (II) in this case, suppose that there is a
big\ page ${{\mathcal Q}}\ne {{\mathcal P}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$ such that  $Q\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Q}}}}\subset V=K$.
Since ${{\mathcal Q}}$ is a page of the book of $I$--bundles
${{\mathcal N}}$, we have $Q\cap\partial N \ne\emptyset$. But we
have $K\cap\partial N  =D_1\cup D_2$, and hence
$Q $ must meet the interior of 
either $D_1$ or $D_2$. 
This contradicts \ref{snores}, 
and completes the proof of the lemma in the case where (a) holds.

We now turn to the case in which (b) holds.
Consider the
subcase in which $F$ is a disk.
In this subcase, 
since ${\Omega_{F}} $ is $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal N}}$ 
(see \S\ref{wuzza book}),
it follows from  Lemma \ref{what about} that there is a topological ball 
$K\subset N$ 
such that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }K=F$, and ${\Omega_{K}} $ is a bindinglike suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$.
Hence $\pi_1({\Omega_{K}} )$ is virtually cyclic.
Since $F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  } P $, either (i) $K$ is a component of $\overline{ N  - P }$ or (ii) $K\supset P $.   If (ii) holds, then  since ${{\mathcal P}}$ is a $\pi_1$--injective suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$ by
\S\ref{wuzza book},
${{\mathcal P}}$ is in particular a $\pi_1$--injective suborbifold of  ${\Omega_{K}}
$,
 and hence the page ${{\mathcal P}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$ has a virtually cyclic (orbifold) fundamental group. This contradicts
an observation made in \S\ref{wuzza book}.
Hence (i) holds, i.e.\ 
$K=V$. In particular 
$V$ is a topological ball and its frontier is the single disk $F$. Thus 
$V$ is harmless, and 
Assertion (I) is established in this subcase. 


To prove Assertion (II) in this
subcase,
suppose that for some big\ page ${{\mathcal Q}}\ne {{\mathcal P}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$ we have ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Q}}}} \subset V$. 
Since ${{\mathcal Q}}$ is a $\pi_1$--injective suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$ by
\S\ref{wuzza book},
${{\mathcal Q}}$ is in particular a $\pi_1$--injective suborbifold of  ${\Omega_{K}}
$, and hence the page ${{\mathcal Q}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$ has a virtually cyclic
(orbifold) fundamental group. Again this contradicts
an observation made in \S\ref{wuzza book}.

There remains the subcase in which $F$ is an annulus. Let ${{\mathcal B}}$
denote the binding of ${{\mathcal N}}$ containing ${\Omega_{F}}$. 
Since (b) holds,
$B\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal B}}}}$ is a topological ball. It therefore follows from Lemma
\ref{more four}
and Remark \ref{what weight 4 means}
that 
every component of $\partial F$ bounds a disk in $\partial N$ that has weight\ $4$.
Thus, by Lemma \ref{just four simpler}, $F$ is the full frontier of
$B$ relative to $N$. 
It follows that $V=B$ in
this case, so that $V$ is a topological ball whose frontier is $F$. This means that
$V$ is harmless, and 
Assertion (I) is established
in this subcase. 
Assertion (II) follows immediately, because $V$ is the underlying space of the binding ${{\mathcal B}}$,
and so cannot contain the underlying space of any page.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- claim-18: body_md -->
\label{snores} 
For $i=1,2$, the interior of $D_i$ is disjoint from 
the underlying manifold of every big\ page of $ {{\mathcal N}}$, 
including ${{\mathcal P}}$.
<!-- end claim-18 -->
<!-- claim-19: body_md -->
\label{shores} 
For $i=1,2$, the disk $D_i$ is a component of $\overline{(\partial N )-( P\cap \partial N )}$.
<!-- end claim-19 -->
<!-- custom-61: body_md -->
{Global structure: the proof of Theorem \ref{Thm:HomeoTypeSpherePieces}}\label{ChaiProof}

In \S\S\ref{not more than one, now}--\ref{both verses}, we
have seen how the hypotheses laid out in \S\ref{standing} give
information about the book of $I$--bundles ${{\mathcal N}}$. We shall now assemble
these facts to prove Theorem~\ref{Thm:HomeoTypeSpherePieces}, which describes the
topological type of $N={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$ under these hypotheses. 
In outline, the proof runs as follows. For every big page ${{\mathcal P}}_j$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$, we adjoin certain harmless components to the underlying space $P_j$ to form a set ${\widehat P}_j$ that is itself a classical $I$--bundle. It turns out that $N$ is the union of the classical $I$--bundle s $\hat P_1, \ldots, {\widehat P}_k$ with
certain solid torus bindings. We then show that every ${\widehat P}_j$ is a classical $I$--bundle\ over ${\mathbb S}^2$, ${\mathbb R}{\mathbb P}^2$, or ${\mathbb B}^2$, and in the latter case $N$ is formed by attaching one or two 
$2$--handles to a solid torus.  
The theorem then follows easily.


\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{Thm:HomeoTypeSpherePieces}]
As in \S\ref{standing}, we set 
$n=\mathop{\rm size}(S)$.
Let ${{\mathcal P}}_1,\ldots,{{\mathcal P}}_k$ be the big pages of ${{\mathcal N}}$, and observe that $k \geq 1$ by Lemma \ref{big ol' lemma}.
For
$j=1,\ldots,k$, 
we set $ P_j={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}_j}}$, and we
let ${\bf F}_j$ denote the set of all components $F$  of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
} P_j $ such that either 
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(a)]
\item $F$ is an annulus  with
${\rm spanning size}(F)<n/2$, or 
\item
the underlying space of the binding  of ${{\mathcal N}}$ 
containing  ${\Omega_{F}}$ is homeomorphic to a ball.
\end{enumerate}
For each $F\in{\bf F}_j$, let $V_F$ denote the component of $\overline{ N  - P_j}$ containing $F$. Then  Lemma \ref{both verses} implies:
\begin{claim}\label{zeero}
For each $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and each $F\in{\bf F}_j$, the component
$V_F$ of $\overline{ N  - P_j}$ is harmless, and is disjoint
from $ P_{j'}$ 
for every $j'\ne j$.
\end{claim}

Let an index $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ be given.
According to the definition of a harmless component,
 for each 
$F\in{\bf F}_j$, the frontier of $V_F$ is
connected and is therefore equal to $F$. In particular, if we fix an
index $j$, then for any distinct elements $F$ and $F'$ of ${\bf F}_j$ we
have $V_F\ne V_{F'}$. For each $j$ we set $ {\widehat P} 
_j= P_j\cup\bigcup_{F\in{\bf F}_j}V_F$. We apply 
 Proposition \ref{Prop:ExpandedPage}, letting ${{\mathcal P}}_j$ play the role of
 ${{\mathcal P}}$, and letting ${\bf V}_j\doteq \bigcup_{F\in{\bf F}_j} V_F$
 play  the role of   ${\bf V}$.   
 Proposition \ref{Prop:ExpandedPage}\eqref{ExpandedPageIsBundle} implies 
that the  manifold $ {\widehat P}_j$ may be given the structure of
a classical $I$--bundle\ in such a way that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  } {\widehat P}_j$ is a vertical
subset of $\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} {\widehat P}_j$. As we observed in \S\ref{Def:Harmless}, 
${\widehat{{\mathcal P}}}_j\doteq{\Omega_{ {\widehat P} _j}}$ is a well-defined clean\ suborbifold
with corners of ${{\mathcal N}}$, so that ${\widehat P} _j$ 
is a clean submanifold with corners of $N$.
Furthermore, Proposition \ref{Prop:ExpandedPage}\eqref{ExpandedPageFrontier} and the definition of ${\bf V}_j$ imply that
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\widehat P} _j$ is the union of all components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
} P_j$ that do not belong to ${\bf F}_j$, i.e.\ do not satisfy (a) or (b). A component $E$ of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
} P_j$ fails to satisfy (b) if and only if  the underlying set 
of the
binding containing ${\Omega_{E}}$ 
is
a  topological solid torus, which by 
\S\ref{spherical etc}
implies
in particular that $E$ is
an annulus. An annulus component $E$ of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
} P_j$ fails to satisfy (a) if and only if  
${\rm spanning size}(E)=n/2$. Hence we have shown:

\begin{claim}\label{jeepers}
 $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\widehat P} _j$ is the union of all components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
 } P_j$ which are annuli of spanning size\ $n/2$
and are contained in 
topological
solid 
tori that are underlying manifolds of bindings.
\end{claim}

We claim:

\begin{claim}\label{fish and chips}
The 
sets
$ {\widehat P}  _1,\ldots, {\widehat P}  _k$ are pairwise disjoint.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{fish and chips}, we must
 check that when  $j,j'\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ are distinct indices, three conditions hold: first, $ P_j\cap  P_{j'}=\emptyset$; second, $ P_{j'}\cap V_F=\emptyset$ for each $F\in{\bf F}_j$; and third, $V_F\cap V_{F'}=\emptyset$ for all $F\in{\bf F}_j$ and $F'\in{\bf F}_{j'}$.
If  $F\in{\bf F}_j$ and $F'\in{\bf F}_{j'}$, it
is immediate that $ P_j\cap  P_{j'}=\emptyset$ since ${{\mathcal P}}_j$ and ${{\mathcal P}}_{j'}$ are distinct pages of ${{\mathcal N}}$. According to Lemma \ref{both verses}, $V_F$ is  disjoint from every big\ page of ${{\mathcal N}}$ other than ${{\mathcal P}}_j$; in particular $V_F\cap {{\mathcal P}}_{j'}=\emptyset$. Finally, to show that the connected, proper subsets $V_F$ and $V_{F'}$ of $ N  $ are disjoint, 
it is enough to prove that each is disjoint from the frontier of the other; and by symmetry, we need only prove that  $V_F$ is disjoint from $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }V_{F'}$. But this follows from the fact that 
$V_F$ is disjoint from ${{\mathcal P}}_{j'}$, as the latter set contains $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }V_{F'}$. Thus
\ref{fish and chips} is established.

Next, we claim:

\begin{claim}\label{Claim:IfEmptyFrontier}
If $\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j = \emptyset$ for some $j$, then $N$ is homeomorphic to either ${\mathbb S}^2 \times I$ or the $3$--manifold obtained by removing 
the interior of a closed
 $3$--ball from ${\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^3$.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{Claim:IfEmptyFrontier}, assume that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j = \emptyset$. Since $N$ is connected, it follows that ${\widehat P}_j = N$ (and that $j=k =1$). Thus $N$ is homeomorphic to a classical $I$--bundle\ over some closed surface of positive Euler characteristic. 
Thus $ N  $ is homeomorphic
either to the trivial classical $I$--bundle\ 
${\mathbb S}^2 \times I$ or to a twisted classical $I$--bundle\ over
${\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^2$. In the second case, $N$ is homeomorphic to the $3$--manifold obtained by removing 
the interior of a closed
 $3$--ball from ${\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^3$. 
 
 According to \ref{Claim:IfEmptyFrontier}, the conclusion of the theorem holds if
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j = \emptyset$ for some $j$. Thus, for the remainder of the proof, we 
assume:
\begin{claim}\label{non-empty frontiers}
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j \neq \emptyset$ for every $j$.
\end{claim} 


For $j=1,\ldots,k$, let $H_j$ denote the base of the
classical $I$--bundle\ 
${\widehat P} _j$.
Then $H_j$ is connected since ${\widehat P} _j$ is connected.
If for some $j$ the surface $H_j$  is closed, then we have 
$\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} {\widehat P}_{j}=\emptyset$. In particular,
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  } {\widehat P}_{j}
\subset\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} {\widehat P}_{j}$ is empty, 
contradicting
\ref{non-empty frontiers}. This proves:

\begin{claim}\label{not closed}
For $j=1,\ldots,k$ we have $\partial H_j\ne\emptyset$.
\end{claim}



Now set $\widehat{\bf P} = {\widehat P}  _1\cup\cdots\cup {\widehat P}  _k$, which is a disjoint union
according to \ref{fish and chips}. The 
classical $I$--bundle\ structures on the
${\widehat P} _j$ define a classical $I$--bundle\ structure
 on $\widehat{\bf P}$. 
As in the statement of Lemma \ref{not more than one, now}, we
let
${{\mathscr B}^\ast}$ 
denote the union of all bindings 
of ${{\mathcal N}}$ which have 
topological
solid tori as underlying 
sets
and have  spanning size\
$n/2$.
Set ${\bf B}^\ast={{\rm X}_{{{\mathscr B}^\ast}}}$.
We claim:

\begin{claim}\label{and whaddya got}
We have $N=\widehat{\bf P}\cup{\bf B}^\ast$ and
$\widehat{\bf P}\cap{\bf B}^\ast=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N } \widehat{\bf P}=\mathop{\rm Fr}{\bf B}^\ast$. Furthermore, each component of
$\widehat{\bf P}\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ is an annulus which is vertical in the
classical $I$--bundle\ $\widehat{\bf P}$ 
and has non-zero winding number on the 
(topological solid torus) 
component of ${\bf B}^\ast$ containing it.
\end{claim}


To prove \ref{and whaddya got}, first note that  
if $F$ is any component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }\widehat{\bf P}$, then
by \ref{fish and chips},
$F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\widehat P}_j$ for some $j\le k$;
and according to \ref{jeepers},
$F$ is therefore an annulus  component of 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N  P_j$ 
having spanning size\ $n/2$. Let ${{\mathcal B}} $ denote the binding of ${{\mathcal N}}$
such that $B\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal B}}}}  $ 
shares the frontier component $F$ with $ P_j$.
Then \ref{jeepers} also implies that 
$B  $ is a topological solid torus
(so that ${\rm spanning size}({{\mathcal B}}  )$ is defined by \S\ref{what's the point}),
and that ${\rm spanning size}({{\mathcal B}}  )={\rm spanning size}(F)=n/2$. 
Thus by definition ${{\mathcal B}} $ is a component of ${ {{\mathscr B}^\ast}}$. 
This shows that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }\widehat{\bf P}\subset\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast$.


Conversely, suppose that $F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }
{\bf B}^\ast$. Then $F$
is an annulus of spanning size\ $n/2$, and is a frontier component of
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}} $ for some page ${{\mathcal P}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$. By Lemma
\ref{middle-sized lemma}, ${{\mathcal P}}$ is a big\ page of ${{\mathcal N}}$, so that
${{\mathcal P}}={{\mathcal P}}_j$ for some $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$. 
Since $F$ is a spanning size--$n/2$ component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP_j$, and
since  the
component of ${\bf B}^\ast$ containing $F$ is a topological solid torus by the
definition of ${\bf B}^\ast$, it follows from
\ref{jeepers} that $F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_N{\widehat P} _j$. 
This establishes the reverse inclusion $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast\subset\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }\widehat{\bf P}$.

Thus we have $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast = \mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }\widehat{\bf P}$. 
To prove that this set coincides with $\widehat{\bf P} \cap {\bf B}^\ast$, it suffices to show that 
if  $F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast = \mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }\widehat{\bf P}$, and $W$ is  a tubular neighborhood of $F$ in $N$, then $(W-F)\cap\widehat{\bf P}$ and $(W-F)\cap {\bf B}^\ast$ are contained in different components of $W-F$. But \ref{jeepers} implies that $(W-F) \cap \widehat{\bf P}$ is contained in some $P_j$, which is the underlying space of a page ${{\mathcal P}}_j$, while $(W-F) \cap {\bf B}^\ast$ is contained in the underlying space of a binding ${{\mathcal B}} \subset {{\mathscr B}^\ast}$. Thus 
$(W-F)\cap\widehat{\bf P}$ and $(W-F)\cap {\bf B}^\ast$ are disjoint, 
and we have shown that $\widehat{\bf P}\cap{\bf B}^\ast=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N} \widehat{\bf P}=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast$. 

Since
$\widehat{\bf P}\cap{\bf B}^\ast=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
}\widehat{\bf P}=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast$, the
compact  subset
$\widehat{\bf P}\cup{\bf B}^\ast$ of $ N  $ is an open subset of $ N $. Since we have seen (via a crucial application of 
Lemma \ref{big ol' lemma}) that $k\ge1$, we have $\emptyset \ne P_1\cup\cdots \cup P_k\subset\widehat{\bf P}$, and in particular
$\widehat{\bf P}\cup{\bf B}^\ast\ne\emptyset$. Since $ N  $ is connected it
follows that $\widehat{\bf P}\cup{\bf B}^\ast= N  $, and the 
first sentence of \ref{and whaddya got} is proved. 

To prove the second sentence of \ref{and whaddya got}, consider an arbitrary component $F$ of
$\widehat{\bf P}\cap{\bf B}^\ast$. Then according to 
the first sentence of \ref{and whaddya got},
$F$ is both a component of the
frontier of some component $B$ of ${\bf B}^\ast$, and a component of the
frontier of  ${\widehat P} _j$ for some $j$.
The definition of
${\bf B}^\ast$ implies that ${{\mathcal B}}\doteq{\Omega_{B}}$ is a binding of
${{\mathcal N}}$, 
and that $B$ is a topological solid torus.
According to an observation made in \S\ref{wuzza book},
$F$ is an annulus which has non-zero winding number in
the topological solid torus $B$. 
On the other hand, since $F$ is a component of
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N{\widehat P} _j$, our choice of the $I$--bundle structure on ${\widehat P} _j$ guarantees
that $F$ is a vertical 
subset
of $\partial {\widehat P} _j$ and therefore of
$\partial\widehat{\bf P}$.
The proof of \ref{and whaddya got} is now complete.

Now we claim: 
\begin{claim}\label{one annulus}
For each component $K$ of $\partial N$, the intersection $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ is a single annulus.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{one annulus}, we first note that \ref{and whaddya got} directly implies that each component of $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ is an annulus. Furthermore, it follows from Lemma \ref{not more than one, now} that $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ has at most one component. It remains only to show that $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast\ne\emptyset$. If we assume that $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ is empty, then since $N=\widehat{\bf P}\cup{\bf B}^\ast$ by \ref{and whaddya got}, we  have $K\subset\widehat{\bf P}$. But the component $K$ of $\partial N$ is a $2$--sphere, and in particular a closed surface. Hence $K$ must be a full boundary component of ${\widehat P}_{j}$ for some $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$. 
Thus the classical $I$--bundle\ ${\widehat P}_{j}$ has a boundary component which is a sphere; and the base $H_{j}$ of the classical $I$--bundle\ has non-empty boundary by \ref{not closed}. It follows that $H_j$ must be a disk. But then ${\widehat P}_j$ is a topological ball whose full boundary is the sphere $K$; this contradicts the essentiality of the sphere $S$ in $M$. Thus \ref{one annulus} is proved.

Now consider an arbitrary component $K$ of $\partial N$. By \ref{one annulus}, $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ is an annulus, and it follows from \ref{and whaddya got} that $K\cap\widehat{\bf P}=\overline{K-(K\cap {\bf B}^\ast)}$. 
Since $K$ is a sphere, it follows that $K\cap\widehat{\bf P}$ is the union of two disjoint disks. In particular:
\begin{claim}\label{They're disks}
Every component of $\widehat{\bf P}\cap\partial N$ is a disk.
\end{claim}

Now we claim:
\begin{claim}\label{each hatpj is a ball}
For each $j\le k$, the manifold with corners ${\widehat P}_j$ is a topological ball, and ${\widehat P}_j\cap{\bf B}^\ast$  is a single annulus.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{each hatpj is a ball}, we first recall that 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j \neq \emptyset$ for every $j$
by \ref{non-empty frontiers}. We choose a component $F$ of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j$, which by \ref{and whaddya got} is an annulus. Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ denote the components of $\partial F$. For $i=1,2$, it follows from \ref{and whaddya got} 
that $C_i$ is contained in a component $D_i$ of $\widehat{\bf P}\cap\partial N$. By \ref{They're disks}, each $D_i$ is a disk. In particular we have $\partial D_i=C_i$ for $i=1,2$. Since $D_i\subset\widehat{\bf P}$ and $C_i\subset{\widehat P}_j$, we have $D_i\subset{\widehat P}_j$. It now follows that $R \doteq D_1\cup F\cup D_2$ 
is a topological $2$--sphere contained in $\partial {\widehat P}_j$. But ${\widehat P}_j$ is a classical $I$--bundle\ over the compact surface $H_j$, which by \ref{not closed} has non-empty boundary. It follows that the manifold obtained by straightening the angles\ of ${\widehat P}_j$ is irreducible. Since $\partial{\widehat P}_j$ contains the $2$--sphere $R$, we deduce that ${\widehat P}_j$ is a topological ball with boundary $R$. We have ${\widehat P}_j\cap{\bf B}^\ast= R \cap{\bf B}^\ast=F$. This completes the proof of \ref{each hatpj is a ball}.  

It follows from \ref{each hatpj is a ball} that
$ N  $ is homeomorphic 
to a topological manifold obtained from ${\bf B}^\ast$ by
adding $k$ topological $2$--handles.
As $ N  $ is connected, it follows that ${\bf B}^\ast$ is connected,
i.e.\ is a single topological solid torus. A topological manifold
obtained by adding $k$ topological $2$--handles to a solid torus along 
annuli with non-zero winding number
 is homeomorphic to 
a manifold obtained from a (possibly trivial) lens space by removing
 the interiors of $k$ disjoint closed $3$--balls. 
In particular, $k$ is the number of boundary components of $N$, and is therefore equal to $1$ if $S$ separates $M$, and to $2$ otherwise.
If $k=1$, then $N$ is homeomorphic to a manifold obtained from a lens space by
removing  the interior of a closed $3$--ball; and in this case, since
$S$ is essential, the lens space in question must be non-trivial.  If
$k=2$, then $N$ is homeomorphic 
to a manifold obtained from a (possibly trivial) lens space by
removing the interiors of two disjoint closed $3$--balls.
In either case, the conclusion of the theorem follows.

(We remark that the above proof shows that $N$ has at most two big pages. Indeed, if $\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j = \emptyset$ for some $j$, then there is exactly one big page, and otherwise the number $k$ of  big pages is equal to the number of components of $\partial N$.)
\end{proof}

As in \S\ref{standing}, we set 
$n=\mathop{\rm size}(S)$.
Let ${{\mathcal P}}_1,\ldots,{{\mathcal P}}_k$ be the big pages of ${{\mathcal N}}$, and observe that $k \geq 1$ by Lemma \ref{big ol' lemma}.
For
$j=1,\ldots,k$, 
we set $ P_j={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}_j}}$, and we
let ${\bf F}_j$ denote the set of all components $F$  of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
} P_j $ such that either 
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(a)]
\item $F$ is an annulus  with
${\rm spanning size}(F)<n/2$, or 
\item
the underlying space of the binding  of ${{\mathcal N}}$ 
containing  ${\Omega_{F}}$ is homeomorphic to a ball.
\end{enumerate}
For each $F\in{\bf F}_j$, let $V_F$ denote the component of $\overline{ N  - P_j}$ containing $F$. Then  Lemma \ref{both verses} implies:
\begin{claim}\label{zeero}
For each $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and each $F\in{\bf F}_j$, the component
$V_F$ of $\overline{ N  - P_j}$ is harmless, and is disjoint
from $ P_{j'}$ 
for every $j'\ne j$.
\end{claim}

Let an index $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ be given.
According to the definition of a harmless component,
 for each 
$F\in{\bf F}_j$, the frontier of $V_F$ is
connected and is therefore equal to $F$. In particular, if we fix an
index $j$, then for any distinct elements $F$ and $F'$ of ${\bf F}_j$ we
have $V_F\ne V_{F'}$. For each $j$ we set $ {\widehat P} 
_j= P_j\cup\bigcup_{F\in{\bf F}_j}V_F$. We apply 
 Proposition \ref{Prop:ExpandedPage}, letting ${{\mathcal P}}_j$ play the role of
 ${{\mathcal P}}$, and letting ${\bf V}_j\doteq \bigcup_{F\in{\bf F}_j} V_F$
 play  the role of   ${\bf V}$.   
 Proposition \ref{Prop:ExpandedPage}\eqref{ExpandedPageIsBundle} implies 
that the  manifold $ {\widehat P}_j$ may be given the structure of
a classical $I$--bundle\ in such a way that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  } {\widehat P}_j$ is a vertical
subset of $\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} {\widehat P}_j$. As we observed in \S\ref{Def:Harmless}, 
${\widehat{{\mathcal P}}}_j\doteq{\Omega_{ {\widehat P} _j}}$ is a well-defined clean\ suborbifold
with corners of ${{\mathcal N}}$, so that ${\widehat P} _j$ 
is a clean submanifold with corners of $N$.
Furthermore, Proposition \ref{Prop:ExpandedPage}\eqref{ExpandedPageFrontier} and the definition of ${\bf V}_j$ imply that
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\widehat P} _j$ is the union of all components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
} P_j$ that do not belong to ${\bf F}_j$, i.e.\ do not satisfy (a) or (b). A component $E$ of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
} P_j$ fails to satisfy (b) if and only if  the underlying set 
of the
binding containing ${\Omega_{E}}$ 
is
a  topological solid torus, which by 
\S\ref{spherical etc}
implies
in particular that $E$ is
an annulus. An annulus component $E$ of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
} P_j$ fails to satisfy (a) if and only if  
${\rm spanning size}(E)=n/2$. Hence we have shown:

\begin{claim}\label{jeepers}
 $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\widehat P} _j$ is the union of all components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
 } P_j$ which are annuli of spanning size\ $n/2$
and are contained in 
topological
solid 
tori that are underlying manifolds of bindings.
\end{claim}

We claim:

\begin{claim}\label{fish and chips}
The 
sets
$ {\widehat P}  _1,\ldots, {\widehat P}  _k$ are pairwise disjoint.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{fish and chips}, we must
 check that when  $j,j'\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ are distinct indices, three conditions hold: first, $ P_j\cap  P_{j'}=\emptyset$; second, $ P_{j'}\cap V_F=\emptyset$ for each $F\in{\bf F}_j$; and third, $V_F\cap V_{F'}=\emptyset$ for all $F\in{\bf F}_j$ and $F'\in{\bf F}_{j'}$.
If  $F\in{\bf F}_j$ and $F'\in{\bf F}_{j'}$, it
is immediate that $ P_j\cap  P_{j'}=\emptyset$ since ${{\mathcal P}}_j$ and ${{\mathcal P}}_{j'}$ are distinct pages of ${{\mathcal N}}$. According to Lemma \ref{both verses}, $V_F$ is  disjoint from every big\ page of ${{\mathcal N}}$ other than ${{\mathcal P}}_j$; in particular $V_F\cap {{\mathcal P}}_{j'}=\emptyset$. Finally, to show that the connected, proper subsets $V_F$ and $V_{F'}$ of $ N  $ are disjoint, 
it is enough to prove that each is disjoint from the frontier of the other; and by symmetry, we need only prove that  $V_F$ is disjoint from $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }V_{F'}$. But this follows from the fact that 
$V_F$ is disjoint from ${{\mathcal P}}_{j'}$, as the latter set contains $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }V_{F'}$. Thus
\ref{fish and chips} is established.

Next, we claim:

\begin{claim}\label{Claim:IfEmptyFrontier}
If $\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j = \emptyset$ for some $j$, then $N$ is homeomorphic to either ${\mathbb S}^2 \times I$ or the $3$--manifold obtained by removing 
the interior of a closed
 $3$--ball from ${\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^3$.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{Claim:IfEmptyFrontier}, assume that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j = \emptyset$. Since $N$ is connected, it follows that ${\widehat P}_j = N$ (and that $j=k =1$). Thus $N$ is homeomorphic to a classical $I$--bundle\ over some closed surface of positive Euler characteristic. 
Thus $ N  $ is homeomorphic
either to the trivial classical $I$--bundle\ 
${\mathbb S}^2 \times I$ or to a twisted classical $I$--bundle\ over
${\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^2$. In the second case, $N$ is homeomorphic to the $3$--manifold obtained by removing 
the interior of a closed
 $3$--ball from ${\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^3$. 
 
 According to \ref{Claim:IfEmptyFrontier}, the conclusion of the theorem holds if
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j = \emptyset$ for some $j$. Thus, for the remainder of the proof, we 
assume:
\begin{claim}\label{non-empty frontiers}
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j \neq \emptyset$ for every $j$.
\end{claim} 


For $j=1,\ldots,k$, let $H_j$ denote the base of the
classical $I$--bundle\ 
${\widehat P} _j$.
Then $H_j$ is connected since ${\widehat P} _j$ is connected.
If for some $j$ the surface $H_j$  is closed, then we have 
$\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} {\widehat P}_{j}=\emptyset$. In particular,
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  } {\widehat P}_{j}
\subset\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} {\widehat P}_{j}$ is empty, 
contradicting
\ref{non-empty frontiers}. This proves:

\begin{claim}\label{not closed}
For $j=1,\ldots,k$ we have $\partial H_j\ne\emptyset$.
\end{claim}



Now set $\widehat{\bf P} = {\widehat P}  _1\cup\cdots\cup {\widehat P}  _k$, which is a disjoint union
according to \ref{fish and chips}. The 
classical $I$--bundle\ structures on the
${\widehat P} _j$ define a classical $I$--bundle\ structure
 on $\widehat{\bf P}$. 
As in the statement of Lemma \ref{not more than one, now}, we
let
${{\mathscr B}^\ast}$ 
denote the union of all bindings 
of ${{\mathcal N}}$ which have 
topological
solid tori as underlying 
sets
and have  spanning size\
$n/2$.
Set ${\bf B}^\ast={{\rm X}_{{{\mathscr B}^\ast}}}$.
We claim:

\begin{claim}\label{and whaddya got}
We have $N=\widehat{\bf P}\cup{\bf B}^\ast$ and
$\widehat{\bf P}\cap{\bf B}^\ast=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N } \widehat{\bf P}=\mathop{\rm Fr}{\bf B}^\ast$. Furthermore, each component of
$\widehat{\bf P}\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ is an annulus which is vertical in the
classical $I$--bundle\ $\widehat{\bf P}$ 
and has non-zero winding number on the 
(topological solid torus) 
component of ${\bf B}^\ast$ containing it.
\end{claim}


To prove \ref{and whaddya got}, first note that  
if $F$ is any component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }\widehat{\bf P}$, then
by \ref{fish and chips},
$F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\widehat P}_j$ for some $j\le k$;
and according to \ref{jeepers},
$F$ is therefore an annulus  component of 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N  P_j$ 
having spanning size\ $n/2$. Let ${{\mathcal B}} $ denote the binding of ${{\mathcal N}}$
such that $B\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal B}}}}  $ 
shares the frontier component $F$ with $ P_j$.
Then \ref{jeepers} also implies that 
$B  $ is a topological solid torus
(so that ${\rm spanning size}({{\mathcal B}}  )$ is defined by \S\ref{what's the point}),
and that ${\rm spanning size}({{\mathcal B}}  )={\rm spanning size}(F)=n/2$. 
Thus by definition ${{\mathcal B}} $ is a component of ${ {{\mathscr B}^\ast}}$. 
This shows that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }\widehat{\bf P}\subset\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast$.


Conversely, suppose that $F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }
{\bf B}^\ast$. Then $F$
is an annulus of spanning size\ $n/2$, and is a frontier component of
${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}} $ for some page ${{\mathcal P}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$. By Lemma
\ref{middle-sized lemma}, ${{\mathcal P}}$ is a big\ page of ${{\mathcal N}}$, so that
${{\mathcal P}}={{\mathcal P}}_j$ for some $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$. 
Since $F$ is a spanning size--$n/2$ component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP_j$, and
since  the
component of ${\bf B}^\ast$ containing $F$ is a topological solid torus by the
definition of ${\bf B}^\ast$, it follows from
\ref{jeepers} that $F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_N{\widehat P} _j$. 
This establishes the reverse inclusion $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast\subset\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }\widehat{\bf P}$.

Thus we have $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast = \mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }\widehat{\bf P}$. 
To prove that this set coincides with $\widehat{\bf P} \cap {\bf B}^\ast$, it suffices to show that 
if  $F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast = \mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }\widehat{\bf P}$, and $W$ is  a tubular neighborhood of $F$ in $N$, then $(W-F)\cap\widehat{\bf P}$ and $(W-F)\cap {\bf B}^\ast$ are contained in different components of $W-F$. But \ref{jeepers} implies that $(W-F) \cap \widehat{\bf P}$ is contained in some $P_j$, which is the underlying space of a page ${{\mathcal P}}_j$, while $(W-F) \cap {\bf B}^\ast$ is contained in the underlying space of a binding ${{\mathcal B}} \subset {{\mathscr B}^\ast}$. Thus 
$(W-F)\cap\widehat{\bf P}$ and $(W-F)\cap {\bf B}^\ast$ are disjoint, 
and we have shown that $\widehat{\bf P}\cap{\bf B}^\ast=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N} \widehat{\bf P}=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast$. 

Since
$\widehat{\bf P}\cap{\bf B}^\ast=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
}\widehat{\bf P}=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\bf B}^\ast$, the
compact  subset
$\widehat{\bf P}\cup{\bf B}^\ast$ of $ N  $ is an open subset of $ N $. Since we have seen (via a crucial application of 
Lemma \ref{big ol' lemma}) that $k\ge1$, we have $\emptyset \ne P_1\cup\cdots \cup P_k\subset\widehat{\bf P}$, and in particular
$\widehat{\bf P}\cup{\bf B}^\ast\ne\emptyset$. Since $ N  $ is connected it
follows that $\widehat{\bf P}\cup{\bf B}^\ast= N  $, and the 
first sentence of \ref{and whaddya got} is proved. 

To prove the second sentence of \ref{and whaddya got}, consider an arbitrary component $F$ of
$\widehat{\bf P}\cap{\bf B}^\ast$. Then according to 
the first sentence of \ref{and whaddya got},
$F$ is both a component of the
frontier of some component $B$ of ${\bf B}^\ast$, and a component of the
frontier of  ${\widehat P} _j$ for some $j$.
The definition of
${\bf B}^\ast$ implies that ${{\mathcal B}}\doteq{\Omega_{B}}$ is a binding of
${{\mathcal N}}$, 
and that $B$ is a topological solid torus.
According to an observation made in \S\ref{wuzza book},
$F$ is an annulus which has non-zero winding number in
the topological solid torus $B$. 
On the other hand, since $F$ is a component of
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N{\widehat P} _j$, our choice of the $I$--bundle structure on ${\widehat P} _j$ guarantees
that $F$ is a vertical 
subset
of $\partial {\widehat P} _j$ and therefore of
$\partial\widehat{\bf P}$.
The proof of \ref{and whaddya got} is now complete.

Now we claim: 
\begin{claim}\label{one annulus}
For each component $K$ of $\partial N$, the intersection $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ is a single annulus.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{one annulus}, we first note that \ref{and whaddya got} directly implies that each component of $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ is an annulus. Furthermore, it follows from Lemma \ref{not more than one, now} that $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ has at most one component. It remains only to show that $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast\ne\emptyset$. If we assume that $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ is empty, then since $N=\widehat{\bf P}\cup{\bf B}^\ast$ by \ref{and whaddya got}, we  have $K\subset\widehat{\bf P}$. But the component $K$ of $\partial N$ is a $2$--sphere, and in particular a closed surface. Hence $K$ must be a full boundary component of ${\widehat P}_{j}$ for some $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$. 
Thus the classical $I$--bundle\ ${\widehat P}_{j}$ has a boundary component which is a sphere; and the base $H_{j}$ of the classical $I$--bundle\ has non-empty boundary by \ref{not closed}. It follows that $H_j$ must be a disk. But then ${\widehat P}_j$ is a topological ball whose full boundary is the sphere $K$; this contradicts the essentiality of the sphere $S$ in $M$. Thus \ref{one annulus} is proved.

Now consider an arbitrary component $K$ of $\partial N$. By \ref{one annulus}, $K\cap{\bf B}^\ast$ is an annulus, and it follows from \ref{and whaddya got} that $K\cap\widehat{\bf P}=\overline{K-(K\cap {\bf B}^\ast)}$. 
Since $K$ is a sphere, it follows that $K\cap\widehat{\bf P}$ is the union of two disjoint disks. In particular:
\begin{claim}\label{They're disks}
Every component of $\widehat{\bf P}\cap\partial N$ is a disk.
\end{claim}

Now we claim:
\begin{claim}\label{each hatpj is a ball}
For each $j\le k$, the manifold with corners ${\widehat P}_j$ is a topological ball, and ${\widehat P}_j\cap{\bf B}^\ast$  is a single annulus.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{each hatpj is a ball}, we first recall that 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j \neq \emptyset$ for every $j$
by \ref{non-empty frontiers}. We choose a component $F$ of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j$, which by \ref{and whaddya got} is an annulus. Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ denote the components of $\partial F$. For $i=1,2$, it follows from \ref{and whaddya got} 
that $C_i$ is contained in a component $D_i$ of $\widehat{\bf P}\cap\partial N$. By \ref{They're disks}, each $D_i$ is a disk. In particular we have $\partial D_i=C_i$ for $i=1,2$. Since $D_i\subset\widehat{\bf P}$ and $C_i\subset{\widehat P}_j$, we have $D_i\subset{\widehat P}_j$. It now follows that $R \doteq D_1\cup F\cup D_2$ 
is a topological $2$--sphere contained in $\partial {\widehat P}_j$. But ${\widehat P}_j$ is a classical $I$--bundle\ over the compact surface $H_j$, which by \ref{not closed} has non-empty boundary. It follows that the manifold obtained by straightening the angles\ of ${\widehat P}_j$ is irreducible. Since $\partial{\widehat P}_j$ contains the $2$--sphere $R$, we deduce that ${\widehat P}_j$ is a topological ball with boundary $R$. We have ${\widehat P}_j\cap{\bf B}^\ast= R \cap{\bf B}^\ast=F$. This completes the proof of \ref{each hatpj is a ball}.  

It follows from \ref{each hatpj is a ball} that
$ N  $ is homeomorphic 
to a topological manifold obtained from ${\bf B}^\ast$ by
adding $k$ topological $2$--handles.
As $ N  $ is connected, it follows that ${\bf B}^\ast$ is connected,
i.e.\ is a single topological solid torus. A topological manifold
obtained by adding $k$ topological $2$--handles to a solid torus along 
annuli with non-zero winding number
 is homeomorphic to 
a manifold obtained from a (possibly trivial) lens space by removing
 the interiors of $k$ disjoint closed $3$--balls. 
In particular, $k$ is the number of boundary components of $N$, and is therefore equal to $1$ if $S$ separates $M$, and to $2$ otherwise.
If $k=1$, then $N$ is homeomorphic to a manifold obtained from a lens space by
removing  the interior of a closed $3$--ball; and in this case, since
$S$ is essential, the lens space in question must be non-trivial.  If
$k=2$, then $N$ is homeomorphic 
to a manifold obtained from a (possibly trivial) lens space by
removing the interiors of two disjoint closed $3$--balls.
In either case, the conclusion of the theorem follows.

(We remark that the above proof shows that $N$ has at most two big pages. Indeed, if $\mathop{\rm Fr}_N {\widehat P}_j = \emptyset$ for some $j$, then there is exactly one big page, and otherwise the number $k$ of  big pages is equal to the number of components of $\partial N$.)
<!-- end proof-39 -->

<!-- custom-62: body_md -->
{Complexity and ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal tori}\label{TorusComplexity}
 Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable, hyperbolic $3$--orbifold such that
$M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}} $ is irreducible. 
According to the conventions laid out in \S\ref{AccordantConvention},
${{\mathcal M}}$ is understood to be equipped with an ${{\mathcal M}}$--accordant
smooth structure.
Suppose that $M$ contains a $\pi_1$--injective torus $T$ that is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$. Define the \emph{complexity} of $T$ to be
\[
{\rm comp}(T) = 
\begin{cases}
\mathop{\rm size}(T) & \text{if $T$ is separating,} \\
2 \mathop{\rm size}(T) & \text{if $T$ is non-separating}.
\end{cases}
\]
A torus $T \subset M$ is called \emph{${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal} if $T$ 
\begin{enumerate}
\item\label{Itm:Comp1} is $\pi_1$--injective, 
\item\label{Itm:Comp2} is transverse to the singular locus, and 
\item\label{Itm:Comp3} has the smallest complexity among all tori in $M$ satisfying \eqref{Itm:Comp1} and \eqref{Itm:Comp2}.
\end{enumerate}
Observe that if $M$ contains a $\pi_1$--injective torus, then it contains an ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal one.
<!-- end custom-62 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{it's still incompressible}
Let 
${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable, hyperbolic $3$--orbifold such that
$M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ is irreducible, and let
$T$ be an ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal
torus in $M$.
Then ${\Omega_{T}} $ is essential in ${{\mathcal M}}$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Set ${{\mathcal T}} = {\Omega_{T}} $.
We first observe that since $T$ is a torus,
${{\mathcal T}}$ 
cannot be spherical, and thus cannot bound a discal $3$--orbifold. 
It remains
to show that 
${{\mathcal T}}$ is $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal M}}$. According to
Proposition \ref{when injective},
this amounts to showing that
if ${{\mathcal D}}$ is a two-dimensional orientable discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$ with ${{\mathcal D}} \cap {{\mathcal T}} = \partial {{\mathcal D}}$, then ${{\mathcal C}}\doteq\partial {{\mathcal D}}$ bounds a discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal T}}$. 


Since ${{\mathcal D}}$ is an orientable discal suborbifold, $ D \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal D}}}}$ is a 
disk, transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$,
 with $\mathop{\rm size}(D)\le 1$ and $\mathop{\rm size}(\partial D) = 0$.
(See \S\ref{Suborbifolds-of-3orbifolds}.)
 
Now since $T$ is ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal and therefore $\pi_1$--injective, 
the curve $C\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal C}}}}=\partial D$ 
bounds a disk
$D'\subset T$. 
Then
 $S \doteq D\cup D'$ is a 
smoothable 
topological
$2$--sphere
with $S\cap T=D'$. 
Since $M$ is irreducible, $S$ bounds a
topological ball $H\subset M$.
The $\pi_1$--injectivity of $T$ 
in $M$ implies that 
$T$ cannot be
contained in
$H$; hence $H\cap T=D'$. It follows that
the torus $T_1$ obtained by smoothing $(T-D')\cup D$ (which
by \S\ref{what's smoothing} has the same size as $(T-D')\cup D$)
is smoothly 
isotopic to $T$ in
$M$. Thus $T_1$  is $\pi_1$--injective, which is property \eqref{Itm:Comp1} of \S\ref{TorusComplexity}.
By construction, $T_1$ also satisfies property \eqref{Itm:Comp2} of \S\ref{TorusComplexity}.

The minimality of $T$ now implies ${\rm comp}(T) \leq {\rm comp}(T_1)$. Since $T$ and $T_1$ are isotopic, they are either both separating or both non-separating; hence $\mathop{\rm size}(T) \leq \mathop{\rm size}(T_1)$.
Thus
\[
\mathop{\rm size}(T) \leq \mathop{\rm size}(T_1)=\mathop{\rm size}(\overline{T-D'})+\mathop{\rm size}(D) = \mathop{\rm size}(T) - \mathop{\rm size}(D') + \mathop{\rm size}(D).
\]
Hence
$\mathop{\rm size}(D')\le\mathop{\rm size}(D)\le1$. Thus ${\Omega_{D'}}$ is the
required discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal T}}$ bounded by ${{\mathcal C}}$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- custom-63: body_md -->
{Dominant pages}
Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be an orbifold book of $I$--bundles, and let $N \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$.
A page ${{\mathcal P}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$ is called \emph{dominant} if for every component $K$ of ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}} \cap \partial N$, the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1(K)\to\pi_1(N)$ is
non-trivial.
<!-- end custom-63 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{Lem:DominantExists}
Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be an orbifold book of $I$--bundles, and
  set $N = {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$.
Suppose that $N$ is irreducible and that every component of $\partial N$ is a $\pi_1$--injective torus. Then ${{\mathcal N}}$ has a dominant page ${{\mathcal P}}$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Choose a component $T$ of $\partial N $, and set ${{\mathcal T}}={\Omega_{T}}$.
Using the notation of \S\ref{wuzza book}, set
${\mathscr A}={\mathscr A}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal T}}}$, ${\mathscr H}={\mathscr H}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal T}}}$, and ${\bf C} = {\bf C}_{{{\mathcal N}},{{\mathcal T}}}$.
Then ${\bf H}\doteq{{\rm X}_{{\mathscr H}}}$ and ${\bf A}\doteq{{\rm X}_{{\mathscr A}}}$
are $2$--manifolds with boundary whose union is $T$,
and
${\bf C} = {\bf H}\cap{\bf A}=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{T}{\bf H}=\mathop{\rm Fr}_{T}{\bf A}$
is a closed $1$--manifold.

We claim:

\begin{claim}\label{Claim:PartiallyDominant}
There is a component $H$ of ${\bf H}$ such that the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1(H)\to\pi_1(T)$ is
non-trivial. 
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{Claim:PartiallyDominant}, we consider two cases. First, suppose that
 some component $C$ of ${\bf C}$ is
homotopically non-trivial on the torus $T$. 
If $H$ denotes the component of 
${\bf H}$
containing $C$, the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1(H )\to\pi_1( T  )$ is
non-trivial, as desired.


Next, suppose that
 every component of ${\bf C}$ is
homotopically trivial in $T$.
In this case,  
${\bf C}$ is a finite union of simple closed curves
in the torus $T$,  each of which bounds a disk in $T$. Hence
there is
a compact submanifold $\Delta$ of $T$, each component of which is a
disk, such that $\partial\Delta\subset{\bf C}\subset\Delta$.
It follows that
$L\doteq\overline{T-\Delta}$ is connected,  that 
the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1(L )\to\pi_1( T  )$ is
surjective, and that
$\mathop{\rm int} L$ 
is disjoint from
${\bf C}$. 
Since the $2$--manifold $L\subset T$ is connected, has boundary
contained in ${\bf C}$ and has interior disjoint from ${\bf C}$, we deduce
that $L$ is a
component of either ${\bf A}$ or ${\bf H}$. 
But every component $A$ of ${\bf A}$ is either a disk or an annulus, so in particular $\pi_1(A)$ cannot surject onto $\pi_1(T)$. 
Thus $L$ must be a component of  ${\bf H}$, and setting $H = L$ completes the proof of \ref{Claim:PartiallyDominant}.

Now, let ${{\mathcal P}}$
  denote
the unique page of ${{\mathcal N}}$ whose underlying space $P$ contains $H$. 
  Set
  ${\bf K}= P\cap \partial N \subset {\bf H}$, so that $H$ is a component of ${\bf K}$. 
We claim:

\begin{claim}\label{Claim:ConnectOrClassic}
Either ${\bf K}$ is connected, or $ P$ may be given the structure of
a trivial
classical $I$--bundle\ 
 in such a way that 
${\bf K}=\partial_\mathrm{h}^{\rm cl} P$.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{Claim:ConnectOrClassic}, recall  
from 
\S\ref{PagelikeBindinglike}
that the page ${{\mathcal P}}$ has the structure of an orbifold $I$--bundle in
which 
${\Omega_{{\bf K}}}=\partial_\mathrm{h}{{\mathcal P}}$  and 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal P}}=\partial_\mathrm{v}{{\mathcal P}}$.
In particular, according to Corollary \ref{Cor:VertBoundaryStructure},
each component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal P}}$
is an annular orbifold, and hence each component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP$  is an annulus or a disk. 


It follows from Proposition  \ref{Prop:IBundleTotalSpace} that
the topological $3$--manifold $ P$ may be given
the structure of a
classical $I$--bundle\ 
in such a way that
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP$ is a vertical subset of $\partial_\mathrm{v}^{\rm cl} P$.
In particular,
 if $V$ denotes the vertical boundary of the 
classical $I$--bundle\  $P$, 
we have $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP\subset V$, and $Z\doteq \overline{V-\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP}$ is
also a vertical submanifold. If $Y$ denotes the horizontal boundary 
 of the classical $I$--bundle\  $P$,  we have ${\bf K}=Y\cup Z$. 
In a classical $I$--bundle, each
 component of a
 vertical
  subset
meets each component of the horizontal boundary;
 hence if $Z\ne\emptyset$, or if $Y$ is connected, then ${\bf K}$ is
 connected. But $Y$ is disconnected if and only if $P$ is a trivial
classical $I$--bundle;
and $Z = \emptyset$ if and only if ${\bf K}=Y$. 
This proves \ref{Claim:ConnectOrClassic}.


To prove the lemma, we claim that ${{\mathcal P}}$ is a dominant page.
That is, for every component $K$ of
 ${\bf K} = P \cap \partial N$, the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1(K )\to\pi_1( N  )$ is
  non-trivial.
Observe that if $K = H$, the assertion follows 
from \ref{Claim:PartiallyDominant} and the $\pi_1$--injectivity
 of $T$ in $N$. In particular, the assertion is true if ${\bf K}$ is
connected. If ${\bf K}$ is not connected, then by \ref{Claim:ConnectOrClassic},
$ P$ may be given the structure of
a trivial 
classical $I$--bundle\ 
in such a way that 
${\bf K}=\partial_\mathrm{h}^{\rm cl} P$.
In this case, ${\bf K}$ has two
components, one of which is $H$. We need only prove the assertion in
the subcase when
$K$ is the other component of ${\bf K}$. But then the 
classical $I$--bundle\ 
structure of $ P$ gives a homeomorphism of $K$ onto $H$ which,
regarded as a map from $K$ to $N$, is homotopic to the inclusion
$K\hookrightarrow N$. Since the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1(H)\to\pi_1( N  )$ is
non-trivial, 
we conclude that the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1(K )\to\pi_1( N  )$ is
also non-trivial, 
and the lemma is proved.
<!-- end proof-41 -->

non-trivial.
<!-- end claim-30 -->

<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{doughnut hole}
Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be an orbifold book of $I$--bundles, and let $N \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal N}}}}$. Suppose that $N$ is irreducible and that every component of $\partial N$ is a $\pi_1$--injective torus.  Let ${{\mathcal P}}$ be a dominant page in ${{\mathcal N}}$, which exists by Lemma~\ref{Lem:DominantExists}. Set 
$P = {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}$, and let ${\widehat P}$  denote
 the union of $ P$ with all harmless\
components 
of $\overline{ N  - P }$ (see \S\ref{Def:Harmless}).
Then every component of  
$\partial({\widehat P}\cap \partial N)=\partial(\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\widehat P})$ 
is $\pi_1$--injective in $ N  $.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Following the notation of 
Lemma~\ref{Lem:DominantExists}, 
set ${\bf K} = P \cap \partial N$. We claim:

\begin{claim}\label{i just did}
If $Q$ is any component of $\partial{\bf K}$ which is a homotopically trivial
simple closed curve in $N$, then $Q$  bounds a disk which is a component of
$\overline{\partial N -{\bf K}}$.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{i just did}, first note that since 
$Q\subset\partial N$ is homotopically
trivial in $N$, and $\partial N$ is $\pi_1$--injective in $N$, the curve $Q$ 
bounds a disk $D\subset\partial N$. Since 
$Q$ is a component of $\partial{\bf K}$, either (a) $D$
is a component of
$\overline{\partial N -{\bf K}}$, or (b) $D$
contains some component $K$ of ${\bf K}$. But since $D$
is a disk, (b) would imply that the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1(K )\to\pi_1( N  )$ is
trivial, 
contradicting the assumption that ${{\mathcal P}}$ is dominant.
Hence (a) must hold,
and \ref{i just did} is established.


We also claim:
\begin{claim}\label{kiddly divy}
If $F$ is any component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP$ such that the inclusion
homomorphism $\pi_1(F)\to\pi_1(N)$ is trivial, then there is a smoothable 
$2$--sphere
$S\subset N$ which is the union of $F$ with some subsurface of
$\partial N$.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{kiddly divy}, suppose that $F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP$
such that the inclusion
homomorphism $\pi_1(F)\to\pi_1(N)$ is trivial. Then each component of
$\partial F$ is a simple closed curve in $\partial N$, homotopically trivial in
$N$, which is also a component of $\partial{\bf K}$. 
By \ref{i just did}, each such component bounds  
a disk which is a component of
$\overline{\partial N -{\bf K}}$.

In the
case where $F$ is an annulus, let $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ denote its boundary
components. Each $Q_i$  bounds a disk $D_i$ which is a component of
$\overline{\partial N -{\bf K}}$. Since $Q_1\ne
Q_2$, the components $D_1$ and $D_2$ of $\overline{(\partial
  N)-{\bf K}}$ are distinct and therefore
disjoint. The conclusion
of \ref{kiddly divy}
 then follows upon setting $S=D_1\cup F\cup D_2$.

In the
case where $F$ is a disk,
$Q\doteq\partial F$ bounds a disk $D$ which is a component of
$\overline{\partial N -{\bf K}}$. 
In this case the  conclusion 
of \ref{kiddly divy}
follows upon setting $S=D\cup F$. 

Now we claim:
\begin{claim}\label{who wants to know}
If $F$ is any component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP$ such that the inclusion
homomorphism $\pi_1(F)\to\pi_1(N)$ is trivial, then the component of
$\overline{N -P}$ 
containing $F$ is harmless. 
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{who wants to know}, suppose that $F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP$ such that the inclusion
homomorphism $\pi_1(F)\to\pi_1(N)$ is trivial, and let $S$ be the
smoothable $2$--sphere given by \ref{kiddly divy}. Since $N$ is irreducible, $S$
bounds a topological ball $J\subset N$. 
According to \ref{kiddly divy}, $S=\partial
J$ is the union of $F$ with some subsurface of
$\partial N$. It now follows that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NJ=F$. 

Since $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NJ=F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP$, either $J$ is  a component of $\overline{N-P}$, or 
$J \supset P$. But if
$J\supset P$ then in particular 
${\bf K}\ne\emptyset$ and is contained in the topological ball $J\subset
N$; this is impossible since the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_1(K)\to\pi_1( N  )$ is 
non-trivial for each component $K$ of ${\bf K}$, by the definition of  a dominant page. 
Hence $J$ is  a component of $\overline{N-P}$. Since $J$
is a topological ball and $F=\mathop{\rm Fr}_NJ$ is connected, it now follows from the
definition that $J$ is a harmless component of $\overline{N-P}$, and
\ref{who wants to know} is proved.

To complete the proof of the lemma, suppose
that $C$ is a component of  $\partial({\widehat P}\cap\partial N
)=\partial(\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N  }{\widehat P})$.
The component $F$ of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ N 
}{\widehat P}$ containing $C$ is in particular a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP$.
Assume that $C$
is not $\pi_1$--injective in $ N  $.  Since 
$C$ is contained in the $\pi_1$--injective submanifold $\partial N$ of $N$,
the  simple closed curve
$C\subset T\subset N$ is homotopically trivial in $N$. Since 
$F$ is a disk or an
annulus, it follows that the inclusion homomorphism
$\pi_1(F)\to\pi_1(N)$ is trivial. Hence by \ref{who wants to know},
$F$ is contained in a harmless component of $\overline{N-P}$. But this
contradicts the fact that $F$ is a component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{N} {\widehat P}$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
