\label{who wants to know}
If $F$ is any component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_NP$ such that the inclusion
homomorphism $\pi_1(F)\to\pi_1(N)$ is trivial, then the component of
$\overline{N -P}$ 
containing $F$ is harmless.
<!-- end claim-34 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{Prop:TorusBooksTotalSpace}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable, hyperbolic $3$--orbifold such that $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}} $ is irreducible.
Suppose that $T$ is an ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal torus in $M$. 
Let $N$ be a component of $M {\backslash \backslash} T$, and assume 
that ${{\mathcal N}} \doteq {\Omega_{N}}$ admits the structure of  a book of $I$--bundles. 
Then either
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(i)]
\item 
$T$ is separating, and 
$N$ admits a Seifert fibration over a disk with exactly two
singular fibers; or
\item $T$ is non-separating, 
and $N$ admits a Seifert fibration over an annulus  with at most
one singular fiber.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Let $R$  be a tubular neighborhood of $T$ in $M$. Then $N$ is diffeomorphic to a component $N_0$ of $\overline{M-R}$. We shall show that the conclusions of the proposition hold with $N_0$ in place of $N$, thereby proving the proposition.

We may suppose $R$ to have been chosen in such a way that $\partial N_0$ is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, and that each component of $\partial N_0$ has the same size as $T$. Since $\partial N_0$ has one component if $T$ is separating, and has two components if $T$ is non-separating, the definition of complexity now implies:
\begin{equation}\label{size is complexity}
\mathop{\rm size}(\partial N_0)={\rm comp}(T). 
\end{equation}



We set ${{{\mathcal N}}_0}={\Omega_{{N_0}}}$, and  fix a structure of a book of $I$--bundles on ${{{\mathcal N}}_0}$.

First note that 
$T   $ is $\pi_1$--injective in $M $ by the definition of an ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal torus. It follows that ${N_0} $ is irreducible and that 
every component of  
$\partial {N_0} $ is a $\pi_1$--injective torus
 in ${N_0} $.
In particular:

\begin{claim}\label{sickle}
 $ {N_0}  $ is not a solid torus. 
Therefore
 $ {N_0}  $ admits no Seifert fibration over a disk with at most one singular fiber.
\end{claim} 


We also observe that since $T$ is essential in $M$, 
the manifold case of Lemma~\ref{split injective} implies
that
\begin{claim}\label{that too}
$N_0$ is $\pi_1$--injective in $M$.
\end{claim}



Now according to Lemma \ref{Lem:DominantExists},  we may fix a 
dominant page ${{\mathcal P}}$  of ${{{\mathcal N}}_0}$.
We set $P={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal P}}}}$.
We apply Proposition \ref{Prop:ExpandedPage}\eqref{ExpandedPageIsBundle}, taking ${\bf V}$ to be the union of
all harmless components of $\overline{{N_0} -P}$.
This shows that ${\widehat P} 
\doteq P \cup {\bf V}
$ may be given the structure of a
classical $I$--bundle\ in
such a way that 
$F\doteq\mathop{\rm Fr}_{ {N_0}   }{\widehat P}$
is a vertical submanifold of 
$\partial{\widehat P}$. 

We let 
$W$ denote the $3$--manifold with corners  $\overline{ {N_0}   - {\widehat P}}$. It may happen that $W$ is empty. On the other hand,  since ${N_0}$ is connected and ${\widehat P}\supset P\ne\emptyset$, we have that
\begin{claim}\label{cooties}
Each component of $W$ contains a component of $F$. 
\end{claim}
We set
$C=\partial F=\partial({\widehat P}\cap\partial {N_0}   )$. It follows from Lemma \ref{doughnut hole} that
\begin{claim}\label{ronly honly bing}
 $C$
is $\pi_1$--injective in $ {N_0}   $. 
\end{claim}

It follows from \ref{ronly honly bing} that no component of $F$ is  a disk.
The components of $F$ must therefore be annuli, and, again by \ref{ronly honly bing}, these annuli are $\pi_1$--injective. But a vertical annulus in the boundary of a classical $I$--bundle\ must be a component of the vertical boundary.  
 Hence, if $E$ denotes the vertical boundary of the classical $I$--bundle\ ${\widehat P}$, we may state: 
\begin{claim}\label{frugal me}
$F$ is a union of components of  $E$, and each component of $F$ is a $\pi_1$--injective annulus in $N_0$.
\end{claim}

It follows from \ref{ronly honly bing}
that the
boundary components of ${\widehat P}\cap\partial {N_0}   $ are homotopically
non-trivial simple closed curves in 
${N_0} $, and in particular in $\partial {N_0}   $. 
Since 
$\partial {N_0} $ consists of tori,
it follows that each component of ${\widehat P}\cap\partial {N_0}   $ or
$W\cap\partial {N_0}   $
 is a torus or an annulus. Since the components of
 $F$ are annuli by
  \ref{frugal me},
  it now follows that:
\begin{claim}\label{spell it out}
All of the
boundary components of the topological manifolds ${\widehat P}$ and $W$ are
smoothable tori. 
\end{claim}

In particular we have
$\chi({\widehat P})=0$, so that the base of the classical $I$--bundle\ ${\widehat P}$ is a
topological torus,  Klein bottle,  annulus, or M\"obius band. 

If the base of  ${\widehat P}$ is a topological torus or  Klein bottle, then
$E=\emptyset$, and in particular  \ref{frugal me} implies
$F=\emptyset$. Hence $ {N_0}   ={\widehat P}$, i.e.\ ${N_0}$ is either a
trivial classical $I$--bundle\ over $T^2$ or a twisted classical $I$--bundle\ over the topological Klein
bottle. 
If ${N_0}$ is a
trivial classical $I$--bundle\ over $T^2$, then
${N_0}$ admits a Seifert fibration over an
annulus with no singular fibers.
If  ${N_0}$ is a twisted classical $I$--bundle\ over the Klein
bottle, then
${N_0}$ admits a
Seifert fibration over a disk with two singular fibers (see
\cite[Theorem 2.3(b)]{hatcher3M}).
Thus the conclusion of the proposition holds if  the base of  ${\widehat P}$ is a topological torus or Klein bottle.

For the rest of the proof, we assume that the base of ${\widehat P}$ is a topological annulus or M\"obius band. 
Since $M $ is orientable, ${\widehat P}$  is either a trivial classical $I$--bundle\
over a
topological annulus or a twisted classical $I$--bundle\ over a topological M\"obius band. In
particular ${\widehat P}$ is a topological solid torus,  $E$ has at most two components, and if $E$ has two components then each of them is an annulus whose winding number in ${\widehat P}$ is $1$. By \ref{frugal me}
$F$ is a union of components of  $E$. We must have
$F\ne\emptyset$, for otherwise $ {N_0}   $ would be equal to the
topological solid torus ${\widehat P}$, a contradiction to \ref{sickle}. 
Hence:
\begin{claim}\label{pour chanter en choeur}
${\widehat P}$ is a topological solid torus, and  either (a) $F$ is a single annulus, or (b) $F$ is the union of
two disjoint annuli and ${\widehat P}$ is a parallelism (see \S\ref{Pi1Injective})  between these two annuli. 
\end{claim}


According to Proposition~\ref{Prop:ExpandedPage}\eqref{ExpandedPageEuler}, each component of $F$ is the underlying surface of an annular $2$--orbifold. Since  every component of $F$ is an annulus, we have $\mathop{\rm size}(F)=0$, and therefore 
$\mathop{\rm size}(\partial{\widehat P})+\mathop{\rm size}(\partial W) =\mathop{\rm size}(\partial {N_0})$. 

On the other hand,
Proposition~\ref{Prop:ExpandedPage}\eqref{ExpandedPageEuler} also gives that 
$\chi({\Omega_{{\widehat P}}})<0$, which implies that  $\chi({\Omega_{\partial{\widehat P}}})=2\chi({\Omega_{{\widehat P}}})<0$. Since ${\widehat P}$ is a topological solid torus, we have $\chi(\partial{\widehat P})=0$. Hence  $\mathop{\rm size}(\partial{\widehat P})>0$. It now follows that $\mathop{\rm size}(\partial W)<\mathop{\rm size}(\partial  {N_0}   )$,
which with \eqref{size is complexity} gives
\begin{equation}\label{and therefore}
\mathop{\rm size}(\partial W)<{\rm comp}(T). 
\end{equation}


We claim:
\begin{claim}\label{they separate}
Every  component of $\partial W$  is a separating
smoothable
 torus in $M$.
\end{claim}


To prove \ref{they separate}, first note that each component of $\partial W$ is a 
smoothable
torus by \ref{spell it out}. Next, note that since the $3$--submanifold $W$ of the closed $3$--manifold $M$ is compact, $\partial W$ cannot have \emph{exactly} one non-separating component. Assume  that $\partial W$ has at least two non-separating components. Choose two such components, and smooth them to obtain tori $T_1$ and $T_2$, with $\mathop{\rm size} (T_1)\le\mathop{\rm size}(T_2)$.
Using the definition of complexity and \eqref{and therefore}, we find
$${\rm comp}(T_1)=2\mathop{\rm size}(T_1)\le\mathop{\rm size}(T_1)+\mathop{\rm size}(T_2)\le\mathop{\rm size}(\partial W)<{\rm comp}(T).$$
Since $T$ is an ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal torus, and $T_1\subset M$ is a torus transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, it follows that $T_1$ is not $\pi_1$--injective in $M$. Since $M$ is irreducible, any non-$\pi_1$--injective torus in $M$ either bounds a solid torus in $M$ or is contained in a $3$--ball in $M$. In either case, $T_1$ must separate $M$, and we have a contradiction. This proves \eqref{they separate}.


On the other hand, we claim:
\begin{claim}\label{connected complement}
For every component $K$ of $W$, the manifold $\overline{M-K}$ is connected. 
\end{claim}

Let $K$ be a component of $W = \overline{N_0-{\widehat P}}$.
Note that $\overline{N_0-K}$ is the union of ${\widehat P}$ with all components of $\overline{N_0-{\widehat P}}$ distinct from $K$. Each such component meets ${\widehat P}$, since $N_0$ is connected. Hence $\overline{N_0-K}$ is connected. But $\overline{M-N_0}$ is connected by construction, and $\overline{N_0-K}\cap\overline{M-N_0}$ contains $P \cap\partial N_0$, which is the underlying set of the horizontal boundary of an orbifold $I$--bundle ${{\mathcal P}}$, and is therefore 
non-empty. 
It follows that $\overline{M-K}=\overline{N_0-K}\cup\overline{M-N_0}$ is connected, and \ref{connected complement} is proved.

We now claim more:
\begin{claim}\label{how's this?}
Each component of $W$ is a topological solid torus.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{how's this?}, 
let $K$ be any component  of $W$. 
It follows from \ref{they separate} and \ref{connected complement} that
 $\partial K$ is 
 a single smoothable torus, which in particular  
separates $M$. Let $T'$ denote a torus obtained by smoothing $\partial K$. By definition
 $T'$ is transverse to the singular set of ${{\mathcal M}}$. 

By \eqref{and therefore}
we have 
\[
\mathop{\rm size}(T')=\mathop{\rm size}(\partial K)\le\mathop{\rm size}(\partial W)<{\rm comp}(T).
\]
 But $T'$ separates $M$, so we have ${\rm comp}(T')=\mathop{\rm size}(T')$, hence ${\rm comp}(T')<{\rm comp}(T)$. If $T'$ were $\pi_1$--injective in $M $, we would now have a contradiction to the ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimality of $T$. Hence $T'$ is not $\pi_1$--injective in $M $. Since $M $ is irreducible, $T'$ either bounds a 
solid torus in $M $ or is contained in a 
ball in $M $. But $T'$ is topologically isotopic to $\partial K$, which by \ref{cooties}  contains a component of $F\supset C$;
and by \ref{ronly honly bing}, $C$ is a $\pi_1$--injective closed one-dimensional submanifold of ${N_0}$, and hence of $M $ by \ref{that too}. 
Hence $T'$ cannot be contained in a ball. Since $T'$ is isotopic to the full boundary of $K $, it follows that either $K$ or $\overline{M -K}$ is a topological solid torus. 
But $\overline{M -K}$ contains $T$, which 
is an ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal torus and is thus 
$\pi_1$--injective in $M $. Hence $K$ must be a topological solid torus, and \ref{how's this?} is proved.

To establish the conclusion of the proposition, it suffices to show that $N_0$ has a Seifert fibration such that either (i) the base is a disk and there are two singular fibers, or (ii) the base is an annulus and there is at most one singular fiber. Indeed, if (i) holds then $\partial N_0\cong\partial N$ is connected, and hence $T$ is separating; and if (ii) holds then $\partial N_0\cong \partial N$ has two components, and hence $T$ is non-separating.

First consider the case in which Alternative (a) of \ref{pour chanter en choeur} holds. Since $ {N_0}   $ is connected, it then follows from \ref{how's this?} that $W$ is a single topological solid torus. The topological solid tori ${\widehat P}$ and $W$ meet in $F$, which by
  \ref{frugal me}
  is an annulus, $\pi_1$--injective in $ {N_0}    $ and therefore in both ${\widehat P}$ and $W$. Hence $ {N_0}   ={\widehat P}\cup W$ admits a Seifert fibration over the disk with at most two singular fibers. It follows from \ref{sickle} that this Seifert fibration must have exactly two singular fibers, and conclusion (i) follows in this case.

Now  consider the case in which Alternative (b) of \ref{pour chanter en choeur} holds. 
Let $F_1$ and $F_2$ denote the components of $F={\widehat P}\cap W=\partial {\widehat P}\cap \partial W$,
which by
  \ref{frugal me}
are  annuli, and are $\pi_1$--injective in $ {N_0}   $ and hence in $W$.
Since $ {N_0} $ is connected, it then follows from  \ref{how's this?} that either 
(1) $W$ is the disjoint union of two topological solid tori $W_1$ and $W_2$, and we have $F_i\subset W_i$ for $i=1,2$, or
(2) $W$ is a single topological solid torus.
Since Alternative (b) includes the assertion that ${\widehat P}$ is a parallelism between $F_1$ and $F_2$, the manifold $ {N_0}  $ is homeomorphic to a topological
manifold obtained from $W$ by gluing the annuli $F_1$ and $F_2$ together by some homeomorphism.
 In Subcase (1) it follows that $ {N_0}  $ admits a Seifert fibration over the disk with at most two singular fibers, and by \ref{sickle}  this Seifert fibration must have exactly two singular fibers. In Subcase (2) it follows that $ {N_0}  $ admits a Seifert fibration over
the annulus with at most one singular fiber.
<!-- end proof-43 -->

Therefore
