<!-- custom-64: body_md -->
{Definitions}\label{GS review}
We shall
generalize to the context of orbifolds some definitions that
are stated in Guzman and Shalen \cite[Section 3]{GS-homotoping} in the context of
manifolds. 

We shall say that a $3$--orbifold is \emph{simple} if
it is compact, orientable, irreducible
and boundary-irreducible, 
 is not discal, and has a fundamental group containing no rank--$2$ abelian
subgroup. 
Since irreducible $3$--orbifolds are connected by Definition~\ref{Pi1Injective}, every simple $3$--orbifold is also connected.
We observe that if a closed $2$--orbifold ${{\mathcal R}}$   in a
closed hyperbolic $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}$ is essential, then every component of
${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal R}}$ is simple. 


 Let ${{\mathcal Q}}$ be a compact, orientable $3$--orbifold.
The notion of a bindinglike (or purely  bindinglike)
suborbifold ${\mathcal K}$ of ${\mathcal Q}$, and that of a pagelike (or purely  pagelike)
suborbifold of ${\mathcal Q}$, were defined in \S\ref{PagelikeBindinglike}.
(The definition of ``pagelike'' in \S\ref{PagelikeBindinglike}, when specialized to the manifold case, differs slightly from
the definition of a ``pagelike submanifold'' $P$ in \cite{GS-homotoping}, in that it requires non-positive Euler characteristic. However, this does not affect our quotation of any result from \cite{GS-homotoping}.)
According to \S\ref{PagelikeBindinglike},  if ${\mathcal K}$ is a pagelike or bindinglike suborbifold  of ${\mathcal Q}$ then
the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{\mathcal Q}{\mathcal K}$ are neatly\  embedded 
annular $2$--orbifolds 
in ${\mathcal Q}$. We
shall say that ${\mathcal K}$ has \emph{essential frontier} if all the
components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{\mathcal Q}{\mathcal K}$ are essential 
annular orbifolds 
in ${\mathcal Q}$. 

A \emph{thickened annular orbifold} in ${\mathcal Q}$ is a 
clean\ 
suborbifold with corners
${\mathcal Y}$ of ${\mathcal Q}$ which is 
diffeomorphic to ${{\mathcal A}} \times[0,1]$, for some annular orbifold ${{\mathcal A}}$,
under a diffeomorphism that maps $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal Q}}{{\mathcal Y}}$ onto
${{\mathcal A}} \times\{0,1\}$.

By specializing the notions of simple orbifold, 
(purely) pagelike\ or bindinglike\  suborbifold (with essential frontier),
essential annular orbifold,   and thickened annular orbifold
to the manifold case, one obtains the
notions of simple manifold, 
 (purely) pagelike or bindinglike submanifold (with essential frontier),
essential annulus, and thickened annulus.
After translating between the PL and smooth categories, these
specialized notions coincide with the notions for manifolds that are used in
\cite{GS-homotoping}.
<!-- end custom-64 -->
<!-- custom-65: body_md -->
{Acylindrical pairs}\label{only manifolds}
Next,
we review some notions involving manifolds which
are defined in \cite{GS-homotoping}. Unlike the notions discussed in
\S\ref{GS review}, these notions will not need to be generalized to
orbifolds.


An \emph{acylindrical pair} is a 
clean\ manifold pair $({\bf L} ,{\bf E})$ 
satisfying the following conditions: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item each component of
the manifold obtained by straightening the angles\ of
 ${\bf L} $ is irreducible, no  component of ${\bf L}$ is a 
topological ball, 
and no component has a fundamental group with a rank--$2$ free abelian subgroup;
\item each component of ${\bf E}$ is an annulus and is $\pi_1$--injective
  in ${\bf L} $;
\item no component (see \S\ref{Clean pairs}) of $({\bf L} ,{\bf E})$
  is  diffeomorphic
to a pair of the form $(L,E)$, where $L$ is an $I$--bundle
over a (possibly non-orientable) surface and $E$ is the vertical
boundary of the $I$--bundle $L$;
\item no component of ${\bf L} $ is a
topological solid torus; and
\item for every neatly\  embedded, $\pi_1$--injective annulus
  $\Delta$ in $ {\bf L} -{\bf E}$, either
(a) $\Delta$ is boundary-parallel in ${\bf L}-{\bf E}$, or
(b) there is a component $E$ of ${\bf E}$ such that  $\Delta$ is
parallel  to $E$ in $({\bf L} -{\bf E})\cup E$. See \S\ref{Pi1Injective} for the notion of \emph{parallel}.
\end{enumerate}

We remark that the notion of an acylindrical pair is extremely similar to the notion of an \emph{acylindrical pared manifold} $(M, P)$ that is commonly used in the literature on Kleinian groups. See e.g.\ Namazi and Souto~\cite[Sections 3.1--3.2]{NamaziSouto:Density}.
<!-- end custom-65 -->
<!-- custom-66: body_md -->
{Characteristic submanifolds}\label{char-submflds}
Our treatment of characteristic submanifolds follows the point of view of 
Guzman and Shalen
 \cite[Section 3]{GS-homotoping}, which is based on
Jaco--Shalen \cite{JS}. In \cite{GS-homotoping}, 
the authors
consider a class of manifolds which includes all manifolds that are simple in the sense of this paper;
and for each manifold $Q$ in this
class the characteristic submanifold is described as a certain clean\
submanifold with corners ${\bf V} \subset Q$, 
 which is well-defined up to smooth isotopy. 

When
$Q$ is simple, ${\bf V}$ may be thought of as
a clean\ submanifold with corners, each of whose components is either bindinglike or pagelike
and satisfies certain nondegeneracy conditions; and
among all such submanifolds, ${\bf V}$ is maximal in a suitable sense.

While the formal definition of the characteristic submanifold will not
be quoted directly in this paper, we will make strong use of the
following characterization of the characteristic submanifold of a
simple manifold, which is proved in
\cite{GS-homotoping}.
<!-- end custom-66 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{char-submflds, GS edition}
Let $Q$ be a simple $3$--manifold with non-empty boundary, 
and let ${\bf V}$ be a
clean\  submanifold
  with corners
of $Q$. Then ${\bf V}$ is
isotopic to the characteristic submanifold of
$Q$ if and only if it has the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Each component of ${\bf V}$ 
is either bindinglike\ or pagelike, and has essential frontier
relative to $Q$.
\item
For each component $L$ of $\overline{Q-{\bf V}}$, 
either the pair $(L,\mathop{\rm Fr}_Q L)$  is acylindrical, or $L$ is a thickened annulus;
and in the latter case,  the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_Q L$ are contained in
distinct components of ${\bf V}$, of which one is purely
bindinglike\ and the other is purely pagelike.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
This is a direct translation of \cite[Proposition 3.12]{GS-homotoping} to the smooth category.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{what about manifolds}
Let $Q$ be a simple $3$--manifold with non-empty boundary, and let ${\bf V}$ denote its
characteristic submanifold. Let $L$ be a component of $\overline{Q -  {\bf V}}$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:$(1)$]
\item Every component of $\partial L$ (where we think of $L$ as a topological manifold) has non-positive Euler characteristic.
\item $\chi(L) \leq 0$.
\item If $\chi(L)=0$, then $L$ is a thickened annulus; and  
the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_Q L$ are contained in
distinct components of ${\bf V}$, of which one is purely
bindinglike\ and the other  is purely pagelike.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
According to Proposition \ref{char-submflds, GS edition},
each component
  of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_Q{\bf V}$ is 
an essential annulus in $Q$.
In particular, the boundary
  components of $\overline{Q -  {\bf V}}\cap\partial Q$ are $\pi_1$--injective simple closed
  curves in $\partial Q$.
Furthermore, the simplicity of $Q$ implies that no component of
$\partial Q$ is a $2$--sphere. Hence each component of $L\cap\partial
Q$ has non-positive Euler characteristic. 
Again using that 
the frontier
components of ${\bf V}$ are annuli, we deduce:
\begin{claim}\label{easy part}
Each boundary component of the topological manifold $\overline{Q -  {\bf V}}$ has non-positive
Euler characteristic.
\end{claim}

In particular, the claim implies Conclusion (1). Furthermore, 
since  $\chi(L)=\chi(\partial L)/2$, 
claim \ref{easy part} also establishes Conclusion (2).


To prove the last assertion of the lemma, suppose that $L$ is a
component of $\overline{Q -  {\bf V}}$ such that
  $\chi(L)=0$. Then $\chi(\partial L)=0$, and in view of \ref{easy part} it follows that every component of $\partial L$ is a
  topological torus. 

The components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_QL$ are among the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_Q{\bf V}$; hence they are
 essential annuli in $Q$, and  in particular are
$\pi_1$--injective annuli. The
$\pi_1$--injectivity of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_QL$, together with the simplicity of $Q$, implies that $L$ is irreducible and
$\pi_1$--injective in $Q$ and that $\partial L\ne\emptyset$. Since $Q$
is simple, any component of $\partial L$ fails to be $\pi_1$--injective
in $Q$, and therefore fails to be $\pi_1$--injective in $L$. But it is a standard
consequence of the Loop Theorem that a compact, orientable,
irreducible $3$--manifold, whose boundary contains a torus which is not
$\pi_1$--injective, is a solid torus. 
Hence $L$ is a topological solid torus.

According to Proposition \ref{char-submflds, GS edition}, 
either the pair $(L,\mathop{\rm Fr}_Q L)$  is acylindrical,
or $L$ is a thickened annulus. Since $L$ is a topological solid torus, the
definition implies that $(L,\mathop{\rm Fr}_Q L)$  is not acylindrical. Thus
$L$ is a thickened annulus. It also follows from 
Proposition \ref{char-submflds, GS edition} that
the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_Q L$ are contained in
distinct components of ${\bf V}$, of which one is purely
bindinglike, and the other is purely pagelike.
This
completes the proof of Conclusion (3).
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- claim-45: body_md -->
\label{easy part}
Each boundary component of the topological manifold $\overline{Q -  {\bf V}}$ has non-positive
Euler characteristic.
<!-- end claim-45 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{still simple}
Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be a simple $3$--orbifold, and suppose that $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$ is a
regular,
finite-sheeted covering of ${{\mathcal N}}$ which is a manifold. Then $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$
is simple.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
The compactness, orientability, 
boundary-irreducibility and non-discality of $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$, 
as well as the non-existence of  rank--$2$ abelian
subgroups in $\pi_1(\widetilde{{\mathcal N}})$, follow immediately from the
corresponding properties of ${{\mathcal N}}$.
It remains to show that  $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$ is irreducible. Since
${{\mathcal N}}$ is irreducible, it follows from the equivariant sphere theorem \cite[Theorem 7]{MY-sphere}
that $\pi_2(\widetilde{{\mathcal N}})=0$. 
Hence 
every $2$--sphere in $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$ bounds a contractible, compact
$3$--manifold $H\subset\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$
(see \cite[proof of Theorem 2]{Milnor}).
By the solution to the Poincar\'e Conjecture \cite{Morgan-Tian},
$H$ is a $3$--ball, and irreducibility is established.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{CharSuborbifold}
Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be a simple $3$--orbifold with non-empty boundary, suppose that $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$ is a regular, finite-sheeted manifold cover of ${{\mathcal N}}$
(so that $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$ is simple by Lemma \ref{still simple}, and therefore
has a well-defined characteristic submanifold, up to isotopy,
according to \S\ref{char-submflds}).
Then there is a  
clean suborbifold 
with corners
${{\mathscr C}} \subset {{\mathcal N}}$ 
whose preimage in $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$ is isotopic to the characteristic submanifold of $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$.
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Let $G$ 
denote
the deck group of the 
covering space $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$,
and let $p\colon\thinspace\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}\to{{\mathcal N}}$ denote the covering projection.
Let ${\bf V}$ denote the characteristic submanifold of
$\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$. By a theorem of Meeks
and Scott~\cite[Theorem 8.6]{MeeksScott}, 
we may choose ${\bf V}$ within its isotopy class in such a way that it is
$G$--invariant. Then 
by an observation made in \S\ref{Suborbifolds}, ${{\mathscr C}}\doteq{\Omega_{{\bf V} / G}}$ is defined (as a weak suborbifold with corners of ${{\mathcal N}}$). Since ${\bf V}$ is a clean submanifold of $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$, 
the  frontier of  ${\bf V}=p^{-1}({{\mathscr C}})$ 
    is a neatly\ 
    embedded submanifold of $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$, and
$({\bf V},\mathop{\rm Fr}_{\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}}{\bf V})=(p^{-1}({{\mathscr C}}),p^{-1}(\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}}{{\mathscr C}}))$ is a clean pair. It then  follows formally from the definitions that 
$\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}}{{\mathscr C}}$ is defined and is a neatly embedded suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$, and that
$({{\mathscr C}},\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}}{{\mathscr C}})$ is a clean pair. In view of the discussion in \S\ref{clean},
it follows
that ${{\mathscr C}}$ is a clean suborbifold with corners of ${{\mathcal N}}$, and is in particular a suborbifold with corners in the strong sense.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- custom-67: body_md -->
{Characteristic suborbifolds}
\label{called characteristic part one}
Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be a simple $3$--orbifold with non-empty boundary.
We define \emph{a
  characteristic suborbifold} of ${{\mathcal N}}$ to be a clean 
suborbifold with corners
${{\mathscr C}} \subset {{\mathcal N}}$ with the property that
there exists a finite-sheeted regular manifold cover $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$
(which is simple by Lemma \ref{still simple}), such that
the preimage of ${{\mathscr C}}$ in  $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$  is isotopic to the characteristic submanifold of
$\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$.
<!-- end custom-67 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{characteristic corollary}
Every very good, simple $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$ with non-empty boundary has a characteristic suborbifold.
{\hfill$\square$}
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- remarks-1: body_md -->
\label{called characteristic part two}
It is a consequence of the Orbifold Theorem, included in \cite[Corollary
3.28]{BoileauMaillotPorti}, that every irreducible
 $3$--orbifold is very good.  Given that every simple $3$--orbifold is irreducible by \S\ref{GS review}, it follows that every simple  $3$--orbifold is very good. Using this fact,
the hypothesis ``very good'' could be removed from Corollary
\ref{characteristic corollary}. We will not need to do this, because
in all applications of  Corollary \ref{characteristic corollary},
${{\mathcal N}}$ will be a suborbifold of a hyperbolic $3$--orbifold; hence the fact that ${{\mathcal N}}$ is very good will follow directly from observations that were
made in 
\S\ref{Orbifold covers}.

Similarly, in
this paper, we will not address the issue of uniqueness of a characteristic suborbifold
up to orbifold isotopy, because we will not need such a uniqueness
result. An argument for the uniqueness of ${{\mathscr C}}$ is sketched 
in Bonahon and Siebenmann's paper \cite{bon-sie} (see the paragraph
on page 445 beginning ``More generally \ldots'').
<!-- end remarks-1 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{Prop:CharSuborbifoldPieces}
Suppose that ${{\mathscr C}}$ is a characteristic suborbifold of a simple
$3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$ with non-empty boundary. Then
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:$(1)$]
\item \label{EveryFrontAnnular} every component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathscr C}}$
is a $\pi_1$--injective annular $2$--orbifold in
${{\mathcal N}}$;
\item \label{EveryPiecePageOrBinding}
every component of ${{\mathscr C}}$ is
either pagelike or bindinglike as a suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$;
\item \label{EveryCompNonPos}
every component of 
$\overline{{{\mathcal N}} -  {{\mathscr C}}}$ 
has non-positive Euler characteristic; and
\item \label{ZeroEulerProduct}
if ${{\mathcal Y}} $ is a component of 
$\overline{{{\mathcal N}} -  {{\mathscr C}}}$ 
with $\chi({{\mathcal Y}} )=0$, then 
${{\mathcal Y}} $ is a thickened annular orbifold;
and  the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}} {{\mathcal Y}} $ are contained in
distinct components of ${{\mathscr C}}$, of which one is purely
bindinglike\ and the other is purely pagelike.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Since ${{\mathscr C}}$ is a characteristic
suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$, we may fix
a finite-sheeted regular covering space $p \colon\thinspace \widetilde{{\mathcal N}}\to{{\mathcal N}}$
such that 
$\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$ is a manifold 
(and is therefore simple by 
Lemma \ref{still simple}), and such that  ${\bf V}\doteq p^{-1}({{\mathscr C}})$ is isotopic to the characteristic
submanifold of $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$.  
Let $G$ be the deck group of the cover $p$.

If
${{\mathcal F}}$ is any component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}} {{\mathscr C}}$, we may choose a component
$\widetilde{{\mathcal F}}$ of $p^{-1}({{\mathcal F}})$; 
it follows from Proposition \ref{char-submflds, GS edition}
that the component $\widetilde{{\mathcal F}}$ of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}}{\bf V}$ is
an essential annulus in $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$, and is in particular a $\pi_1$--injective annulus. 
Hence ${{\mathcal F}}$ is annular; and the inclusion homomorphism
$\iota\colon\thinspace \pi_1({{\mathcal F}})\to\pi_1({{\mathcal N}})$, whose domain group is infinite cyclic
or infinite dihedral, restricts to an injection on some finite-index
subgroup. It follows that $\iota$ is itself injective, and 
Assertion \eqref{EveryFrontAnnular} is proved.

 Proposition \ref{char-submflds, GS edition} also gives:
\begin{claim}\label{components above bigorbC} Every component of 
$p^{-1}({{\mathscr C}})$
is a bindinglike or pagelike submanifold of $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$.
\end{claim}

We claim:
\begin{claim}\label{down to business}
Let ${{\mathcal C}}$ be any component of ${{\mathscr C}}$, and let $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ be any component
of $p^{-1}({{\mathcal C}})$. Then ${{\mathcal C}}$ is bindinglike if and only if
 $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ is bindinglike, and ${{\mathcal C}}$ is pagelike if and only if
 $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ is pagelike.
\end{claim}

In the following proof of \ref{down to business}, we shall implicitly use the facts that ${{\mathcal C}}$ is a clean suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$, and that ${\bf V}$ is a clean submanifold of $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$.
First 
suppose that ${{\mathcal C}}$ is
pagelike. Then ${{\mathcal C}}$ has an $I$--bundle structure in which
${{\mathcal C}}\cap\partial{{\mathcal N}}=\partial_\mathrm{h}{{\mathcal C}}$. 
The $I$--bundle
structure of ${{\mathcal C}}$ induces an $I$--bundle structure on $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ whose
horizontal boundary is $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}\cap\partial\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$, and hence $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$
is pagelike.

Conversely, suppose that $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$
is pagelike. Then $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$
may be given the
structure of an $I$--bundle  over a surface $F$
in such a way that 
$\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}\cap\partial \widetilde{{\mathcal N}}= \partial_\mathrm{h}\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$. 
Since $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ is simple, $F$
cannot be a sphere or projective plane.
We may fix 
a
finite-sheeted covering $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}'$ of $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ such that (a) the $I$--bundle
structure which $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}'$ inherits from $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ is trivial, and (b)
the covering projection $p' \colon\thinspace \widetilde{{\mathcal C}}'\to{{\mathcal C}}$ is regular. Let $G'$ denote the deck group of $p'$.

The horizontal
boundary of the trivial $I$--bundle $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}'$ is the preimage of
${{\mathcal C}}\cap\partial {{\mathcal N}}$ under the covering projection $p'$.
Hence the deck group $G'$ leaves 
$\partial_\mathrm{h} \widetilde{{\mathcal C}}'$ invariant. 
Furthermore, since $F$ is not a sphere or projective plane, the  base
of the $I$--bundle $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}'$ is
not a sphere or projective plane.
It then follows
from Meeks and Scott's result
\cite[Theorem 8.1]{MeeksScott} that, after possibly modifying
the $I$--fibration of $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}'$, without changing its
vertical boundary, we may assume that the action of $G'$ preserves the
$I$--fibration. 
(The assertion about vertical boundaries is not stated in \cite[Theorem 8.1]{MeeksScott}, but it follows from the proof of that theorem, which is derived from \cite[Theorem 2.2]{MeeksScott} by a doubling argument.)
                                           
                                                                             
                                                                                    
                                                                                   
                                                                         
                                                                                     
                                                                                       
                                                                                           
                                                                                               
                                                                                                
                                           
It now follows from Proposition \ref{FiberPreservingAction} that
the $I$--fibration of $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}'$ then induces an $I$--fibration of
${{\mathcal C}}$ in which the horizontal boundary is ${{\mathcal C}}\cap\partial{{\mathcal N}}$. 
Hence the vertical boundary of ${{\mathcal C}}$ in this fibration is $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathcal C}}$. This
shows that ${{\mathcal C}}$ is pagelike,
and the first assertion of \ref{down to business} is proved.

To prove the second assertion of \ref{down to business}, note that the manifold  $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}_0$ obtained by straightening the angles\ of $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ is a finite-sheeted covering of the manifold ${{\mathcal C}}_0$ obtained by straightening the angles\ of ${{\mathcal C}}$. Hence $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}_0$ is a solid torus if and only if ${{\mathcal C}}_0$ is a solid toric orbifold. Since the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}} {{\mathcal C}}$ are annular by \eqref{EveryFrontAnnular}, and the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}} \widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ are therefore annuli, the second assertion follows, and the proof of \ref{down to business} is complete.

Assertion \eqref{EveryPiecePageOrBinding} of the present proposition follows immediately from \ref{components above bigorbC} and \ref{down to business}.


We record the following direct consequence of \ref{down to business}:

\begin{claim}\label{and purely so}
If ${{\mathcal C}}$ is a component of ${{\mathscr C}}$, and some component of
$p^{-1}({{\mathcal C}})$ is purely pagelike or purely bindinglike, then ${{\mathcal C}}$
is, respectively, purely pagelike or purely bindinglike.
\end{claim}

To prove Assertion \eqref{EveryCompNonPos}, we need only note that if ${{\mathcal Y}} $ is a component of 
$\overline{{{\mathcal N}} -  {{\mathscr C}}}$, then every component of
$p^{-1}({{\mathcal Y}})$ is a component of $\overline{\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}-{\bf V}}$, and
therefore has non-positive Euler characteristic by Lemma \ref{what about manifolds}; 
it follows that $\chi({{\mathcal Y}})\le0$.

To prove Assertion \eqref{ZeroEulerProduct}, suppose that ${{\mathcal Y}} $ is a component of 
$\overline{{{\mathcal N}} -  {{\mathscr C}}}$ 
with $\chi({{\mathcal Y}} )=0$.
If we choose a component $L$ of
$p^{-1}({{\mathcal Y}})$, then
$\chi(L)=0$. Hence  
Lemma \ref{what about manifolds} gives that 
$L$ is a thickened annulus, and that the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}}L$ are contained
in distinct components $V_{\rm p}$ and $V_{\rm b}$ of ${\bf V}$, where $V_{\rm p}$ is
purely pagelike and $V_{\rm b}$ is purely bindinglike.

Since $L$ is a thickened annulus, it may be
given the structure of a trivial $I$--bundle over an annulus in such a
way that $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}} L= \partial_\mathrm{h} L$.
It follows from \cite[Theorem 8.1]{MeeksScott} that, after possibly modifying
the $I$--fibration of $L$, without changing its horizontal or
vertical boundary, 
we may assume that the action on $L$ of
${\rm Stab}_G(L)$
preserves the $I$--fibration. 
(Recall that $G$ denotes the deck group of $p$.)
It now follows from Proposition \ref{FiberPreservingAction} that
the $I$--fibration of $L$ induces an $I$--fibration
of ${{\mathcal Y}}$, whose base is an annular orbifold.
But since  $V_{\rm p}$ is
purely pagelike and $V_{\rm b}$ is purely bindinglike,
no element of ${\rm Stab}_G(L)$ can interchange the two 
components of $\partial_\mathrm{h} L$. Hence
the $I$--bundle ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is trivial, i.e.\ ${{\mathcal Y}}$ is a thickened annular
orbifold. 

It now also follows that the components of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{{\mathcal N}}}{{\mathcal Y}}$ are
contained in distinct components of ${{\mathscr C}}$, which may be labeled
as ${{\mathcal C}}_{\rm p}$ and ${{\mathcal C}}_{\rm b}$ in such a way that $V_{\rm p}$ and
$V_{\rm b}$ are components of $p^{-1}({{\mathcal C}}_{\rm p})$ and $p^{-1}({{\mathcal C}}_{\rm
  b})$ respectively. Hence  by \ref{and purely so},
${{\mathcal C}}_{\rm p}$ is purely pagelike and ${{\mathcal C}}_{\rm b}$
is purely bindinglike. This establishes Assertion \eqref{ZeroEulerProduct}.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- claim-46: body_md -->
\label{components above bigorbC} Every component of 
$p^{-1}({{\mathscr C}})$
is a bindinglike or pagelike submanifold of $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$.
<!-- end claim-46 -->
<!-- claim-47: body_md -->
\label{down to business}
Let ${{\mathcal C}}$ be any component of ${{\mathscr C}}$, and let $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ be any component
of $p^{-1}({{\mathcal C}})$. Then ${{\mathcal C}}$ is bindinglike if and only if
 $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ is bindinglike, and ${{\mathcal C}}$ is pagelike if and only if
 $\widetilde{{\mathcal C}}$ is pagelike.
<!-- end claim-47 -->
<!-- claim-48: body_md -->
\label{and purely so}
If ${{\mathcal C}}$ is a component of ${{\mathscr C}}$, and some component of
$p^{-1}({{\mathcal C}})$ is purely pagelike or purely bindinglike, then ${{\mathcal C}}$
is, respectively, purely pagelike or purely bindinglike.
<!-- end claim-48 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{nothing like a book}
Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be a simple $3$--orbifold with non-empty boundary, and suppose that
${{\mathscr C}}$ is a characteristic suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$. Then we have
$\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}})\le0$, and if $\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}})=0$ then ${{\mathcal N}}$ admits the
structure of a book of $I$--bundles.
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
According to Assertion \eqref{EveryCompNonPos} of
Proposition \ref{Prop:CharSuborbifoldPieces}, each
component of $\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}}$ has non-positive
  Euler characteristic. 
Thus
  $\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}})\le0$.

Now suppose that $\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}})=0$. Then
each component of $\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}}$ must have Euler
characteristic $0$. 
According to Assertions \eqref{EveryFrontAnnular}, \eqref{EveryPiecePageOrBinding} and \eqref{ZeroEulerProduct} of
Proposition \ref{Prop:CharSuborbifoldPieces},
 every component of $\mathop{\rm Fr}_{{\mathcal N}}{{\mathscr C}}$
is a $\pi_1$--injective annular $2$--orbifold in
${{\mathcal N}}$;
every component of ${{\mathscr C}}$ is a
 pagelike or bindinglike suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$;
and  every  component of 
$\overline{{{\mathcal N}} -  {{\mathscr C}}}$ 
is a 
thickened annulus\ whose frontier components are contained in
distinct components of ${{\mathscr C}}$, of which one is purely
bindinglike\ and the other is purely pagelike. It now follows from
Definition~\ref{wuzza book} that  ${{\mathcal N}}$ admits the
structure of a book of $I$--bundles.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- custom-68: body_md -->
{The Gromov volume}
\label{gromov volume}
If $Q$ is a compact, orientable $3$--manifold, we define the \emph{Gromov
  volume} of $Q$, denoted $\mathop{\rm vol_G}(Q)$, to be the number
${v_{\rm tet}}\cdot\|DQ\|/2$, where $DQ$ denotes the double of $Q$, 
and $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the Gromov
norm 
(see \S\ref{Gromov norm}). 
This definition is inspired by \eqref{genuine gromov}, which implies
that if $Q$ is closed and hyperbolic then $\mathop{\rm vol_G}(Q)=\mathop{\rm vol} Q$.

Suppose that $d$ is a positive integer and that $\widetilde Q$ is a $d$--sheeted cover
of a
compact, orientable topological $3$--manifold $Q$. Then the double
$D\widetilde Q$ of $\widetilde Q$ is a $d$--sheeted cover of $DQ$, and according to \cite[Section 0.2]{gromov}
we have $\|D\widetilde Q\|= d\cdot\|DQ\|$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gromov multiplicative}
\mathop{\rm vol_G}(\widetilde Q)=d\cdot\mathop{\rm vol_G}(Q).
\end{equation}


Using \eqref{gromov multiplicative}, we can extend the definition of
$\mathop{\rm vol_G}$ to all very good, orientable compact $3$--orbifolds: for any
such orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$ we set $\mathop{\rm vol_G}({{\mathcal N}})=\mathop{\rm vol_G}(\widetilde{{\mathcal N}})/d$, where
$\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$ is an arbitrary finite-sheeted manifold cover of ${{\mathcal N}}$ and
$d$ is the degree of the covering. If $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_1$ and $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_2$ are
two finite-sheeted manifold covers of ${{\mathcal N}}$, and $d_i$ denotes the
degree of the covering $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_i \to {{\mathcal N}}$ for $i=1,2$, we may choose a 
finite covering  $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_3$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$ whose covering
projection factors through those of $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_1$ and $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_2$. If
we let $n_i$ denote the degree of $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_3 \to {{\mathcal N}}_i$
then $d_1 n_1= d_2 n_2$. But by \eqref{gromov multiplicative}  we have
$n_1\mathop{\rm vol_G}(\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_1)=\mathop{\rm vol_G}(\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_3)=n_2\mathop{\rm vol_G}(\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_2)$. Hence
$\mathop{\rm vol_G}(\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_1)/d_1=\mathop{\rm vol_G}(\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_2)/d_2$, and we have shown that
$\mathop{\rm vol_G}({{\mathcal N}})$ is well-defined.

The definitions given above do not require the
manifolds involved to be  connected. (A closed, 
orientable manifold with $n$ components
has $2^n$ fundamental classes, but they all have the same Gromov
norm. Furthermore, the existence of a common finite-sheeted covering $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_3$ of
$\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_1$ and $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}_2$ does not depend on connectedness.) We remark that if $\mathscr{N}$ is a disconnected $3$--orbifold, then $\mathop{\rm vol_G} (\mathscr{N}) = \sum_{{\mathcal N}} \mathop{\rm vol_G}({{\mathcal N}})$, where ${{\mathcal N}}$ ranges over the connected components of $\mathscr{N}$.
<!-- end custom-68 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{orbifold 7.2}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable hyperbolic $3$--orbifold,
and let ${{\mathcal R}}$ be an essential two-dimensional suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$.
Then
$\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} \geq  \mathop{\rm vol_G}({{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal R}})$.
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
In the special case where ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a manifold (so that
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}=\emptyset$ and ${{\mathcal R}}$ is an essential surface in
${{\mathcal M}}$), this is a result of Agol, Storm, and Thurston~\cite{AST}. See, specifically, the first inequality in the statement of \cite[Theorem 9.1]{AST}. 

To prove the general case of the proposition, fix a 
regular
manifold cover
$p\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}\to{{\mathcal M}}$ of some degree $n<\infty$. 
Then $\widetilde{{\mathcal R}}\doteq
p^{-1}({{\mathcal R}})$ is an essential $2$--manifold in ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$,
and ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}{\backslash \backslash}\widetilde{{\mathcal R}}$ is an $n$--sheeted manifold cover of ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal R}}$.
Thus we have
\[
n\cdot\mathop{\rm vol}{{\mathcal M}} = \mathop{\rm vol}{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}
\geq \mathop{\rm vol_G}({\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}{\backslash \backslash}\widetilde{{\mathcal R}}) = n \cdot \mathop{\rm vol_G}({{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal R}}).
\]
Here, the inequality follows from the manifold case of the
proposition, and the last equality follows from \S\ref{gromov volume}. Now, dividing the first and last terms by $n$ gives the conclusion.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- proposition-25: body_md -->
\label{Prop:GromovVolEuler}
Suppose that ${{\mathcal N}}$ is a simple $3$--orbifold with non-empty boundary, and that 
${{\mathscr C}}$ is a
characteristic suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$. 
Then $\mathop{\rm vol_G}({{\mathcal N}})\ge{v_{\rm oct}}\cdot(-\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}}-{{\mathscr C}}}))$.
<!-- end proposition-25 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
According to the definition of a characteristic suborbifold,
we may fix a regular manifold cover $p\colon\thinspace  Q \to{{\mathcal N}}$ such
that    ${\bf V}\doteq p^{-1}({{\mathscr C}})$ is (up to isotopy) the
characteristic submanifold of $Q$. 
In the notation of Agol, Storm, and Thurston \cite{AST},
the union of all components of $\overline{Q  -  {\bf V}}$ that are not thickened annuli is denoted by ${\rm Guts}(Q)$. (This rephrasing of \cite[Definition 2.1]{AST} essentially matches our characterization of the characteristic submanifold ${\bf V}$ in Proposition~\ref{char-submflds, GS edition}.)

Note that
$\chi({\rm Guts}(Q))=\chi(\overline{Q -  {\bf V}})$.
If $d$ denotes the degree of the covering $Q$ of ${{\mathcal N}}$, then
$\overline{Q -  {\bf V}}$ is a (possibly disconnected) $d$--sheeted covering of
$\overline{{{\mathcal N}}-{{\mathscr C}} }$, and hence $\chi({\rm Guts}(Q))=d\cdot\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}}-{{\mathscr C}} })$.

Agol, Storm, and Thurston point out 
in the short proof of \cite[Theorem 9.1]{AST} that,
as a consequence of \cite[Theorem 6.5.5]{Thurston:notes} and Miyamoto's inequality \cite{Miyamoto},
every simple $3$--manifold $Q$ satisfies
$\mathop{\rm vol_G}(Q)\ge{v_{\rm oct}}(-\chi({\rm Guts}(Q)))$. 
Thus in the context of the present
argument, using the definition of the Gromov volume of the orbifold
${{\mathcal N}}$ (see \S\ref{gromov volume}), we have
\[
\mathop{\rm vol_G}({{\mathcal N}}) = \tfrac{1}{d}
\mathop{\rm vol_G}(Q)
\geq \tfrac{1}{d}
{v_{\rm oct}} \cdot (-\chi({\rm Guts}(Q))) = {v_{\rm oct}}\cdot(-\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}}-{{\mathscr C}} })),
\]
as required.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{orbifold AST}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable hyperbolic $3$--orbifold. Let
${{\mathcal R}}$ be a non-empty, 
essential 
$2$--suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$.
Then each component ${{\mathcal N}}$  of ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash}
{{\mathcal R}} $ 
is simple and very good, and hence
has a characteristic suborbifold ${{\mathscr C}}_{{\mathcal N}}$ by Corollary \ref{characteristic corollary}.
Furthermore, 
we have
$$\mathop{\rm vol}{{\mathcal M}}\ge{v_{\rm oct}}\cdot\sum_{{\mathcal N}}(-\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}}-{{\mathscr C}}_{{\mathcal N}}})),$$
where ${{\mathcal N}}$ ranges over the components of ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal R}}$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Since ${{\mathcal M}}$ is hyperbolic and ${{\mathcal R}}$ is essential, it follows from
an observation made in
\S\ref{GS review} that each component ${{\mathcal N}}$ of ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal R}}$ is simple. Likewise, since ${{\mathcal M}}$ is hyperbolic, it follows from the discussion in
\S\ref{Orbifold covers} 
that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is  very good, hence every ${{\mathcal N}}$ is very good. The displayed
inequality now follows 
immediately from Propositions \ref{orbifold 7.2} and
\ref{Prop:GromovVolEuler},
together with the observation that orbifold Euler characteristic is
additive over components.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{requark}
Note that Proposition \ref{Prop:GromovVolEuler} and Theorem \ref{orbifold AST}
involve quantities of the form $\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}}  - 
  {{\mathscr C}}})$, where ${{\mathcal N}}$ is a simple $3$--orbifold with non-empty boundary and ${{\mathscr C}}$ is a characteristic suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$. For the arguments in
this paper, we do not need to know that the quantity $\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}}  - 
  {{\mathscr C}}})$ is an invariant of the simple $3$--orbifold ${{\mathcal N}}$,
i.e.\ that it is independent of  ${{\mathscr C}}$. The assertion of invariance
of  $\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}}  - 
  {{\mathscr C}}})$
is weaker than the
assertion that ${{\mathscr C}}$ is unique up to orbifold isotopy; as we 
mentioned in \S\ref{called characteristic part two}, a proof of the stronger
assertion is sketched in \cite{bon-sie}. Here, for the benefit of the
interested reader, we sketch a proof of the weaker assertion
that $\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}}  - 
  {{\mathscr C}}})$ is an invariant of  ${{\mathcal N}}$. Using arguments similar to
those invoked in \S\ref{gromov volume} to show
the Gromov volume of an orbifold is well-defined, one can reduce the
proof of invariance of $\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}}  - 
  {{\mathscr C}}})$ to showing that if $p\colon\thinspace \widetilde Q\to Q$ is an $n$--fold covering of
simple $3$--manifolds, and if ${\bf V}$ and $\widetilde {\bf V}$ denote the
respective characteristic submanifolds of $Q$ and $\widetilde Q$, then $\chi(\overline{\widetilde Q  - 
  \widetilde {\bf V}})=n\cdot \chi(\overline{Q  - 
  {\bf V}})$. For this purpose it is enough to know that $p^{-1}({\bf V})$ is
isotopic in $\widetilde Q$ to $\widetilde {\bf V}$; and the latter fact is not hard to deduce
from \cite[Theorems 8.1 and 8.6]{MeeksScott} and the characteristic submanifold theory.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- proposition-26: body_md -->
\label{what if no book}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed, orientable hyperbolic $3$--orbifold containing
no essential turnovers. Let
$ R$ be a closed orientable surface in $M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$  which is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$. 
Suppose that the two-dimensional suborbifold ${{\mathcal R}}\doteq{\Omega_{R}} $ is essential in ${{\mathcal M}}$. Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be a component of ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal R}} $, and suppose that 
${{\mathcal N}}$
does not admit the structure of 
an orbifold book of $I$--bundles.
Let ${{\mathscr C}}$ be a characteristic suborbifold of ${{\mathcal N}}$.  
Then $\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}})\le-1/12$. 
Furthermore, if ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a link orbifold then
 $\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}})\le-1/6$.
<!-- end proposition-26 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Under the hypotheses of the proposition, 
let ${{\mathcal Z}}$ denote the $3$--orbifold obtained by straightening the angles\ 
of
$\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}}$. Set $Z={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal Z}}}}$.
Observe that  $\partial Z$ can be identified with the smooth surface obtained by smoothing the boundary of the topological manifold ${{\rm X}_{\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}}}}$.


We first claim:

\begin{claim}\label{big enough}
Every component of $\partial {{\mathcal Z}}$ has non-positive Euler characteristic.
\end{claim}


To prove \ref{big enough}, recall from Proposition~\ref{CharSuborbifold} and Definition~\ref{called characteristic part one} that ${{\mathcal N}}$ has a regular, finite-sheeted manifold cover $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$, such that ${\mathscr C}$ is covered by the characteristic submanifold ${\bf V}$ of $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$. Thus every component of $\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}}$ is covered by a component of $\overline{\widetilde{{\mathcal N}} - {\bf V}}$.
Now, by Lemma~\ref{what about manifolds}, every boundary component of the manifold obtained by straightening the angles\ of  $\overline{\widetilde{{\mathcal N}} - {\bf V}}$ has non-positive Euler characteristic, and \ref{big enough} follows.


Next, we claim:

\begin{claim}\label{four or more}
Every 
component of $\partial Z $ which is a topological $2$--sphere
has size\ at least $4$.
\end{claim}



To prove \ref{four or more}, suppose that $S$ is a $2$--sphere component of $\partial Z$, and that 
$\mathop{\rm size}(S)\le 3$. 
By Proposition \ref{if three},  ${\Omega_{S}} $ is $\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal M}}$, and by \ref{big enough} we have $\chi({\Omega_{S}} )\le0$. If $\chi({\Omega_{S}} )=0$ then ${\Omega_{S}} $ is a $\pi_1$--injective toric suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$, a contradiction to hyperbolicity. If $\chi({\Omega_{S}} )<0$ then ${\Omega_{S}} $ is an essential turnover
in ${{\mathcal M}}$, a contradiction to the hypotheses. This completes the proof of \ref{four or more}.

Next, we recall that
\begin{equation}\label{chi oh my}
\chi(\partial {{\mathcal Z}})=2 \chi({{\mathcal Z}}).
\end{equation}
On the other hand, the orbifold Euler characteristic formula 
\eqref{hurwitz} implies that every component ${{\mathcal W}}$ of $\partial {{\mathcal Z}}$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{snub ya}
\chi({{\mathcal W}})=\chi({{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal W}}}} )-
\sum_{x\in\Sigma_{{\mathcal W}}}\bigg(1-\frac1{\mathop{\rm ord}(x)}\bigg).
\end{equation}
Observe that each term of the sum 
in 
\eqref{snub ya} is at least $1/2$.

Now if $\partial {{\mathcal Z}}$ has a component ${{\mathcal W}}$ such that 
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(a)]
\item $W\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal W}}}} $ has genus $g > 1$, or 
\item $W $ has genus $1$ and $\mathop{\rm size}(W )>0$, or 
\item $W $ has genus $0$ and $\mathop{\rm size}(W )\ge5$, 
\end{enumerate}
then 
it follows from \eqref{snub ya} that $\chi({{\mathcal W}})\le-1/2$; hence by \ref{big enough} we have $\chi(\partial {{\mathcal Z}})\le -1/2$, and by \eqref{chi oh my} we have $\chi({{\mathcal Z}})\le-1/4<-1/6$. Thus both conclusions of the proposition are true if (a), (b) or (c) holds. For the rest of the proof we assume that none of the alternatives (a), (b) or (c) holds. In view of \ref{four or more}, 
we may now assume that:

\begin{claim}\label{four, basically}
Every component of $\partial Z $ is either a size--$4$ topological $2$--sphere or a size--$0$  topological  torus.
\end{claim}


Now by hypothesis ${{\mathcal N}}$ 
does not admit the structure of a
book of $I$--bundles, which by
Proposition \ref{nothing like a book} implies
that $\chi({{\mathcal Z}})<0$. Hence 
$\partial {{\mathcal Z}}$ has a component ${{\mathcal W}}_0$ such that $\chi({{\mathcal W}}_0)<0$. By
 \ref{four, basically}, ${{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal W}}_0}}$ is a sphere of size\ $4$. If
 each of the singular points of ${{\mathcal W}}_0$ had order $2$, it would follow
 from \eqref{snub ya} that $\chi({{\mathcal W}}_0)=0$, a contradiction. Hence
 some singular point 
$x_0$ of ${{\mathcal W}}_0$ has order at least $3$. Since each of the other three singular points is of order at least $2$, \eqref{snub ya} gives $\chi({{\mathcal W}}_0)\le-1/6$; \eqref{big enough} then gives $\chi(\partial {{\mathcal Z}})\le-1/6$, and \eqref{chi oh my} gives $\chi({{\mathcal Z}})\le-1/12$. This proves the first assertion of the proposition.

To prove the second assertion, suppose that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a link
orbifold. Then the component of $Z \cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ containing
$x_0$ is an arc, having $x_0$ as one endpoint. Let $x_1$ denote the
other endpoint. Then $x_1\in\Sigma_{\partial {{\mathcal Z}}}$ and $\mathop{\rm ord} x_1=\mathop{\rm ord}
x_0\ge 3$. If $x_1$ lies in the component ${{\rm X}_{ {{\mathcal W}}_0}}$ of $\partial
Z $, then ${{\mathcal W}}_0$ has two singular points of order at least $3$,
while each of the other two has order at least $2$. In this case
\eqref{snub ya} gives $\chi({{\mathcal W}}_0)\le-1/3$; 
hence  $\chi(\partial {{\mathcal Z}})\le-1/3$ and
$\chi({{\mathcal Z}})\le-1/6$, as required.   If $x_1\in{{\rm X}_{ {{\mathcal W}}_1}}$ for some component ${{\mathcal W}}_1\ne {{\mathcal W}}_0$ of $\partial {{\mathcal Z}}$, then ${{\mathcal W}}_1$ has a singular point of order at least $3$, while each of the other three has order at least $2$. In this case \eqref{snub ya} gives $\chi({{\mathcal W}}_1)\le-1/6$; 
hence  $\chi(\partial {{\mathcal Z}})\le-1/3$ and
$\chi({{\mathcal Z}})\le-1/6$. Thus the proof of the second assertion is complete.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- claim-49: body_md -->
\label{big enough}
Every component of $\partial {{\mathcal Z}}$ has non-positive Euler characteristic.
<!-- end claim-49 -->
<!-- claim-50: body_md -->
\label{four or more}
Every 
component of $\partial Z $ which is a topological $2$--sphere
has size\ at least $4$.
<!-- end claim-50 -->
<!-- claim-51: body_md -->
\label{four, basically}
Every component of $\partial Z $ is either a size--$4$ topological $2$--sphere or a size--$0$  topological  torus.
<!-- end claim-51 -->
<!-- proposition-27: body_md -->
\label{why a book}
Suppose that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a closed, orientable hyperbolic $3$--orbifold containing
no essential turnovers, and that
either 
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:(a)]
\item
$\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} < {v_{\rm oct}} / 12$, or 
\item ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a link orbifold and $\mathop{\rm vol}
{{\mathcal M}} < {v_{\rm oct}} / 6$. 
\end{enumerate}
Let $R $ be a closed, orientable surface in
$M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ which is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$. Suppose
that the two-dimensional suborbifold 
${{\mathcal R}}\doteq{\Omega_{R}} $ 
is essential in ${{\mathcal M}}$. Then every component of  ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal R}} $ 
admits  the structure of
an orbifold 
book of $I$--bundles.
<!-- end proposition-27 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Let us define a number $\alpha$ by setting $\alpha=1/6$ if ${{\mathcal M}}$ is
a link orbifold, and $\alpha=1/12$ otherwise. Then the volume hypothesis
implies that $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} <\alpha\,{v_{\rm oct}}$.

For each component ${{\mathcal N}}$ of ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal R}} $, 
we use 
Corollary~\ref{characteristic corollary}
to choose 
a characteristic suborbifold ${{\mathscr C}}_{{\mathcal N}} \subset {{\mathcal N}}$.
(The hypothesis that ${{\mathcal N}}$ is very good follows from the hyperbolicity of ${{\mathcal M}}$.)

Assume that the conclusion is false, so that ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal R}} $ has
a component ${{\mathcal N}}_0$ which does not
admit  the structure of
an orbifold 
book of $I$--bundles. Since ${{\mathcal M}}$ contains no essential turnovers,
it follows from Proposition \ref{what if no book} that
$\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}}_0 - {{\mathscr C}}_{{{\mathcal N}}_0}})\le-\alpha$. For any component
${{\mathcal N}}\ne{{\mathcal N}}_0$ of ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal R}} $, we have
$\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}_{{\mathcal N}}})\le0$. Hence
$\sum_{{\mathcal N}}(-\chi(\overline{{{\mathcal N}} - {{\mathscr C}}_{{\mathcal N}}}))\ge\alpha$,
where ${{\mathcal N}}$ ranges over the components of ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal R}}$.
It therefore follows from 
Theorem \ref{orbifold AST} that 
$\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}}\ge\alpha{v_{\rm oct}}$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{Thm:NoTurnoverMain}
Suppose that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a closed, orientable hyperbolic $3$--orbifold containing
no essential turnovers, and that
either $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} < {v_{\rm oct}} / 12$, or  ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a link orbifold and $\mathop{\rm vol}
{{\mathcal M}} < {v_{\rm oct}} / 6$. Set $M = {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}} $. Then   one of the following alternatives holds.

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $M$ admits a Seifert fibration 
over ${\mathbb S}^2$
and having at most
three singular fibers. 

\item $M$ is homeomorphic to  a connected sum of two non-trivial lens spaces, or the connected sum of ${\mathbb S}^2\times {\mathbb S}^1$ with a non-trivial lens space.


\item
$M$ contains 
a separating essential torus $T$ such that each component of $M {\backslash \backslash} T$ 
admits a Seifert fibration over ${\mathbb B}^2$
having exactly two singular fibers.

\item
$M$ contains 
a non-separating essential torus $T$  such that  $M {\backslash \backslash} T $ 
admits a Seifert fibration 
over an annulus
having at most one singular fiber.
\end{enumerate}


\noindent Furthermore, if Alternative (i) does not hold, then every node of
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ is dihedral.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
We begin by observing that the volume hypotheses of the present theorem are stronger than those of Corollary~\ref{Cor:SimpleVolBound}, because $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} < {v_{\rm oct}}/6 =0.61\ldots < {V_{\rm Weeks}}$. 
Thus, by Corollary~\ref{Cor:SimpleVolBound}, $M$ cannot be a
hyperbolic manifold. Hence, according to Proposition \ref{because Perelman},
we must be in one of the following cases:

{\bf Case I.} $M$ admits a Seifert fibration over ${\mathbb S}^2$ with at most three singular fibers.

{\bf Case II.} $M$ is reducible, i.e.\ it contains an essential $2$--sphere. 

{\bf Case III.} $M$ is irreducible and contains an essential torus. 

In Case I, Alternative (i) of the conclusion of the theorem holds.


Next, observe that the volume hypotheses of the present theorem include those of Proposition \ref{why a book}. Once we find an essential two-dimensional suborbifold  ${{\mathcal R}} \subset {{\mathcal M}}$ (as we will in cases II and III), we can apply that proposition.

In Case II, it follows from an observation made in \S\ref{minimal} that
$M$ contains a strongly ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal $2$--sphere $S$. According
to Lemma \ref{it's incompressible}, 
${{\mathcal S}}\doteq{\Omega_{S}} $ 
is essential in ${{\mathcal M}}$. Now
we apply Proposition \ref{why a book},
taking $R=S$, to deduce that
each
component of ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal S}}$ admits the structure of an orbifold
book of $I$--bundles. It then follows from Corollary
\ref{Cor:HomeoTypeReducible}
that $M$ is homeomorphic to either (a) a connected sum of two non-trivial lens spaces, or (b) the connected sum of ${\mathbb S}^2\times {\mathbb S}^1$ with a possibly trivial lens space. In Subcase (a), Alternative (ii) of the present theorem holds. In Subcase (b), 
either Alternative (i) or Alternative (ii) holds.

In Case III, it follows from 
an observation made in \S\ref{TorusComplexity}
that  $M $ contains an ${{\mathcal M}}$--minimal torus $T$ (which is in particular an essential torus).
 According to Lemma \ref{it's still incompressible}, 
${{\mathcal T}} = {\Omega_{T}} $ 
is essential in ${{\mathcal M}}$.
Now, we apply   Proposition \ref{why a book},
  this time taking  
$R=T$, to deduce that
each component of ${{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal T}}$ admits the structure of an orbifold
book of $I$--bundles. If  $T$ 
separates $M$, then Proposition~\ref{Prop:TorusBooksTotalSpace} implies that
each component of $M {\backslash \backslash} T$ 
admits a Seifert fibration 
over ${\mathbb B}^2$
having exactly two singular fibers.
If  $T$ does not
separate $M$, then Proposition~\ref{Prop:TorusBooksTotalSpace} implies that
$M {\backslash \backslash}
T $ 
admits a Seifert fibration 
over an annulus
having at most one singular fiber.
Thus one of the alternatives (iii) and (iv) of the present theorem holds in this case.


This completes the proof that, under the hypotheses of the theorem,
one of the alternatives (i)--(iv) must hold. 

To complete the proof of
the theorem, it suffices to show that in Cases II and III, every node of
${{\mathcal M}}$ is dihedral. To this end, we observe that, in each of
these cases, the arguments given above provide a closed $2$--manifold
$R \subset M$, transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, such that ${{\mathcal R}} \doteq {\Omega_{R}}$ is
essential in ${{\mathcal M}}$, and each component of ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal R}}$ admits
the structure of a book of $I$--bundles. By transversality, every node of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is  a
node of ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal R}}$. But by Proposition
\ref{nodes of a book}, every node of ${{\mathcal M}}{\backslash \backslash}{{\mathcal R}}$ is
dihedral.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
$M$ admits a Seifert fibration over ${\mathbb S}^2$ with at most three singular fibers.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
$M$ is reducible, i.e.\ it contains an essential $2$--sphere.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
$M$ is irreducible and contains an essential torus.
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- custom-69: body_md -->
{Orbifolds with geodesic boundary}\label{Def:TotallyGeodesic}
Fix a dimension $n \geq 2$. A \emph{truncated hyperbolic space} is a closed, connected submanifold of ${\mathbb H}^n$ whose boundary is a (non-empty) disjoint union of totally geodesic copies of ${\mathbb H}^{n-1}$. A \emph{hyperbolic $n$--orbifold with totally geodesic boundary} is a very good $n$--orbifold ${{\mathcal M}}$ such that each component of ${{\mathcal M}}$ is the quotient of a truncated hyperbolic space by a 
discrete
group of isometries.
We remark that a hyperbolic orbifold with totally geodesic boundary does not satisfy the definition of ``hyperbolic orbifold'' given in \S\ref{Orbifold covers}, because the universal cover is not all of ${\mathbb H}^n$. This departure from our usual convention (whereby boundaries are implicitly permitted) will only be needed in Theorem~\ref{MiyamotoOrbifold} and Lemma~\ref{Turnover volume}.
<!-- end custom-69 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{MiyamotoOrbifold}
Let ${{\mathcal N}}$ be a hyperbolic $3$--orbifold with totally geodesic boundary. Then $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal N}} \geq ({v_{\rm oct}} / 2) \cdot | \chi(\partial {{\mathcal N}}) |$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
As volume and Euler characteristic are additive over components, we
may assume that ${{\mathcal N}}$ is connected. Let $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}}$ be a
$d$--sheeted manifold cover of ${{\mathcal N}}$. In \cite[Theorem
4.2]{Miyamoto}, Miyamoto proved that
$\mathop{\rm vol} \widetilde{{\mathcal N}} \geq ({v_{\rm oct}}/4\pi) \mathop{\rm area}(\partial
\widetilde{{\mathcal N}})$.
Since volume and Euler characteristic are both multiplicative in the cover $\widetilde{{\mathcal N}} \to {{\mathcal N}}$, we obtain
\[
d \cdot \mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal N}} = \mathop{\rm vol} \widetilde{{\mathcal N}} \geq \frac{{v_{\rm oct}}}{4\pi} \mathop{\rm area}(\partial \widetilde{{\mathcal N}}) = \frac{{v_{\rm oct}}}{2}  | \chi(\partial \widetilde{{\mathcal N}}) | = d \cdot \frac{{v_{\rm oct}}}{2}  | \chi(\partial {{\mathcal N}}) |,
\]
as desired.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{Turnover volume}
Let ${{\mathcal M}}$ be a closed hyperbolic $3$--orbifold that contains an essential turnover ${{\mathcal S}}$. Then we have the following volume estimates:
\begin{enumerate}[\:\:$(1)$]
\item\label{TurnoverVolSmallest} In all cases, $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} \geq 0.1491$.
\item\label{TurnoverVolNot7} If ${{\mathcal S}}$ is not a $(2,3,7)$ turnover, then $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} \geq  {v_{\rm oct}} / 20 \approx 0.1831$.
\item\label{TurnoverVolLink} If ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a link orbifold, then $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} \geq 0.1658$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
By a result of Adams and Schoenfeld \cite[Theorem
2.1]{AdamsSchoenfeld}, 
we may assume after an isotopy that
${{\mathcal S}}$ is totally geodesic in ${{\mathcal M}}$. Let ${{\mathcal N}} =  {{\mathcal M}} {\backslash \backslash} {{\mathcal S}}$, 
and observe that the hyperbolic metric on ${{\mathcal M}}$ endows ${{\mathcal N}}$ with the structure of a (possibly disconnected) hyperbolic $3$--orbifold with totally geodesic boundary. Furthermore, $\partial {{\mathcal N}}$ consists of two copies of ${{\mathcal S}}$, and  $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} = \mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal N}}$. 


Let $p,q,r$ be the orders of the three points of $\Sigma_{{\mathcal S}}$, and arrange the labels so that $p \leq q \leq r$. We consider two cases.

First, suppose that $(p,q,r) \in \{(2,3,7), \, (2,3,8)\}$. In this case, we apply a volume estimate of Atkinson and Rafalski \cite[Theorem 3.4]{AtkinsonRafalski}, which builds on the work of Miyamoto \cite[Section 4]{Miyamoto}  by incorporating not only $\chi(\partial {{\mathcal N}})$ but also the largest order of torsion in $\partial {{\mathcal N}}$.
Their theorem says that $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal N}} \geq 0.1491$ if $(p,q,r) = (2,3,7)$ and $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal N}} \geq 0.2204$ if $(p,q,r) = (2,3,8)$.

Next, suppose that $(p,q,r) \notin \{(2,3,7), \, (2,3,8)\}$. Since $\chi({{\mathcal S}}) < 0$, we have $\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q} + \frac{1}{r} < 1$. There are three subcases:
\[
p = 2, \: q = 3, \: r \geq 9;
\qquad
p = 2, \: q \geq 4, \: r \geq 5;
\qquad
p \geq 3, \:  q \geq 3, \: r \geq 4.
\]
In all three of these subcases, we have $\chi({{\mathcal S}}) \leq -1/20$, hence $\chi(\partial {{\mathcal N}}) \leq -1/10$. Now, Theorem \ref{MiyamotoOrbifold} implies $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal N}} \geq {v_{\rm oct}}/20$.

We conclude that $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} \geq 0.1491$ if $(p,q,r) = (2,3,7)$, and $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} \geq {v_{\rm oct}}/20 \approx 0.1831$ otherwise, establishing conclusions \eqref{TurnoverVolSmallest} and \eqref{TurnoverVolNot7}.

It remains to establish conclusion \eqref{TurnoverVolLink}. By
\eqref{TurnoverVolNot7}, 
a stronger estimate holds if ${{\mathcal S}}$ is not a $(2,3,7)$ turnover. If
${{\mathcal S}}$ is a $(2,3,7)$ turnover, then in particular ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a
hyperbolic link orbifold with $7$--torsion. By a lemma of
Atkinson and Futer~\cite[Lemma 2.3]{af}, any such orbifold has volume
at least $0.1658$.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{Thm:VolWithTurnover}
Suppose that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a closed, orientable hyperbolic $3$--orbifold with $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} < 0.1491$. Then 
$M
\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ 
satisfies one of the alternatives (i)--(iv) of Theorem \ref{Thm:NoTurnoverMain}.
Furthermore, if Alternative (i) does not hold, then every node of
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ is dihedral.
{\hfill$\square$}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{essential or not}
If   ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a (closed, orientable) link orbifold, then every
turnover in  ${{\mathcal M}}$ is  essential.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
If ${{\mathcal S}}\subset{{\mathcal M}}$ is a turnover, then
  by Proposition \ref{if three}, ${{\mathcal S}}$ is
$\pi_1$--injective in ${{\mathcal M}}$. It remains to show that ${{\mathcal S}}$ does not
bound a discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$.
Since ${{\mathcal S}}$ is an orientable $2$--suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$, it follows
from an observation
made in \S\ref{Suborbifolds-of-3orbifolds} that the $2$--sphere
$S\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal S}}}}$ is transverse to $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$.
If
${{\mathcal H}}$ is a discal suborbifold of ${{\mathcal M}}$ with $\partial{{\mathcal H}}={{\mathcal S}}$,
then since ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a link orbifold, each component of the intersection
of $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ with $H\doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal H}}}}$ is an arc or a simple closed
curve. This implies that $S\cap\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}=\Sigma_{{\mathcal S}}$ consists of an
even number of points, which contradicts the fact that ${{\mathcal S}}$ is a turnover.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- custom-70: body_md -->
{Constructing orbifold coverings from covering spaces}
  \label{orbi cover from mani cover}
Suppose that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is an orbifold and that $Q\colon\thinspace \widetilde M\to M$ is a covering space of
$M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$. If $( U , W, \Phi, G)$ is a chart for ${{\mathcal M}}$ such that
$U\subset M$ is connected and evenly covered by $Q$, if $V$ is a
component of $Q^{-1}(U)$, and if $R$ denotes the inverse of the
homeomorphism $Q|V\colon\thinspace V\to U$, then $(V, W, R\circ\Phi, G)$ is an
orbifold chart in $\widetilde M$ (in the abstract sense defined in
\S\ref{Def:OrbifoldChart}). The orbifold charts of this form, as
$( U , W, \Phi, G)$ ranges over charts for ${{\mathcal M}}$ such that
$U\subset M$ is connected and evenly covered by $Q$, and  $V$ ranges over
components of $Q^{-1}(U)$, form an orbifold atlas for $\widetilde M$, which
defines an orbifold ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ with ${{\rm X}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}}}=\widetilde M$. We then have $\Sigma_{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}=Q^{-1}(\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}})$, and $Q$ 
defines an orbifold covering $q\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}\to{{\mathcal M}}$ having the same
degree as $Q$.
<!-- end custom-70 -->
<!-- proposition-28: body_md -->
\label{uses Agol}
Suppose that   ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a 
hyperbolic link
orbifold containing no turnovers, and that  $Q\colon\thinspace \widetilde M\to M$ is a
finite-sheeted covering space of
$M\doteq{{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$. Let  $q\colon\thinspace {\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}\to{{\mathcal M}}$ denote the orbifold
covering given by the construction of \S\ref{orbi cover from mani cover}.
Then ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ is a link
orbifold and contains no turnovers.
<!-- end proposition-28 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
Since by \S\ref{orbi cover from mani cover} we have
$\Sigma_{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}=Q^{-1}(\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}})$, and since ${{\mathcal M}}$ is
a link orbifold, ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ is also
a link orbifold. It remains to show that 
${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ contains no turnovers.

Let us fix a tubular neighborhood $J$ of the link $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ in
$M$. Since
$\Sigma_{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}=Q^{-1}(\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}})$, the set ${\widetilde J}\doteq Q^{-1}(J)$ is a
tubular neighborhood of  the link $\Sigma_{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ in
$\widetilde M$. We set $N=\overline{M-J}$ and $\widetilde N=\overline{\widetilde M-{\widetilde J}}$. The restriction
$Q|\widetilde N \colon\thinspace \widetilde N\to N$ is a covering map.  If
$\mu\subset\partial\widetilde N$ is a meridian of $\Sigma_{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ (i.e.\ a simple closed curve
bounding a neatly\  embedded disk in ${\widetilde J}$ which meets $\Sigma_{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ transversely in exactly one point),
then $Q$ maps $\mu$ to a closed curve which, although not necessarily
simple, is homotopic in $\partial N$ to a meridian of
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$.  


By the work of Kojima~\cite{Kojima:Deformations}, the $3$--manifold $M  -  \Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$
admits a finite-volume complete hyperbolic metric.
The manifold
$N$ is a compact core of $M  -  \Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$.  

If ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ contains a turnover, then $\widetilde N$ contains a neatly\ 
embedded pair of pants $P$ whose boundary curves are meridians of 
$\Sigma_{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$. If $P$ is not $\pi_1$--injective in $\widetilde N$, then the
loop theorem provides a compressing disk $D$ for $P$. The boundary of
$D$ is a homotopically non-trivial simple closed curve on $P$, and is
therefore parallel to a boundary curve of $P$. This implies that some
meridian of $\Sigma_{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ is homotopically trivial in $\widetilde N$, and
therefore that some
meridian of $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ is homotopically trivial in $N$; but this
contradicts
the hyperbolicity of $M  - \Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$.
Hence $P$ is  $\pi_1$--injective in $\widetilde N$.

Since $Q|\widetilde N$ is a covering map, it now follows that  $f\doteq Q|P$ is a
$\pi_1$--injective map from the pair of pants $P$ to $N$. We have
$f(\partial P)\subset\partial N$; and $f$ maps each boundary curve of
$\partial P$ to a closed curve which is homotopic in $\partial N$ to a meridian of
$\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$.  

We now apply a theorem due to Agol~\cite[Theorem 4.1]{Agol:Pants},
which asserts that if $N$ is a compact core of a finite-volume orientable
hyperbolic $3$--manifold, and $f$ is a $\pi_1$--injective map of a pair
of pants $P$ into $N$ such that $f(\partial P)\subset\partial N$, then
one of two possibilities must hold:

\begin{enumerate}
\item The map of pairs $f\colon\thinspace (P,\partial P) \to (N,\partial N)$ is
  homotopic to an embedding of pairs.
\item 
The interior of
$N$ is obtained by (possibly empty) Dehn filling on the exterior
$W$ of the Whitehead
link. That is, there is a $3$--manifold $K \subset\mathop{\rm int} N$, which is
either empty or a solid torus, such that $\overline{N- K}$ is
homeomorphic to $W$. Furthermore,  $f(P)$ is disjoint from $K$, and
$f$ is homotopic in $N-K$ to a clasp of $W$, as in \cite[Figure
2]{Agol:Pants}. In particular, 
after modifying the map of pairs $f\colon\thinspace (P,\partial P) \to (N,\partial N)$
within its homotopy class, we may assume that $f$ maps the 
boundary components of $P$ homeomorphically to three simple closed curves in
the same 
component $T$ of $\partial N$, and that these curves represent exactly
two distinct homotopy classes on $T$.
\end{enumerate}

In our setting,
  Alternative
(2) leads to a contradiction, because the simple
closed curves which are the images of the components of $\partial P$
under $f$
must all be meridians of $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$, and hence
no two of them can represent distinct homotopy classes on the same boundary torus of
$N$.
  Now suppose that Alternative (1) holds, so that
the map of pairs $f\colon\thinspace (P,\partial P) \to (N,\partial N)$ is
  homotopic to an embedding $g$. In particular, $g|\partial
  P\colon\thinspace \partial P\to \partial N$ is homotopic to $f|\partial
  P\colon\thinspace \partial P\to \partial N$, so that each boundary component of the pair of
  pants $E\doteq g(P)$ is a meridian curve of $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$.   Hence
  the components of $\partial E$ bound disjoint neatly\  embedded disks in $J$,
  each of which meets $\Sigma_{{\mathcal M}}$ transversely in one point. The
  union of $E$ with these disks is the underlying set of a turnover
  contained in ${{\mathcal M}}$.
  Since by hypothesis ${{\mathcal M}}$ contains no
  turnovers, we have a contradiction in this case as well.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{MainConnectSum}
Suppose that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a closed,
orientable hyperbolic link orbifold, and
that $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} \le {V_{\rm Weeks}} / 6$. 
If  $M \doteq {{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}}$ is a non-trivial connected sum, then $M$ is homeomorphic  to 
either ${\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^3 \# {\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^3$, or to ${\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^3 \# L(p,q)$, where $p > 1$ is relatively prime to $6$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
We first note that
since $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} \leq {V_{\rm Weeks}} / 6 < 0.1658$, 
it follows from Lemma~\ref{Turnover volume}
that ${{\mathcal M}}$ contains no essential turnovers, 
and hence by Lemma \ref{essential or not} it contains no turnovers at
all.

Since $M$ is a non-trivial connected sum, it must satisfy alternative (ii) of 
Theorem \ref{Thm:NoTurnoverMain}, i.e.\ $M$ is
 homeomorphic to a connected sum
$Y_1 \# Y_2$, where each $Y_i$ is a non-trivial lens space or ${\mathbb S}^1
\times  {\mathbb S}^2$.
Hence for $i = 1,2$, we have $\pi_1(Y_i) \cong {\mathbb Z}/p_i{\mathbb Z}$ for some integer $p_i\ge0$,
so $\pi_1(M) \cong {\mathbb Z}/p_1 {\mathbb Z} * {\mathbb Z}/p_2 {\mathbb Z}$. If $p_i=0$ then $Y_i$ is
homeomorphic to ${\mathbb S}^2\times {\mathbb S}^1$, and if $p_i>1$ then $Y_i$ is homeomorphic to $L(p_i,q_i)$ for
some positive integer $q_i$ which is relatively prime to $p_i$. 
 Since neither $Y_1$ nor $Y_2$ is the $3$--sphere, we have
$p_i \neq 1$ for $i=1,2$.


Next, we claim:

\begin{claim}\label{however}
For each $i\in\{1,2\}$, either $p_i$ is relatively prime to $6$, or  $p_i=2$.
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{however}, it suffices by symmetry to prove that either
$p_1$ is relatively prime to $6$, or  $p_1=2$. Assume that  $p_1\ne2$
and that $p_1$ is not relatively prime to $6$.
Then $p_1$ is divisible by some $d\in\{2,3\}$. 
Set ${\widetilde{p}}_1=p_1/d$. Then  $Y_1$ has a
$d$--sheeted covering space $\widetilde Y_1$, which is a lens space with
fundamental group isomorphic to ${\mathbb Z}/{\widetilde{p}}_1{\mathbb Z}$ if $p_1\ne0$, and is
homeomorphic to ${\mathbb S}^1\times {\mathbb S}^2$ if $p_1=0$. It follows that $M$, which is
homeomorphic to $Y_1 \# Y_2$, has a $d$--sheeted covering $\widetilde M$ which is
homeomorphic to the connected sum of $\widetilde Y_1$ with $d$ homeomorphic
copies of $Y_2$. 
Since $p_1\ne2$, we have either $d=3$ or ${\widetilde{p}}_1 \neq 1$. Thus 
$\widetilde M$ is homeomorphic to a connected sum of three or more
prime, non-trivial $3$--manifolds.

Since ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a closed orientable link
$3$--orbifold containing no turnovers, and $\widetilde M$ is a
$d$--sheeted covering of $M$, \S\ref{orbi cover from mani cover} provides a
$d$--sheeted orbifold covering 
${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$
of ${{\mathcal M}}$ such that ${{\rm X}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}}}=\widetilde M$. According to Proposition \ref{uses Agol}, ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ is a
link orbifold containing no  turnovers. 
We have $\mathop{\rm vol} {\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}} =d\cdot\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}}\le 3
\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} < {V_{\rm Weeks}} / 2 < {v_{\rm oct}} / 6$.
Thus the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{Thm:NoTurnoverMain}
hold with ${\widetilde{{\mathcal M}}}$ in place of ${{\mathcal M}}$. Hence one of the alternatives (i),
(ii), (iii), (iv) of the conclusion of Theorem \ref{Thm:NoTurnoverMain} holds with $\widetilde M$ in place of $M$. But each of these
conditions implies that  $\widetilde M$ 
has a prime decomposition with at most two summands.
As we have already
shown that $\widetilde M$ is 
homeomorphic 
to the
connected sum of  three or more prime, non-trivial $3$--manifolds, this
contradicts the uniqueness of the prime decomposition for a
closed oriented $3$--manifold and proves \ref{however}.


To complete the proof, we claim:

\begin{claim}\label{one's divisible}
At least one of the integers $p_1,p_2$ is equal to $2$. 
\end{claim}

To prove \ref{one's divisible}, let us assume for a contradiction that neither $p_1$ nor
$p_2$ is equal to $2$. Then by \ref{however}, $p_1$ and $p_2$ are both
relatively prime to $6$. Since $H_1(M;{\mathbb Z})$ is
isomorphic to $({\mathbb Z}/p_1{\mathbb Z})\oplus ({\mathbb Z}/p_2{\mathbb Z})$, it follows that $M$
is a ${\mathbb Z}/6{\mathbb Z}$--homology $3$--sphere. But by hypothesis we have
$\mathop{\rm vol}{{\mathcal M}}\le {V_{\rm Weeks}} / 6$; and
according to a theorem of Atkinson and Futer \cite[Theorem 1.5]{af}, a link orbifold which has volume at most ${V_{\rm Weeks}} /
6$,  and whose underlying manifold is a
${\mathbb Z}/6{\mathbb Z}$--homology $3$--sphere, 
must be the orbifold ${\mathcal O}_L$ depicted in Figure~\ref{Fig:OL}. The underlying space of ${\mathcal O}_L$ is ${\mathbb S}^3$. This contradicts the hypothesis that $M$ is a non-trivial connected sum, proving \ref{one's divisible} and the theorem.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- claim-52: body_md -->
\label{however}
For each $i\in\{1,2\}$, either $p_i$ is relatively prime to $6$, or  $p_i=2$.
<!-- end claim-52 -->
<!-- claim-53: body_md -->
\label{one's divisible}
At least one of the integers $p_1,p_2$ is equal to $2$.
<!-- end claim-53 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{second main} Suppose that ${{\mathcal M}}$ is a closed,
orientable hyperbolic link orbifold, and
that $\mathop{\rm vol} {{\mathcal M}} \le {V_{\rm Weeks}} / 6$. 
Set $M={{\rm X}_{{{\mathcal M}}}} $. Then either  one of the alternatives (i),  (iii), or (iv)
of  Theorem \ref{Thm:NoTurnoverMain}
holds, 
or we have the following specialization of (ii):
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(ii$'$)]
$M$ is homeomorphic either  to ${\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^3 \# {\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^3$, or to a connected
sum ${\mathbb R} {\mathbb P}^3 \# L(p,q)$, where $p > 1$ is relatively prime to $6$.  {\hfill$\square$}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
